News.title: Girl, 3, dies after ‘being shot by five-year-old sister’ – as horrified parents woken by gunfire & cops seize weapon
News.content:
GUN HORROR Girl, 3, dies after ‘being shot by five-year-old sister’ – as horrified parents woken by gunfire & cops seize weapon







Next

A THREE-year-old girl has died after being struck by a bullet allegedly fired by her five-year-old sister.

The children’s parents woke up to the sound of a gunshot and raced to their daughter’s room to find the little girl injured.



The older sister said she had been playing with the pistol – kept at home by her father who was authorised as collector, sports shooter and hunter.

She said she had been playing with the gun when it went off and hit her sister at the family’s home in Rio de Janeiro, Brazil.



The parents drove the three-year-old to Rocha Faria Municipal Hospital where doctors said she was admitted while under cardiorespiratory arrest.

Despite frantic efforts to save her, the little girl tragically succumbed to her injuries this morning.



Local military police unity confirmed the child’s death at the hospital.

The Capital Homicide Division has launched an investigation into the horrifying incident which will include a forensic examination of the family’s home.

It is not yet clear where the weapon was stored, whether it had any safety precautions or how the girl accessed the pistol.

Due to the girl’s young age she cannot be prosecuted for criminal charges.



It comes just one day after a teenager was shot in the head during a game involving a firearm elsewhere in Brazil.

A 16-year-old had allegedly been handling the gun when Daniel Antunes da Rocha, 15, was struck.

The boy was raced to hospital – but did not survive his injuries.

Police have not yet recovered the weapon used in the shooting.

Last year a two-year-old boy accidentally shot his mum dead after picking up his dad’s gun and playing with it.



Horror footage shows the boy grabbing the firearm from a table before pulling the trigger as his mum turned to look at him.

The couple, who were at their home in the Brazilian state of Mato Grosso do Sul at the time, appeared so deep in conversation that they failed to notice their son holding the Glock 9mm pistol.

She initially seemed to have survived the shooting but after briefly standing up to examine her wounds she is quickly seen falling to the ground.

In a state of shock the youngster is captured running to his mum’s aid as his dad grabs the lethal weapon from the floor.

News.title: Labour minister admits closer EU ties will come at a cost as fears grow over Burnham’s Brexit reset
News.content:
Next

A LABOUR Cabinet ­minister has admitted there will be costs to closer ties with the EU.

Lisa Nandy said she wants a stronger relationship with Brussels but said there would be trade-offs to having a more aligned trading partnership.



The comments by the Culture Secretary come ahead of the UK-EU “reset” summit on November 20 — fuelling fears Labour is edging Britain closer to the bloc without ­coming clean about the price.

Ms Nandy said: “There are trade-offs and ­choices to be made here in the relationship with the European Union.



“The Prime Minister has made no secret of the fact that he, like me, wants to see a closer relationship. We think that is in Britain’s interest.”

She added: “It is right to say there are costs as well as benefits to a closer relationship with the European Union.



“There are trade-offs to be made and we can’t cut people out of that conversation.”

After the Brussels summit, PM Andy Burnham is expected to set out options for a closer relationship with the EU.

Labour’s mixed messaging on Europe comes with Britain set to rejoin the Erasmus ­Plus student scheme in January, six years after leaving.

Labour faced a furious backlash after they said that “as we mark Remembrance Sunday, Erasmus Plus will give a new ­generation the chance to build connections across Europe”.



Tory Party chairman Kevin Hollinrake said the comments were “tone deaf”.

News.title: Labour must stop obsessing over reversing Brexit and start tackling the real problems facing Britain
News.content:
POLITICS FIX Labour must stop obsessing over reversing Brexit and start tackling the real problems facing Britain







Next

LABOUR is still trying to work out what its position on Brexit should be.

Andy Burnham before becoming PM said he wanted to see Britain rejoin the European Union within his lifetime.



Since taking office, he has called for an “honest discussion” about the possibility of restoring free movement between the UK and EU as part of a closer relationship with the bloc.

This is despite the fact Labour won the election promising not to bring back free movement this Parliament.



Mr Burnham has been keen to blame many of the country’s ills on Brexit, arguing that rejoining would help put Britain back on a path to growth.

But yesterday, close ally Lisa Nandy warned there would be trade-offs involved in any move towards rejoining.



A major UK-EU summit at the end of November is looming over the PM, with the immediate focus on securing new agreements in areas such as food and youth mobility.

But it remains unclear what Mr Burnham ultimately wants to achieve, or what compromises he would be prepared to make to get there.

Politically it may make sense.

A tougher line on Brexit could unite Labour’s left-wing factions and backbenchers who are desperate to reverse the freedoms Britain gained by leaving the EU.



But without a clear campaign capable of changing the minds of millions of people, it risks becoming a debate which goes nowhere.

Worse, it could take the oxygen away from more pressing issues, including securing Britain’s borders and tackling the soaring welfare bill.

Talking about Brexit may pay dividends in the short term.

But Labour risks exhausting a public that simply wants the Government to get on with running the country.

News.title: Man in his 60s dies after fire erupts at flat in residential street – as cops launch probe into ‘devastating’ tragedy
News.content:
Add us as a preferred source

FIRE TRAGEDY Man in his 60s dies after fire erupts at flat in residential street – as cops launch probe into ‘devastating’ tragedy







Next

A MAN in his 60s has died in a flat fire in a residential street, as cops launch an investigation.

The emergency services were alerted to the blaze in Baguley Crescent, Middleton at around 2.45pm on Saturday, Greater Manchester Police said.

The man died at the scene and his next of kin have been informed.



A neighbour, Ian Walsh, told the BBC: “The firefighters managed to get him out and then they did CPR on him outside the flat.”



He added: “There was a lot of smoke. We are all shocked.”

The 73-year-old said paramedics and an air ambulance team tried to save the man

He said: “It’s very sad and bewildering that he died.

“You don’t expect it to happen opposite you. There were forensics here and all sorts.”

Another neighbour, who did not want to be named, said: “I know they managed to get him out and they tried to save him.

“I saw the air ambulance arrive. It’s devastating that he died.”

The force added that investigations into the incident were ongoing.

News.title: How Thomas Markle was described as ‘mentally sharp’ by daughter Samantha just weeks before child abuse image arrest
News.content:
Next

THOMAS Markle Snr was “mentally sharp” shortly before he was linked to a child sex abuse stash, his eldest daughter said.

Samantha Markle, 61, gave the update to her brother Thomas Jnr, 60, after he called to ask about his wellbeing.



Markle Snr — also dad to Meghan, Duchess of Sussex, 45 — had left his home in the Philippines in May after a blood clot led to the amputation of his left leg, and he was being treated in a rehabilitation centre in Lakeland, Florida.

Samantha told Thomas Jnr in June that their 82-year-old dad was recovering “really well”.



But last week, as Markle Snr faced shocking allegations he hoarded thousands of images and videos of child sex abuse, he claimed to have “cognitive issues”.

The day after The Sun broke the news about the allegations, he strenuously denied any wrongdoing and also claimed he had been diagnosed with dementia.



But Thomas Jnr says his father’s dementia claim flies in the face of what his sister told him.

He said: “I called Samantha and asked how Dad was doing in Florida and she couldn’t have been more positive.

“She said he was doing great and in good health and had recovered really well. She said that he was mentally sharp and he was like Dad of old, making jokes and laughing.

“Then when I find this stash of horrific child abuse images he suddenly has dementia. Something doesn’t ring true.”



He added: “It’s very convenient that he suddenly has memory issues.”

Markle Snr was taken to a Florida nursing home, which specialises in “memory care”, a week ago.

He was arrested there by the FBI on Friday and has since been charged on one count of possession of an indecent image of children.

News.title: GTA VI launch set to cost bosses £12m as workers book 83,000 days off to play long-awaited game
News.content:
Next

BOSSES fear a business slump as tens of thousands of staff take annual leave to play the new Grand Theft Auto VI.

Experts say the launch on November 19 — 13 years after the last game’s release — has sparked a surge in requests for days off and could cost firms £12million.



Staff absence tracker BrightHR revealed 83,000 days have been booked off for GTA-related reasons this month and next.

The projected cost to firms on the launch day alone is £3.14million.



Some 4.63 per cent of time off requests for that day mention GTA as a reason.

Many fans have even threatened to quit if they are not given the time off by bosses.



The findings were taken from absence data from more than 1.2million employees at 70,000 UK businesses.

More than twice as many people have booked launch day off compared to those who will be away on a honeymoon.

One die-hard gamer has gone full throttle, saving up enough annual leave to disappear for a whole fortnight in a bid to complete the game.

The last full game in the action-adventure crime series, Grand Theft Auto V, was released on September 17, 2013.



BrightHR boss Alan Price said: “This launch is going to cost businesses more than £12million, which is a big loss in a short space of time.

“Some bosses might roll their eyes at taking time off work to game, but it is every bit as valid as booking annual leave to attend a football match, concert or hen do. Fans have waited 13 years for this.”

Time off requests have included: “GTA — week on the sofa in my pants”, “GTA Release — I’ll resign if this is denied”, and “GTA day. Game on, losers”.

GTA, published by Rockstar Games, is one of the biggest-selling video games of all time.

The newest release is said to be the most expensive ever, costing as much as £1.12billion ($1.5billion) to make.



Gaming and tech expert at AO.com, Nick Bunce, said: “It’s rare for a game launch to generate this level of anticipation.

“A lot of fans want to experience it from day one. It’s shaping up to be one of those cultural moments.”

News.content:
Russell Brand remains caged inside HMP Wandsworth in South London as the disgraced star awaits his sentencing for rape and sexual assault on Monday

News.title: Dad with 'sore throat’ forced to leave family holiday after shock doctor's call
News.content:
Dad with 'sore throat’ forced to leave family holiday after shock doctor's call

Dean Flinn, 41, from West Derby, was told his persistent sore throat which had lasted around six to eight weeks was actually cancer

View 6 Images Dean Flinn, from Lydiate, 41, with his wife Sarah, 35, and two children Theo, eight, and Ella, six (Image: liverpoolecho/Amy Newsham)

A dad-of-two has told of the moment he was told that his sore throat was actually tonsil cancer.

‌



‌



Dean Flinn, 41, from West Derby, was told the awful news in October 2024 after he developed a persistent sore throat which had lasted around six to eight weeks.

‌



Dean, who has spent the past two years battling cancer is facing his toughest fight yet after the disease returned and spread rapidly, the Liverpool Echo reports.

‌



He initially visited his GP who reassured him there was no cause for concern however after seeking a second opinion through his private healthcare, further tests were carried out.

Dean was on a two-week family holiday in Turkey with his wife, Sarah Flinn, 35, two children, Theo eight, Ella, six, and his sister-in-law Amy Newsham, 33, from Lydiate, during October half term when he received a phone call telling him he needed to return home for further tests.

View 6 Images Dean, Sarah, Theo and Ella with sister-in-law Amy Newsham (Image: liverpoolecho/Amy Newsham)

‌



Amy said: “We were away with the whole family and we didn't really have any answers at this point they just said they wanted to investigate a bit further.”

Five days into the holiday, Dean flew home to have a scan before returning to the holiday but three days before they were due to fly home, Dean received another phone call.

‌



Amy said: “They said to him that they would like to see him in the clinic as soon as he gets back. So as you can imagine Dean was sat watching his two little kids in the pool thinking the worst, basically."

As they tried to enjoy their break, the uncertainty quickly became overwhelming. After the family pushed for some indication of what the tests had revealed, Dean was told over the phone that the results were cancerous and he needed to attend an appointment as soon as he returned.

‌



Amy said: "He was absolutely devastated. We all were absolutely devastated. We were just in utter shock because Dean just went to see his GP because he had a sore throat. Cancer wasn't even something he thought it could be."

View 6 Images Dean with Theo and Ella (Image: liverpoolecho/Amy Newsham)

‌



After arriving home, Dean went on to undergo months of gruelling intensive chemotherapy alongside radiotherapy. Then in spring 2025, the family thought they had reached the end of a devastating chapter when Dean completed his treatment and rang the bell.

Theo and Ella joined him for the milestone, wearing t-shirts bearing the words, ‘You did it Daddy’.

‌



Amy said: “He was so strong and positive throughout that he was going to beat it. He did absolutely amazing. When he rang the bell, we all thought that was the end of it and that was the last time we were going to see cancer.”

But the relief was unfortunately short-lived after Dean was offered a full-body MRI scan in December 2025 as part of a clinical trial, which revealed the cancer had returned and spread to his neck and lung.

‌



Amy said: “We were told it was a treatable cancer, so we had high hopes that it was going to go away and he was going to be ok."

View 6 Images The couple, who have been together for more than 10 years, married in May this year (Image: liverpoolecho/Amy Newsham)

‌



Dean went on to have major surgery to remove the cancer in his neck but was left unable to swallow or eat food.

Amy said: “Eating is a massive thing. It's everyday life and even the social side of things, so it's had a massive effect on Dean and the family.

‌



"He lost so much weight. His sleep is disturbed every night because he’s choking on his own spit because he can’t swallow.”

Dean also began immunotherapy, but further devastating news followed when he started experiencing dizziness, collapsing, and paralysis down one side of his face.

‌



A visible lump appeared along his jawline and, after further scans and a biopsy, doctors discovered the cancer had grown rapidly.

It had spread up the back of his skull, wrapped around his carotid artery and returned in his neck.

‌



Doctors planned to begin another course of chemotherapy, but Dean developed an infection which meant treatment had to be delayed.

View 6 Images Dean and Sarah on holiday (Image: liverpoolecho/Amy Newsham)

‌



He has now spent almost four weeks in hospital at Clatterbridge Cancer Centre.

Amy said the delay had been another crushing blow for Dean, who was desperate to begin treatment.

‌



She said: "He just wanted to get the treatments. He was desperate to get chemotherapy because he wants to be here for his kids."

Away from hospital, his wife Sarah has been trying to keep life as normal as possible for their children while supporting her husband through the ordeal.

‌



The couple, who have been together for more than 10 years, married in May this year.

Amy said Dean had always been a hands-on dad, involved in every aspect of Theo and Ella's lives, from school pickups to their activities.

‌



But his illness has meant a huge change for the family, with the children having to adjust to seeing their dad unwell and unable to do the things they once took for granted.

View 6 Images Dean also began immunotherapy, but further devastating news followed when he started experiencing dizziness, collapsing, and paralysis down one side of his face (Image: liverpoolecho/Amy Newsham)

‌



Amy said: "Dean was a dad who was involved in absolutely every aspect of the kids' lives. He did everything, every activity, every school pick-up.

"There was a massive change. The kids are aware and understand small amounts, but not to the extent where we'd want to scare them. We want to protect them."

‌



Sarah, who works as a pharmacist in a hospital, has remained by Dean's side throughout his treatment while also trying to be there for their children. But Amy said the emotional toll on her sister had been immense.

She said: "Sarah has tried to remain positive the last two years. Every hurdle they’ve faced, they’ve overcome and been strong. She’s fought with him and been at his side every minute of every day.

‌



“But behind closed doors, we see as a family where she's a broken mum and a broken wife. She's hurt for her whole family. She thinks, ‘Why are their kids going to go through something like this?'

"They've got such a loving dad, and they don't deserve this."

‌



Now Amy has launched a fundraiser to help the family explore further treatment options and give Dean, his wife Sarah and their two young children the chance to make precious memories together.

The appeal has already raised more than £30,000, with thousands of people rallying around the family.

‌



Amy said: "The GoFundMe page is basically to help explore alternative treatment options, if there are any available to Dean.

"Sarah made an appointment with a professor down at the Royal Marsden in London to explore some alternative treatments and see what Dean’s options are but unfortunately with him being in hospital they’ve had to cancel it because Dean was too unwell to travel.

‌



"But they've been strong, they've been hopeful. They've been like, 'We're going to do this, let's crack on, let's keep going.'

"I think this GoFundMe page will just give them that bit of hope again when all other hope was lost. The support they’ve had so far is absolutely amazing.

Article continues below

"He's got two small children, he's got a lovely family, a young family with so much life left to give and to live.

"We’re such a close-knit family, so It's just absolutely devastating."

News.title: 'I was attacked on shift and humiliated online by 150 strangers’

This week, the Daily Mirror joins forces with the Retail Trust as the charity launches their Let's Respect Retail campaign, and calls on ministers fast-track tough new legal protections before the Christmas shopping rush.

Filmed, abused, and posted online

3 View 3 Images Shropshire store assistant Charles Davies, 23, was pushed and filmed by an aggressive customer before the clip was posted on Facebook for strangers to ridicule 3 View 3 Images He has called for a ban on filming staff on shop premises.

What began as an ordinary shift turned violent when an aggressive shopper demanding a refund pushed him and hurled threats.

"He pulled out his phone, started recording me, and got really in my face, quite aggressive, a bit brutish,” Charles, a Usdaw representative, said. "It was a very harrowing experience.”

While Charles hoped the confrontation was over once the customer left, days later, the video was uploaded to a local community Facebook page, sparking a barrage of vile comments ridiculing his competence.

Attacked at work

Shopkeeper Benedict Selvaratnam was left needing stitches on the back of his head after confronting a shoplifter. The 43-year-old dad of three runs two convenience stores in Croydon, south London.

"I tried to retrieve a stolen wine bottle from a shoplifter and he started attacking me and hitting me with it," he said.

Benedict - who is a member of the Association of Convenience Stores, which has joined forces with the Retail Trust - has witnessed a steep rise in hostility.

‌



"When we opened our town centre store 10 years ago, there were about two to three instances of abuse per week. Now it’s two to three every day,” he said, describing young female colleagues being spat on and customers threatening to wait outside after their shifts.

"It’s very disheartening coming to work and not knowing what kind of day it’s going to be," he said. "It's worse for my team members - this is my life and how I support my children; I have to put up with it. I have complete sympathy for my staff."

The intimidation and shoplifting became so unbearable that he almost walked away altogether: "Two years ago, I put the town centre site up for sale when it was really bad," he admitted.

But tensions have eased slightly since Croydon became one of the first areas to introduce live facial recognition earlier this year, bringing a noticeable drop in shoplifting.

‌



Despite the pressure he remains under, Benedict says it is local goodwill that keeps him going: "One of the perks of working in a community store is when you receive supportive feedback from customers. It always cheers me up. I think, why should I be grumpy when the previous customer treated me really nicely? It’s a morale boost."

Find out more about the campaign: retailtrust.org.uk/respect

News.title: Man found dead during police probe into string of burglaries as murder arrest made
News.content:
Man found dead during police probe into string of burglaries as murder arrest made

A suspected burglar has now been arrested on suspicion of murder after police discovered the body of a man in his 70s at a home linked to a suspected string of break-ins

View Image Whitstable Close, Oldham (Image: ASP)

Detectives investigating a series of burglaries discovered the body of a man in his 70s when they visited a property suspected of being targeted.

Police had been investigating a string of break-ins in Oldham, Greater Manchester, in which a burglar allegedly demanded bank cards and PIN numbers from householders. Officers arrested a man in his 30s on suspicion of aggravated burglary on Saturday night (November 7), following four linked incidents.

But the investigation took a shocking turn when detectives visited a fifth address suspected of being connected to the series on Sunday and discovered the body of a man in his 70s, the Manchester Evening News reported.

The man's death is being treated as suspicious, and the arrested suspect has since also been arrested on suspicion of murder. The discovery was made at a property on Whitstable Close in Chadderton, Oldham, after officers visited the address as part of their enquiries.

Greater Manchester Police (GMP) said the man's next of kin had been informed and were being supported by specially trained officers. The incident at Whitstable Close is believed to have occurred between Wednesday, November 4, and Saturday, November 7, 2026.

Detective Superintendent Amber Waywell said: "First and foremost, our thoughts are with the gentleman who has sadly died and with his family and loved ones at what will be an incredibly difficult and distressing time.

"This remains a complex and developing investigation, and we are working hard to establish the full circumstances surrounding his death. I would like to thank the outstanding work of our detectives, who have shown real determination and persistence throughout this investigation.

"We are also extremely grateful to everyone who came forward following our media appeals, with the most recent one being on Friday. We received a number of calls from members of the public, and the information provided has been invaluable in supporting our ongoing enquiries."

Police have linked four burglaries between January and March this year, followed by a fifth incident in October. In each case, victims were targeted in a similar way, with the suspect attempting to or successfully gaining entry to their properties before demanding they hand over bank cards and PIN codes, according to GMP.

Det Supt Waywell added: "Protecting our communities and safeguarding vulnerable people remains an absolute priority for us. We understand the concern incidents of this nature can cause, particularly when offenders are accused of targeting elderly people in their own homes.

"Let me be clear: we take offences like these incredibly seriously, and we will not tolerate those who seek to prey on vulnerable members of our communities.

"If you feel like you have been a victim of this type of crime that may possibly be linked to this investigation, or if you know of anything suspicious that matches these crimes, please get in touch with us.

Article continues below

"You can call our office in confidence on 0161 856 9577, quoting the log number 2908 of 30/10/2026. Information can also be submitted online at www.gmp.police.uk. Alternatively, you can call the independent charity Crimestoppers anonymously on 0800 555 111."

News.title: Seven teens injured after car mounts pavement in Dublin as eight rushed to hospital
News.content:
Seven teens injured after car mounts pavement in Dublin as eight rushed to hospital

According to multiple reports, a car is understood to have mounted a footpath outside shops on Oliver Plunkett Road with several people, including a number of teenagers, understood to be injured

View Image A car is understood to have mounted a footpath outside shops on Oliver Plunkett Road (Image: Dublin Live)

Seven teenagers are among those injured after a car reportedly mounted the pavement near shops in Dublin.

‌



‌



The incident happened at around 3:30pm with eight people reportedly injured, including the driver - seven of the victims are teenagers, Dublin Live reports. All of the injured have been taken to hospital - some of the teenagers involved have been described as 'critical'.

‌



A Garda spokesperson said: "Gardaí are investigating a serious road traffic collision involving a car and seven pedestrians on Oliver Plunkett Road, Dún Laoghaire, today, Sunday 8th November 2026 at approximately 3:00pm.

‌



"The seven juvenile pedestrians, all teenagers, and the driver of the car, a woman aged in her 40s, sustained varying degrees of injuries. All eight individuals have been taken to different hospitals for treatment. Gardaí are continuing to investigate the circumstances surrounding the collision."

The teenagers are being treated at Children’s Health Ireland Temple Street and Crumlin, where some of the injuries were later described as “critical”.

The road remains closed for a 'technical examination' as of 11.30pm on Sunday, November 8.

‌



Local Fine Gael Councillor Dan Carson said: "I am aware of a serious vehicle incident in Monkstown farm. My thoughts are with the first responders currently on scene and the families of those affected."

Fianna Fáil councillor Justin Moylan said there was a “surreal sense of shock in the area”.

‌



He said: “Our thoughts are with those that are injured and their families, hoping for a recovery for them as quick as possible.”

According to multiple reports, a car is understood to have mounted a footpath outside shops on Oliver Plunkett Road. Several people, including a number of teenagers, are understood to have been injured in the incident.

Article continues below

Six people reportedly injured in the incident. It is understood five of the victims are teenagers aged between 14 and 15. Gardai, paramedics and firefighters are at the scene and at least one person has been rushed to hospital.

A Garda spokeswoman told Dublin Live: "Gardaí are at the scene of a serious road traffic collision." No further information has been released by officials.

News.title: More than 300 teachers, parents and doctors demand pause on plans to use AI school tutors
News.content:
More than 300 teachers, parents and doctors demand pause on plans to use AI school tutors

EXCLUSIVE: More than 300 teachers, parents, academics and doctors have demanded Andy Burnham halt plans to roll out artificial tutoring tools in schools

View 2 Images Up to 450,000 children from disadvantaged backgrounds could be provided with AI powered tutoring tools (Image: Getty Images)

More than 300 teachers, parents, academics and doctors have demanded Andy Burnham halt plans to roll out artificial tutoring tools in schools.

‌



‌



Up to 450,000 children from disadvantaged backgrounds could be provided with AI powered tutoring tools from next year in a bid to improve poorer families' access to unaffordable private tutors. But experts have sounded the alarm over a lack of evidence about the effectiveness and safety of AI amid recent apocalyptic warnings about its risk.

‌



In a letter to Mr Burnham and Education Secretary Lucy Powell, experts including neuroscientists, psychologists and special needs educators said disadvantaged children should not be the first to bear the risks of "an unproven and contested technology". They said children’s struggles such as food poverty or mental health issues cannot be solved through tech.

‌



View 2 Images Experts warned disadvantaged children should not be the first to bear the risks of 'an unproven and contested technology' (Image: PA)

The letter reads: “Children who are hungry, persistently absent, struggling with their mental health, experiencing a combination of these factors, or lacking foundational skills need the right conditions for learning. These are not technological problems and they don’t have technological solutions.

“They need excellent teachers, nutritious food, physical activity, safe schools, relationships and support. Every pound, every hour of policy attention and every institutional resource devoted to making an uncertain technology work is a resource that cannot be devoted to addressing the conditions we already know children need in order to learn.”

‌



It added: “Children with the fewest alternatives should not be the first to bear the risks of an unproven and contested technology.”

Signatories include Jane Rowland, director of the SafeScreens Campaign, Dr Rebecca Foljambe, an NHS GP and founder of Health Professionals for Safer Screens, and Lila Byock, founder of Schools Beyond Screens.

‌



Co-author of the letter Dr Velislava Hillman, founder of the EDDS Institute which examines tech use in education, told The Mirror: "The most disadvantaged children don’t need a chatbot, but excellent teachers, safe schools and proper support.

"Every pound spent trying to make an unproven technology work is a pound not spent on what we already know helps children learn. The government should pause this rollout, invest in what works, and only come back to AI tutoring if it can prove it does more good than harm.”

Article continues below

A Government spokesman said: “Children’s safety has to come first. This is not a national rollout of AI tutors, but a carefully controlled trial to build the evidence about what works and make sure these tools are safe for pupils before anything is scaled up.

“We know that generative AI tools are readily available and are not always designed for learning. That’s why we are taking action, working with schools and established technology companies to make sure tools designed for education are properly tested."

News.title: Pharmacist ‘life threatening’ warning over ‘dangerous’ ramipril side effect
News.content:
Pharmacist ‘life threatening’ warning over ‘dangerous’ ramipril side effect

A TikTok pharmacist has highlighted a potentially life-threatening reaction that can develop even after years

View 2 Images Ramipril is one of the most commonly prescribed blood pressure medications in Ireland. (stock image) (Image: Pexels)

People taking a common blood pressure tablet have been warned about a potentially life-threatening side effect that can strike long after treatment begins. Raj Patel, known as the Straight-Talking Pharmacist on TikTok, has urged patients to recognise the warning signs and act quickly if they develop swelling around their mouth or face.

‌



‌



Ramipril belongs to a group of medicines called ACE inhibitors, which are prescribed to treat high blood pressure and certain heart conditions. Mr Patel told his more than 100,000 followers that the reaction can happen even when someone has taken their medication for years without problems.

‌



"A blood pressure tablet could cause a life-threatening reaction long after you thought the risk had gone," he said in one of his videos. "If you take Ramipril, Lisinopril or any other ACE inhibitors, this really matters and you may want to watch this video till the end."

‌



Blood test could reveal Alzheimer’s risk 10 years early, common drugs secretly helping viruses, and liquid painted onto kids’ teeth in seconds can stop cavities - all this and more in our science newsletter

View 2 Images A box of generic Ramipril pills. Ramipril is a prescription drug primarily used for the treatment of high blood pressure. - white background

‌



The Medicines and Healthcare products Regulatory Agency (MHRA) issued a safety update in June 2026 highlighting the risk of angioedema associated with ACE inhibitors. Its warning explains that swelling of the lips, tongue, face or throat can develop at any point during treatment, including after weeks or years of use.

Such swelling can obstruct the airway and cause difficulty breathing or swallowing, making prompt medical attention essential. Mr Patel noted "Here's the important bit, this is not a normal allergy, so taking an antihistamine is probably not going to work."

‌



The MHRA explains that some cases are caused by a mechanism involving bradykinin rather than histamine, meaning standard allergy treatments may not be effective. Anyone who develops sudden swelling of the lips, mouth, tongue or throat should call 999, particularly if breathing or swallowing becomes difficult, as per the NHS.

Content cannot be displayed without consent

Article continues below

Mr Patel urged viewers: "If you get swelling of the lips, tongue, face or throat, get urgent help straight away and please don't take another tablet." The MHRA advises people with suspected ACE inhibitor-related angioedema not to take further doses and to inform a healthcare professional immediately.

The reaction is uncommon, and patients should not stop prescribed ramipril simply because they have seen the warning. Anyone with concerns about their medication should speak to a healthcare professional, while suspected angioedema requires urgent assessment rather than waiting for a routine appointment.

News.title: Nvidia launches investigation into CEO's affair with suspected Chinese spy
News.content:
US tech giant Nvidia has opened an independent investigation following reports its CEO Jensen Huang had a relationship with a suspected Chinese spy.

The company, one of the most valuable in the world, said its board had no reason to believe the company's secrets or national security were compromised, adding that the CEO was committed to continuing to lead the company.

Separately, Jensen Huang admitted to having been "unfaithful" to his wife and apologised for hurting her and their children.

US intelligence officials believed that Chinese businesswoman Alice Huang, who had a close relationship with Jensen Huang, was a spy for Beijing, according to a New York Times report.

Jensen Huang said he took "full responsibility" for what he did, adding that he had fallen short of his responsibilities to Nvidia's employees, board and shareholders.

Nvidia is one of the world's largest companies and seen as central to making the hardware for emerging AI technologies, and Jensen Huang has been in charge of it for more than 30 years.

He said: "I was unfaithful to my wife. My actions hurt her and our children. There is no excuse for what I did. I am deeply sorry."

His statement continued: "Regarding the national security concerns raised in news reports, Nvidia's Board of Directors has initiated an independent investigation. I support the investigation and will cooperate fully.

"I love our country and our company. I am committed to protecting Nvidia and supporting America's national security. I am proud and grateful to be an American."

A separate statement issued by Nvidia's board of directors said it would begin an investigation in "light of recent reporting that founder and CEO Jensen Huang has been the target of a foreign intelligence effort".

It continued: "The Board prioritises US national and economic security, which is paramount to the interests of Nvidia and its shareholders.

"While the Board has no reason to believe that either national security or Nvidia secrets were compromised, the Board's inquiry will examine all available information."

Jensen Huang rescued Nvidia from almost going broke on more than one occasion, and he took a punt on AI a long time before the rest of the world did.

His decision to make Nvidia chips, originally designed for gaming, become the best in the business for AI development, has now paid off in spades and the company is worth trillions.

This is a big blow for a man who is renowned for being a workaholic, a perfectionist and someone who expects incredibly high standards from his staff.

Alice Huang, who is of no relation to Jensen Huang, is linked to Singapore-based data centre firm Megaspeed.

The company told the New York Times last month its current leadership took the allegations seriously and had appointed external legal advisers to conduct an internal investigation.

Nvidia is a central player in AI infrastructure, providing chips to leading AI model developers including OpenAI and Meta.

The microchip manufacturer is worth some $4.5 trillion, making it one of the most valuable companies ever.

China has previously rejected allegations of an espionage operation targeting Nvidia's chief, describing the claims as "groundless speculation".

US intelligence agencies had been monitoring Alice Huang and concluded that she was acting on behalf of the Chinese government, according to unnamed sources cited by The New York Times.

Surveillance reportedly revealed communications between Alice Huang and an American citizen, who was subsequently identified as Jensen Huang through a process known as "unmasking".

It remains unclear what information Alice Huang â who is also known as Huang Le â allegedly passed to Beijing, how valuable it was, or when she is believed to have begun gathering intelligence.

Alice Huang did not respond to the paper's request for comment.

Last week, members of Congress wrote to Jensen Huang, asking him to appear before them in the light of the reported relationship.

Three House Republican committee leaders asked the CEO to appear later in the month, to talk about Nvidia's "security protocols against foreign adversary espionage" given his reported relationship with Alice Huang.

"Recent reports raise significant national security concerns regarding the PRC's [China's] access to sensitive US technology and information.

"The issue of PRC infiltration and access to cutting-edge US technology is core to the investigative work of our three committees this Congress," the letter said.

Nvidia's AI chips have been a major focus of the rivalry between the US and China, and Washington has previously imposed controls on where its advanced products can be sold.

The H200, Nvidia's second most advanced semiconductor, had previously been restricted by Washington over concerns that it would give China's technology industry an edge over the US.

In January, the Trump administration said it would allow the company to sell its H200 chips to Chinese customers under certain conditions.

News.title: King leads solemn Remembrance Sunday service at Cenotaph
News.content:
King Charles III led the nation in a solemn two-minute silence on Remembrance Sunday in London to honour veterans who had died in conflict.

On a stone-grey autumn morning, he laid a wreath at the Cenotaph in Whitehall before a march-past by 10,000 armed forces veterans.

That included a shrinking number of World War Two veterans, with 12 taking part this year, including 103-year-old Annie Duplock, who described it as a "very emotional day".

Meanwhile, the number of former prime ministers reached a record high, with nine lined up to lay wreaths, while Andy Burnham attended for the first time as the current occupant of No 10 Downing Street.

And for the first time, the leader of Reform UK, Nigel Farage, had enough MPs in Parliament to qualify to lay a wreath alongside other major party leaders.

News.title: Maya Jama steps down as host of reality TV show Love Island
News.content:
Presenter Maya Jama has announced she is stepping down as the host of reality TV show Love Island after three years.

The 32-year-old wrote on Instagram alongside a highlights reel of her on the programme that it was "time to throw myself into something new".

"While my own Love Island journey has come to an end, I wish the show and the team all the success in the world, I'll be cheering you lot on from the sidelines forever," the TV and radio presenter said.

Jama's announcement comes hot on the heels of an appearance as a contestant on Celebrity Traitors that won her praise and speculation in the Times, external that she could "get Â£1m per deal" thanks to her success.

Thanking fans and the production team on Love Island, she said she had an "unforgettable time" on the programme.

"I started hosting the show aged 28 and during the nine incredible series met the most wonderful humans along the way. I've loved every slow-mo walk, fire pit and live show.

But she added: "I've always believed that to truly grow, you have to take a leap every now and then."

Jama landed her biggest presenting role to date as the host of the reality TV show in 2023, taking over from Laura Whitmore.

The programme couples contestants together who then complete a range of tasks and keep swapping in the hope of meeting the love of their life.

An ITV spokesperson said: "Maya has been a fantastic and much loved host on Love Island - we thank her for everything she has brought to the show over the last three years and wish her every continued success."

Love Island is one of the most popular reality TV shows in the UK but the series has polarised viewers, with some arguing the show is misogynistic and raising concerns about the welfare of contestants.

News.title: Top House Democrat 'a hard yes' on impeaching Pete Hegseth
News.content:
The top Democrat widely expected to be the next US House of Representatives Speaker has said he is "a hard yes" for impeaching Defence Secretary Pete Hegseth.

New York congressman Hakeem Jeffries told ABC's programme This Week that Hegseth had "abused his power, undermined our national security, and engineered this reckless and costly war of choice in Iran".

Outgoing Republican congressman Thomas Massie, a foe of President Donald Trump, has said he plans as early as Monday to introduce a resolution to impeach Hegseth, which could result in his removal from office.

The Pentagon told the BBC it had followed the law and that Hegseth would not be deterred by "phony investigations".

As the current Democratic minority leader in the House, Jeffries is favourite to become Speaker when his party takes control of Congress in January following their landslide victory in last week's midterm elections.

"I'm a hard yes on the Hegseth resolution," Jeffries told ABC on Sunday.

"Pete Hegseth has got to go," he continued.

Kentucky congressman Massie's resolution contains eight articles of impeachment against Hegseth, alleging that he made war on Iran without the required congressional authorisation under the War Powers Resolution of 1973.

News.title: 'Time is up': Minister warns media industry to take abuse seriously in wake of Brand case
News.content:
Abuse in the media industry is probably still happening as organisations are not doing enough to protect women, the culture secretary has warned in the wake of Russell Brand's conviction.

Lisa Nandy told the BBC's Sunday with Laura Kuenssberg programme: "Time is up, it really is time for the media industry to take this seriously."

She added that since entering government, "many people" from within the industry had reached out to her "to allege that things have happened to them".

Brand was found guilty of rape and sexual assault after a four-week trial, following allegations from multiple women spanning the decade between 1999 and 2009.

Nandy was asked whether she believed there was still exploitation and abuse within the media industry, following the Brand trial and cancellation of Channel 4 reality show Married at First Sight after the BBC revealed rape allegations.

She said: "I do not see that much has changed in terms of the way that institutions in the media industry and across public life, including politics, deal with women who very bravely come forward to allege abuse."

Nandy added that there was often no protection and a "very heavy cost" for women who speak up in industries such as media and politics, pointing to power imbalances and short-term contracts some staff members are given.

"Hand on heart, I can't say to you as the culture secretary that this is not happening today. In fact, if I had to wager, I would say it is," she said.

Nandy said many had come forward from within the industry, including from the BBC.

But she added that the BBC had been an "exemplar" in signing up to the industry body to protect whistleblowers - the Creative Industries Independent Standards Authority - and urged other organisations to follow suit.

A BBC spokesperson said the broadcaster "has made a significant commitment to improve its culture, processes and standards".

"Last year, following an independent culture review, we set out the behavioural expectations for everyone who works with or for the BBC and we were clear action would be taken if these were not met," the spokesperson added.

News.title: Nandy defends linking Erasmus student scheme to Remembrance Sunday after backlash
News.content:
Culture Secretary Lisa Nandy has rejected accusations of politicising Remembrance Sunday after being criticised for linking the event to the UK rejoining the European Union's Erasmus scheme.

Her department announced on Saturday night that "as we mark Remembrance Sunday, Erasmus+ will give a new generation the chance to build connections across Europe".

That sparked a backlash from the Conservatives, who said "veterans did not fight for a student exchange scheme" and accused her of making an "EU membership pitch".

Nandy said she was "horrified" by the Tory response and insisted that the expanded EU scheme for study and work would help young Britons recognise wartime sacrifice.

The UK is rejoining the scheme in January, six years after leaving it as part of the Brexit deal.

On Saturday, the Department for Culture, Media and Sport drew comparisons between that scheme and events on Sunday to commemorate veterans who had died in conflict.

Referring to the scheme, Nandy said in her department's press release: "As we remember the immense courage of those who served our country, we honour them by building the best opportunities for the next generation through closeness and collaboration with our allies."

Conservative Party chairman Kevin Hollinrake described her comments as "tone deaf and frankly shameful" and called on Nandy to apologise.

He said the bonds that veterans forged "run far deeper" than Erasmus.

"It is not a day for a Labour minister to try to make an EU membership pitch," he added.

Reform leader Nigel Farage told the BBC: "For Lisa Nandy to use Remembrance Sunday to announce this and say it's all about peace, it's all about the war - I find that very, very poor taste."

Peter Sharples, chief executive of the Veterans Institute, told the Telegraph that people should "just honour the fallen" on Remembrance Sunday rather than discussing "party political matters".

Asked about the criticism on the BBC's Sunday with Laura Kuenssberg programme, Nandy stood by her initial remarks.

"It was Winston Churchill after the Second World War who talked about extending the hand of friendship across Europe and making sure that we honoured the legacy of that generation," she said.

She said that after Brexit "we closed off opportunities for young people from this country to understand not just the impact that generation made here in the UK, but the way in which they went off and fought for the freedom of people across Europe".

Asked to respond to accusations she had chosen Remembrance Sunday to "promote part of the new deal the government has done with the EU", Nandy said she was "not choosing today or any day actually to promote a deal with the EU".

Pressed about linking the day to what the government believes are the cultural benefits of the scheme, Nandy said: "There was a time where that wouldn't have even raised an eyebrow as somehow political, it was just common sense - and it is common sense."

News.title: Government looking at banning under-16s from Vinted and eBay
News.content:
Vinted and eBay could be included in the list of platforms set to be banned for children aged under 16, the culture secretary has said.

Lisa Nandy said the government was "looking seriously" at including the retailing websites in the social media ban "to keep children safe".

The UK's social media ban for under-16s is set to come into force in March next year, with children barred from accessing platforms such as Instagram, TikTok and Snapchat.

In response, eBay said it was looking forward to "understanding more and continuing to work constructively with the government". Vinted said it welcomed "open dialogue" with ministers and the regulator on the issue.

Asked on the BBC's Sunday with Laura Kuenssberg programme whether the government was looking to ban under-16s from Vinted and eBay, Nandy said: "We are looking seriously at doing so in order to keep children safe."

It came after the Sunday Times reported, external that the UK's social media ban was being expanded to include the popular second-hand online marketplaces.

The move was due to fears that messaging functions on the platforms allowed strangers to groom children, according to the newspaper. It suggested similar reselling platforms, Depop and Facebook Marketplace, would also be included in the list of banned sites.

Businesses and individuals sell a host of goods on eBay, which has been a major global player in the online reselling market for years. The platform states on its website that it currently requires all of its members to be over 18 years old because listings involve "entering into a contract".

Vinted is aimed at over 18s, but its terms and conditions do allow parents or guardians to create accounts for their children, which must be used under parental supervision.

The site, on which users mostly buy and sell unwanted clothes and other fashion items, has grown rapidly recently to reach 17 million UK users.

A Vinted spokesperson said direct messaging was "part of how the platform works" but that it had a "zero tolerance for harmful or explicit content" and had moderation teams and tools to spot and remove "activity that breaks our rules".

"When we identify inappropriate behaviour, we take action, up to a permanent ban or reporting to the relevant authorities," they said.

An eBay spokesperson said the company was "focused on providing a trusted and safe marketplace experience for our millions of customers".

"While the details of the proposed legislation are not yet clear, we look forward to understanding more and continuing to work constructively with the government," they added.

News.title: Two arrested after police officers hurt in brawl outside bare-knuckle fighting event
News.content:
Two men have been arrested and three police officers injured during a street disturbance outside a bare-knuckle fighting championship in Glasgow.

Footage circulating on social media shows a group of men trading punches in the street outside the Ovo Hydro where the event was held on Saturday evening.

More than 20 police vehicles and a police helicopter converged on the area. Three officers were hurt, two of them requiring medical treatment, as they responded to the disorder.

Police Scotland said two men, aged 32 and 27, had been arrested and charged with offences including assault, obstructing police and threatening and abusive behaviour.

News.title: Briton among six killed in 'far-right' shooting in Krakow
News.content:
A gunman believed to have been inspired by far-right ideology has killed six people and injured more than a dozen others in an attack in the busy centre of Poland's second largest city.

Police said the attacker drove on to Main Market Square in Krakow, a popular tourist attraction, on Saturday afternoon and fired randomly at people.

Four women and two men were killed. Three were Polish, one was British and two have not been identified.

Among the 16 injured are five foreign nationals from Austria, Germany, Portugal, Russia and Britain.

Another three bodies were found when counter-terrorism police searched the suspect's home around 125 miles (200km) away, Polish Prime Minister Donald Tusk said.

A massive armed police presence was deployed across Krakow on Saturday evening, as security measures were ramped up in the capital Warsaw and elsewhere.

A period of mourning has been declared in Krakow until 11 November.

Two police officers are also among those injured, one critically.

The suspect, who was equipped with military-style weapons and attire, is a 25-year-old Polish man - described by a minister as "ultra-nationalist".

Police shot and arrested him and he remains in hospital having undergone surgery.

Tusk said there were "strong indications" the two women and one man found dead at the suspect's home in Ostrowiec ÅwiÄtokrzyski were his immediate family members.

He said: "Until now in Poland we haven't had such drastic cases of terrorism... that's what we have to call this cruel attack on people's lives here in Krakow."

UK Prime Minister Andy Burnham said: "I'm shocked and saddened by the appalling shooting in KrakÃ³w today."

"My thoughts are with the families of those who have lost their lives, everyone injured and all those affected by this senseless violence. The United Kingdom stands in solidarity with the people of Poland," he added.

The rampage began shortly before 15:00 local time (14:00 GMT) in the historic centre of Krakow, an ornate square which has long been a draw for tourists.

Footage showed the attacker's vehicle speeding through the centre of the city, and people fleeing as the sound of gunfire rang out.

The glass front of shops were shattered by bullets and a tram was shot at during the attack, which police say lasted for around three minutes.

Images from the scene show overturned tables and scattered belongings left behind as people ran for their lives.

Armed police officers pursued the attacker's car until it crashed, at which point they engaged him in a firefight.

Distressing footage authenticated by BBC Verify captured the moment a police officer confronted the suspect as he lay on the ground.

The officer, who is visibly injured, can then be seen falling to the ground.

News.title: Secondary schools told to stop teaching GCSEs before Year 10
News.content:
Secondary schools will be told not to teach GCSEs early as part of a major shake-up of how children in Years 7 to 9 are taught.

The government plans to make Key Stage 3 a more distinct education phase, urging schools to focus less on exams and more on a "richer, more engaging" experience.

The changes come in response to two reviews that found pupils were increasingly becoming disengaged in their early teenage years, affecting attendance and achievement, the Department for Education (DfE) said.

The move will mark a reversal of the approach taken by the previous Conservative government to focus the first three years of secondary school on core subjects and on doing well in assessments.

Former Education Secretary Michael Gove prioritised English, maths and science, while raising grade boundaries, making exams harder and limiting resits.

He also made GCSEs linear, meaning they are sat all in one go at the end of Year 11 instead of over the course of Key Stage 4.

These reforms meant teachers started preparing pupils for exams at an earlier stage at the expense of teaching unexamined parts of their subject.

Education Secretary Lucy Powell said: "The early years of secondary school should be a time when children are excited to go to school and engage in the specialist and much broader teaching on offer, and where they find their passion and develop a love of learning."

She added that ringfencing Key Stage 3 studies would allow for "more time to develop deeper understanding, as well as a richer experience that will engage more young people in their passions".

The DfE has pledged a "more engaging offer" in subjects like drama, PE, music and languages, which have seen a decline in students taking them, when it publishes its new curriculum later this year.

It says persistent absence nearly doubles among pupils between Year 6 and Year 9, from 13% to 15%.

The department pointed to a recent survey commissioned by the International Baccalaureate that found GCSE prep dominated Key Stage 3 learning in England, with 57% of teachers saying it was the leading influence on the curriculum.

"The pressures of GCSEs and an overcrowded curriculum are resulting in too many children receiving a narrower offer during Key Stage 3 and being rushed towards exams without grasping the fundamentals or developing deeper understanding," Powell said. "I'm putting a stop to that."

A 2015 Ofsted report suggested that Key Stage 3 may be "wasted years", echoing the view at the time that pupils aged 11-14 lacked a clear motivation to work hard.

However, the government faced criticism at the time that its reforms made each exam far more significant, meaning teachers refocused lessons only on what could come up in them.

Reacting to the DfE's announcement on Sunday, Lib Dem education spokeswoman Munira Wilson MP said school was "more than drilling kids for exams" but cautioned against "micromanaging" teachers.

She added that a new curriculum "alone won't get children back into the classroom", noting that "too many pupils are missing school because of anxiety and unmet mental health needs" while "schools can't offer more drama, music and languages without the teachers to teach them".

News.title: We face paying £9,000 tax even though our second home is in a war zone
News.content:
A Ukrainian woman who fled to Scotland after Russia invaded her homeland has been told she could face a Â£9,000 property tax charge because she still owns a flat in Kyiv.

Kateryna Stepanovych, 38, discovered the potential charge when she tried to buy a house in North Ayrshire with her Scottish partner Mattias Lindgren.

The couple were told the Additional Dwelling Supplement (ADS) charge would apply because she already owned a property overseas.

Kateryna bought the small flat in 2018, before Russia's invasion. She fled the war zone in 2023, leaving the property behind.

News.title: I won't let my daughter's killer live in my head, says Sarah Payne's mum
News.content:
The mother of murdered schoolgirl Sarah Payne says she wants to change how people see victims of crime.

Sara Payne's daughter was abducted while playing with her siblings and murdered in July 2000, aged just eight.

Roy Whiting - a convicted sex offender - was jailed for life in December 2001 for her killing.

Sara told BBC South East there were many reasons behind how people behaved, but they "still have choices".

"You have to choose which path you're going to take," she said.

"I chose not to allow him [Whiting] to live in my head.

"It had to be her - so I keep Sarah."

Sarah's body was found 17 days after she went missing from a field near her grandparents' house in West Sussex.

Her disappearance prompted one of the most heavily publicised searches in UK history and led to landmark legal changes.

"I don't have anger. I don't have aggression. I don't want to bring back hanging or any of those things," Sara continued.

"I just want to go forward in a humane way and be human."

News.title: Veterans shouldn't sleep rough this Christmas, Burnham says
News.content:
No one who served in the UK armed forces should have to sleep on the streets this Christmas, Andy Burnham has said.

Downing Street said the PM would personally write to councils across England on Armistice Day (11 November) to urge them to draw up plans to offer accommodation for veterans sleeping rough ahead of the festive period.

He will say that national and local government should work under the "simple principle" that "no one who has served our country should ever be left to sleep rough on our streets".

The Conservatives have meanwhile criticised Culture Secretary Lisa Nandy for linking participation in an EU scheme for young people with the armed forces' sacrifices on Remembrance Sunday.

Burnham will ask local authorities to use part of the additional Â£874m already announced to tackle homelessness specifically for housing veterans.

"People who stepped forward prepared to put their lives on the line for the rest of us should never lack a roof over their head," Burnham said in a statement issued on Saturday.

"When they need help, the country owes them more than warm words. It owes them a bed every night, a proper plan and someone in their corner from day one."

The PM will ask councils to work with local organisations and charities to tackle homelessness amongst veterans.

Downing Street said an additional Â£8.7m in funding would be allocated to eight organisations across the UK to help housing providers offer assistance to veterans with complex needs, including those with health or addiction problems.

Among them are Veteran Housing Scotland, Launchpad and SSAFA, the Armed Forces Charity.

News.title: Two seriously hurt in 30-vehicle crash on the M20 in Kent
News.content:
More than 30 vehicles were involved in a crash which left two people seriously injured on the M20 in Kent on Saturday evening.

The crash happened in foggy conditions just after 18:40 GMT on the London-bound carriageway between junctions eight (Maidstone) and nine (Ashford).

Paramedics attended to 11 people, and two were taken to hospital, Kent Fire and Rescue Service said.

The road was shut in both directions early on Sunday, but has since reopened.

An air ambulance crew, three fire engines and a "technical rescue unit" were sent to the scene, where National Highways said "thick fog" had been confirmed.

Kent Police said one of the two people seriously injured had been taken to a hospital locally, and the other to a London hospital.

"Other drivers have sustained injuries not believed to be serious," it said in a statement.

The force has asked anyone with information about the incident or dashcam footage to come forward.

News.title: School Street fines at one location exceed £1m
News.content:
A London council has issued more than Â£1m worth of penalty charge notices (PCNs) to drivers under a School Street scheme in less than two years.

Brent Council issued PCNs totalling Â£1.15m after introducing the scheme outside Manor School in Kensal Rise in November 2024, saying it would improve road safety and the environment.

Ward councillor Barbara Want raised concerns about the scheme and claimed that the signs were "too high and not properly visible".

Brent Council said the signs in place complied with Department for Transport guidelines, but that it had decided to install extra lower-level signs and gateway features to give more clarity to drivers.

In the 21 months the scheme has been in place, the north-west London council has collected Â£54,799 on average per month, with the scheme only in place during term time.

School Streets are being trialled across the borough to enforce road closures during drop-off and pick-up times, policed by CCTV cameras and mobile enforcement teams. Those caught face a PCN of Â£160, reduced to Â£80 if paid within 14 days.

Previously, it was reported that 70,000 PCNs were issued in 12 months, at a rate of 384 per school day.

In July 2025, the two cameras enforcing the scheme outside Manor School raised more than Â£107,000 in a single month, according to the Local Democracy Reporting Service.

Want said: "For months I have been highlighting the huge volume of PCNs issued to drivers on the Manor School Street. The fact that it has raked in more than Â£1m in two years should have told them something wasn't right.

"It is failing children's safety if drivers are still using the road. I fear the scheme is more about revenue generation than improving road safety or air quality."

Promise Knight, the council's cabinet member for cleaner streets, transport and public realm, said School Streets existed in the borough "to make the journey to and from school safer for children and families".

"The purpose of the scheme is to protect children by reducing congestion and improving air quality.

"We will continue to review the scheme and make practical improvements where they can help drivers comply."

News.title: Grenfell NHS support service faces funding cut
News.content:
NHS England committed Â£50m to the community's recovery in 2018, which funded the service. The ICB has bid for Â£1.8m to continue it, the Local Democracy Reporting Service said.

The fire in June 2017 killed 72 people. The Crown Prosecution Service (CPS) has said it will make charging decisions before the 10th anniversary on 14 June 2027.

Lucy Knight, the Kensington and Chelsea council's lead member for adult social care and public health, said "no-one should be left worrying" about whether their care would still be there.

She said the NHS accepted the period ahead could be especially hard for the community, and now was not the time to change the model of care to fit a smaller budget unless it could still meet people's needs.

A cross-party motion asked the council to tell the ICB and local NHS trust that survivors and the bereaved remained a top priority, and to urge NHS England to confirm long-term funding.

Representatives of the ICB and Central and North West London NHS Foundation Trust (CNWL), which runs the service, will attend a council scrutiny meeting in December.

In a September update, the service said support would "not simply stop".

The ICB said its priority was making sure future arrangements met the needs of those affected. It said local people were helping to shape proposals, which it aimed to finalise as soon as possible.

NHS England said it supported efforts to ensure people affected could continue to get the care they needed.
