World.title: President Milei welcomes Pope Leo during historic visit to Argentina
World.content:
Pope Leo XIV’s visit marks the first papal trip to Argentina in nearly four decades, amid tensions with the Milei government.

Argentinian President Javier Milei has welcomed the head of the Catholic Church, Pope Leo XIV, upon his arrival at Jorge Newbery airport near Buenos Aires.

Milei and his sister, presidential secretary Karina Milei, greeted the pope on Sunday amid tensions between the government and Argentina’s Catholic Church over austerity measures.

Prior to his arrival, the pope spent three days in Uruguay, the first stop on his tour of Latin America.

He is the first pontiff to visit Argentina in nearly four decades, since John Paul II’s trip in 1987.

“Without a doubt, it gives us great joy that this pope is visiting us,” said Jorge Silanes, religious director at the Pequeno Cottolengo Don Orione, a home for people with disabilities in the Buenos Aires province.

In Argentina, Pope Leo’s schedule includes attending a welcome ceremony at Plaza San Martin and a meeting with Milei at the Casa Rosada, the official presidential palace.

But the pontiff’s visit comes amid shrinking membership in the Catholic Church in Latin America, as well as a sometimes fractious relationship with politicians like Milei.

Catholics comprise the largest religious group in Latin America, with as many as 425 million people identifying with the church.

But their numbers have shrunk over the last decade. A Pew Research Center survey found that, in Argentina, the percentage of self-identifying Catholics slipped from 71 percent in the 2013-2014 year to 58 percent a decade later.

Milei himself has suggested he considered converting to Judaism, though he was raised in the Catholic faith.



The Catholic Church has also criticised Milei’s austerity measures, which included slashing social spending and safety-net programmes for the poor.

Milei has defended the budget cuts as necessary to bring inflation under control.

Some members of the Catholic clergy, however, have taken a visible role in the protests against Milei’s measures.

Leo, 71, the first US-born pope, will remain in Argentina until Wednesday and meet with officials, diplomats and civil society representatives.

He will also visit a prison and celebrate mass in Buenos Aires, Lujan, and the province of Cordoba, before travelling to Peru, where he spent years serving as a bishop.

The previous pope, Francis, was born in Buenos Aires in 1936 and was the first pope from the Americas, but he never visited his home country as head of the Catholic Church. Francis died in 2025.

He and Milei had a notably contentious relationship, with the Argentinian president calling the late pontiff a “communist” and an “imbecile who defends social justice”.

“Leo is going to make the visit that Francis never did,” said Reverend Lorenzo “Toto” de Vedia, who works with poor communities in a neighbourhood of Buenos Aires.

World.title: US chipmaker Nvidia investigates CEO Jensen Huang over affair
World.content:
Huang has confirmed he had been having an affair with a woman accused of spying for China.

United States-based chipmaker Nvidia is investigating its chief executive officer, billionaire Jensen Huang, after he confirmed he had an intimate relationship with a woman accused of working for Chinese intelligence.

In an announcement on Sunday, Nvidia said the probe would be conducted by a “committee of independent directors” with outside counsel.

“While the board has no reason to believe that either national security or Nvidia secrets were compromised, the board’s inquiry will examine all available information,” Nvidia’s board of directors said.

It said the board continued to have “confidence in Jensen and his leadership team”. Huang will continue to lead Nvidia during the probe.

The investigation follows a report in The New York Times last month that Jensen may have been the target of a Chinese espionage plot.

China and the US have been in competition to dominate key tech sectors like artificial intelligence (AI).

Amid the AI boom, Nvidia has seen demand for its chips and programming interfaces explode, resulting in the company being valued in the trillions of dollars.

For years, the US has sought to restrict the export of advanced chips to China, fearing the Asian superpower could gain an edge over its technology and military sectors.

But on October 29, The New York Times said it had obtained exclusive information that a Chinese woman named Alice Huang, or Huang Le, sought to cultivate close ties with Jensen Huang in an effort to glean information about Nvidia’s technology.

The Chinese Embassy in Washington, DC, has denied any allegations of spying in the case.



The New York Times also reported that Alice Huang’s employer, Megaspeed, had become one of Nvidia’s largest buyers, purchasing some $4.8bn in equipment from the US firm.

Jensen Huang’s ties to Alice Huang, who is of no relation, spurred fierce bipartisan backlash in the US Congress in the aftermath of the report.

“For months, bipartisan members of Congress have raised concerns about NVIDIA’s advanced AI chips going to China,” Democratic Senator Elizabeth Warren wrote in a statement.

“NVIDIA’s Jensen Huang and NVIDIA’s board owe Congress answers. And we need to pass bipartisan legislation we have ready to stop advanced American technology from going to China.”

Republican lawmakers in the House of Representatives also called on Huang to appear and testify before Congress about the affair on November 18.

“It is vital that Congress determines the extent to which US national security has been placed at risk,” Republicans John Moolenaar, Brian Mast and Rick Crawford said in a statement.

In an email to Nvidia staff on Sunday, Huang had admitted to having an extramarital relationship.

“I was unfaithful to my wife. My actions hurt her and our children. There is no excuse ‌for what I did,” Huang said.

Nvidia has grown rapidly in recent years with the rise of AI, producing chips for large language models developed by companies like OpenAI, Anthropic, Meta and Google.

Huang has also been closely working with US President Donald Trump since the Republican leader returned to office in 2025.

In August of that year, the Trump administration announced it would take a 15 percent cut of certain Nvidia chip sales to China.

Trump reportedly bought as much as $1.6m in Nvidia stock and sold about $1m in August, ahead of November’s midterm elections.

After the midterm races last Tuesday, stocks for AI-related companies, including Nvidia, tumbled in reaction to widespread Republican losses.

Trump has pushed back against calls to regulate AI companies, but many Democrats during the midterms campaigned on placing restrictions on the companies, including on the construction of data centres.

Nvidia lost $450bn in market value in a single trading day last week, but it rebounded on Friday, regaining 4 percent of its losses.

World.title: Why Trump wants UFC chief Dana White as his new White House press secretary
World.content:
The two have business ties going back decades, and White has helped Trump reach out to younger voters.

Share Why Trump wants UFC chief Dana White as his new White House press secretary on social media

Ultimate Fighting Championship (UFC) chief executive Dana White is set to meet United States President Donald Trump on Monday to discuss taking the job of White House press secretary.

Trump announced the offer on Saturday, days after his Republican Party suffered record losses in midterm elections. In a post on Truth Social, the president praised White as “a violent Fighter and Warrior” who would bring along leading UFC fighters as “assistants” to “defend us against the Lunatic Left”.

But it remains unclear how serious the offer is. In a news conference on Saturday, White confirmed he would travel to Washington, DC, to meet with Trump. But he also signalled concerns about his existing workload.

“I got a lot of jobs already,” White, a Trump ally and donor, said. “We have a meeting on Monday, so I’m sure I’ll have more to talk about after that.”

White also posted a photo to Instagram Stories of himself standing behind the White House podium. Its caption read, “On to the next chapter.”

Trump, too, posted his own AI-generated memes about the potential hire.

On Sunday, he shared an animated cartoon of White in the White House briefing room, flanked by a row of fighters. One of them body-slams a reporter who asks, “Is Trump a threat to democracy?”

The press secretary role has been vacant since Katie Zacharia’s brief tenure ended ‌last ⁠month. She left the post within five days of being hired after facing criticism that she presented herself as a lawyer without being licensed in the US.

Zacharia succeeded Karoline Leavitt, who stepped down from the role at the end of August, citing the needs of her growing family.



But why is the head of a mixed martial arts franchise being considered for the new public face of the Trump administration? Al Jazeera explains that and more in this brief explainer.

Who is Dana White?

A former bouncer and small-time boxer, White began his career as a businessman by opening a boxing gym in Boston where he trained other fighters.

He later moved to Las Vegas, where he continued to run gyms and manage emerging fighters.

The UFC was founded in 1993, at about the time White resettled in Las Vegas. The organisation sought to offer an arena for fighters from different disciplines – from boxing to wrestling to jujitsu – to face each other in “no-holds-barred” competition.

In 2001, White convinced two casino magnate friends to buy the UFC for $2m and name him president. Since then, he has built the company up through big fights and lucrative pay-per-view television deals.

He has been a fixture in the UFC in the more than two decades since. White has been credited with turning the fledgling franchise into a global business that brought mixed martial arts into the mainstream.

In 2016, the UFC was sold for $4bn, and in 2023, White became its CEO after a merger with World Wrestling Entertainment valued at some $21bn.

How do Trump and White know each other?

White has been a longtime supporter of Trump, appearing by his side at campaign events for nearly a decade.

Trump, in turn, has a history of hosting UFC fights as far back as 2001. At the time, UFC was struggling against criticism that the sport was too violent.

White had just taken up his position as UFC president, and he and Trump came to an agreement to host that year’s UFC championship at Trump’s Taj Mahal casino in Atlantic City, New Jersey.

The next year, the UFC returned to the Taj Mahal.

Speaking in support of Trump at the 2016 Republican National Convention, White recalled how the early collaboration helped open doors for the UFC, making other venues more accessible.

“No arenas wanted us,” White said at the time. “This guy reached out, and he’s always been a friend to me.”

The 2016 election cycle would mark Trump’s first successful bid for public office. In 2018, White was invited to visit the White House during Trump’s inaugural term as president.

During the 2020 elections, White again endorsed Trump as he sought a second term as president. White also donated $1m to Trump’s campaign and was a key speaker at the Republican Party’s national convention that year.

“I’ve known this man for 20 years. We’ve actually become even closer since he’s become the president of the United States,” White told supporters at a rally in Colorado. “He’s a fighter. He loves this country. He’s doing great things for this country, and we’ve got to win this election again.”



Trump lost the 2020 race to Democrat Joe Biden. But four years later, in 2024, he launched another re-election bid, and successfully won a second term.

During that campaign, Trump credited White with helping him connect with younger voters.

“He introduced me to people I never heard of, young kids,” Trump told Time Magazine in May. “I was being interviewed by 20-year-old kids. I’m saying, ‘Where the hell did you meet these people?’ They’re called influencers.”

How has UFC shaped Trump’s second term?

Experts say Trump’s 2024 campaign benefitted significantly from his UFC connections.

Ahead of his victory, Trump courted influencers like UFC fan Theo Von and UFC host Joe Rogan, whose podcast boasts about 11 million listeners per episode.

Trump has also used his second term as president to elevate the UFC’s profile, weaving one of its events into plans to celebrate the 250th US Independence Day.

Dubbed “UFC Freedom 250”, the tournament was given unusual access to national monuments for a commercial event.

White, for instance, hosted a weigh-in for fighters on the steps of the Lincoln Memorial, with uniformed military personnel standing as an honour guard. The fights themselves were held on the lawn of the White House.

Trump called the event “one of the most exciting days in the history of our fabled White House”.

But critics warned the event could constitute a conflict of interest: In the months before the fight, Trump reportedly bought up to $50,000 of stock in TKO Holding, the UFC’s parent company.

A lawsuit also challenged the UFC’s use of public facilities, calling the event “deeply corrupt”.

How is the announcement being received?

Some opposition figures have dismissed Trump’s idea of appointing White as press secretary as a way to distract attention from the midterm elections.

During the November 3 elections, Trump’s Republican Party suffered record losses, losing majorities in both the House of Representatives and the Senate.

Melat Kiros, a Democrat elected to represent Colorado in the House, said on Saturday that Trump’s offer to White “demonstrates how deeply unserious this man is, how ridiculous this administration is”.

Democratic Senator Mark Kelly, meanwhile, said Trump’s choice raised questions about the president’s wellbeing.

“It would be really funny if it wasn’t dangerous, if he wasn’t the president,” Kelly said. “Countries around the world are continuing to laugh at us because of what he’s doing.”

There has also been some speculation that Trump may have tapped the wrong Dana White.

A woman by the same name formerly worked as a Pentagon spokesperson during Trump’s first term. She has denied being approached for the press secretary role.

“To everyone texting me congratulations: thank you, but you have the wrong Dana White,” she wrote on LinkedIn.

World.title: Surgeon having lunch near Krakow shooting undoubtedly saved officer's life, colleague says
World.content:
One of two surgeons who treated victims on the streets in the aftermath of a mass shooting in Krakow, Poland said his colleague"undoubtedly" saved the life of a gravely injured police officer.

The pair were eating near the city's Main Market Square on Saturday when a gunman began firing at random, killing six and injuring 15.

The doctors raced to treat both the attacker and two officers shot while subduing the perpetrator.

On Sunday, the officers - both hailed as "true heroes" by the prime minister for preventing further deaths - emerged from comas.

Prosecutors launched a terror investigation after ministers previously said the 24-year-old Polish attacker - who remains in a critical condition - was apparently inspired by "far-right ideologies".

A British national and Austrian woman were among those killed alongside four Poles.

Professor Michal PÄdziwiatr and Dr Mateusz Wierdak were having lunch in central Krakow with their families when they heard gunshots, local media reported.

"Suddenly my son ran up and said: 'Dad, they're shooting at people there, people are falling to the ground'," PÄdziwiatr told news outlet Fakt.

PÄdziwiatr said when they got to the scene, they treated both the apparent attacker and the police officers.

"When it comes to saving lives, it doesn't matter who is who," he added.

Once the shooting stopped, PÄdziwiatr said he took care of the other victims and the perpetrator, while Wierdak began working on the police officer who was shot in the chest during the gunfight.

World.title: Seven dead and more than 100 injured after trains collide in Egypt
World.content:
At least seven people have died in a train crash near the Egyptian city of Giza, with more than 100 injured.

The country's railway authority said two trains travelling south from Giza and Cairo collided, causing several carriages to derail and fall down an embankment.

Images from the scene showed people looking inside overturned carriages for injured passengers as a massive emergency response was launched.

Egyptian President Abdul Fattah al-Sisi said he had ordered state authorities to "investigate the circumstances of the accident, and hold accountable anyone found to have been negligent".

The public prosecutor's office warned the death toll could rise.

World.title: Homes and temples glow across India to mark Diwali
World.content:
Millions across India are celebrating Diwali, the Hindu festival of lights, illuminating homes, temples, offices and streets with oil lamps and colourful lights to symbolise the triumph of light over darkness.

The festival falls on the darkest night of the Hindu lunar month of Kartik, when the moon is not visible in the sky.

Although Diwali traditions vary across India's regions and communities, the festival is widely marked by prayers, family gatherings, the exchange of sweets and the lighting of firecrackers.

But the celebrations come amid growing concerns over air pollution, particularly in northern India.

Seasonal weather conditions and the burning of crop residue contribute to deteriorating air quality, while firecrackers set off during Diwali can make the situation worse.

Air pollution in the Indian capital Delhi has reached such hazardous levels that it is the most polluted Diwali festival in a decade. New measures to improve air quality do not seem to have been successful.

India's financial capital, Mumbai, has also experienced high pollution levels in recent weeks.

In an effort to limit pollution, India's Supreme Court on Monday permitted the manufacture, sale and use of certified "green" firecrackers in Delhi and surrounding areas for a limited period.

These firecrackers are designed to produce 20-30% fewer emissions than conventional fireworks. But critics have questioned how effective they are at reducing pollution and raised concerns that conventional firecrackers could still make their way into the capital from neighbouring states.

World.title: Iran executes three men for 'armed unrest' after January protests
World.content:
Iran has executed three men accused of carrying out armed unrest during January's anti-government protests, according to state media.

Hassan Dioband, Hamid Kazemi and Reza Zanganeh were accused of throwing Molotov cocktails and grenades, using bladed weapons and firearms, and setting fire to public facilities in the city of Karaj, west of Tehran, Iran's state news agency Tasnim, external reported.

The executions are the latest in a series linked to the protests, including those of people accused of having ties to Israel and the United States.

The number of executions in Iran has increased since US-Israeli strikes on the Islamic Republic began in late February.

The protest movement initially sparked in December last year by the high cost of living rapidly evolved into widespread anti-government demonstrations that peaked on 8 and 9 of January.

Iranian authorities reported more than 3,000 deaths, and blamed the violence on "terrorist acts" orchestrated by the US and Israel.

However foreign-based NGOs gave higher figures and the BBC received multiple accounts from Iranians of security forces opening fire on unarmed protesters.

Tasnim reported that the three men were executed after the Supreme Court upheld their convictions and found them guilty of "participating in operational activities on behalf of the Israeli Zionist regime, the United States and hostile groups".

The damage allegedly included an electricity substation in Karaj which caused power outages in some areas.

Dioband was arrested on 11 January after investigations identified him as a suspect in attacks on public property and incitement to violence.

Ten others accused of taking part in the unrest under his supervision were later arrested.

Reuters news agency reports that they received prison terms of 5 to 10 years.

The latest executions in Iran come after the UN human rights chief Volker TÃ¼rk said he was alarmed by the rise in death penalties.

In August, TÃ¼rk said at least 56 people had been executed on national security-related charges since 19 March, including 27 in cases linked to January's nationwide anti-government protests.

Iran is thought to be the world's second-most prolific executioner after China. Last year, it put to death at least 2,159 people, according to Amnesty International.

The human rights group said that was the highest figure on record since 1981 and included 45 executions of suspected dissidents on national security-related charges.

World.title: Houthis say at least 33 killed in Saudi air strike
World.content:
Media linked to the Houthi movement in Yemen say at least 33 people, including women and children, have been killed in air strikes by Saudi Arabia.

There has been no comment from the Saudi-led coalition backing the internationally recognised government in Yemen.

Live video footage on Al Masirah - a television station run by the Houthis - has shown rescuers pulling bodies out of the rubble of several buildings in al-Shariyah, a town to the east of the capital, Sanaa.

The bodies of young children can be seen among those dug out from the ruins.

The television station has also shown a number of injured people being carried on stretchers to hospital.

Saba news agency, which is also run by the Houthis, said the attack was carried out by Saudi Arabia on Saturday. It added that 39 people had been injured.

The Saudis have led a coalition that has been fighting the Houthis for more than a decade in support of Yemen's internationally recognised government.

The war in Yemen had been dormant for several years but reignited as a result of the Iran war.

A truce began to fall apart when Saudi Arabia struck the airport in Sanaa - which is controlled by the Houthis - to prevent an Iranian plane landing there.

The Tehran-backed Houthis subsequently targeted Abha airport in Saudi Arabia, then began hitting Saudi ships that have been using the Red Sea off the coast of Yemen as an alternative oil export route to the Strait of Hormuz.

Major fighting has since resumed in Yemen between the Houthis and forces fighting for the Saudi-backed government of Yemen.

On Friday, an attack on a market in Taiz province, which has been the focus of much of the recent fighting, is reported to have killed 30 people.

The Houthis accused the Saudis of carrying out the strike, while government forces accused the Houthis of having fired a missile at the site.

The United Nations says more than 1,600 people have been killed and more than 300,000 displaced since fighting resumed.

The Saudis have regularly bombed Houthi positions, while the group has fired multiple missiles at targets inside Saudi Arabia, including airports and oil facilities.

Hours before the strike that hit al-Shariyah, the Saudi-led coalition said it intercepted a missile heading towards Riyadh.

The Saudi Ministry of Energy later said the Aramco tower had been hit by falling shrapnel in what it said was an attempted attack.

The state-owned oil company's building suffered minor damage.

A Houthi leader, Mahdi al-Mashat, has vowed that the group will take revenge for the latest attacks in Yemen.

World.title: 'Flat', 'tired', 'cynical': Unusually gloomy Kiwis deliver New Zealand's tightest election in years
World.content:
New Zealand voted in a new government as fog choked the capital, Wellington, on Saturday - and the mood was as palpable as the grey weather.

"It's pretty flat," 21-year-old Imogen Vlutger says. "There's this kind of apathy and a bit of dread."

"Tired. I think we're all tired," Symone, 28, admits.

"I didn't even vote," one man in his 40s sheepishly confesses. He couldn't bring himself to tick any of the boxes, he explains, declining to chat further.

"Wellington's a bit of a bubble," another voter says, expressing a caveat I heard often, before describing feeling disillusioned.

But polling shows this is a pervasive sentiment across the country: the national mood is low and faith in politics is even lower.

More than half the country no longer sees it as a land of opportunity, a recent study found, while a similar portion fears that the future looks even worse.

Many Kiwis feel the economy is in ruins, there are no jobs, the cost of living has become sky high, the sense of community that used to be a source of national pride is breaking down and there's no sense of genuine progress on policy solutions.

A record number of them are abandoning ship in search of brighter futures elsewhere.

Saturday's election also saw a record number of voters desert the two major parties, giving neither a clear mandate.

But it brought new highs for parties across the spectrum: the left-leaning Greens, the right-wing libertarian Act Party and the centrist Opportunity Party â the latter of which had never won a seat in parliament before but could now hold the balance of power with seven.

World.title: Paraguay's former president charged after bank collapse
World.content:
Prosecutors in Paraguay have charged former president Santiago PeÃ±a over his alleged role in a banking scandal that led to his impeachment.

He has been accused of breach of trust and administration for personal gain.

PeÃ±a, who denies any wrongdoing, was forced from office after a bank collapse triggered a crisis that left more than half of the country's population without access to their accounts.

He was arrested on Friday minutes after lawmakers, including from his own party, unanimously voted to remove him from office following the collapse of Ueno Bank, which has links to his private business interests.

He had offered to step down but rather than accept his resignation, senators impeached PeÃ±a and charged him with misconduct, meaning he has been stripped of the immunity usually granted to ex-presidents.

PeÃ±a, who until last year held shares in the company that owned the bank, has denied any wrongdoing.

The impeachment charges that led to PeÃ±a's removal alleged he had conflicts of interest, manipulated regulatory oversight, diverted pension funds, and participated in an institutional cover-up involving the central bank.

PeÃ±a's deputy, Pedro Alliana, has been sworn in as the new interim president and promised not to "abandon" the millions of people affected by the scandal.

"Compatriots who are now going through a difficult time as a result of the financial collapse will be fully compensated," said Alliana, who will serve as president until 2028.

The demise of the digital bank left more than half of Paraguay's population without access to their savings after it was seized by Paraguay's central bank.

Long lines of people trying to withdraw money from Ueno branches snaked down the streets of the capital Asuncion on Tuesday and Wednesday.

An estimated three million depositors remain unable to access their savings and pensions, prompting public outrage particularly in the capital, AsunciÃ³n.

Protests erupted across the country in response, with thousands taking to the streets on Thursday to demand their money.

Earlier demonstrations featured clashes with the police, who used tear gas and water cannons on the crowd.

PeÃ±a's impeachment passed with 44 out of 45 senators voting in favour of it. One lawmaker was absent.

"It was never my intention to betray the trust you placed in me," PeÃ±a said in a video posted on X announcing his resignation, adding his priority was "the peace of mind of Paraguayans who entrusted their savings to our financial system".

Afterwards, senate president Basilio NÃºÃ±ez said PeÃ±a was found guilty of "dereliction of duty".

World.title: Pope in 'pretty good health' as he starts Latin America tour
World.content:
Pope Leo XIV has told reporters travelling with him to Latin America he is "in pretty good health", in his first comments on his condition since having surgery for lung cancer.

The Pope has arrived in Uruguay, the first stop of a 12-day tour which he is undertaking only three weeks after his operation.

The pontiff, 71, also said he was "very happy" to be able to make the trip which was thrown into doubt last month when doctors discovered a tumour during a routine scan.

The tour will cover Argentina and a much anticipated return to Peru, which the Vatican described as a "homecoming" as the Pope was based there for many years as a missionary, then a bishop.

"I must confess that, from the very first day, I never had any doubts; I was convinced that this journey had to go forward," the Pope told journalists on his plane to Uruguay.

"Thanks to the marvellous medical staff... I believe I am in quite good health," Pope Leo confirmed.

Last month's operation to remove a tumour was successful and his doctors say the cancer has not spread.

On Friday, he arrived in Monetevideo to a seafront lined with crowds shouting his name as his Popemobile passed.

In his first speech of the trip, the Pope said universal healthcare should be "accessible to everyone".

He told the crowd in Plaza Independencia the care he received made him think of the "many men and women who lack the means to obtain a timely diagnosis" or receive treatment.

He capped his day with a prayer at the Montevideo Cathedral.

Pope Leo will cover more than 20,000 miles on his sixth international tour.

On Sunday he will travel to Argentina, the homeland of his predecessor Pope Francis who did not return during his own papacy.

The Pope said his visit was about being near the people who were looking to the Church for a message of "hope".

World.title: Lagos police ask political parties to notify command ahead of 2027 rallies
World.content:
The Lagos State Police Command has asked political parties to send it notice ahead of rallies, campaigns, processions and other political gatherings as preparations for the 2027 general elections gather pace.

The Commissioner of Police, Tijani Fatai, said the notice would enable the command to make security arrangements and deploy personnel to cover the events.

Mr Fatai made the appeal in a statement shared on X on Sunday by the police spokesperson, Abimbola Adebisi.

He stated that the command would provide security for all political parties, candidates and their supporters without discrimination. He, however, warned that activities capable of disrupting public peace would not be tolerated.

The commissioner said parties that failed to notify the police or disregarded security arrangements, resulting in a breach of peace, would be held accountable under the law.

He also referred to a security meeting held on 15 October ahead of the elections, where political parties and other stakeholders were urged to cooperate with security agencies and comply with security guidelines.

The police’s appeal comes against the backdrop of their statutory responsibility to provide security for political activities. Section 91 of the Electoral Act 2022 requires the police to provide adequate security for the peaceful conduct of rallies and processions.

Stay Ahead with Premium Times 

READ ALSO: Lagos police foil plot to traffic Kaduna girls to Ivory Coast

It also protects the right of registered political parties, aspirants and candidates to hold lawful rallies.

Mr Fatai urged political parties to cooperate with the command to ensure that political activities across the state were conducted peacefully.

The notice, as framed by the police command, is not a request for permission to conduct political activities.

The position of the law based on subsisting court judgements is that police permits are not required to hold such political activities or organise protests.

World.title: Abiodun commends DSS, Police for rescuing kidnap victims, vows Ogun won’t be criminals’ safe haven
World.content:
Ogun State Governor, Prince Dapo Abiodun, has commended the Director-General of the Department of State Services (DSS), Mr Oluwatosin Adeola Ajayi and the Inspector-General of Police, Olatunji Rilwan Disu, for their roles in the safe rescue of 10 passengers abducted from a commercial vehicle around Orita Fufu, Awa-Ijebu, in Ijebu North-East Local Government Area of the state.

Abiodun particularly applauded the DSS Director-General for providing critical intelligence and sophisticated security equipment that aided the tracking of the kidnappers and facilitated the rescue operation.

He also commended the Inspector-General of Police for his prompt directives and intervention, which galvanised the Ogun State Police Command and other security operatives into action, culminating in the release of the victims unharmed.

The governor, in a statement, declared that his administration would not allow kidnappers and other criminal elements to turn any part of the state into a safe haven, assuring residents that the government was intensifying efforts to ensure that criminals had no place in Ogun.

He warned that those who threatened the security of residents and commuters would be relentlessly pursued until they were brought to justice. He also urged residents to support security agencies by providing timely and credible information about suspicious persons, movements and activities in their communities.

Abiodun reiterated his administration’s commitment to strengthening collaboration with security agencies and providing the necessary support to protect lives and property across the state.

He called on residents to remain vigilant and cooperate with security operatives, stressing that collective action and prompt information-sharing were essential to preventing crime and maintaining peace in Ogun State.

World.title: Lagos governorship candidates clash over waste management, defend political records
World.content:
Lagos governorship candidates on Sunday disagreed over how to address the state’s waste management crisis, with proposals ranging from returning a greater role to local governments to investing in recycling and waste recovery facilities.

The candidates spoke at a governorship debate in Lagos, where they also faced questions about their political records, experience in public office, party affiliations and the 2020 #EndSARS protests.

Gbadebo Rhodes-Vivour of the African Democratic Congress (ADC) described Lagos as a state that stinks, blaming years of poor management for the deterioration in refuse collection.

He rejected the argument that population growth was mainly responsible, saying the state had managed its waste more effectively in the past despite the increasing number of residents.

Mr Rhodes-Vivour said Lagos had about 1,000 waste collection trucks under former Governor Babatunde Fashola, but that the number had fallen to about 200, according to information available to him.

He blamed the decline partly on the centralisation of waste management, which he said had weakened the role of local governments.

“We don’t actually have a waste management system. We have a waste pick and dump system,” he said.

Stay Ahead with Premium Times 

He proposed involving local governments in refuse collection and requiring households to separate their waste so that recyclable materials could be collected and processed.

He said the arrangement would create economic opportunities and allow residents and the different levels of government to benefit from waste recycling.

Lagos introduced its Private Sector Participation (PSP) scheme for domestic waste collection in 1997, beginning with a pilot in Kosofe and Bariga local government areas. The scheme was later extended across the state, with the Lagos Waste Management Authority (LAWMA) taking over its management in 2007. LAWMA has identified unreliable service delivery and difficulties enforcing standards as among the scheme’s weaknesses.

Deputy Governor Obafemi Hamzat, the All Progressives Congress (APC) candidate, defended the government’s approach, saying Lagos was moving away from the practice of collecting refuse and dumping it in landfills.

He said the volume of waste generated in the state, coupled with limited land for disposal, made it necessary to invest in facilities that could recover useful materials.

Mr Hamzat said the government was developing Olusosun and Solous 3 in Alimosho as transfer stations, while a material recovery facility had been established at Erekiti. Similar facilities, he added, were planned for Kinsinki and Chikurudu.

The explanation came against the backdrop of the state’s continuing waste collection problems. In September, Governor Babajide Sanwo-Olu declared a state of emergency on waste collection after acknowledging delays in refuse evacuation.

During an inspection of the Olusosun dumpsite, the governor announced plans to increase disposal capacity, deploy additional equipment and improve the operations of PSP operators. Transfer-loading stations were also proposed for Olusosun and Solous 3.

Responding to the description of Lagos as a smelly city, Mr Hamzat said it would be unfair to apply that description to the entire state, although he acknowledged that some areas had unpleasant odours.

He admitted that waste management remained a challenge, pointing to inadequate collection trucks, reception facilities and transfer stations.

Funso Doherty, the Nigeria Democratic Congress (NDC) candidate, said waste was accumulating faster than it was being collected.

He argued that the problem extended beyond household refuse to liquid and human waste, and raised concerns about pollution from the Olusosun dumpsite and its effects on nearby communities.

Candidates defend political records

Beyond waste management, the candidates faced questions about their political histories and whether their experience prepared them to govern Lagos.

Mr Rhodes-Vivour, who came second in the 2023 governorship election on the Labour Party platform before moving to the ADC, was asked whether his performance in that election and subsequent defection could affect his chances in 2027.

He said he was focused on reaching voters and learning from the mistakes of his previous campaign. He also questioned the conduct of the 2023 election, arguing that a credible process would be important in determining the outcome of the next poll.

The Independent National Electoral Commission declared Mr Sanwo-Olu the winner in 2023 with 762,134 votes. Mr Rhodes-Vivour polled 312,329 votes, while the Peoples Democratic Party candidate, Abdul-Azeez Adediran, popularly known as Jandor, secured 62,449 votes.

On his preparedness for office, Mr Rhodes-Vivour pointed to his work in urban development and housing, including proposals for low-income housing developed with the Chinese and American governments and Temple Housing.

He also challenged the emphasis on previous executive experience, citing former Lagos Governor Lateef Jakande as an example of a leader whose vision and commitment shaped his administration.

Mr Hamzat faced questions about whether he would govern independently or remain under the influence of the political establishment that has controlled Lagos since 1999.

He defended his capacity to make independent decisions, citing his academic and professional background, including earning a PhD at 27 and serving as an executive director in an American organisation. He also referred to his family’s political background and his experience in public administration, transport and budgeting.

His record in government also came under scrutiny, with questions about why residents should trust him to tackle flooding, traffic congestion, housing shortages, waste collection and the rising cost of living after nearly eight years as deputy governor and in previous positions in the state government.

Mr Hamzat said he was proud of the state’s achievements but acknowledged that more needed to be done.

He cited the Lekki-Ikoyi Bridge, which he said was delivered while he served as commissioner for transport and works, as well as the Bus Rapid Transit system and the establishment of transport agencies.

He attributed the pressure on public infrastructure to Lagos’s growing population, which he said was approaching 25 million, while the state’s land area remained unchanged.

Hamzat questioned over #EndSARS

The 20 October 2020 shooting at the Lekki Toll Gate also featured in the debate, with Mr Hamzat asked what he knew about the incident and what he did as deputy governor at the time.

He described the day as a sad one and said the Lagos State Government established an independent judicial panel of inquiry, funded its work and later published a White Paper on its recommendations.

Mr Hamzat argued that responsibility for the military rested with the Federal Government but maintained that the state government had not ignored the pain caused by the incident.

In November 2021, the Lagos government said it had accepted 11 of the panel’s 32 recommendations, accepted six with modifications, rejected one and referred 14 to the Federal Government, saying they fell outside the state’s powers.

Mr Rhodes-Vivour, in his closing remarks, recalled being tear-gassed while laying flowers at the Lekki Toll Gate. He criticised what he described as violence against opposition figures and questioned the treatment of people who participated in the protests despite political leaders’ public statements about #EndSARS.

Funso Doherty addresses NDC primary dispute

The NDC candidate also faced questions about a dispute over the party’s governorship primary.

The moderator raised an allegation by Naheem Balogun that he had won the primary but was subsequently displaced.

Mr Doherty rejected the allegation, insisting that he had won the ticket. He said anyone dissatisfied with the outcome could approach the courts.

His movement between political parties also came under scrutiny, with questions about whether it was consistent with the principled leadership he promised Lagos residents.

Mr Doherty argued that opposition parties operated in a difficult political environment, where court cases and interference sometimes made it difficult for politicians to pursue their ambitions on their original platforms.

His political movements have included leaving the ADC for the PDP in 2024, returning to the ADC and later joining the NDC in May 2026.

In announcing his latest move, he said he had initially hoped the ADC would unite the opposition but concluded that it would no longer serve that purpose.

Deji Doherty speaks on Wike’s influence

The PDP candidate, Deji Doherty, was challenged over his relationship with the Minister of the Federal Capital Territory, Nyesom Wike, and whether it would undermine his independence if elected governor.

Mr Wike remains a member of the PDP but serves in the APC-led Federal Government and has publicly declared support for President Bola Tinubu.

Mr Doherty attributed his emergence as the PDP candidate to 26 years of political activity and grassroots support, rather than the influence of any individual.

However, he described Mr Wike as his national leader and said he would continue to recognise him in that capacity.

He argued that political cooperation could bring benefits to Lagos, including improved funding and development.

On his business background, Mr Doherty said his business group was established in 1986 and would mark its 40th anniversary in December.

He said he had worked with major organisations and experienced financial difficulties, including a period when he owed banks about N3.8 billion.

Describing himself as a debt manager, he argued that his experience handling business debts would help him manage the state’s finances.

Candidates make final appeals

In their closing remarks, the candidates returned to their campaign promises.

Mr Rhodes-Vivour called for people-centred policies, greater investment in human development and a government that would protect residents’ welfare and rights.

Mr Hamzat asked voters to assess him against the commitments in his manifesto, The Lagos Promise.

Mr Doherty of the NDC urged residents to decide whether they were satisfied with Lagos after 27 years of political dominance by the same political bloc or wanted a change in direction. He described his party’s programme as The New Way.

Mr Doherty of the PDP promised to remove some levies imposed on residents, including what he described as solar and pothole levies. He also called for a review of charges imposed on minors receiving treatment in hospitals.

He pledged to prioritise education and improve support for teachers and medical workers.

World.title: I’m impressed with Gov Lawal’s performance in Zamfara, says Emir of Kano
World.content:
The Emir of Kano, His Royal Highness Khalifah Muhammad Sunusi II, has expressed satisfaction with Governor Dauda Lawal’s performance in Zamfara State.

The Emir was the guest of honour at the commissioning of the rebuilt and equipped Zawiyya Mosque and Islamiyya School in Gusau.

The Zawiyya is one of the oldest Islamic institutions in Zamfara, with a long history of producing scholars across various fields.

In his Friday sermon at the rebuilt mosque, Professor Ibrahim Maqari emphasised peaceful coexistence among people and the importance of cleanliness, particularly in places of worship.

At the commissioning ceremony, the Emir of Kano, Khalifah Muhammadu Sunusi II, said that only those familiar with the Zawiyya’s former structure could fully appreciate the scale and quality of Governor Lawal’s work.

He also emphasised the importance of keeping the rebuilt mosque clean and well maintained.

He said, “The mosque should be kept clean and in good condition. We must maintain cleanliness when we come here because the mosque is a symbol of Islam.

Stay Ahead with Premium Times 

“I am delighted with this work. May Almighty Allah reward His Excellency.

“I can see the good work you are doing in Zamfara State in education, health, security, and infrastructure.

“I am not surprised, as I have known your governor since his days in the banking industry. I know his capabilities, and I am impressed by his performance and happy to see him doing such wonderful work as governor.”

World.title: Lagos governorship candidates offer competing plans on transport, healthcare
World.content:
Candidates in the Lagos State governorship debate have outlined different approaches to tackling traffic congestion and improving healthcare, with proposals ranging from expanding public transportation to increasing hospital funding and providing free treatment for mothers and children.

The World Bank has identified traffic congestion as a persistent problem in Lagos, where commuters spend an average of about four hours daily travelling. Its September 2025 brief examined the city’s public transport challenges and efforts to expand mass transit.

African Democratic Congress (ADC) candidate Gbadebo Rhodes-Vivour on Sunday at the debate said poor urban planning and an inadequate transport network were partly responsible for the long hours residents spend commuting.

He stated that traffic had become so much a part of daily life that residents had come to accept spending several hours travelling to and from work, often at the expense of time with their families.

“Traffic is not a lifestyle and we should not have to work to get to work,” Mr Rhodes-Vivour said.

He proposed spreading development across the state and expanding the rail network with private-sector funding.

According to him, infrastructure finance companies could provide the money for the expansion, allowing the projects to be completed within two and a half years and repaid over 30 years without placing the entire financial burden on the state government.

Stay Ahead with Premium Times 

He also proposed shorter bridges linking the eastern foreshore with the Ibeju-Lekki axis to provide alternative routes for motorists.

On water transportation, Mr Rhodes-Vivour called for more ferry services, accessible terminals and cable cars to complement the rail network. He said commuters should be able to park their vehicles at ferry terminals and continue their journeys by water.

He also proposed dedicated bicycle lanes, improved roads within communities and the development of local centres across local governments to reduce the need for residents to travel long distances to access basic services.

Deputy Governor Obafemi Hamzat, the All Progressives Congress (APC) candidate, said his administration would build on the existing bus rapid transit (BRT) system and improve connections between road, rail and water transportation.

He noted that the BRT system had recorded 77 million passenger journeys since its introduction. He proposed increasing the number of buses from about 1,000 to 4,000, mainly using compressed natural gas (CNG), to move about one million passengers daily.

Mr Hamzat also proposed dedicated BRT lanes linking Marina with Epe and Badagry, among other routes.

He said commuters should be able to use ferries, trains and BRT buses with a single payment system, allowing them to move between different transport services without making separate payments.

He proposed deploying electric ferries to reduce operating costs and increase passenger capacity, with routes linking Oworonshoki, Ikorodu, Epe and Badagry.

Mr Hamzat added that the government had identified traffic junctions for intervention to ease congestion.

The proposals are linked to the Lagos State Government’s broader transport plans. The Lagos Metropolitan Area Transport Authority (LAMATA) says its Strategic Transport Master Plan provides for an integrated system involving rail, BRT, waterways and other transport services.

Disagreement over rail financing

The candidates disagreed over whether private investors could finance the expansion of Lagos’s rail network without substantial government funding.

Mr Rhodes-Vivour said private financing was possible, adding that he had held discussions with infrastructure financiers who had presented proposals to the Lagos State Government.

He argued that the project was commercially viable and should not take decades to complete.

Mr Hamzat disagreed, saying no sub-national government in Africa had successfully built a rail network entirely through private-sector financing.

He recalled that the Lagos government spent three years under former Governor Babatunde Fashola seeking private investors to finance the Blue and Red rail lines but was unsuccessful.

He stated that government must first invest in rail infrastructure before considering concessions to private operators.

Mr Hamzat also warned that relying on passenger fares alone to finance rail projects could make transportation too expensive for ordinary residents.

Agbero system and public transportation

Funso Doherty of the Nigeria Democratic Congress (NDC) blamed part of Lagos’s traffic problem on poor management of existing infrastructure and the failure to modernise public transportation.

He criticised the condition of commercial buses operating in the state, describing many as dilapidated and poorly managed. He said the government needed to replace the fragmented system with modern buses that offered safer and more comfortable journeys.

Mr Doherty also alleged that vested interests had benefited from the existing transport arrangement and that political considerations had prevented successive administrations from confronting the informal network associated with transport union levies and touts.

He noted that he would have the political will to reform the system because his administration would depend on voters rather than the informal transport network for political support.

Research by the International Growth Centre has examined the effects of Lagos’s Bus Reform Initiative on private minibus operators. A 2025 study found that the introduction of public buses affected minibus services and drivers’ earnings, highlighting the need to consider informal operators when planning transport reforms.

Deji Doherty of the People Democratic Party (PDP) also identified heavy-duty truck movements, transport union activities, poor roads and delays in completing the Fourth Mainland Bridge as factors contributing to congestion.

He said several local government areas had roads in poor condition, making it difficult to ease traffic without improving the road network.

He proposed additional bridges, including routes linking Oworonshoki with Epe and Ibeju-Lekki, to provide alternative routes for motorists.

Mr Doherty stated that Lagos’s population meant commercial buses, motorcycles, tricycles and private vehicles would continue to operate, making it necessary to improve roads and provide more options for commuters.

On the informal transport system, the NDC candidate said reform would require addressing the livelihoods of people who depended on it.

He proposed expanding vocational and skills acquisition programmes to help them find alternative sources of income.

He also said modernising public transportation would create jobs for drivers, conductors, mechanics and other workers, providing opportunities for some people currently working in the informal system to move into more organised employment.

Fact-checkers challenge candidates’ claims

The debate’s independent fact-checking team challenged some of the candidates’ claims, including statements about Lagos’s revenue and elevation above sea level.

The team rated as false a claim attributed to the NDC candidate that Lagos’s internally generated revenue (IGR) was higher than the combined revenue of 31 other states.

According to figures presented by the fact-checkers, Lagos generated N1.77 trillion in 2025, while all 36 states and the Federal Capital Territory generated a combined N5.15 trillion.

The other 35 states and the FCT accounted for N3.38 trillion, meaning Lagos contributed about 34 per cent of the total.

The National Bureau of Statistics’ 2025 IGR figures, reported by PREMIUM TIMES, also showed that Lagos generated N1.77 trillion out of the combined N5.15 trillion.

The fact-checking team also rated

Mr Hamzat’s claim that Lagos was two metres below sea level as false. It said the state was a low-lying coastal area but was not below sea level.

Candidates differ over healthcare funding

On healthcare, the candidates proposed different ways to address funding shortages, improve hospital services and make treatment more accessible to residents.

The moderator raised concerns about Lagos’s health budget, noting that the state allocated between five and eight per cent of its annual budget to healthcare, below the 15 per cent target under the Abuja Declaration.

The candidates were asked how they would increase funding and ensure that allocations were released and properly spent.

Mr Rhodes-Vivour proposed establishing emergency response centres in all 245 wards, each equipped with two ambulances.

He said the centres would reduce the time residents spend moving between hospitals in search of beds, oxygen and other emergency services.

He also proposed preventive healthcare programmes to identify illnesses early and provide basic health education at the ward level. The centres, he said, would include wellness facilities where residents, particularly older people and pensioners, could exercise and receive guidance on healthy living.

Mr Rhodes-Vivour said he would increase healthcare funding towards 15 per cent of the state budget, improve doctors’ salaries, train support staff and introduce artificial intelligence to support diagnosis and healthcare delivery.

Mr Hamzat stated that his administration would expand health insurance coverage, increase hospital capacity and upgrade primary healthcare centres.

He said the Ilera Eko health insurance scheme currently covered about 1.4 million people and proposed extending coverage to one in every three Lagos residents.

He also cited ongoing hospital projects, including a 150-bed general hospital and the Massey Street children’s hospital, as part of efforts to increase capacity.

Mr Hamzat said Lagos had more than 300 primary healthcare centres, but only 87 were operating as flagship facilities. He proposed increasing the number to about 150 and expanding round-the-clock services so residents could access medical attention at any time.

He also proposed establishing a new university of medicine, with a target of producing up to 1,000 doctors.

However, he said increasing the number of trained doctors alone would not address the problem unless the government also improved hospital facilities and working conditions to retain medical professionals.

The state government has acknowledged the funding challenges. At a ministerial briefing in May 2026, Commissioner for Health Akin Abayomi said Lagos spent about eight per cent of its budget on health and faced an estimated N100 billion gap between available funding and projected healthcare needs.

The NDC candidate called for increased government spending on healthcare and education, proposing that their combined allocation should rise from about 15 per cent to 28 per cent of the state budget during his first term.

He also promised free maternal and child healthcare, including drugs and diagnostic tests.

Mr Doherty said some government hospitals provided consultations but required patients to obtain tests elsewhere and buy prescribed drugs themselves, making treatment unaffordable for many families.

He argued that free healthcare should cover essential treatment rather than depend mainly on insurance schemes. While acknowledging the role of health insurance in expanding coverage, he said the government should directly fund treatment for residents who could not afford medical expenses.

The PDP candidate said improving healthcare would require more investment in medical personnel, hospital equipment and pharmaceutical production.

He called for the training of more doctors and nurses, saying the available number of medical professionals and hospitals was inadequate for a state with an estimated population of 25 million.

He also proposed supporting local manufacturers of hospital beds, medical equipment and drugs.

Mr Doherty said reducing charges imposed on pharmaceutical manufacturers would encourage local production and make medicines more affordable.

He identified malaria, cancer, hypertension and HIV as health challenges requiring greater attention from the state.

World.title: Lagos governorship candidates disagree over rent control, housing, flooding
World.content:
Candidates in the Lagos State governorship debate on Sunday disagreed over how to address rising rents, the shortage of affordable housing and recurrent flooding, with proposals ranging from rent regulation and government-backed housing to better drainage management and protection of wetlands.

African Democratic Congress (ADC) candidate Gbadebo Rhodes-Vivour called for legislation to protect tenants from arbitrary rent increases.

He proposed that landlords give tenants at least six months’ notice before increasing rents, with the government setting guidelines to limit increases to between 20 and 30 per cent.

“There must be legislation that ensures that tenants are protected from arbitrary rent increases, at least given six months’ notice before that happens,” Mr Rhodes-Vivour said.

He also complained about excessive agency and legal fees charged by estate agents. Citing a self-contained apartment with an annual rent of N500,000, he said some agents demanded an additional N500,000 in fees.

He proposed a system that would allow tenants to report such practices to the government for investigation.

To increase the supply of affordable housing, Mr Rhodes-Vivour noted that his administration would consider financing the completion or renovation of unfinished private buildings in exchange for temporary ownership rights. The properties would then be made available as affordable rental accommodation.

Stay Ahead with Premium Times 

The proposal comes against the backdrop of a housing deficit estimated at more than 2.7 million units in Lagos. A report said 34,800 housing units were in the development pipeline.

Deputy Governor Obafemi Hamzat, who is seeking to succeed Governor Babajide Sanwo-Olu on the platform of the All Progressives Congress (APC), stated that the state had already introduced regulations for estate agents and that the focus should now be on enforcing them.

He said agents were required to register with the relevant government agency and urged residents to report those who violated the rules through its online platform.

Mr Hamzat also promised to complete ongoing housing projects, speed up the processing of property documents and work with private developers to increase housing supply.

He said developers of luxury properties would be encouraged to include lower-cost housing in their projects.

His reference to existing estate agency regulations is separate from the Lagos State Tenancy and Recovery of Premises Bill 2025.

PREMIUM TIMES reported that the proposed bill sought to address issues including advance rent payments, agency fees and disputes between landlords and tenants. A report also stated that the bill was still at the committee stage in the state assembly.

Funso Doherty of the Nigeria Democratic Congress (NDC) said the government needed to play a more direct role in providing affordable housing, arguing that private developers alone could not meet the needs of low- and middle-income residents.

“Private sector, you know, will not drive the number of units that are required to do this,” he said.

He proposed an ombudsman’s office to handle complaints about exploitative practices in the property market and cited the housing programme of former Governor Lateef Jakande as an example of government-led intervention.

Mr Doherty also accused the current administration of leaving too much responsibility for essential services, including housing, transport and healthcare, to private businesses.

Deji Doherty of the People Democratic Party (PDP) proposed that the government rent properties from landlords and sublet them to residents at affordable rates. He said government intervention was necessary because landlords could not be compelled to charge rents that ordinary workers could afford.

He also called for long-term leases and more low-cost housing, questioning how residents earning about N120,000 a month could afford accommodation in Lagos.

Flooding and the environment

The candidates also disagreed over the causes of flooding in Lagos and the measures needed to address it.

Mr Doherty blamed the problem partly on climate change and poor drainage management. He called for regular maintenance of drainage channels and proper water disposal, while urging residents to stop dumping refuse into drains. He acknowledged the government’s efforts to clear the channels.

The NDC candidate blamed poor environmental planning, particularly the destruction of wetlands, which he described as natural drainage systems that help absorb excess water during rainfall.

“Your wetlands are your natural absorptive mechanism in a city like Lagos. That’s what nature has provided for you to soak moisture when rains fall,” he said.

He accused the government of allowing buildings to spring up on drainage channels and flood-prone areas before moving to demolish them.

In October, the Lagos State Government warned that the destruction and reclamation of wetlands, floodplains and lagoon fronts could worsen flooding and coastal erosion.

Mr Dowarned of the NDC also questioned whether an environmental impact assessment had been conducted before construction began on the Lagos-Calabar Coastal Highway.

He said the Lagos State Government had a responsibility to protect residents from environmental risks, even though the federal government was executing the project.

Mr Hamzat rejected the criticism, saying an environmental impact assessment had been conducted for the coastal road alignment when he served as commissioner for works and infrastructure.

He attributed Lagos’s flooding problems to its low-lying geography, population density and increasing rainfall. He said rainfall had risen from 2.2 metres in the previous year to 2.7 metres in 2026, putting additional pressure on the drainage system.

He said Lagos had an extensive drainage network but stressed that its effectiveness depended on keeping the channels clear and allowing water to flow into the creeks and lagoon. He also defended the removal of buildings obstructing waterways.

Rhodes-Vivour called for a longer-term approach to flood management, suggesting that Lagos study how cities such as Venice and those in the Netherlands manage water and protect communities in low-lying areas.

He criticised the quality of road construction and poor maintenance, saying some newly constructed roads developed potholes after the next rainy season.

“You see a road is done newly. By next year, when the rainy season comes, it’s like you’re playing a computer game, dodging potholes on the road,” he said.

He also called for better weather forecasting and early-warning systems to help residents prepare for heavy rainfall. To protect wetlands, he proposed converting some into parks or solar farms to discourage indiscriminate reclamation.

Disagreement over coastal highway assessment

The disagreement over the Lagos-Calabar Coastal Highway centred on whether the environmental assessment conducted for the project covered the route currently under construction.

Mr Doherty of the NDC said information he obtained from the Bureau of Public Procurement showed that a due-process report indicated that an environmental impact assessment had not been presented when the project was submitted to the bureau.

He argued that an assessment conducted years earlier for a different alignment could not automatically be treated as the assessment for the current route.

However, a notice published by the Federal Ministry of Environment shows that a draft Environmental and Social Impact Assessment for Section One of the highway, covering the 0–47.5-kilometre stretch, was placed on public display on 27 August 2024 for public review and comments.

Mr Hamzat maintained that the federal government had the authority to execute the project and insisted that an assessment had been conducted for the alignment approved during his tenure as commissioner.

World.title: Major shakeup in Nigerian Air Force, 67 senior officers redeployed
World.content:
The Nigerian Air Force (NAF) has reshuffled 67 senior officers across its operational commands, military training institutions and strategic defence establishments in a major leadership realignment it says is aimed at strengthening its operational effectiveness and support for ongoing military campaigns against insurgency and other security threats.

The reshuffle includes the appointment of a new leader for Operation Hadin Kai, a joint task force fighting against Boko Haram and Islamic State West Africa Province (ISWAP) insurgents in Nigeria’s North-east. The air force has been a key agency in the fight against the insurgents, deploying air assets to support ground troops.

The Chief of the Air Staff (CAS), Kelvin Aneke, an air marshal, approved the appointments on 7 November, affecting key positions at NAF headquarters, operational commands, Defence Headquarters, and the Office of the National Security Adviser (ONSA), among other institutions.

In a statement on Sunday, the NAF spokesperson, Ehimen Ejodame, said the exercise was designed to align officers’ professional competencies and experience with the service’s evolving operational and institutional priorities.

He stated that all affected officers are expected to assume their new appointments and complete the necessary handover and takeover formalities by 13 November.

The affected officers all hold the rank of Air Vice Marshal (AVM).

At the NAF headquarters, Adeniran Ademuwagun was appointed chief of transformation and innovation, while Nnamdi Ananaba became chief of operations.

Stay Ahead with Premium Times 

Other appointments include Precious Amadi as chief of air intelligence, Enebong Efiom as chief of training, Ahmed Bakari as air provost marshal and John Laoye as chief of aircraft engineering.

Mohammed Ibrahim was appointed chairman, air expo and international liaison, while Adebayo Kehinde became chief of civil-military relations. Other appointments include MA Sulaiman as chief of communications and information systems and Simon Peters as coordinator, project implementation team.

New commanders for operational units

The reshuffle also affects the leadership of the NAF’s operational commands.

Nnaemeka Ilo was appointed air officer commanding, Tactical Air Command, while Bashir Mamman took over Mobility Command.

Olufemi Ogunsina became air officer commanding, Logistics Command, while Michael Onyebashi was appointed to head Special Operations Command. FCS Nwakara took over as air officer commanding, Ground Training Command.

John Ukeh was also appointed commander of the Nigerian Air Defence Corps (NADC).

Additionally, Garba Jibia was appointed deputy force commander of Operation Hadin Kai.

Defence Headquarters, intelligence appointments

Several officers were also deployed to strategic positions at Defence Headquarters and other national security institutions.

Usman Abdullahi was appointed director of defence operations at Defence Headquarters, while Elijah Ebiowe moved to the ONSA as deputy coordinator, national intelligence.

Other appointments include Idi Sani as deputy chief of defence intelligence and David Pwajok as director of technical services at the Defence Intelligence Agency (DIA).

At the Defence Headquarters, ZA Usman took over as director of cyber operations, while Edward Gabkwet was appointed director of civil-military relations.

Other appointments include Ahmed Shinkafi as director of liaison, Alfred Shogbamu as director of military strategy, Rasaq Olanrewaju as director of search and rescue, J Usman as director of special duties and John Ijudigal as director of sports.

At the Defence Space Administration, Abubakar Suleh was appointed deputy chief, while OA Oyename and Solomon Lazarus became directors of earth observation and launch vehicles and space operations, respectively.

OT Salami was posted to the Defence Space Command Centre as deputy chief, while AI Hanidu became director of integrated air power studies at the Air Power Centre of Excellence.

Military training institutions get new heads

The leadership changes also extend to military training and professional development institutions.

PB Philips was appointed commandant of the Armed Forces Command and Staff College, while MC Ekwueme became commandant of the Armed Forces Resettlement Centre.

AO Akinbunwa was appointed commandant of the Air Force War College, while A Idris became commandant of the Air Warfare Doctrine Centre.

Other appointments include JA Ekwuribe as commandant of the Regiment Training Centre, OC Ubadike as commandant of the Air Force Institute of Technology and AI Sambo as commandant of the Nigerian Air Force College of Logistics and Management.

M Yusuf was appointed deputy commandant of the Nigerian Defence Academy (NDA), Kaduna State.

The NAF also announced changes across its other commands and strategic establishments, including the appointment of AY Dari as general manager of the Nigerian Air Force Investment Limited Group of Companies and NS Okoro as director general of the Air Force Research and Development Institute.

CE Akubue was appointed managing director of Aircraft Engineering and Technical Services Limited, while CE Akpa became commander of Headquarters NAF Camp.

Other appointments include SA Eyoma as deputy commandant of the Air Force Institute of Technology, FO Ankeli as commandant of the Air Traffic Services Training Centre and U Ariahu as deputy commandant of the Nigerian Air Force College of Logistics and Management.

NAF said the realignment demonstrated its commitment to leadership renewal, institutional accountability and improved operational effectiveness.

The CAS, Mr Aneke, expressed confidence that the newly appointed officers would advance his command philosophy and strengthen the air force’s capacity to deliver decisive airpower in support of joint military operations and national security objectives.

World.title: 2027: PDP factional chairman accuses judiciary of favouring APC against opposition
World.content:
Kabiru Turaki, factional chairman of the Peoples Democratic Party (PDP), has accused President Bola Tinubu and the ruling All Progressives Congress (APC) of influencing the judiciary to make pronouncements on disputes involving opposition parties in ways that destabilise them and favour the government.

Mr Turaki, a former minister of Special Duties and Inter-Governmental Affairs, said court judgments against opposition parties were often delivered in a “brazen and shameless manner” to favour factions whose members support the ruling party.

He referenced the recognition of the Nyesom Wike-backed PDP faction, led by Abdulrahman Mohammed, as the authentic leadership of the party. The faction is now backing the Rainbow Coalition being promoted by Mr Wike, a member of the party but serving as minister of the Federal Capital Territory (FCT), to campaign for Mr Tinubu’s re-election in 2027.

Mr Turaki made the allegations at a press briefing in Abuja on Sunday.

“Another trick from the APC playbook is the judicialisation of politics, wherein the courts are used to erect hurdles on the path of the opposition and to remove the institutionalised uncertainty that a keenly contested election generates. How else can one explain the numerous cases and judgments that led to the derecognition, deregistration and destabilisation of opposition parties?

“All opposition parties have had their share of this anomaly, where the judiciary is used to answer political questions, in a way and manner that favours the ruling party. This is done in a brazen and shameless manner that the beneficiaries in the opposition are known supporters of the governing APC, championing an anti-democratic coven called Rainbow Coalition,” he said.

Mr Turaki warned that the alleged actions could undermine Nigeria’s democracy and pave the way for authoritarian rule.

Stay Ahead with Premium Times 

“Today, the governing party, the All Progressives Congress, and the Presidency, led by a pseudo-democrat, are speeding down the infamous lane that leads to democratic destruction: the lanes of constriction of the political space, violence against the opposition, the ‘buying’ and co-optation of opposition leaders, and the judicialisation of politics.

“History, both local and foreign, has shown that these lanes lead to only one destination: the death of democracy and the birth of full authoritarian rule, which subjugates the people and destroys the nation,” he added.

The factional chairman urged the president to desist from allegedly influencing the judiciary and allow voters to freely choose their leaders without intimidation.

“Nigerians should be allowed to freely choose their leaders at all levels, not the current situation where public officials threaten voters to leave their jurisdictions if they do not vote for the APC. This threat has been widespread across the country, and some have now made their threats real by unleashing violence against the opposition,” he said.

The Court of Appeal, in a unanimous judgement delivered last Wednesday, upheld the earlier decision of the Federal High Court dismissing a suit challenging the leadership of the Wike-backed faction of the PDP, chaired by Mr Mohammed.

The appeal was filed by the PDP Board of Trustees (BoT), led by former Senate President Adolphus Wabara, which sought to compel the Independent National Electoral Commission (INEC) to recognise the interim National Working Committee (NWC) led by Mr Turaki.

The appellants had argued that the committee emerged from a National Executive Committee meeting convened after an earlier Supreme Court judgement on the party’s leadership crisis. However, the appellate court upheld the lower court’s dismissal of their suit.

Mr Turaki’s faction has indicated that it is considering approaching the Supreme Court to challenge the latest Court of Appeal decision.

The PDP’s legal battle comes amid a similar crisis in the African Democratic Congress (ADC), where a Federal High Court in Abuja, on 5 November, nullified its NWC led by a former Senate President, David Mark, and invalidated decisions taken by the faction.

Peter Lifu, the judge, who delivered the judgment, held that the Mark-led NWC, which organised the party’s presidential primary that produced former Vice-President Atiku Abubakar as its candidate for the 2027 presidential election, was illegally constituted.

The suit was instituted by Nafiu Bala Gombe, a former deputy national chairman of the ADC, who challenged the process through which Mr Mark and other members assumed the party’s leadership. He argued that following the resignation of the party’s former National Chairman, Ralph Nwosu, he was constitutionally entitled to take over its leadership.

The court granted the plaintiff’s prayers, sacked the party’s national officers under the Mark-led leadership and invalidated the nomination of candidates presented by the faction to INEC for the 2027 elections.

The judgment also directed INEC not to recognise decisions taken at the party’s 99th National Executive Committee meeting of 27 July 2025 and subsequent actions, including the nomination of candidates.

The decision, however, does not mean that the ADC itself has been deregistered or outlawed. Rather, it invalidates the leadership structure that produced its candidates, including Atiku, and places the party’s participation in the 2027 elections in serious legal uncertainty pending the outcome of an appeal.

The development is particularly significant because the ADC has become a coalition platform for prominent opposition figures seeking to challenge President Bola Tinubu and the APC in 2027. The party has indicated that it will challenge the judgement at the appellate courts.

Tactics weakening opposition parties

Mr Turaki also accused the president and the APC of using various tactics to weaken opposition parties ahead of the 2027 elections.

“This is a very ugly development that undermines democratic consolidation and paves the way for the enthronement of authoritarian rule. It is evident that President Tinubu and the APC are not ready for competitive elections, which is why they are deploying every tactic, in and out of the book, to ground any credible opposition party,” he added.

He urged President Tinubu to reconsider his approach, warning that he could not force himself on Nigerians in the 2027 elections.

“We draw the attention of the president, his handlers, INEC and the security agencies to the fact that they can foist a result on the people, but they cannot compel the country to legitimise their act. As we have said before, and it bears repeating here, there are two elections coming up: the first for the heart of the country, and the second for the office of the President.
