World.title: Gov. Josh Shapiro urges Democrats to prioritize healthcare, food assistance
World.content:
Pennsylvania Gov. Josh Shapiro said he hopes Democrats prioritize healthcare and food assistance when they take control of Congress in January, though he urged them not to forget to hold the Trump administration accountable.

“I hope one of the first things that the Congress does is to stop these Medicaid cuts, stop the SNAP cuts, roll back the cuts, the effective cuts in the Affordable Care Act,” Shapiro said in an interview with NBC News’ “Meet the Press” that aired Sunday.

Shapiro said that in Pennsylvania alone, 510,000 people are losing healthcare and 143,000 more are losing SNAP or food assistance because of cuts approved during President Donald Trump’s second term.

“In general, though, I think Democrats need to have an aggressive agenda that cuts costs, that ends the war, that gets put on the president’s desk,” he said. “Hopefully, he will sign it, because it’ll be commonsense stuff that makes people’s lives better.”

Trump has said he intends to work with Democrats when Congress begins its new term, though he has also touted a new “VETO”-branded hat since Republicans lost the majority in the midterm elections.

Shapiro said that if Trump chooses to veto Democrats’ legislation, “it’s yet another signal to the American people the president actually doesn’t care about their well-being.”

While he stressed the importance of revitalizing Medicaid and SNAP programs, Shapiro also said Democrats shouldn’t forget to hold the Trump administration accountable.

“I think the Congress needs to be responsive to where voters are on corruption, and there has to be real accountability for this administration,” he said, adding that Democrats need to “walk and chew gum at the same time” to pass effective legislation and “have real accountability for the corruption that exists in Washington.”

“It can’t be either/or,” he said. “It has to be both/and.”

Shapiro said Rep. Hakeem Jeffries, D-N.Y., who is poised to become the next speaker of the House, “has made very clear that both are going to be on the agenda for the first 100 days and for these next two years.”

He said he doesn’t think Democrats should be thinking about the 2028 elections yet. Instead, “we should be thinking about how to make people’s lives better in 2027,” he said.

“It’s incumbent upon the Congress to now do that, and it’s incumbent upon governors now to continue to lead the way in our states,” Shapiro said.

Shapiro, who has been floated as a potential 2028 presidential contender, didn’t commit to running.

Asked whether he is likelier to run than not, Shapiro answered that his focus is on “figuring how we advance policies like raising the minimum wage and many other things that have been blocked by Republicans,” as Pennsylvania Democrats won a majority in the state Legislature on Tuesday.

He also didn’t directly answer whether he was committed to serving his full four-year term.

“Well, I committed to run for governor, and that’s the work I’m focused on doing,” Shapiro said. “And if I’ve got something to say about my future, I’d love to come back on your show and talk about it.”

World.title: House Minority Leader Hakeem Jeffries says he is a ‘hard yes’ on impeaching Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth
World.content:
House Minority Leader Hakeem Jeffries, D-N.Y., said he is a “hard yes” on supporting impeachment efforts against Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth, which are expected to be brought to a vote this week.

Asked in an interview on ABC’s “This Week” whether he would support Rep. Thomas Massie, R-Ky., in his efforts to impeach Hegseth, Jeffries confirmed he supported the push.

“I’m a hard yes on the Hegseth resolution,” Jeffries said. “The so-called secretary of defense has abused his power, undermined our national security and engineered this reckless and costly war of choice in Iran, which has skyrocketed prices on the American people and made the country less safe.”

“Pete Hegseth has got to go,” he added.

Jeffries’ support marks a major endorsement of impeachment efforts against Hegseth and signals how other House Democrats could ultimately vote on the measure. The impeachment push also tests how far lawmakers are willing to go to oust the top Pentagon official after voters have given low marks to the administration’s handling of the war in Iran, which factored into midterms.

Asked on ABC whether Jeffries believed all other House Democrats would support the impeachment resolution, he said that they would “have that conversation Tuesday morning.” The House is back in session this week, and the impeachment resolution is expected to be filed early this week with a vote to follow.

Massie has been a vocal critic of Hegseth and the war in Iran. He previously filed a resolution to impeach Hegseth in September, but Republican leaders canceled planned votes and the House left early, pushing the vote to after the election.

NBC News reported last week that President Donald Trump has told allies that he was considering replacing Hegseth. Trump, though, has publicly denied that he is planning to replace the secretary, telling reporters last week that Hegseth was “doing a very good job.”

At the same time, Hegseth has forcefully pushed back on Massie’s impeachment plans, referring to the congressman in a social media video last week as a “disgruntled, defeated congressman.”

“It’s all about the politics of personal destruction,” Hegseth said in the video. “Didn’t work against President Trump, and it won’t work with me. You can rest assured of that.”

Massie, though, said in a social media post last week that his “Hegseth impeachment resolution is a much gentler version of what’s coming when Dem’s control Congress.” Democrats, Massie said, would “have hearings & trials.”

World.title: Nvidia opens investigation after reports CEO Jensen Huang was targeted by Chinese intelligence
World.content:
Nvidia’s board of directors said Sunday that it is opening an independent investigation following reports that CEO Jensen Huang was targeted by a foreign intelligence effort.

The announcement followed reporting by The New York Times and the Financial Times about Huang’s relationship with Alice Huang, a Chinese businesswoman who the newspapers reported had been recruited to spy for China. The two are not related.

NBC News has not confirmed either report, and it has asked the Trump administration for comment.

“The NVIDIA Board is initiating an independent investigation in light of recent reporting that founder and CEO Jensen Huang has been the target of a foreign intelligence effort,” the company said in a statement.

“A committee of independent directors, assisted by outside independent counsel, will oversee the investigation. The Board prioritizes U.S. national and economic security, which is paramount to the interests of NVIDIA and its shareholders.”

The company added that while it “has no reason to believe that either national security or NVIDIA secrets were compromised, the Board’s inquiry will examine all available information.”

In a memo to Nvidia employees that the company shared with NBC News, Huang said: “I was unfaithful to my wife. My actions hurt her and our children. There is no excuse for what I did.”

The New York Times and the Financial Times reported that Alice Huang, a Chinese citizen whose Singapore-based company was buying Nvidia’s advanced chips, had been under surveillance by U.S. intelligence agencies. Those agencies, the reports said, found that she had been recruited to spy by China’s top intelligence agency.

Jensen Huang and Nvidia, for years, have been at the forefront of the artificial intelligence boom. Nvidia’s products are the most highly sought-after chips in the world; however its top-tier products are mostly restricted from being sold to customers in China because of national security fears.

China has long sought to become a global leader in AI. President Xi Jinping set a 2030 deadline to surpass the capabilities of American AI systems.

Huang, 63, essentially serves as an ambassador for the industry, regularly appearing alongside the likes of President Donald Trump and King Charles III of Great Britain and at conferences to tout his company and what he says will be immense payoff in the future from AI.

In October, Trump awarded Huang the National Medal of Science, one of the nation’s highest honors for achievement in science and technology.

Nvidia is the world’s second-largest publicly traded company as of Friday, worth nearly $4.5 trillion. That’s up more than 500% over the last five years.

Huang’s wealth has also ballooned as he has led the company. His net worth has soared from around $25 billion at the start of 2022 to almost $160 billion, making him the world’s 10th-richest person, according to the Bloomberg Billionaires Index.

In the latest series of reports, published Sunday afternoon, The New York Times reported that concerns inside the U.S. government about Alice Huang and Jensen Huang rose as high as Secretary of State Marco Rubio.

Speaking Sunday to reporters in Florida shortly after Nvidia’s announcement, Rubio said, “I just can’t comment because of the nature of it, and I also can’t comment on an internal corporate matter that’s going on with Nvidia.”

On Friday, the FT reported that the U.S. government believed Jensen Huang had a romantic relationship with Alice Huang. In response to the article, the FT reported that Nvidia declined to comment and said Jensen Huang meets “thousands of customer executives every year,” as any CEO normally does.

Huang previously defended his interactions with Alice Huang, describing them as business-related in a recent statement: “Our relationship, our interactions, have been related to Megaspeed, and it was all completely normal and not unusual.”

In Sunday’s memo, Huang wrote: “To my wife and family: I love you. I know an apology cannot undo what I have done. I hope our family will heal and that, over time, I can earn back your trust.”

The email to employees continued: “To my colleagues at NVIDIA, including those I have worked alongside for decades, and to our board, partners, and shareholders around the world: you deserve better from me. Leading NVIDIA is the privilege of my life. My responsibility is to serve you and be worthy of your trust. I have fallen short of that responsibility. I am fully committed to NVIDIA and will work to earn back your confidence.”

A spokesperson for Nvidia told NBC News that “today’s news will not slow” the company and that Huang is “committed to continuing to lead NVIDIA as CEO without interruption.”

Before Sunday’s announcement, Nvidia and Huang were already facing congressional scrutiny over the reports about Megaspeed and its executive. On Thursday, top House Republicans requested a briefing from Huang about the reports.

“Recent reports raise significant national security concerns regarding the PRC’s access to sensitive U.S. technology and information,” said Rep. John Moolenaar, R-Mich., who is also chairman of the House Select Committee on China. “PRC” is shorthand for the People’s Republic of China.

“It is vital that Congress determines the extent to which U.S. national security has been placed at risk,” a letter to Nvidia read.

World.title: Tensions rise in Philadelphia over boycott of Jewish-owned restaurants
World.content:
A bike ride organized to promote a boycott of several Jewish-owned restaurants drew opposing demonstrators to Philadelphia on Sunday, with people waving Palestinian and Israeli flags exchanging heated words.

NBC Philadelphia witnessed several verbal confrontations between the groups in the city’s Rittenhouse Square.

A line of Philadelphia police officers worked to keep the groups separated as tensions continued to build before the bike ride had even begun.

Three people were arrested Sunday, according to a spokesperson for the Philadelphia Police Department, as approximately 300 pro-Palestinian protesters clashed with roughly 200 pro-Israeli counter-protesters.

One adult woman was arrested for assault, one adult man for disorderly conduct and one 17-year-old teenage boy for assault on police, according to the spokesperson.

Meanwhile, some of the restaurants targeted by the boycott were seeing long lines of customers supporting.

By early afternoon, all demonstrators had dispersed, police said, with no property damage reported.

The protest was organized by Philly Bike On Your Left, a group that describes itself as an “anti-fascist, anti-Zionist social cycling collective.”

Philadelphia police officers attempted to separate the groups on Sunday. WCAU

On Oct. 31, the group announced plans to boycott what it called “Zionist establishments” in Rittenhouse Square in solidarity with the Palestinian community.

The restaurants named in the boycott include Mac Mart, K’Far Café, Huda, Goldie, Schlesinger’s and Dizengoff.

Half of the establishments targeted are owned by Philadelphia restaurant group CookNSolo, whose Israeli co-owners have publicly supported and fundraised for Israel’s military efforts.

The restaurant group has already been the target of a local “Boycott CookNSolo” campaign that says it protests the restaurateurs for “materially and ideologically support[ing] the ongoing occupation and genocide of Palestinians.”

“We stand with the organizers of the Boycott Ride, a small group of bicyclists against genocide who have been doxxed and villainized by social media Zionists and self-serving politicians,” Boycott CookNSolo wrote in an Instagram post this weekend.

On Sunday, a group of protesters holding a “Boycott CookNSolo” banner was seen marching in the city while raising a Palestinian flag, according to footage shared on the public safety app Citizen. In it, a counter-protester appeared to walk in front of the group carrying a large Israeli flag.

The planned boycott ride by Philly Bike On Your Left drew widespread criticism, including from Philadelphia Mayor Cherelle Parker and Pennsylvania Attorney General Dave Sunday, who condemned the boycott on social media.

The Anti-Defamation League also encouraged people to show their support by dining at the targeted restaurants and other Jewish-owned businesses.

“This protest is an attempt to intimidate a Jewish community that has faced generations of violence, exclusion and antisemitism. It’s the latest in a string of incidents that hold Jewish businesses responsible for events in the Middle East,” the ADL wrote. “That’s antisemitic, plain and simple. But we refuse to let hate win.”

Billboards urge Philadelphians to ‘boycott the boycott’

In response to the planned ride, nonprofit organization JewBelong installed billboards at 14 locations across Philadelphia urging people to support Jewish-owned businesses.

The billboards read, “Running over Jewish businesses isn’t a peace plan,” and encourage residents to “boycott the boycott ride.”

At least one person was arrested amid the crowd in Rittenhouse Square. WCAU

The demonstration also falls on the eve of the anniversary of Kristallnacht, or the “Night of Broken Glass,” when Nazi-organized antisemitic attacks targeted Jewish communities in Germany, Austria and Sudetenland on Nov. 9 and 10, 1938.

In a statement posted to Instagram, Philly Bike On Your Left said the ride had been “grossly misrepresented.”

“We stand firmly against racism and oppression of all forms, including fascism, antisemitism, islamophobia and colonialism.”

It added that the ride was planned “around people’s schedules” and that any implications “about the timing of our ride are simply false.”

“There are business owners in our community who have raised funds for the Israeli military, hosted Israeli soldiers, were praised by Benjamin Netanyahu, or expressed support for Israel,” the organization wrote. “How we spend our money is a reflection of our values.”

Ahead of the bike ride, Governor Josh Shapiro on Friday joined in on the condemnations.

“Hate and antisemitism have no place in our Commonwealth,” Shapiro wrote on X. “And I’m grateful to state and local law enforcement who will work to make sure our neighborhoods remain safe this weekend.”

After the demonstration on Sunday, Mac Mart’s owner Marti Lieberman wrote in an email that although she did spot some protesters, the group eventually moved on without direct confrontation. She added that local customers, supporters and police officers “shielded us from the commotion.”

“We were truly overwhelmed by the wonderful crowd of people who came out to line up and show their support at our shop throughout the entire day—it was absolutely amazing!” Lieberman said. “We are so deeply grateful for all the love and strength we’ve received from our community.”

World.title: We want to hear your experience with changes to student loan repayment plans
World.content:
President Donald Trump’s “big, beautiful bill” has transformed the sprawling federal student loan system — and student borrowers are feeling the effects of the most consequential changes.

This year, the approximately 7.5 million student borrowers under the Biden-era Saving on a Valuable Education, or SAVE, plan had to select a new one. So far, about 2 million borrowers have done so, after the Education Department warned that the SAVE plan was “illegal” and would be discontinued. The remaining borrowers who did not select a new plan were set to start receiving notices this month informing them that they missed a final deadline and were automatically moved to a new plan.

The Trump administration has said ending the SAVE plan would help streamline repayment programs while ensuring borrowers are paying off what they owe to the federal government. But student advocacy groups fear lower-income borrowers who had benefited from smaller monthly payments — or even qualified to make no payments at all based on their income — will end up with significantly higher bills under the other available plans.

We want to hear from you, whether you’re in this situation or are facing another challenge related to the recent student loan changes. Please share your experience by filling out the form below.

World.title: The human touch: Luxury brands embrace craftsmanship as ‘AI slop’ floods the internet
World.content:
The sound of pencil putting lines to paper. The geometric shapes of a cartoon animal before it comes to life on the page.

Those were the opening shots of a teaser for Prada’s 2026 holiday campaign, which introduced a series of films made “using the anachronistic craft of hand-drawn animation,” working with longtime Disney animator John Pomeroy.

“I learned my craft with pencil and paper, old-school analog drawing with pencil and paper,” Pomeroy, who left Disney in 2003, says in the teaser video.

It’s that kind of skill that some artists say has become a greater asset than ever. In the age of widespread and accessible AI, artists say they’ve noticed more brands leaning into handcrafted art as a selling point.

In recent weeks, the luxury fashion houses Prada and Hermès touted their human-made art projects in social media campaigns — even tagging the artists behind the work to showcase their authenticity.

A still from the Prada Holiday 2026 campaign. Glen Luchford for PRADA

Alina Golovlova, a stop-motion artist in Prague, said that recently, she has felt that her work is actually “appreciated more than in previous years” as brands try to separate themselves from the AI content flooding the internet.

“In previous years, I felt like I was just some hired content creator. No one really cared to tag me or make a [collaborative post],” Golovlova said. “And I think now for brands, it becomes valuable to bring the artists together with the brand to show that they are working with real people.”

Golovlova directed a short film for Anthropologie last month, featuring a needle-felted bunny, embroidered stars and stop-motion movements — all designed and put together entirely by hand by a team of artists.

And the choice proved to be an effective marketing strategy, as support rolled in from commenters online.

“Beautiful! Love the creativity and seeing something human made and NOT AI 👏❤️,” a user wrote on Anthropologie’s post, accruing thousands of likes.

“AI = Broke, cheap, lazy,” another user posted in response to Prada’s campaign. “Art from human hands = High-end, luxurious, high quality.”

Animator Jon Densk, who worked on the hand-drawn Prada campaign under Pomeroy, said that while he suspects AI still has a way to go before it can be used successfully in animation, he has seen signs of it in commercials. Coca-Cola, he said, comes to mind as a major company that has leaned into AI for its s.

“After the first one I saw two years ago, I was like, I’m not buying Coke until they stop it. I still haven’t bought a Coke in two years,” Densk said. “So having a stance against [AI], I think, is a smart move for brands.”

Coca-Cola’s use of AI stirred some controversy, as attitudes about the technology remain divided over labor and environmental concerns, as well as fatigue over the swath of mass-produced content commonly described as “AI slop.”

Still, Densk said he wasn’t expecting the explosion of support that Prada’s hand-drawn campaign would attract online.

“I think people that see people like us who are still drawing things, and even people working in CG animation, as true craftsmen, because that stuff really does take hours and hours and hours of practicing to get to a proficient level,” Densk said.

World.title: OC fishermen find cruise ship employee treading water miles off coast
World.content:
Two Newport Beach fishermen found a Royal Caribbean cruise ship employee treading water nearly 20 miles off the coast while returning home from a fishing trip near Catalina Island on Friday.

Sean Norton and Grant Garrett were fishing for marlin in the morning. By noon, they had rescued the man who had been treading water nearly 20 miles off the coast in the middle of the Pacific Ocean.

"I'm like, 'Yeah, it's a human being. Stop the boat; let's get all of our lines in," Garrett said, recalling the moment the boat's captain spotted the man in the water.

"Grant and I each got an arm and lifted him up," Norton said. "He was in total shock."

Garrett said when the man came to, he told them he was a pianist on the 14-deck Royal Caribbean cruise ship called the "Ovation of the Seas."

"The only thing he said to me was, 'Thank you. I thought I was gonna die,'" Norton said.

After pulling him from the water, the crew put out an emergency maritime call, and a group of Newport Beach lifeguards responded to help.

"It was approximately 15 to 20 miles offshore, pretty much in the middle of the ocean," Battalion Chief Adam Yacenda said. They believe he may have gone overboard from the ship about nine hours before he was found, at around 2:30 a.m.

The man, who still hasn't been identified, was hospitalized after the ordeal and is expected to survive, according to the U.S. Coast Guard, which is investigating the incident and how he went overboard.

"You have this crazy super El Niño year. This guy was in the water for probably 10 hours, but the water's 76 degrees," Norton said. "A different year, no way he makes it."

In a statement to CBS LA, a Royal Caribbean Group spokesperson shared, "We are providing support and assistance to our crew member during this difficult time. To respect the privacy of our employee, we have no additional details to share."

World.title: Nvidia investigates CEO Jensen Huang over Chinese espionage concerns
World.content:
Nvidia has launched an independent investigation of its co-founder and CEO, Jensen Huang, over allegations that he was the target of an intelligence effort by China.

"The NVIDIA Board is initiating an independent investigation in light of recent reporting that founder and CEO Jensen Huang has been the target of a foreign intelligence effort," Nvidia's board of directors said in a statement Sunday. "A committee of independent directors, assisted by outside independent counsel, will oversee the investigation."

The board said it had no reason to believe that the company's secrets or national security were compromised.

"The Board prioritizes U.S. national and economic security, which is paramount to the interests of NVIDIA and its shareholders," the statement said.

A company spokesperson said Huang "fully supports the review" and is committed to continuing to lead the company.

The New York Times reported last month that U.S. authorities were investigating Chinese businesswoman Alice Huang, a former executive of the Singapore-based Megaspeed, which buys AI chips from Nvidia. The report claims Jensen Huang had a close relationship with Alice Huang, who U.S. intelligence officials believe was a spy for China's Ministry of State Security.

Last month, China rejected allegations of a Chinese espionage operation targeting Jensen Huang, describing the claims as "groundless speculation," CBS News partner BBC News reported.

Separately, in a message to employees, Jensen Huang admitted to being "unfaithful" to his wife and apologized for hurting her and their children.

"There is no excuse for what I did. I am deeply sorry," he said in a statement.

Jensen Huang said he had fallen short of his responsibilities to the company's employees, board and shareholders. He said he is "fully committed to NVIDIA" and will work to earn back their trust.

"Regarding the national security concerns raised in news reports, NVIDIA's Board of Directors has initiated an independent investigation," he said in a statement. "I support the investigation and will cooperate fully."

"I love our country and our company. I am committed to protecting NVIDIA and supporting America's national security. I am proud and grateful to be an American," he added.

Alice Huang was previously a television reporter in China before becoming a top executive at Singapore-based data center company Megaspeed, which has become one of Nvidia's biggest customers in Southeast Asia. Megaspeed bought more than $4.8 billion worth of Nvidia chips over the past two years, according to the Times.

Asked about the report on Sunday, Secretary of State Marco Rubio said he couldn't comment, saying it was an "internal corporate matter."

Nvidia, the world's most valuable company, has regularly surpassed Wall Street's earnings expectations in the past three years since its high-end chips emerged as AI's best building blocks. The Santa Clara, California-based company reported quarterly profits of $59.69 billion in August.

World.title: New House members on their top priorities: "Cannot be afraid to do big things"
World.content:
Newly elected House members arrived in Washington on Sunday for orientation, and freshman lawmakers on both sides of the aisle say they want to focus on lowering the cost of living for Americans following the seismic midterm election that shifted control of both chambers to the Democrats.

CBS News spoke with several Democratic representatives-elect who say their priority is making life affordable for the American people, but they also plan to hold the Trump administration accountable.

"We can walk and chew gum, but lowering people's cost of living is the most important," said Scott Wiener, who was elected to succeed Nancy Pelosi in California's 11th Congressional District.

As for House Republicans who have suddenly found themselves a minority despite a historic effort to redraw several states' congressional districts in their favor, they say the party has to figure out a way forward.

"There was a message sent last Tuesday night, and I hope, as a new member, I can be on the ground level of figuring out how we can reconnect and better message to the needs of the American people," GOP Rep.-elect Chris Stigall of Missouri's 6th Congressional District said Sunday.

Newly elected House members on affordability

Adrian Boafo, the Democratic Rep.-elect for Maryland's 5th Congressional District, said Sunday that the question for the House caucus is "what's the affordability agenda going to look like?"

Boafo said his focus will be on federal workers in his district.

"Federal workers are extraordinarily important ... 85,000 federal workers in my district, 30,000 in the state who have been laid off. I mean, so federal workers is probably the number one, two and three priority for me," he said.

For Connecticut's 1st Congressional District, Democrat Luke Bronin said Democrats "cannot be afraid to do big things."

"I think as a Democratic Party, we have to bring a whole new energy to this fight," Bronin told CBS News on Sunday. "You know, when things are deeply broken, like healthcare or the housing market, or electricity prices going through the roof, we cannot be afraid to offer bold answers and be courageous about pushing through. And I want to see us go on offense.

"At the same time, I think we do have to be serious about oversight and accountability. The type of corruption we're seeing right now is unlike anything we've seen in our history, and the American people just made pretty clear that they're disgusted by it and they want to see an end to it," he added.

GOP Rep.-elect Charlie Hatcher of Tennessee's 5th Congressional District — who defeated Andy Ogles in the primary after Ogles sparked backlash for saying "Muslims don't belong in American society" on social media — said he wants to focus on diesel prices.

"Price of diesel fuel is affecting most everybody, especially farmers. And I'm a farmer, and that's one of my top issues as well," Hatcher said. "So it's a price of fuel that's affecting everything all the way down the line. Transportation, logistics, groceries ... It's all connected to that."

GOP House members on working with Democrats

With Democrats flipping more than three dozen Republican-held seats, ranging from suburban areas in the northeastern United States to areas of South Texas that were once viewed as increasingly GOP-friendly, new Republican House members say they have to work with Democratic colleagues to get things done for constituents.

"I think first and foremost we have to recognize that my party is now in a significant minority," said Chris McGowan, GOP rep.-elect for Iowa's 4th Congressional District. "So we're going to have to work very, very hard to meet the new legislators representing the Democratic Party and where we can collaborate, cooperate, communicate on issues of shared interest, we certainly look forward to doing so."

Rep.-elect Jon Bonck of Texas' 38th Congressional District told CBS News on Sunday that he's also willing to work on bipartisanship.

"If it's fixing housing affordability, deregulating industries, or getting the government out of healthcare, I'd love to meet Democrats that will do those kinds of things — cut taxes, give more money back to people," Bonck said.

Progressive Caucus on its priorities

The Congressional Progressive Caucus held an introductory press briefing on Sunday with the new members-elect who will join the progressive group.

Rep. Greg Casar, the chair of the Caucus, announced the Caucus is welcoming at least 25 new members, "the largest class of progressive members." Casar also said that, with a big majority, the Democrats will deliver on promises they have "failed" to keep in the past.

"In the past, Democrats, with a narrow majority, have failed to pass Social Security expansion or taxing billionaires because special interests have been able to peel off just one or two members," he said.

Rep. Pramila Jayapal, Chair Emerita, further explained the Caucus' priorities: "Taking on corruption, taking on affordability, making sure we end endless wars."

World.title: Former RFK Jr. adviser accuses Trump officials of corruption
World.content:
The full transcript of Margaret Brennan's interview with Calley Means is available on cbsnews.com.

A former senior White House adviser and top aide to Health and Human Services Secretary Robert F. Kennedy Jr. is accusing several Trump administration officials, including the recently resigned White House chief of staff Susie Wiles, of prioritizing industry interests over the health of voters as part of the White House's midterm elections strategy.

"Underneath Trump's nose, in many cases, you had a group of former lobbyists, catering to the vaping industry, catering to the ultra-processed food industry, catering to the pharmaceutical industry, catering to the pesticide industry and doing their bidding with an excuse that we need their money for the midterms and really need to actually go against what voters said," Calley Means told "Face the Nation" moderator Margaret Brennan in an interview that aired Sunday.

Means helped found the "Make America Healthy Again" movement and helped form the winning alliance between Mr. Trump and Kennedy in 2024 before serving as Kennedy's top aide. Means helped lead the Department of Health and Human Services' efforts to revise the country's dietary guidelines and remove soda and candy from SNAP benefits before resigning last month.

He told CBS News that Wiles and "a very close-knit crew" of other White House advisers "were taking money from the industries we ran on fighting against."

Means went public Friday with very specific allegations of corruption against Wiles and a call for President Trump to "clear his house" in an interview he taped Thursday for "The Joe Rogan Experience" podcast.

He claimed Wiles and her deputy, James Blair, relentlessly pushed HHS to find a pathway to approve fruit-flavored vapes. In early May, the Food and Drug Administration approved some fruit-flavored e-cigarettes.

Blair denied Means' characterization of his role in the vape debate in a statement to CBS News.

"I didn't promote flavored vaping specifically at all," Blair said. "I was tasked with driving FDA to make its process for approving or denying nicotine delivery device applications work the way current federal law dictates it works, which is that applicants get a yes or no answer on approval in six months. Calley is intentionally misrepresenting my role and my responsibility because he opposes the issue entirely. Even though the president himself has made his position on smoking and smoking alternatives known very publicly and has provided clear direction. Calley just doesn't like it."

Two sources familiar with the process told CBS News that Blair was tasked by Mr. Trump with driving then-FDA Commissioner Dr. Marty Makary to more quickly respond to applications from the nicotine industry, but also acknowledged that the president sought to make flavored vapes more available.

As a 2024 presidential candidate, Mr. Trump vowed to "save" vaping and mentioned his past efforts on behalf of flavored vaping during his first administration, which he said in a social media post was intended to get people off smoking. Mr. Trump won backing from e-cigarette companies, shop owners and vaping enthusiasts.

In May, Makary was pressed to resign his post as FDA commissioner amid reports that he had been pressured by the White House to approve the fruit-flavored vapes.

"Big tobacco exploited their connections to administration and HHS officials to put repeated pressure on me to approve fruit-flavored vapes that appeal to children—I wouldn't do it," Makary said in a statement to CBS News. "The Kratom/7-OH lobby ran the same playbook to undermine my efforts to make this new 'gas station heroin' illegal. As FDA commissioner, I always rejected political corruption just as voters across the political spectrum did last week."

Multiple sources confirmed to CBS News the New York Times' reporting in May that tobacco lobbyists had been at the president's Florida golf course with him at lunch and pushed him on the way e-cigarettes were being regulated by the FDA. Means claimed Wiles set up the meeting.

Wiles submitted her resignation to Mr. Trump on Thursday night, a U.S. official and a senior White House adviser told CBS News. Her resignation was tied to Republicans' midterm defeats, according to three sources familiar with the matter. The departure became public shortly after Mr. Trump taped an interview with 60 Minutes midday Friday.

When asked if it was his intention to get Wiles removed from her position, Means responded, "Yes. I think President Trump has been subverted by people that are beholden to special interests and not what President Trump ran on, and what voters voted for." It is not clear at this time whether the public remarks factored into the president's decision to expedite Wiles' departure.

In a statement to CBS News, Wiles denied Means' allegations that she arranged for tobacco industry representatives to meet with the president at his golf course to discuss vape policy.

Earlier this year, Mr. Trump signed an executive order to boost production of glyphosate, a herbicide that is included in the weedkiller Roundup and which has been found to be linked to cancer. WHO has deemed glyphosate to be "probably carcinogenic to humans."

For decades as a private attorney, Kennedy had spearheaded a legal challenge to the chemical giant Monsanto for its use of the herbicide. In a statement on social media at the time of the president's order, Kennedy said: "Our agricultural system depends heavily on these chemicals."

Kennedy testified to Congress in March that he was "very clear with the president about my own displeasure with the executive order." Kennedy said in that testimony the executive order on glyphosate "came from the Pentagon," and "the president felt it was necessary for national security reasons."

In June, the Supreme Court sided with Monsanto, ruling that it cannot be held liable for failing to warn consumers about alleged cancer risks in Roundup. On "Face the Nation," Means accused White House adviser Heidi Overton of working with the Department of Justice to write a brief to the Supreme Court, urging them to take the case prior to Mr. Trump's executive order.

A senior White House official told CBS News that the solicitor general wrote the brief for the Supreme Court at the request of the court. The official also said that Dr. Overton did weigh in on the brief in the final stages but just made changes to "tone." The Trump administration argued in court filings that federal standards supersede state-level liability claims, which was the same position taken by glyphosate-maker Monsanto, now known as Bayer.

There is an ongoing EPA review of glyphosate, expected to conclude in early 2027. Means alleged the prior EPA review of glyphosate was "thrown out because it had ghostwritten research showing Bayer bribed EPA officials."

Means resigned last month and said he is leaving "with tremendous respect for President Trump and Robert F. Kennedy Jr."

Food stocks rallied on the day of his departure. Means told "Face the Nation" that he was frustrated with his stalled efforts to create a federal definition of ultra-processed food, which he argues is poisoning American children.

"There was relentless lobbying against this because the industry and they said this in meetings with me and other people, they just don't want a definition because they don't want Americans to have more transparency into what they're eating because there's a shift away from ultra-processed food right now."

Means said on "Face the Nation" that he is confident of Mr. Trump's stance on the "issue of improving health for children," but claimed that the president's advisers gave him poor advice and "treated him like a baby in many respects and used him."

"They would block access to and information to him all the time," Means alleged. "I would be not surprised at all, you know, if they had very short conversations on these issues, you know, where the president's extremely busy and the president said, 'OK, whatever.'"

Mr. Trump's top adviser Stephen Miller, who is set to take over the White House chief of staff role on Monday, wasn't among them, according to Means.

"Stephen Miller wants to get transformative things done with Bobby Kennedy and President Trump that are not partisan, but structural," he said. "He wants to get the same things done that Elizabeth Warren and (Abdul) El-Sayed and other people are running on. And I think there is a major opportunity to come together and get some big things done, which, quite frankly, we have to do."

In August, Mr. Trump nominated policy aide Dr. Heidi Overton to be the next FDA commissioner. Kennedy has endorsed Overton's nomination.

However, Means told CBS News that Overton "was the biggest block to MAHA policies I encountered in the government," alleging she "did whatever" Wiles "told her to do."

Means alleged that in one particular meeting, Overton told Makary — whom Means described as Overton's "mentor" — that she "couldn't help" him on other policies unless he approved "a drug that he thought scientifically should not be approved," Moderna's mRNA flu vaccine, mFLUSIVA.

In August, the FDA approved mFLUSIVA for adults ages 50 and older. It was the first influenza vaccine using mRNA technology to receive FDA approval.

The approval came despite repeated criticism of mRNA technology by Kennedy, who in 2025 canceled 22 vaccine development projects that use mRNA technology. The FDA had earlier this year said it would refuse to consider Moderna's application. But it reversed course about a week later. Clinical trials found mFLUSIVA to be slightly more effective than the standard flu shot.

"It's just a factual statement that after Marty left, partly due to the vaping issue, she drove the creation of the relaxed vaping strategy," Means said, adding that he does not believe Overton has the "character or integrity" to be FDA commissioner.

A spokesman for Overton responded to Means' criticism of her qualifications and told CBS News that "two former FDA commissioners think otherwise."

Calley Means is the brother of Dr. Casey Means, also a close ally of Kennedy. CBS News previously reported that both played a key role in coordinating Kennedy's endorsement of Mr. Trump during the 2024 presidential campaign. Casey Means was briefly Mr. Trump's pick for surgeon general, but her name was withdrawn in April because her bid stalled in the Senate.

World.title: NYC schools employee faces murder charge in Brooklyn jogger's killing
World.content:
A New York City Department of Education employee is facing a murder charge in the stabbing death of a 28-year-old woman last week in Brooklyn, authorities announced Saturday.

Katie Suarez was stabbed while jogging along the Shore Parkway greenway in Brooklyn on the evening of Oct. 30.

Her father found Suarez injured along the path. She was rushed to the hospital with a stab wound to her neck but ultimately died from her injuries.

On Saturday, the NYPD said it had arrested 27-year-old Sayed Mohassib, of Bath Beach, Brooklyn. Mohassib is charged with second-degree murder, tampering with physical evidence, and criminal possession of a weapon. Mohassib, wearing flip flops and a red jacket, did not answer any questions when police walked him out of the 62nd Precinct Saturday afternoon.

The circumstances leading to Suarez's killing were not immediately clear. It also wasn't immediately clear what led police to Mohassib.

NYPD sources say he made statements claiming he "blacked out" and doesn't remember hurting anyone. Mohassib was taken in for questioning Friday, police sources said, but they have not yet shared details on how they tied him to the crime.

Police sources say Mohassib and Suarez both attended Brooklyn College at the same time, but right now there's no evidence that they knew each other.

Katie Suarez NYPD

Police sources say the suspect worked at Public School 200 in Brooklyn, and that he was also a member of the NYPD in field training in the Bronx from October to November 2022.

Elected officials said he was employed as a teacher's aide and police sources say he was on the job at PS 200 near the precinct this past week.

"The safety of our students is our very top priority. We have suspended this individual and will move to terminate employment pending the outcome of the conviction. We are supporting the NYPD in their investigation however is needed," the Department of Education said in a statement.

Mohassib's employment with the DOE has raised questions by elected officials. City Councilmember Kayla Santosuosso, state Sen. Andrew Gounardes and Assemblymember-elect Chris McCreight said in a joint statement Mohassib "was evidently a mentally disturbed man with no criminal record" who had been "an ex-NYPD officer and ex-Marine who was discharged from the military on psychiatric grounds."

"Troublingly though, at the time of the attack, he was a DOE employee, serving as a teacher's aide in a public school," they said. "This last revelation raises serious questions about how he came to be employed in a local public school and warrants a full investigation into the circumstances of his hiring and continued employment."

Suarez's killing prompted shock and outrage throughout New York City, along with an intense search by the NYPD for her killer.

Pedestrians on the greenway reacted to word of the arrest Saturday.

"Definitely a relief," said Anatoly Bogdanov. "Everybody was concerned that he is out there and he is dangerous."

"I was very surprised, because I feel it's a very safe area," said Yana Tomacheva. "I think it's a little bit of relief. I guess relief and hopefully, potentially, some closure for her family."

"We want to make sure that he's held accountable," the Rev. Erick Salgado said. "We hope that justice is done. I know that nothing is going to give them back their daughter, but he will be praying that at least this will come to a closure."

"My younger one is still at PS 200 and this is really disturbing," Bogdanov said.

Earlier this week, Katie's anguished mother Yasira Suarez had called on the suspect to turn themselves in, saying "you took an angel."

World.title: Transcript: Calley Means on "Face the Nation with Margaret Brennan," Nov. 8, 2026
World.content:
The following is the full transcript of the interview with Calley Means, former senior adviser to Health Secretary Robert F. Kennedy Jr., a portion of which aired on "Face the Nation with Margaret Brennan" on Nov. 8, 2026.

MARGARET BRENNAN: Calley, thank you for coming in and talking to us. President Trump has announced that Chief of Staff Susie Wiles has left the White House. The departure coincides with this resounding Republican loss in the midterms. But also, you went public with some very specific allegations of corruption and a call to clean house. Was it your intention to get her removed?

CALLEY MEANS: Yes. I think President Trump has been subverted by people that are beholden to special interests and not what President Trump ran on, and what voters voted for. I led the MAHA initiative at the White House. And Stephen Miller said it recently in his speech, the heart of MAHA is that we are the only primate humans that deal with pediatric cancer and rampant cancer rates. And it's obviously because of our environment. It's because of pesticides. It's because of that- 70% of a child's diet is ultra-processed food. It's because we're not out in the sun. It's basic, basic stuff. And that, I think, was really the heart of the MAHA movement. I think a heart of what President Trump ran on. And there's very simple things. And Americans voted to change those things. And I think underneath Trump's nose, in many cases, you had a group of former lobbyists, catering to the vaping industry, catering to the ultra-processed food industry, catering to the pharmaceutical industry, catering to the pesticide industry and doing their bidding with an excuse that we need their money for the midterms and really need to actually go against what voters said, but need their money explicitly. That's what they said. And I think that--

MARGARET BRENNAN: --Who's they?

CALLEY MEANS: Susie and her cohort. Susie and Richard Walters, who is actually not someone most people know, but was one of the most powerful people in the country, was the de facto chief of staff when Susie was getting cancer treatment. Walker Barrett and James Blair, a very close knit crew, who explicitly catered to special interests against the will of the voters. I think a lot of this happened without Trump's full knowledge. I don't think President Trump fully knew that some of these advisors were taking money from the industries we ran on fighting against. At the time, they're giving explicit policy advice--

MARGARET BRENNAN: Directly taking money?

CALLEY MEANS: Directly, of course. Yes. Tony Fabrizio--

(NOTE: Richard Walters told CBS News he submitted his resignation Friday. Susie Wiles told CBS News that President Trump "did more for MAHA than any president before or likely any president in the future.")

MARGARET BRENNAN: --he's a pollster. (CROSSTALK)

CALLEY MEANS: --is one of the most powerful people in the country. And every single cabinet secretary was conniving on how to convince Tony Fabrizio of their policy positions because any policy went through Tony Fabrizio for a political check. You know, he was in the White House all the time, every single week. And--

MARGARET BRENNAN: He runs an outside polling firm that the White House relies on.

CALLEY MEANS: Yeah, but- but that's- that's a name- I mean, he was- he was one of the most impactful players in White House policy making. One of the most powerful people in the country. He had a huge say in any policy that got done. And as he is opining on the political relevance of doing, you know, healthy food and healthy school lunches or, you know, taking on the pesticide industry or taking on big pharma, which President Trump ran on. He was getting paid by Pfizer or by Pepsi. To this day, it's on his website right now. You can see it on the Joe Rogan podcast I just did, we pulled up his website. It's advertised right now. He solicits clients right now and lists those people as his clients.

MARGARET BRENNAN: So you think all of his polling is compromised?

CALLEY MEANS: I'm just stating facts. I'm just stating--

MARGARET BRENNAN: But that's your theory that you're putting forward.

CALLEY MEANS: Yeah, I'm just stating a fact that we were trying to get a 90% support policy done of defining ultra-processed food, and he said the juice isn't worth the squeeze on this, and advised against it, while being paid by Pepsi.

(NOTE: Following the conclusion of Face the Nation's broadcast, Tony Fabrizio released the following statement: "Anyone with web access and a couple spare minutes could find ample evidence that Calley Means' allegations that I am in the pocket of Big Pharma is not only ridiculous, but demonstrably false… I have even encouraged GOP Members of Congress to campaign on the MFN issue, which would harm Big Pharma's bottom line").

MARGARET BRENNAN: I want to get into the specifics of ultra-processed food in a moment, because it's an important health initiative that you are pushing for. But let me ask you on this topic of basically corruption. You went on Joe Rogan's podcast and made a lot of these allegations.

CALLEY MEANS: Just factual statements of what I yeah, what I experienced leading the MAHA agenda.

MARGARET BRENNAN: Did the president get word that you were doing that? Do you think that what you laid out publicly was a factor in Susie Wiles' departure?

CALLEY MEANS: I have no idea. I know the president is close with Joe Rogan and appreciates his opinion. You know, people can watch the podcast. I encourage everyone to do so. It goes into details of factual statements.

MARGARET BRENNAN: Because she resigned Thursday.

CALLEY MEANS: But I think that President Trump yeah, you know, I can't speak to what's going through President Trump's head. But I think with his elevation of Stephen Miller and again, speaking for my world, speaking for MAHA, Stephen Miller, who understands the corporate capture of our political system is particularly when it comes to health care, better than any, I would say, government official, that I've ever seen. Who wants to go hard against special interests, who I think made a pitch to President Trump, we're going to go back to campaign promises, America First principles, that President Trump got shot and suffered so much in order to be a historic president and do big things. We're going to get away from the Ballard, which is Susie's lobbying group, controlled policy process and towards an America First policy process. I think that's what Stephen wants to do. I think that's what resonated with President Trump. So I think it's a bold statement that President Trump made, pushing Susie out and- and elevating Stephen Miller. And I think it's a very good sign for America.

MARGARET BRENNAN: So, RFK Jr, the HHS secretary, who you're very, very close to, said "Stephen Miller is the strongest MAHA supporter in the administration. It's time to unleash the Kraken." What- what do you take that to mean?

CALLEY MEANS: What I take it to mean is actually an opening for Republicans and Democrats. "Unleash the Kraken" means doing things that matter to the American people. And when it comes to health care, these are completely nonpartisan things. I mean, I spent every single day with Bobby Kennedy, as you said, probably more time with them than almost anyone. And what he says, what he pushes his team on, is the exact same things that Democrats are running on. It is taking on corporate capture. It's taking on corruption. It's taking on big pharma incentives. It's making our food healthier. That is what he is pushing his team to do. And I think people would be shocked to- if they saw, I think really how wholesome his world is to be quite frank. I mean, these- these are universal, very popular ideas he's trying to push on. So "unleash the Kraken" means understanding the pain Americans are feeling, the frustration they're feeling. And I think we are more closer to a breaking point with our institutions and Americans' frustration with the corruption in Washington, D.C. President Trump identified that issue. And I think what that means is we are- have an open hand. The administration has an open hand, to actually get big things done that are not partisan but actually structural.

MARGARET BRENNAN: So on that point, I hear that you believe Stephen Miller is an ally to the cause, but in terms of being an operator in Washington, I mean, he's radioactive to Democrats. They're already calling for him to be fired. He was the architect of the mass deportation policy that proved very unpopular in these midterms. Why do you think he can actually help you get things done on this cause?

CALLEY MEANS: Yeah, President Trump is the president for the next two years. The next two years are going to be the most consequential two years in American history. And I think we should all realize that our problems are not Trump or no Trump. Stephen Miller, not Stephen Miller. It's the institutional corruption in D.C. that Stephen Miller and President Trump understand. I think there's a lot we can get together on immigration, which is not my issue. I will say that a lot of polls said that that was one of- like actually solving the border crisis. Stephen Miller did do that. That was a core campaign promise. That was an existential issue. He is very competent and he has dramatically reduced those numbers. So I can speak with most authority from the MAHA perspective. Let's talk about health care. Stephen Miller wants to get transformative things done with Bobby Kennedy and President Trump that are not partisan, but structural. He wants to get the same things done that Elizabeth Warren and El-Sayed and other people are running on. And I think there is a major opportunity to come together and get some big things done, which, quite frankly, we have to do.

MARGARET BRENNAN: So you said earlier this week you think the best chance the president has to get things done is to work with Bernie Sanders, and Senator-elect Abdul El-Sayed. You mentioned Elizabeth Warren here, but how do you think those things can get done in this environment? Like, what's the thing that is most tangible here?

CALLEY MEANS: Yeah, I think there are specific bills, specific issues that they're literally saying the same thing. Stephen Miller, President Trump and Bobby Kennedy want to take on the fact that we spend two, three times more than any other developed country on health care and live shorter. That's clearly just corruption.

MARGARET BRENNAN: But the administration pushed-- (CROSSTALK)

CALLEY MEANS: --Pharma prices-- (CROSSTALK)

MARGARET BRENNAN: --Republican bill that pulled funding from premiums, and Medicaid— (CROSSTALK)

CALLEY MEANS: I think- I think Stephen Miller and Bobby Kennedy would be very amenable to meeting with Democrats, meeting with Republicans who aren't beholden to special interests like John Thune. And working out specific wins on drug pricing, on labels for ultra-processed food, on greater disclosures and processes at the FDA so we make sure we have gold star science on the fact that the United States is 4% of the world's population, but in just 20% of the world's herbicides and pesticides, and the recent EPA review of glyphosate was thrown out because it had ghostwritten research showing Bayer bribed EPA officials. Can we have EPA reform?

MARGARET BRENNAN: This is a cancer-linked herbicide.
