In his short life, he explored many parts of the world, including Mexico, Germany, Austria, Italy, Croatia, Malta, the Netherlands, England and Spain.

Reagan Goulding, his aunt, said during the funeral that he often made those around him laugh.

She said it's been hard knowing that he died at a young age.

"This is perhaps one of the hardest parts of losing someone so young," she said. "It's not just the memories we have lost, but the opportunity to make a relationship we still had time to build."

Reagan Goulding said she could see her nephew, who she described as being "smart, ambitious, determined, and resourceful," perhaps becoming a police officer or joining CSIS.

"I truly believe great things were in his future. We wanted him to know that we all saw this in him, that we believed in him and became a proud follower of him," she said.

She said her last message to Goulding was sent on the day of the tragedy, a text message that said, "Aidan, you better be OK."

She never received a reply.

WATCH | Who are the 4 who died in the CFB Wainwright fire?: Who are the 4 service members killed at CFB Wainwright? | Duration closed caption 6:26

Reagan Goulding said if she knew this was her last message she would have said more, including telling him one more time how proud she was.

She also remembered the other soldiers killed in the fire.

They were: Pte. Hayden Lykkemark, 19, of Langley, B.C.; Sgt. Morgan Wong, 26, of Edmonton; and Pte. Shaun Farrell, 23, of Prince Albert, Sask.

"They were young men who matched their calling, who stood beside one another, and who were parts of the family themselves. Their loss is felt by their families, their friends, soldiers, and everyone who has been touched by this tragedy," she said.

"Aidan and his fellow soldiers will not be forgotten," she added.

As the soldiers carried the casket out of the armoury and reloaded it into a hearse to head to the cemetery, the sun broke through the clouds, casting its light over rainy Vancouver.

Monk, who spoke to media after the funeral, said she felt it was a sign from Goulding, encouraging her to move forward with life.

"Because I think through tragedy or hardship, he would always say things like that, 'We'll move forward.' So, I think that's what he was sort of saying to me today, actually, with the sun shining bright in my eyes."

Monk said she felt "supported and lifted" after hearing stories from Goulding's "brothers and sisters" in the army.

"I'm quite tired, I haven't eaten a lot, I haven't slept a lot. But all the support and seeing everybody here today, it's remarkable. I can't find a word other than remarkable," said Monk, adding that "There's lots of love in Canada."

World.title: Weather challenges search for Vancouver Island man who failed to return from canoe trip
World.content:
The audio version of this article is generated by AI-based technology. Mispronunciations can occur. We are working with our partners to continually review and improve the results.

A community-led search is underway off northern Vancouver Island for 34-year-old James "Dakota" Smith, who failed to return from a solo canoe trip amid stormy weather Friday.

Smith, a member of the Ma’amtagila Nation, was last seen around 12 p.m. PCT at Adam River, about 85 kilometres northwest of Campbell River, according to family member and search co-ordinator Matthew Ambers.

Smith had planned to return bones from an earlier hunt to nature by dropping them into the ocean, according to his cousin Seneca Ambers.

Returning bones to nature, Seneca said, is a traditional practice among Ma’amtagila First Nations people.

"We just want him home," she said.

Authorities were called to search for Smith after he was a few hours late to return home to his partner and two young children, Seneca said.

According to Matthew’s post, search and rescue crews located Smith’s canoe about seven-and-a-half hours after the search began — six nautical miles west of Adam River.

His posts also called on the community to assist with the search.

"As soon as the sun came up [Saturday], [Matthew] wanted to make sure that people were out searching for Dakota," said Seneca.

Community search

She said most of those searching Saturday were family and community members, including "a lot of friends" who drove to the Adam River area from various locations across Vancouver Island.

Seneca said Smith and his family are considered "guardians of our territory" and he is experienced in the wilderness.

James "Dakota" Smith is a member of the Ma'amtaglia Nation. (Ma'amtagila Tribe Society/Facebook)

"We don’t know what’s happened," she said.

In a post to on social media, shortly after Smith was last seen, the province issued a high streamflow advisory for parts of B.C., including eastern Vancouver Island.

That stormy weather continued to challenge search efforts Saturday, Seneca said, as rough conditions on the water forced Matthew to retreat from the water and aid in the land search instead.

"We want to think as positive as possible right now. That he’s just found a place to hunker down," she said. "But obviously there’s a lot of fear and worry."

In an email, Victoria’s Joint Rescue Coordination Centre said it received the call on Nov. 6, and two Canadian Coast Guard vessels and two aircraft were tasked with searching for Smith.

The canoe was recovered, however there were no signs of Smith.

The centre said that based on survivability models, a search reduction was ordered at roughly 7:30 p.m. PCT.

"The RCMP has the lead now," read the email.

The RCMP says it received the report about Smith at approximately 4:20 p.m. PCT, as the search continued in the Johnstone Strait.

World.title: Regina councillor shared great replacement conspiracy theory with colleagues during mosque broadcast debate
World.content:
The audio version of this article is generated by AI-based technology. Mispronunciations can occur. We are working with our partners to continually review and improve the results.

As Regina debated a mosque's decision to broadcast a call to prayer , Ward 1 Coun. Dan Rashovich forwarded an email to his colleagues that contained what experts say is the "great replacement" conspiracy theory, which falsely suggests immigrants are attempting to replace a country's white population.

The email, obtained by CBC News through a freedom of information request, says the Islamic call to prayer or adhan is a "strategic tactic" to expand Islam in Canada through changing demographics.

"Thank You for your email. You nailed it!" Rashovich wrote in an email CC'd to every member of Regina city council, as well as Regina police Chief Lorilee Davies, Saskatchewan Premier Scott Moe and provincial Justice Minister Tim McLeod.

Rashovich declined multiple requests for an on-camera interview. Instead, in a series of emailed statements, Rashovich said he did not see the email's entire contents before sharing it.

The city councillor said his "You nailed it!" response was referring to a different email from the same sender — an email that doesn't refer to the great replacement conspiracy theory. That email was redacted when provided to CBC.

But one of Rashovich's colleagues did not interpret Rashovich's comment as reacting to a different email.

Ward 6 Coun. Victoria Flores pushed back on the email containing the Islamophobic screed, saying the City of Regina needed to call the email "exactly what it is."

"This unnamed person is explicitly calling for violence and the destruction of places of worship in our city," Flores wrote.

Rashovich told CBC he could not comment on the "accuracy of religious interpretations," and that he did not respond or agree with the email that contains the passage with the conspiracy theory in it.

Amin Asfari, a professor and researcher at the University of Regina, says the email promotes fears that Europeans or Canadians with European heritage are being replaced through a so-called "white genocide."

WATCH | Regina mosque halts prayer broadcast: Regina mosque halts broadcasting call to prayer after backlash | Duration closed caption 0:56 Regina City Jamia Masjid has decided to temporarily halt broadcasting the Muslim call to prayer from its rooftop speakers after a wave of online threats and pushback.

Jasmin Zine, a professor of sociology and religion at Wilfrid Laurier University who has studied Islamophobia , says the conspiracy theory is prominent among white supremacists, nationalists and neo-nazis.

This example, which hinges on Islamophobia, preys on fears of replacement.

"It assumes there's kind of a nefarious intention by people who are immigrants," Asfari said.

'A glaring hypocrisy': professor

Rashovich made his own views on the broadcast of the adhan clear in an email dated July 6, 2026.

The email shows Rashovich responding to an email that is entirely redacted. Rashovich's response is CC'd to the rest of council.

"I agree this should not be happening," Rashovich said, saying he believes in freedom of worship but not at the "expense of publicly expressing this on everybody."

Rashovich says the country was founded on "Judeo Christian values" and that "Religion and Politics should not mix."

"Every religion has the right to worship who and how they want and this should be done within their church besides some outdoor events or marches that happen," Rashovich said.

He goes on to say that the city's noise bylaw allows the broadcast of the adhan "when it should not be allowed."

"We do not need others religious messages being broadcasted. That is for every Religion," Rashovich wrote.

When asked whether he stands by this email, Rashovich said that it must be read in context.

Asfari said the email is an example of hypocrisy from Rashovich.

The University of Regina professor said the email shows Rashovich acknowledging that religious freedom is a central concept to the Canadian identity, while also stating that certain aspects of faith should be relegated away from the general public.

Asfari said religions often use a call to prayer. In Christianity there is the ringing of church bells, in Judaism the shofar horn is used and Islam uses the adhan.

"There's a glaring hypocrisy, and it comes across rather consistently, when people like this speak about what they believe to be the kind of supreme or dominant narrative that must be there, and then the other, which is foreign, must be tucked away," Asfari said.

The email

Rashovich's email that CC's the Islamophic conspiracy theory was sent on the evening of July 14, 2026. CBC obtained it through a freedom of information request filed with the City of Regina.

At that time, the Regina City Jamia Masjid mosque had recently paused its plans to broadcast the adhan over the noon hour on Fridays.

The mosque had obtained a permit from the Regina Police Service allowing it to broadcast the three-minute call over rooftop speakers once a week, under the city's noise bylaw.

M. Anisur Rahaman, director of the Regina City Jamia Masjid, told media that he later decided to pause broadcasts because the mosque had received threats after the first broadcast .

M. Anisur Rahaman, director of the Regina City Jamia Masjid mosque in downtown Regina, poses for a photo outside of the centre on July 17. (Randi LaRocque/CBC)

The email containing the Islamophic message — including who sent it — is redacted in the emails disclosed by the city, but it is partially quoted by Flores in a later email.

The message says the adhan directs adherents to spread the religion in "non-Muslim lands" through "public assertion" and "demographic presence," according to Flores' quotation.

Zine said the message references the great replacement conspiracy theory and the civilizational jihad conspiracy theory, which falsely claims that Muslims immigrants are attempting to establish social, cultural and political strongholds in nations that they are "infiltrating."

The tying of two different conspiracy theories together in one message paints a picture of a grand Islamophobic plan, he said.

"The idea is that Muslims are a Trojan horse that will unleash these invaders who will infiltrate Western societies. They will install themselves politically as a fifth column and then start installing Sharia law," Zine said.

Asfari said Islamophobic conspiracy theories can be precursor to violence, saying it "does tend to plant seeds in more nefarious circles where the propensity for violence is greater."

Zine and Asfari point to the 2017 Quebec City mosque shooting and the 2021 London truck attack as examples of rhetoric becoming action in Canada.

WATCH | Londoners honour the Afzaal family on the anniversary of their tragic deaths: Londoners honour the Afzaal family on the anniversary of their tragic deaths | Duration closed caption 2:12 Hundreds of Londoners gathered at the site where four members of the Afzaal family were tragically killed five years ago on June 6. The local Muslim community held a vigil at the intersection of South Carriage and Hyde Park Roads, then walked to Oakridge Secondary School. The event honoured the Muslim family known as Our London Family, and also aimed to raise awareness about combating hate and Islamophobia.

Asfari and Zine said it's particularly concerning that a municipal politician — rather than a random person online — is sharing the conspiracy theory.

Zine said municipal leaders and politicians are looked to as trusted sources of information. When they share conspiracy theories that are otherwise circulating in white nationalist echo chambers, it helps to legitimize beliefs that are otherwise clearly false and harmful.

"It does give average people more licence to share those stories. And maybe they believe that those are bona fide," Zine said.

A person within an institution, or an institution itself, sharing a conspiracy theory can help give it more weight, Asfari said.

"When we talk about institutionalized Islamophobia, this is precisely the kind of thing that we're talking about," Asfari said.

Asfari commended other councillors for pushing back against the rhetoric in the email.

In one example, Flores directly confronts Rashovich for sharing it.

"...Differentiate between a noise bylaw concern and someone who is using this opportunity to spread misinformation and hate," Flores wrote.

World.title: University libraries are being swarmed by AI bots, putting public access at risk
World.content:
The audio version of this article is generated by AI-based technology. Mispronunciations can occur. We are working with our partners to continually review and improve the results.

Academic libraries are fighting off swarms of data-scraping bots — that are slowing or crashing sites meant for students, researchers and the public — as AI companies continue hunting for content to feed their large language models.

University libraries say entire collections are being knocked offline by persistent streams of unruly bots trying to access their archives, which include academic, historical and government documents.

"They're just out there on the internet, just bombarding us with trying to grab up as much material as possible," Jill Strykowski, cataloguing and government documents lead at San Jose State University, told CBC News.

The bots are used by both AI and third-party companies to scour websites and retrieve data, often to feed LLMs like Claude, Gemini and ChatGPT.

Libraries, museums and other cultural heritage institutions are prime targets because they have quality, vetted information that is generally not hidden behind paywalls or logins.

The bots are "causing an incredible amount of work and headache for every institution that does digitization work and every institution that is trying to make information openly available," Strykowski says.

Researchers found such reports started appearing in late 2024 across North America, Europe and Oceania and experts tell CBC News the problem continues to get worse.

LISTEN | Even smarter, with even fewer guardrails: The Sunday Magazine 23:41 Inside the global race toward an AI that might kill us all

And new challenges keep arising, says Dean Seeman, director of collections and digital infrastructure at University of Victoria Libraries.

"Sometimes the bot traffic gets so bad that it causes the sites to go down completely for a little while," he said.

Seeman says this creates a "real problem" for public access.

Regular people using library websites are now, effectively, in competition with infinite traffic from bot farms, says Peter Lewis, Canada Research Chair in Trustworthy Artificial Intelligence at Ontario Tech University.

"This is another instance of large, private companies making use of common-good public interest institutions in a way that's very extractive and just assumes that that stuff is available and is free — and then using it to be able to produce highly commercial models that then they can go and sell back to people," he said.

Workers enter data from an old document belonging to the McMillan Memorial Library during a digitization exercise at the Eastland Library in Nairobi on March 24, 2022. Libraries and other cultural heritage institutions are prime targets for AI bots. (Patrick Meinhardt/AFP/Getty Images)

Good bots and bad bots

Eric Hellman, executive director of Project Gutenberg — a U.S.-based volunteer organization that digitizes and archives cultural works and distributes eBooks — wrote in a blog last year that these bots, which he characterizes as poorly programmed "monstrosities," are "destroying open access" on the internet.

He tells CBC News that "everything's gotten worse" since he wrote that.

Hellman says the problem comes down to good bots and bad bots.

He explains that search engines like Google, and archiving sites like Internet Archive, use bots that follow robots.txt — voluntary sets of instructions on websites that tell them what they can and can't do, so they don't disrupt the site's functioning while gathering information.

AI scraping bots, on the other hand, sometimes ignore these rules and overwhelm websites — in some cases requesting thousands of documents a second and downloading them in every available format.

WATCH | Young AI researchers in Ontario: This is what young people studying artificial intelligence are thinking — as the future of AI grabs headlines | Duration closed caption 2:16 Developments in AI, and companies and developers warning about the future of the technology, are grabbing headlines again. But there are young people in Windsor studying the technology. The CBC's Jacob Barker caught up with them to hear their perspective.

As an example, the University of North Carolina at Chapel Hill reported last year that it received more than 11,000 searches for Finnish music from thousands of different internet addresses on the same day. The university said its library catalogue was periodically shutting out students, faculty and staff due to bot traffic.

And because one company or bot farm can work from thousands of IP addresses, Hellman says the old fix of blocking problematic IPs is no longer useful.

Michael Weinberg, co-director of GLAM-E, a collaborative effort focused on open-access policies for cultural institutions, is working to protect public access to information. (Submitted by Michael Weinberg)

He says Project Gutenberg is happy for its materials to be used as AI training data and even offers a one-click download of its entire library of books, "but the bots are too stupid to use it."

"Our material is almost all public domain material. It's exactly the sort of material that they should be training on," he said. "We just wish they would do it in a respectful way that doesn't take down websites."

Open access a 'huge benefit'

Some libraries have set up CAPTCHA challenges or other verification systems to weed out bots.

The problem is, those measures can also weed out the good bots, says Michael Weinberg, co-director of GLAM-E, a collaborative academic initiative at NYU Law School and the University of Warwick focused on open-access policies for cultural institutions.

Some libraries have also begun to require login credentials, a controversial move that those who spoke to CBC News say they want to avoid because it puts barriers on human access to things they believe should be easily accessible.

And as the scraping bots get more advanced, experts say they could also learn to work around these strategies.

The Anthropic logo is displayed at during the Dreamforce technology summit in San Francisco, on Sept. 17. AI firms have broadly argued that scraping publicly available data is permissible under fair use and in the public's best interest. (Carlos Barria/Reuters)

Major AI firms have argued that scraping publicly available data to train their models is permissible under fair use and in the public's best interest.

But faced with widespread criticism and copyright lawsuits, Anthropic, OpenAI, Google and Microsoft expressed support last week for honouring a single, standardized opt-out signal in a website's robots.txt file that could block their web crawlers from harvesting data.

Compliance would be voluntary, however, and the agreement leaves out problematic bots from third-party companies and smaller AI startups.

Weinberg says the digitization of valuable information has been a "fantastic" development for humanity — giving researchers, teachers and curious citizens easy access to resources that, 20 years ago, "would have required driving for flying or a special permission to get access."

Organizations like GLAM-E are trying to figure out long-term solutions to preserve that access for humans and helpful bots alike.

Right now, the bots create "a disincentive for libraries and other institutions to make parts of their collection available online," Weinberg said. "I think it's been a huge benefit to society that libraries and museums and other cultural institutions have put a huge amount of work into making their collections available."

World.title: Colombia’s war crimes tribunal JEP announces steep measures after being forced to cut $53M from its budget
World.content:
The president of the JEP announced radical cuts in the war crimes tribunal’s spending, which was forced to cut $53 million (COP170 billion) from its annual budget by Colombia’s Congress.

In a press statement, JEP president Danilo Rojas said that the court would abandon its 15,000m² main office in Bogota and move to a much smaller building in March of next year.

The court president additionally announced that it would eliminate 85% of its temporary employees and force staff to absorb administrative, technical defense, and psychosocial tasks previously handled by external contractors.

Many of the remaining workers will largely be working from home to facilitate the aforementioned move.

The court will also abandon personal security details for magistrates and the court directors and ask the National Protection Unit to take on the protection of victims, witnesses and defendants.

Last but not least, the court announced partnerships with universities, the Inspector General’s Office and local governments to secure regional presence, which is necessary to investigate war crimes.

The radical austerity measures became a necessity after Congress agreed with President Abelardo de la Espriella and hi far-right National Salvation party to slash the JEP’s budget.

The war crimes tribunal seeks justice for millions of victims of the military and the now-defunct guerrilla group FARC, which agreed to demobilize and disarm in 2016.

The JEP has long been the target of criticism of the far-right, which has historically downplayed the war crimes committed by the State and regional elites that used the armed conflict to accumulate wealth.

World.title: Colombia’s labor unions and social organizations call national strike on November 19
World.content:
Colombia’s main labor unions and a collection of civil society organizations called a national strike “against the fascist government of Abelardo de la Espriella and his tax reform” bill.

In a press statement, the organizations accused De la Espriella of, among other things, dismantling the “social, environmental, trade union, and labor rights achieved during the government of Gustavo Petro,” and surrendering sovereignty and kneeling before the imperialist government of the United States.”

The government of Abelardo, like that of Duque and Carrasquilla, intends to reach into the pockets of the people and privilege the ultra-rich with its “economic rescue” bill, which imposes a 19% VAT on food and other basic goods in the family basket, higher taxes on earned income, raises health contributions up to 8%, and conversely reduces the corporate capital income tax from 35% to 31%, eliminates the wealth tax in 2031, and reduces the capital gains tax to 20% for investments in 2027 and 2028. Civil society organizations

The organizations additionally accused the government of seeking special powers to facilitate the privatization of state-controlled companies like oil firm Ecopetrol.

The organizations said they united with the main opposition party, the Historic Pact, “with the purpose of opposing this fascist government and decisively participating in the National Strike.”

The National Strike on November 19 constitutes a new stage in the organization and expression of growing popular discontent, which was also manifested in the successful national mobilization day of October 14. It is about strengthening a collective action process capable of confronting the Government’s regressive measures, demanding respect for hard-won rights, and opposing the deepening of its neoliberal and authoritarian project. Civil society organizations

The last time a national strike was organized was in 2021 when the labor unions and their allies from civil society shut down parts of the country for months.

At the time, a tax reform propose by former President Ivan Duque triggered the initiative.

World.title: Colombia’s government presents “Economic Rescue Bill”
World.content:
Colombia’s Vice-President Jose Manuel Restrepo on Thursday presented an Economic Rescue Bill that seeks to reduce government spending and increase its revenue.

The bill grants extraordinary powers to President Abelardo de la Espriella to slash government spending by decree and includes a tax reform that includes higher sales tax rates on gasoline, coffee, cigarettes and vegetables.

The bill also includes tax breaks for corporations in an attempt to increase investment.

Abelardo’s extraordinary powers

While on campaign, De la Espriella powers vowed a 40% reduction of the State, which the bill falls short of doing.

Article 7 of the bill does grant the president extraordinary powers to “abolish, merge, and split ministries and administrative departments, as well as to determine or modify their names, objectives, and organizational structure,” and allows De la Espriella to “abolish, merge, split, and change the legal status” of other State bodies like the superintendencies, agencies, special administrative units, and public institutions.

Article 96 allows the government to change the personnel hiring of tax agency DIAN, which “would allow for the elimination of annual competitive exams for entry into the DIAN and a return to the practice of appointing thousands of officials,” according to former DIAN director Luis Carlos Reyes.

Last but not least, the bill mandates a 20% reduction in salaries of State employees, excluding the security forces, and cut half of the costs in temporary contracts.

VAT reforms and squeezing the middle class

The bill seeks to remove popular products like cocoa, coffee, sugar and fruits from a VAT exemption list and introduce a 19% sales tac on them.

An increase in taxes on gasoline will inflate its price.

The bill additionally seeks to charge VAT on vice products like liquor and cigarettes, which would make them up to 53% more expensive.

The bulk of these tax increases wouldn’t take fore until after the November 2027 local and regional elections in an apparent compromise to Congress and Colombia’s political forces.

In an attempt to not impoverish the poor, the bill seeks a mechanism that would refund up to 100% of IVA payments to some 19 million of the country’s poorest citizens.

The increased pressure on the middle class has already resulted in opposition from within De la Espriella’s congressional coalition.

Tax benefits for the capitalists

The government seeks to gradually lower the corporate income tax from 35% to 31% and offer a reduced tax rate for large companies that decide to invest in new enterprises.

According to the Inter-American Development Bank, a similar scheme introduced by former President Alvaro Uribe “was ineffective in promoting investment.”

World.title: Accusations over De la Espriella’s narco ties “lack conclusive or solid evidence,” says Colombia’s justice minister
World.content:
Colombia’s Justice Minister, Ivan Cancino, downplayed the evidence of ties between President Abelardo de la Espriella and drug traffickers that was displayed in Congress by opposition Senator Ivan Cepeda.

In a video, Cancino said that “political oversight is a fundamental tool of our democracy. However, it cannot become an arena for launching accusations without proving and substantiating them.”

The justice minister admitted that the pieces of evidence provided to Congress “may seem serious,” but “lack conclusive or solid evidence, as well as any support that could jeopardize the innocence and the presumption of innocence of our president.”

It is not just about displaying organizational charts, deeds from over a decade ago, and business transactions to construct a narrative that supports neither judicial decisions nor the documentary, testimonial, circumstantial, or expert backing required for these types of accusations. Ivan Cancino

Cancino accused the opposition of remaining “silent regarding the grave scandals involving corruption, drug trafficking, and even alleged sexual abuse, as well as fiscal irresponsibility and possible links to criminal organizations that surrounded the previous government. ”

The justice minister was forced to come out after Cepeda showed Congress evidence of De la Espriella’s business ties with multiple convicted drug traffickers and announced criminal complaints against the president.

De la Espriella’s law firm rose to prominence during the demobilization of paramilitary organization AUC with whom he created a foundation that sought to justify the paramilitary violence that terrorized much of Colombia in the 1990’s and 2000s.

Once the ties between the AUC and elected politicians became known, the president ended up defending many of the “parapoliticians” in court.

According to Cepeda, De la Espriella plays a key role in a “revolving door” system that could end up benefiting the very drug traffickers and corrupt politicians that have paid the president for his legal defense in the past.

World.title: Colombia’s opposition announces criminal charges against De la Espriella over ties to drug traffickers
World.content:
Colombia’s opposition leader, senator Ian Cepeda, accused President Abelardo de la Espriella of leading an agrarian counter-reform designed to benefit land-owning clans and convicted drug traffickers.

During a congressional debate, Cepeda claimed that De la Espriella put allies of drug traffickers and paramilitaries in charge of key state institutions responsible for land distribution and asset forfeiture.

The president and his appointees are part of a revolving door system of people who, before being appointed to government positions, defended the interests of drug traffickers and paramilitaries associated with De la Espriella and his businesses, according to the opposition leader.

For example, the president put Diana Patrica Bravo, a former prosecutor and partner at his law firm De la Espriella Lawyers, in charge of The Society of Special Assets (SAE), which controls assets that were seized from drug traffickers.

The leader of the leftist Historic Pact party showed financial statements of one of De la Espriella’s companies, Dominio De la Espriella, that would prove that in between 38% and 40% of its capital deposits came from the family and corporate network of Hugues Rodríguez, a.k.a. Comandante Barbie, a former paramilitary financier who was charged with drug trafficking in the US.

The SAE would control more than 130 properties of Comandante Barbie.

De la Espriella family construction firm, Cosenza S.A.S., made property purchases in the city of Monteria directly with individuals under investigation for money laundering and illicit enrichment, according to Cepeda.

The president’s ex-wife, Yoly Beatriz Illidge, was appointed Superintendent of Notaries, making her “directly responsible for inspecting and monitoring all land entries and records issued by restitution judges throughout the country,” according to Cepeda.

De la Espriella is an associate of drug traffickers, owns assets purchased from drug traffickers, and defends drug traffickers from within the national government. Senator Ivan Cepeda

Last but not least, Agriculture Minister Indalecio Dangond “arrived at this post to execute an agrarian counter-reform at the service of paramilitary land-grabbers, foreign capital, and agro-industrial partners” while blocking investments for small farmers and displacement victims, the opposition leader stated.

Cepeda vowed that he would give the dossier to the United States Department of Justcie and to “Congressmen of the Democratic Party, given that mister De la Espriella is a US citizen.”

The opposition leader additionally promised to file criminal charges against the president and his agriculture minister in Colombia.

World.title: Colombia’s government claims Petro exploited 48 women as president
World.content:
The administration chief of Colombia’s President Abelardo De la Espriella told Congress that former President Gustavo Petro hired at least 48 women who were “trapped and exploited” for presidential parties.

During a hearing, DAPRE director Carlos Andres Rios claimed that Petro had 48 women “working in the Presidency, who were unfortunately exploited through temporary work contracts.”

We’re going to prove this to the Colombian people: how, unfortunately, the Casa de Nariño was set up, organized, and designed not for governing, but for partying there every day, bringing women there and engaging in behavior we should not be engaging in—behavior that sets a bad example. DAPRE director Carlos Andres Rios

“Forty-eight women are already speaking with us about how, through a contract and an OPS, they were trapped and exploited in order to be with President Petro,” said Rios.

Former DAPRE director Angie Rodriguez, who was sacked by Petro in July, doubled down on her successor’s allegations and asked the former president to prove that the president managed a network of women, including child transvestites.

Were there transvestite children there? Answer me, Mr. President. Were there transvestite children there? I am asking you a question, and I have every right to ask it. Were there? And if there weren’t, uh… prove that what I am saying is a lie. Angie Rodriguez

Last but not least, far-right magazine Semana published an interview with a woman identified as Deicy Jimenez, who claimed she as hired by Petro after meeting him on an adult website.

Jimenez even told Semana’s former presidential candidate Vicky Davila she trafficked drugs for the former president when he was senator.

VD: What happened on the day you say you transported drugs for Petro? DJ: Yes, I was traveling, and he asked me as a favor to bring him some drugs. VD: Were you outside of Bogotá? DJ: Yes. VD: How do you recall that favor Petro asked of you? DJ: He asked me as the favor to bring him some drugs. VD: Did you buy them? DJ: Yes, I bought them somewhere. He gave me money. VD: Did he give it to you in cash or deposit it for you? DJ: In cash. VD: How much money? DJ: Three million pesos. VD: What kind of drugs did you buy? DJ: Cocaine. VD: Where did you buy it? DJ: I bought it from some people. I can’t say (publicly) their names or the location. VD: Is it a gang? DJ: Yes. VD: Did he know you were going to buy the drugs from that gang? DJ: Yes. VD: At that time, was he a senator or the president? DJ: A senator. VD: How did you bring that drug in? DJ: I brought it through the airport. VD: You mean, on a plane? DJ: Yeah. VD: Did you get on a plane with Petro’s drugs? DJ: Yes. VD: How were the drugs packaged? DJ: In bags. VD: Like individual doses? DJ: Yes. VD: And where did you hide the drugs? DJ: In my suitcase.

In a response, Petro denied having hired women for sex and claimed that the far-right attack were the result of authorities’ failure to sustain corruption allegations.

World.title: “Brazil and Colombia need each other,” says De la Espriella
World.content:
Colombia’s President Abelardo de la Espriella recognized the election victory of his Brazilian counterpart Luiz Ignacio Lula, who defeated far-right candidate Flavio Bolsonaro on Sunday.

In a post on social media platform X, the Colombian President said that “in the Colombian presidential campaign, President Lula openly supported Ivan Cepeda, and I won. In the Brazilian campaign, I supported Bolsonaro, and Lula won.”

“Neither does Lula decide for Colombians, nor do I decide for Brazilians. THE PEOPLE DECIDE! And when the people speak at the polls, their will is respected because it is sacred,” the president added.

Lula and I have major and profound political and ideological differences, but we agree on one fundamental point: Brazil and Colombia need each other. No other consideration can take precedence over the interests of our nations. Colombia and Brazil are sister nations, facing enormous shared challenges and opportunities.

President Abelardo de la Espriella

De la Espriella stressed that “we have much to do and much work to carry out for the benefit of our peoples” an ought to “fight against narco-terrorism and illegal mining, the protection of the Amazon, and the well-being of our citizens.”

Lula was the first leftist candidate and critic of US President Donald Trump to win an election, triggering celebrations among leftists throughout the continent.

De la Espriella, a US citizen, has been among the most fanatic among Trump supporter in trying to align his domestic policies to US foreign policy.

World.title: Protesters in Santiago de Cuba Demand Freedom for Activist Who Feeds Those Most in Need
World.content:
An officer attempts to dissuade protesters outside the El Cobre police station, where they are demanding the release of Yoel Perez Serrano. / Social media

Dozens of residents, marched to the police station following the arrest of community activist Yoel Alejandro Perez Serrano.

By 14ymedio

HAVANA TIMES – Dozens of residents of El Cobre, in Santiago de Cuba, took to the streets on Saturday to demand the release of Yoel Alejandro Perez Serrano, a young activist known for his community work who had been arrested hours earlier by State Security during an operation involving armed agents.

Videos shared on social media show mothers, children, and other local residents marching with signs and banging pots and pans while chanting, “The people united will never be defeated!” The slogan, widely used by the Cuban government, has also been heard at other recent anti-government protests. Later, the crowd chants in unison, “Freedom for Yoel, freedom, freedom!” as they advance toward the police station.

Another video shows protesters confronting police officers outside the station’s doors as the officers attempt to discourage the demonstration. Meanwhile, an elderly woman near the camera comments, “They can’t beat them… we’re not living in Batista’s time!”

Opposition leader Jose Daniel Ferrer García, founder of the Patriotic Union of Cuba (Unpacu), was the first to report the young activist’s arrest, during a livestream from Miami. According to information he was receiving directly at the time, Ferrer said agents arrived at Perez Serrano’s home in Guamuta at around six in the morning, carrying assault rifles, and blocked access to the neighborhood, preventing anyone from entering or leaving.

“They stormed in with the Black Berets, armed to the teeth… They turned the house upside down, took the phones, took whatever food they found, took the cooking pots, jewelry, everything they came across,” Ferrer said. He added that officers told people attempting to pass through that “worms were not allowed through,” using the regime’s derogatory term for its opponents.

Perez Serrano, a resident of the rural community of Guamuta, in the Santiago de Cuba municipality of El Cobre, is known locally for promoting the humanitarian project “Save Cuba.” With support from Unpacu and the Cuban Resistance Assembly, the initiative provided at least one daily meal, Monday through Friday, to elderly people, malnourished children, the sick, and vulnerable families. The young man was also promoting the construction of a community medical clinic and a dining facility, which is why some residents call him “the mayor of Guamuta.”

Ferrer also said the activist devoted between 12 and 14 hours a day to his community work. “The dictatorship uses its military forces to repress a peaceful man, a noble, generous, deeply humane man who is sacrificing himself to help the people,” he stated.

Last July, Perez Serrano staged a public protest: he went out into the street barefoot and wearing only underwear, carrying a white sheet bearing the words “Freedom,” “Democracy,” “Justice,” and “Dignity.” Shortly afterward, he was summoned by the police.

Cuban authorities have not publicly disclosed Perez Serrano’s whereabouts or the formal charges against him. Social media users expressing solidarity with the young activist are demanding clarification about where he is being held, the conditions of his detention, and the justification for his arrest.

Perez Serrano’s arrest comes amid a growing wave of repression, with recent harassment and arrests of activists, opposition figures, independent journalists, and other dissident voices. In recent days, several people have been surrounded and confined to their homes, including independent journalists Yoani Sánchez, director of this newspaper, after being detained for nine hours by the political police; Adelth Bonne Gamboa, who was also detained; Camila Acosta, Yunia Figueredo, Marthadela Tamayo, and Osvaldo Navarro, as well as activist Yamilka Lafita (Lara Crofs).

Karel Daniel Hernandez, a member of the independent project Fuera de la Caja Cuba (Outside the Cuba Box), was also arrested. Meanwhile, evangelical pastor Rolando Fidel Perez Lora, known as “Pregonero de Cristo” (Herald of Christ), who is being held at Villa Marista, will be forcibly deported from Havana to Las Tunas.

The protest in El Cobre comes amid a year of intense social unrest in eastern Cuba. In Santiago de Cuba, power outages last more than 24 hours on average, and pot-banging protests have multiplied across neighborhoods. In October, Cubalex recorded 48 public protests throughout Cuba, 11 of which took place in this eastern province, the second-highest number in the country after Havana’s 15.

First published in Spanish by 14ymedio and translated and posted in English by Havana Times.

Read more from Cuba here on Havana Times.

World.title: Controversy Over Aid to Cuba’s Political Prisoners
World.content:
In their September report Prisoners Defenders documents 1,351 political prisoners in Cuba.

By Francisco Acevedo

HAVANA TIMES – This week, the confrontation between influencers Yusmani Companioni Vila and Eliecer Avila over assistance to Cuba’s political prisoners went viral.

It is a thorny issue, and personally, I believe that those who call for insubordination in Cuba do far less than they should. It is very easy, sitting comfortably in a chair in Miami, to ask those of us who live in this country to take to the streets and risk spending several years in prison.

Obviously, the income anyone legitimately earns in the United States or any other country is not meant to solve Cuba’s problems. But just as no one demands anything from them, I don’t understand why they demand personal sacrifices from others. If you ask others to give, you must be willing to give yourself. None of them has thought of creating a fund to help the families of political prisoners.

According to the nongovernmental organization Prisoners Defenders, Cuba had 1,339 political prisoners at the end of August 2026, including 155 women (a record number) and 38 people who were detained when they were minors.

The cases include people imprisoned for protesting shortages of water and electricity, filming government agents, or denouncing abuses, actions that lead to imprisonment, threats, and punishments affecting entire families.

According to the organization’s records, 463 of those still imprisoned suffer from serious medical conditions, while 54 have severe mental health disorders resulting from beatings, forced labor, involuntary psychiatric confinement, and lack of medical care.

This is an extremely high number considering the reasons these people are serving sentences, but economically speaking, it would not be so complicated to ensure that they receive the assistance they deserve for their sacrifices. Mind you, everything they have done has been without asking for anything in return, so this is not about payment, but rather an expression of gratitude and, more importantly, a message to those who are afraid to take to the streets: if they do, they will not be left without support.

I know of people who were imprisoned following July 11, 2021, and spent three years behind bars without their families receiving a single dollar from abroad. That does not seem right to me when it comes to those who continue calling for sacrifices. Those who make so much noise from the comfort of their armchairs should be the first to reach into their pockets to help those who had the courage to express their opposition to the island’s regime.

Instead, many were left to fend for themselves, and only the best-known prisoners have received any kind of assistance, and even that has been sporadic because it depends on individual efforts.

We are not naive. We know that providing assistance also involves many complications, because anyone who approaches these people, considered “untouchables” by the regime, can face consequences such as losing the right to travel to Cuba. But there are many ways to help their families. For example, a bank account can receive money without revealing where it came from.

For years, dissidents living abroad have used these difficulties as an excuse to abandon those who need help the most, including people who have no stable source of employment because the dictatorship denies them that opportunity.

It is legitimate for them to argue that those who should first bear these costs are the Castro regime’s ruling clique, owners of hotels, luxury residences, yachts, and countless other assets, as US representative Mike Waltz denounced last week at the United Nations itself.

We are fully aware that those primarily responsible for alleviating the misery they themselves have created are the dictatorship’s chosen leaders. But then don’t ask others to make sacrifices if you are unwilling to help those who will subsequently face the wrath of the Cuban government. And not just the famous ones, but anyone.

Now Companioni says he wants to create a foundation to serve the Cuban people, according to his announcement, although not specifically to help the families of political prisoners.

The confrontation ended with Companioni asking Ávila to donate $200 to a child with health problems in the central province of Sancti Spíritus. Avila countered by proposing that two children of political prisoners also receive assistance, with all those involved identified by their full names.

The political implications here are considerable, but according to Companioni, he can reach everyone. We will see whether he can actually do so and, above all, whether he is allowed to.

Helping a political prisoner does not always mean performing some grand gesture. Often, it consists of delivering a letter, obtaining medication, accompanying a family to court, keeping a copy of a document, or repeating someone’s name so that it is not erased.

It is also necessary to stand by those left outside, because prison does not confine just one person: its bars extend into the home, to the dinner table, to the bed where someone lies waiting.

Families can lose income, housing, access to medication, or educational opportunities. Sometimes they need money, food, transportation, or simply someone’s presence to remind them that they have not been abandoned. Sitting beside a mother in a waiting room, helping care for her children, listening without demanding that she be strong: these gestures carry a quiet dignity.

But helping also requires thinking about safety, because for years the dictatorship has taken advantage of the recklessness of those who want to do good too quickly.

From outside the country, people can send letters to the authorities, support amnesty campaigns, contact international organizations, share reports from the independent press, and demand that governments, universities, labor unions, and associations keep public attention focused on those behind bars.

But putting food on the table is essential, and providing transportation so that relatives can visit prisoners is indispensable, because international pressure cannot replace the struggle of those who resist from within.

No one can sustain a cause if they are silently breaking down. Dictatorships want terror to isolate us, to make each person believe they are alone, because sometimes simply knowing that they have not been abandoned is enough to make it through the night.

Lee más desde Cuba aquí en Havana Times.

World.title: Brazilian Companies Test the 5 x 2 Work Schedule Before It Takes Effect
World.content:
Brazilian supermarkets have been characterized by intense work and little rest.

By Osmel Almaguer

HAVANA TIMES – Brazil’s Congress has put an end to the “6 x 1” work schedule, guaranteeing by law two days of paid rest per week. The new law will take effect on December 16, two months after its enactment.

However, some companies have already ventured into testing the new arrangement to become familiar with it and adapt. One of them is the supermarket chain where I work.

The first challenge was finding a way to distribute days off without favoring or disadvantaging anyone. The company’s internal rule prohibiting days off on certain strategic days, such as Saturdays, had to be eliminated. Sundays also had to begin being treated like any other day, since previously each employee was entitled to one Sunday off per month.

The number of employees on each shift had to be adjusted, with less priority given to the closing shift, which is the supermarket’s busiest period.

Even so, the challenge remained of deciding when each employee would take their days off, along with uncertainty about whether additional workers would need to be hired or whether we would have to close one day a week.

All these questions were crucial because their answers would determine the company’s future.

Closing one day a week would cause enormous losses, which could eventually lead to layoffs. On the other hand, if the company decided to hire more employees, it would inevitably have to pass the financial burden on to customers through higher product prices, ultimately affecting sales.

The solution, although ingenious, was to place the burden on the workers.

The owner devised a rotating system of days off, creating four teams whose members would take their days off together. Each team would include employees from both the morning and afternoon shifts, with representatives from every department. For example, the meat department would have at least one butcher and one salesperson working each shift every day.

Each team would be identified by a color because fixed weekly days off would disappear. Instead, days off would rotate. For example, the yellow team, which rested on Monday and Thursday this week, would rest on Tuesday and Friday the following week, then Wednesday and Saturday the week after that, and finally Monday and Sunday during the last week of the cycle.

When the schedule connects with the first week of the next cycle, which begins with Monday off, the team gets two consecutive days off. This applies to all four colors. With this ingenious but complicated structure, the company ensured fairness in the distribution of days off, maintained constant staffing, and avoided having to hire additional workers.

Since each of the four teams receives two days off, there was one remaining day on which an additional team could rest. They ultimately assigned it to Monday, the day with the lowest sales. On Mondays, two teams will have the day off.

The hardest part is that, because this is still a trial, we continue working 44 hours a week, meaning an additional hour and 18 minutes has been added to each workday. Starting in December, the workweek will be reduced to 42 hours, so the increase in daily working time compared with the previous schedule will be 40 minutes.

One year after the law takes effect, it requires the weekly workload to be reduced to 40 hours, leaving an increase of just 20 minutes per workday.

The difficulty with this system arises on public holidays because, when the supermarket remains open, the law requires employees who work on those holidays to receive an additional day off as compensation. This comes at a time when staffing is already stretched thin. Some employees will have three days off during those weeks.

The measure seems designed to provide relief, and to some extent it does. But we must not forget the owners’ bottom line, and that is where things get complicated. On the one hand, we will have two days at home to rest, go out, take care of personal matters, or even earn a little extra money. On the other hand, our daily working hours and responsibilities within the company will increase.

There will also be consequences for society as a whole, but we will have to wait a little longer to measure that impact.

Read more from the diary of Osmel Almaguer here on Havana Times

World.title: It Doesn’t Take Much to be Put on the Cuban Gov. Blacklist
World.content:
Imprisoned Cuban independent journalist Henry Constantin, File photo: Facebook / Henry Constantín Ferreiro

By Lien Estrada

HAVANA TIMES – During a visit to a librarian friend in Camagüey, I learned that a meeting had been held at his workplace. At the meeting, employees were informed that everyone who contributed to the independent publication La Hora de Cuba was on the government’s blacklist (a way of saying that you are on the country’s political police watchlist). I remember bursting out laughing. Me, blacklisted by a government that calls itself Communist, just for sharing my opinions in a friend’s independent project? I found the whole thing laughable.

If I were threatening society or causing it harm in some way, whether material or spiritual, it might be understandable. But putting my observations and opinions about what I experience into writing… Is that really so dangerous that I should be blacklisted? At the time, 80% of the contributors were women.

On February 15, 2020, I was prevented from traveling to Bogotá, Colombia. I was pulled out of the line and told to wait. Then I was taken into an office, where I was informed that I was under a travel restriction. In other words, I was unable to make my planned trip, even though I had my ticket and all my documents were in order. That is what it means to be blacklisted in Cuba. Even if you complete all the required procedures, or are theoretically entitled to do so, the Communist government claims the authority to prevent you from taking certain actions or carrying out any process whenever it sees fit.

Right now, independent journalist Henry Constantin Ferreiro has been released from a punishment cell, but he has not yet been freed. He remains at a detention facility in Camagüey known as Kilo 7. He is the director of La Hora de Cuba, founded in 2013. That, too, is an example of what can happen when you are blacklisted.

Another example is when police officers show up at your home with a summons from State Security and order you to meet with them. Failing to appear can be very dangerous: you could be charged with disobedience. Under the guise of a conversation, they try to conceal the reality: it is an interrogation intended to intimidate you into stopping whatever they consider wrong (illegal), even though, from your perspective, you are simply expressing your opinions.

I imagine that, as Cuba continues to fall apart, the number of people placed on these blacklists grows by the day. The exodus becomes ever more intense. Possible solutions to the country’s economic and social chaos remain nowhere in sight. And it is painful to witness the strategies used by State Security to silence an entire people while trying, at all costs, to portray the country as peaceful and full of hope.

For my part, despite all the exhaustion, losses, and fears I have endured, I take pride in being blacklisted in my own country for these reasons. I am grateful to life for the reward I already feel in knowing that I am not among those who repress others for expressing their feelings, but rather among those who, at some point, asked themselves: Why shouldn’t I share my ideas, experiences, and aspirations…? And I did.

I trust, and my intentions and work are devoted to making it happen, that sooner rather than later I will be able to live in a free, democratic country. A country where no one is punished for creating an independent project. Where speaking one’s mind does not come at such a high price.

Read more from Lien Estrada’s diary here on Havana Times.

World.title: Why the Embargo Does Not Explain Repression in Cuba
World.content:
Berta Soler (left), photo: AP / Desmond Boylan. Camila Acosta and Yoani Sánchez, photos: taken from Facebook.

By Eloy Viera Cañive (El Toque)

HAVANA TIMES – When the Cuban government arrests a journalist or puts citizens on trial for organizing independently, a familiar explanation tends to resurface: Cuba faces exceptional circumstances because of the United States embargo, and those circumstances justify restricting rights. That argument can be challenged using legal and theoretical reasoning.

The starting point does not deny that sanctions have consequences. Recognizing that a foreign policy can harm a country is one thing; accepting that this conflict requires its rulers to persecute journalists, prevent independent associations, or prosecute people who organize on their own is quite another.

What Is the Argument for Exceptional Circumstances?

The argument works in three steps: Cuba is under threat, Cuba is subject to an embargo, and therefore those in power can do whatever is necessary to defend themselves. The practical consequence is that Cubans who disagree with government policies are expected to wait until the embargo ends before demanding their rights.

This idea is an old one, and at its core it has a concrete effect: if everything that happens on the island is the fault of the embargo and the exceptional circumstances it creates, then no one bears individual responsibility for what they do in the name of those circumstances. Defending exceptional circumstances as a justification for restricting rights amounts to defending impunity for those who carry out repression.

What Lies Between a Sanction and an Arrest?

Between a US sanction and the arrest of a journalist in Havana lies a series of decisions. Those decisions are made by people and are political in nature: officials issue orders, police officers carry them out, and authorities make choices. For that reason, the embargo cannot erase the individual responsibility of each link in that chain.

An ongoing case illustrates the point. Four men, members of the Freemasons, faced trial on November 5, 2026. The formal charge was an illegal dollar exchange transaction. The amount involved: US $300, which was used to purchase powdered milk for elderly residents of a nursing home. This is a political operation presented as a currency-related crime, and the connection between this case and any US sanction once again runs through a decision made inside Cuba.

The second example involves the independent press. Journalists Camila Acosta and Yoani Sánchez were detained on the street, prevented from moving freely, and had their equipment confiscated. Anyone who justifies these actions by invoking the embargo is siding with those who carry them out.

What Does Hannah Arendt Explain About Terror?

Hannah Arendt, the political thinker who developed the concept of totalitarianism, helps answer the fundamental question: Is violence by a totalitarian state a response to an external enemy? According to Arendt, it is not. Terror under totalitarianism does not arise solely as a reaction to adversaries who threaten the government. Rather, it is part of a system of domination that seeks to destroy pluralism and the individual’s capacity to act independently.

This leads to a conclusion applicable to Cuba: if the objective is to dominate through fear, rather than merely defeat the opposition, repression will continue even after organized opposition has been defeated. Cuba has lacked an organized opposition for years, yet repression continues.

A farm analogy helps explain it: repression functions like herbicide sprayed over an already plowed field to prevent anything from growing except what the owner wants. This interpretation is not new. It has been described since the 1940s by authors who understood totalitarianism as a model for organizing power, rather than a phenomenon tied to any particular country.

Why does a One-Party System clash with any form of autonomy?

A system that claims the right of a single party to direct society has a problem with any space for autonomy. Two examples illustrate this. The independent press is troublesome because it decides for itself what to investigate. Freemasonry is troublesome because its members chose their own leaders regardless of what the Ministry of Justice might say.

Neither case has anything to do with the embargo. With or without a blockade, with or without an embargo, any citizen who decides to organize without asking and receiving permission will run into trouble.

All states have policing functions and use force to maintain order, but that order must be enforced within legal and legitimate frameworks. Political repression in Cuba is not legitimate and often is not even legal under the island’s own laws. Regimes of this kind repress because they need to preserve their existing power structure intact. Allowing citizens to organize, obtain information, and compete politically would mean accepting the possibility of losing control.

Havel and the Independent Life of Society

To conclude, it is worth returning to The Power of the Powerless, the essay by Václav Havel, the first president of post-communist Czechoslovakia. Havel spoke of what he called the “independent life of society”: the lives of those who write, teach, create, practice their religion, or organize according to their convictions. Havel showed that, for regimes such as Czechoslovakia’s at the time or Cuba’s today, that autonomy, that independence of ordinary people, could come into conflict with the system even before it developed into explicit political opposition.

That is the conclusion tying together the arguments presented here. If conflict with those in power begins the moment someone acts independently, as with the Freemasons who buy milk for a nursing home or the journalists who go out to report, the embargo may worsen the country’s difficulties, but it does not explain why people are arrested, prosecuted, or have their belongings confiscated. Those are decisions made by people who bear responsibility for them.

First published in Spanish by El Toque and translated and posted in English by Havana Times.

World.title: Pasquale Grasso & Samara Joy– Song of the Day
World.content:
By Circles Robinson
