Target Dangote said the refinery’s initial public offering (IPO) missed its goal of 10 million retail investors.

Price 4.1 billion shares at NGN 525 (about US$0.39) each, minimum 10 shares (about US$3.90).

Dates The offer opened on 14 September 2026; closing was extended to 27 October 2026 with regulator approval.

Size At full subscription the offer is worth about NGN 2.15 trillion (about US$1.6 billion).

Unknown No official investor count, final allotment result or confirmed allotment date had been published.

What Dangote Said

Dangote spoke in Lagos at the 25th annual conference of WIMBIZ, short for Women in Management, Business and Public Service, a Nigerian business network for women. He said the IPO did not reach its 10 million target and gave two reasons: “We didn’t hit the 10 million because of time constraint, and a lot of people, they didn’t know how to access.”

He added that the number of investors had not yet been established. He also said: “I’m sure we are not that far away.”

Dangote compared the turnout with other offers, and these are his figures, which we could not verify. He said that when GTBank, the Nigerian lender formally called Guaranty Trust Bank, made its own offer, “it was 200,000” investors.

He put Safaricom, the Kenyan mobile phone operator and the largest offer there, at “less than 900,000” investors. He said Saudi Aramco, the Saudi state oil company, drew “about five million” worldwide.

In Plain English IPO An initial public offering, the first time a company sells its shares to the public.

Retail investor An ordinary person buying shares with their own savings, not a fund or bank.

SEC Nigeria’s Securities and Exchange Commission, the national market regulator.

Allotment The step when shares are formally assigned to the people who applied.

How the Offer Worked

The offer, branded The People’s IPO, put 4.1 billion ordinary shares on sale at NGN 525 (about US$0.39) each. Buyers had to take at least 10 shares, a minimum outlay of NGN 5,250 (about US$3.90).

File photo. A dredger and workers at the Dangote refinery site in Lagos, March 2020. Photo: GodwinPaya, CC BY-SA 4.0, Wikimedia Commons.

The offer opened on 14 September 2026, and Nigeria’s Securities and Exchange Commission (SEC), the market regulator, approved an extension of the close to 27 October 2026. At full subscription, 4.1 billion shares at that price come to about NGN 2.15 trillion (about US$1.6 billion).

What Is Not Known

As of 8 November 2026 there is no official investor count and no final allotment result. Applications are not the same as shares granted, so the level of demand that turns into allotted shares is still unclear.

The company and the SEC had not confirmed an allotment date by that day, although one earlier estimate pointed to 10 November. Our earlier report on the allotment and regulator approval covers the process.

What It Means for You

A minimum ticket of NGN 5,250 (about US$3.90) was small by design, so price was not the main barrier on Dangote’s account. He pointed to time and access instead.

For a reader in the United States, the missed target shows how hard it is to bring first-time savers into a young share market. Investors who follow Nigerian assets should watch the final count, because it signals how much local demand stands behind the company.

Our earlier look at how the IPO could lift Nigeria’s investor base set out what a bigger turnout would have meant. Our report on the refinery offer abroad covers how it was pitched beyond Nigeria.

Frequently Asked Questions

Did the Dangote refinery IPO reach 10 million investors?

No, according to Aliko Dangote. He blamed limited time and people not knowing how to access the offer, and said he was sure the shortfall was small.

What did one share cost in the Dangote IPO?

Each share cost NGN 525 (about US$0.39), and buyers needed at least 10 shares. That makes the minimum NGN 5,250 (about US$3.90).

When will Dangote IPO shares be allotted?

No allotment date had been confirmed by 8 November 2026, though one earlier estimate pointed to 10 November. Results then go to Nigeria’s Securities and Exchange Commission for approval.

Sources: Dangote’s remarks at the 25th WIMBIZ conference, Lagos (reported 8 November 2026); offer terms of the Dangote Petroleum Refinery and Petrochemicals FZE IPO (4.1 billion shares at NGN 525; opening 14 September and close 27 October 2026).

World.title: South Africa’s Communists Hold Back Support
World.content:
File photo, 2 March 2024. The Parliament of South Africa in central Cape Town. Photo: Dietmar Rabich, CC BY-SA 4.0, via Wikimedia Commons.

SOUTH AFRICA · POLITICS

South Africa’s Communist Party says it will give no party automatic support in the coalition talks that follow the 4 November local elections. Solly Mapaila, general secretary of the South African Communist Party (SACP), told reporters at the national results centre of the Electoral Commission of South Africa in Midrand, near Johannesburg, on Friday 6 November that the party will bring left-wing forces together.

Who Solly Mapaila leads the SACP, a party founded in 1921 and long allied with the African National Congress (ANC).

What The SACP says no party, including the ANC, gets automatic support.

Why it matters Councils without a majority after the 4 November vote need partners to choose mayors.

Prediction markets Polymarket, a prediction platform, gives Democratic Alliance (DA) candidate Helen Zille 54.5% to be Johannesburg’s next mayor (8 November, 5:00 p.m. ET).

As of 8 November 2026, 22:00 GMT.

What Mapaila Said

Mapaila said there is no automatic support for any single party, a line that includes the ANC, the SACP’s long-time ally. He said the SACP would convene a meeting of the left-wing forces that contested the election as soon as possible.

The party’s own statement of 7 November confirms that he spoke live to the media at the Results Operations Centre on the Friday. It does not set out a coalition position.

In Plain English SACP: a communist party that has long been an ally of the ANC and ran on its own this time. DA: the Democratic Alliance, a centre-right party that sits with the ANC in the national government. Hung council: a council where no party holds more than half the seats. Coalition: a deal between parties to govern together.

Download the PDF checklist

Why the SACP Is Free to Choose

The SACP has long opposed the DA’s place beside the ANC in the national Government of National Unity, the multi-party government formed after the 2024 election. It chose to stand its own candidates in the 2026 local elections rather than campaign under the ANC banner.

The party won council seats in several provinces, which is why its choices now matter. How many seats it finally holds will decide how much leverage it has, and seat counts were still being finalised.

What Happens in Hung Councils

In a hung council, parties must agree among themselves who becomes mayor and who controls the budget. Those deals are negotiated between the parties after the vote.

A street in Maboneng, an inner-city district east of central Johannesburg, in March 2020. Photo: Gsalamander, Wikimedia Commons (CC BY-SA 4.0).

Municipal councils oversee local services such as water and roads. That is why companies and investors with interests in Johannesburg, Tshwane (Pretoria) and Cape Town watch who ends up in charge.

For earlier coverage, see our report on the Johannesburg vote count and our election-day guide. For background, read about the DA’s election strategy.

What Prediction Markets Say

On Polymarket, a crypto-based prediction platform, traders gave Helen Zille, the DA’s Johannesburg mayoral candidate, 54.5% to be the city’s next mayor at 5:00 p.m. ET on 8 November, with about US$151,000 traded across the candidates in that mayoral market. These prices are bets, not polls, and they can move quickly as coalition talks develop.

Why we show this: prediction markets turn real-money bets into a live probability that moves within minutes of the news, which is why investors, campaigns and newsrooms in the United States now follow them closely. We show them next to polls and official results, never instead of them.

What It Means for You

Councils without a majority will be run by whichever coalitions form in the coming weeks. Investors and travellers should watch whether the ANC leans towards the DA, towards the left or towards a mix, because each route points to different budget and service priorities.

An SACP that withholds automatic backing makes the ANC’s coalition arithmetic harder in some councils, but it does not close any door. Much will depend on how many seats the party finally holds.

What Is Not Known

The electoral commission had not declared final results at the time of writing, so seat counts that show who holds the balance are provisional. It is also unclear what conditions the SACP will attach to talks with the ANC.

It is unclear which parties will join the left-wing meeting he proposed. A report that Mapaila also ruled out a coalition with the DA outright has not been matched by a written party statement, so we do not treat it as confirmed.

Frequently Asked Questions

Which party will the SACP back in coalition talks?

None automatically. Solly Mapaila said there is no automatic support for any single party.

What is a hung council?

It is a council where no party holds more than half the seats. Parties must then agree a coalition before a mayor can be elected.

Is the SACP still allied with the ANC?

It is a long-time ally but ran separately in this election. Mapaila said the ANC does not get automatic support.

Sources: South African Communist Party statement of 7 November 2026 (https://www.sacp.org.za/press-statements); public remarks by Solly Mapaila at the national results centre, Midrand; Electoral Commission of South Africa results portal (https://results.elections.org.za); Polymarket market page “Next Mayor of Johannesburg?” (https://polymarket.com/event/next-mayor-of-johannesburg-20260609220245506), read 8 November 2026.

World.title: Colo Colo Forward Faces Charges After Crash
World.content:
Carabineros officers outside the First Police Station in central Santiago. The Calles sin Violencia security plan gets no line of its own in the 2027 budget bill. (Photo: Carlos Figueroa Rojas, CC BY-SA 4.0, via Wikimedia Commons)

Leandro Hernández, a 21-year-old forward for Colo Colo, was arrested in Santiago, the capital of Chile, in the early hours of Sunday 8 November 2026 after a car crash. Colo Colo, a Santiago club with 34 Chilean top-flight titles before this season, went on to win the title that afternoon away at Ñublense, a club from Chillán in southern Chile, to take the Liga de Primera, Chile’s top league, for the 35th time.

Later on Sunday a court formalised the case, the step in Chile where prosecutors formally state the allegations and the court sets measures, over driving under the influence causing serious injuries. Hernández was not in the squad that travelled to Chillán, and reports say he was recovering from a sprain.

Your first month after that is US$1. Start my free brief Yes, email me my free daily brief — I can unsubscribe any time. Who: Leandro Hernández, 21, Colo Colo forward, presumed innocent.

What: Formalised, meaning formally put under investigation, for driving under the influence causing serious injuries.

Where and when: Providencia, a Santiago district, around 05:00 on Sunday 8 November 2026.

Next: The court set 120 days for the investigation. Prosecutors still await the definitive blood test result.

What We Know

The crash happened around 05:00 at the junction of Avenida Los Leones and Avenida Pocuro in Providencia. Carabineros, Chile’s uniformed national police, said a breath test showed 1.2 grams of alcohol per litre of blood.

Lieutenant Francisco Cabezas, head of the police sub-station in Providencia Sur, confirmed the figure. He said Hernández stayed at the scene until police arrived and was then detained.

The driver of the other car was taken by SAMU, Chile’s emergency medical service, to Hospital del Salvador. The driver remains in hospital with several fractures but is out of danger to life.

Andrea Contreras, a prosecutor with Fiscalía Oriente, the eastern Santiago prosecutors’ office, said early on that, preliminarily, one car went through a red light and it was the detained driver’s. Prosecutors later said the legal classification could change as the driver’s condition develops.

What Happened in Court

Patricia Ibarra, a prosecutor handling cases of suspects caught in the act at the same office, said Hernández is investigated for driving under the influence causing damage and serious injuries. At the hearing he was formalised, so the charges were formally put to him.

Ibarra said security-camera footage obtained during the investigation shows Hernández crossed the junction on a red light. She said it also shows him hitting the victim’s car at high speed, displacing it along its path.

This is the prosecution’s account of the footage. Hernández is presumed innocent, and his defence position has not been reported.

The court imposed an arraigo nacional, a nationwide travel ban, and ordered him to sign in monthly. His driving licence was retained, so he may not drive while the measure lasts.

The court set 120 days for the investigation, and prosecutors say they await the blood test results. Ibarra said he faces between 541 days and three years in prison if the serious injuries classification holds.

The prosecutor added that a fine and a possible loss of licence for five years are also possible. No court has ruled on guilt, and Hernández is presumed innocent.

What Is Not Known

The definitive blood test result for Hernández is pending. The 1.2 g/L figure comes from the police breath test, and prosecutors say the blood result is still awaited.

A blood sample was also ordered from the other driver, and no result is available. Prosecutors say the charge could still change with the injured driver’s medical progress.

It is unclear whether anyone else was in Hernández’s car, and his defence position has not been reported. The investigation has 120 days to run.

What It Means for You

Travellers who drive in Chile should note that police ran a breath test in this case. The court then imposed a travel ban, monthly signing and retention of his licence.

Chile’s justice process presumes innocence until a court rules, and none has done so here. The 120-day investigation will test the prosecution’s account of the camera footage.

The blood test result, which prosecutors await, is the next fact to watch. For more on the club, see an earlier report on Colo Colo’s jersey-brand dispute and our Santiago city page.

Frequently Asked Questions

Who is Leandro Hernández?

Leandro Hernández is a 21-year-old forward for Colo Colo, a club from Santiago. He was arrested in Santiago on Sunday 8 November 2026 after a crash.

What are the allegations?

He is investigated for driving under the influence causing damage and serious injuries. He was formalised in court on Sunday and is presumed innocent.

What did the court decide?

The court imposed a nationwide travel ban and monthly signing, and retained his driving licence. The court set 120 days for the investigation.

What did the alcohol test show?

Carabineros reported 1.2 grams of alcohol per litre of blood in a breath test. The result of the blood test has not been reported.

World.title: How Living in Costa Rica Changed the Way I See the World
World.content:
When speaking of the 1980s and 90s, I like to refer to it as the previous century. “In the previous century, we didn’t have high speed internet,” I might say. It lends a sort of historical ring to it, like a time and place long ago and far away. In a sense, it was a long way back. Last night, I laid in my bed and watched the last innings of the final game of the baseball World Series on my cell phone. I couldn’t have done that in the previous century. Times change, things evolve. People too– we change and evolve with the passing of the years as well.

This is relevant to me because I recently reread articles I wrote back in the 1990s about my life in Costa Rica. I was younger then, less patient, more ready to criticize and lampoon Tiquicia. I wrote a column, for two different monthlies that catered to the expat communities here. I was, to put it bluntly, a smart ass.

I cringed while reading some of my more pointed articles. At the time I was writing from the point of view of an American who was frustrated with the things we took for granted up there. Down here, the telephone company was still a monopoly. Cell phones were rare and the still in demand landline phones always had a long waiting list.

Many heavily traveled roads and streets were dirt, which meant dust in the summer and mud and potholes in the rainy season. Cops were either apathetic and poorly trained or corrupt predators, using the badge to solicit bribes. I ridiculed shopkeepers who whipped out their calculators for the simplest addition. The local customs, the local diet, all was fair game. My audience, which consisted mainly of other impatient expats like myself, ate it up.

I was in the early years of my second marriage– to a Tica– and the only time I wrote without a condescending voice was the occasional article about home and family life. Otherwise, I felt like my marriage to a local somehow gave me a free pass to be a self-appointed expert on everything that Ticolandia lacked.

A Tico friend who was fluent in English read my stuff and wasn’t overly offended, mainly because he shared my acerbic sense of humor. He suggested that I turn the tables, and write something from the point of view of a Costa Rican fed up with Gringo arrogance. So I did. I wrote from the perspective of a fictional brother-in-law.

I have numerous brothers-in-law, but none speak English well enough to write like my imaginary cuñado. I laid it on heavy, with over the top mentions of fat, aging gringos, their tongues coated blue from sucking on tablets of viagra, chasing girls young enough to be their granddaughters.

My narrator bragged about all the naive, panting young gringas he happily bedded and then dropped when the next Latino hungry candidate caught his eye. It was a 600 word middle finger in the face of the expat community. I had hoped it would be taken in jest, but I was wrong. One retired military vet angrily asked where my make believe brother-in-law lived, because he was ready to punch him out. Another reader greeted me with a frown and said that visiting tourists would read it and never want to come back. The response was so overwhelmingly negative that I found myself avoiding people on the street until the next edition of the monthly came out.

Imagine writing something and then hoping people did not read it. That month was a turning point in the way I looked at the place I had chosen to live. Just because most Ticos would not be able to read my articles did not make them any less nasty. It was a bit like making faces at a blind person.

I began to write from a more objective and empathetic viewpoint, with an eye toward getting to know the culture and the history. I mined my wife and her family for material– not for laughs but for honest appraisals of their lives and how they differed from my own. I sometimes made myself the butt of the joke and discovered it was okay to laugh at my own occasional ineptitude when it came to adapting to my surroundings.

And so it has followed all these years later. I am no longer an outsider, looking in, ready to ridicule. I am as much Tico as Gringo, on the inside now, where the viewpoint is completely different

World.title: Costa Rica Heads to Ecuador and Argentina Without Keylor Navas
World.content:
Bryan Ruiz will take Costa Rica into its toughest test of the year without Keylor Navas. The veteran goalkeeper was left out of the 23-man squad Ruiz named Friday for friendlies against Ecuador and Argentina, his first matches since the federation confirmed him as permanent head coach.

Costa Rica plays Ecuador on Friday, Nov. 13, at the Estadio Olímpico Atahualpa in Quito, with kickoff at 6 p.m. Costa Rica time (7 p.m. ET). It then faces Argentina on Tuesday, Nov. 17, at the Estadio Mario Alberto Kempes in Córdoba. Ruiz said in television interviews last week that Navas has a minor problem in one knee that requires a medical procedure and about 10 days of rest. The coach said the Pumas UNAM goalkeeper had offered to join the squad anyway, but that his priority was for Navas to recover properly.

Without Navas, the job in goal falls to Patrick Sequeira of Portugal’s Casa Pia, Abraham Madriz of Saprissa and Bayron Mora of Alajuelense. Ruiz has said he wants to use the window to evaluate which goalkeepers he can count on for the World Cup cycle ahead. Two other players are out injured. Defender Jeyland Mitchell of France’s Strasbourg and striker Alonso Martínez of New York City FC were both ruled out with physical problems.

The headline return is Manfred Ugalde. The Spartak Moscow striker is back after serving a suspension and has scored 10 goals this season, six in the Russian league and four in the cup. Copenhagen defender Kenay Myrie also returns to the squad. The group leans heavily on the domestic league, with 16 locally based players and seven playing abroad. Alajuelense has eight players, more than any other club. The squad has an average age of 25.8, and nine players are under 23.

Argentina, runners-up at the 2026 World Cup, will be playing its first matches since Lionel Messi’s farewell from the national team on Oct. 6 against Benin. Coach Lionel Scaloni has named a 28-player squad and will face Uruguay at La Bombonera in Buenos Aires on Nov. 13 before hosting Costa Rica in Córdoba.

The Ecuador match brings its own challenge. Quito sits at roughly 2,850 meters (9,350 feet) above sea level, among the highest capitals in the world, and the match will be Ecuador’s first at the Atahualpa in more than nine years. The two teams have met 12 times, with Ecuador winning six and five ending in draws. Costa Rica’s only win came in their first meeting, in 1992. Ruiz took over as interim coach in late September after the federation fired Fernando Batista. He won both of his Nations League matches, beating Nicaragua 3-0 and Haiti 2-0, before being given the job permanently in October.

The squad begins training Monday, Nov. 9, and travels to Quito on Wednesday, Nov. 11, flying on to Córdoba the day after the Ecuador match. Four more players, Alberth Barahona of Saprissa, Claudio Montero and Geancarlo Castro of Cartaginés, and José Vega of San Carlos, will train with the group through Nov. 11 but are not part of the 23.

Goalkeepers: Abraham Madriz (Saprissa), Bayron Mora (Alajuelense), Patrick Sequeira (Casa Pia, Portugal).

Defenders: Aarón Salazar (Alajuelense), Alexis Gamboa (Alajuelense), Diego Mesén (Cartaginés), Francisco Calvo (Nacional, Uruguay), John Paul Ruiz (Alajuelense), Joseph Mora (Saprissa), Juan Pablo Vargas (Puebla, Mexico), Kenay Myrie (Copenhagen, Denmark), Yerlan Sosa (Alajuelense).

Midfielders: Andrey Soto (Saprissa), Celso Borges (Alajuelense), Douglas López (Cartaginés), Gabriel Leiva (Sporting), Gian Mauro Morera (Cartaginés), Roan Wilson (Alajuelense).

Forwards: Carlos Mora (Universitatea Craiova, Romania), Josimar Alcócer (Sparta Prague, Czech Republic), Josimar Méndez (Sporting), Kenyel Michel (Alajuelense), Manfred Ugalde (Spartak Moscow, Russia).

Both matches will be Ruiz’s first against South American opposition as Costa Rica’s coach, and the trip to Córdoba gives his young squad a measure of how far it has to go.

World.title: Two Bull Sharks Found Dead in a Guanacaste Estuary They Had Never Been Known to Enter
World.content:
Two bull sharks, rays, pufferfish and several other fish species have been found dead in an estuary at Playa Langosta, just south of Tamarindo on Guanacaste’s northern Pacific coast, and environmental authorities are now investigating what killed them. The sharks drew the most attention. There had been no previous record of bull sharks entering this estuary, according to reports from the community.

The animals were found in the San Francisco Estuary at Playa Langosta, not the better-known Tamarindo Estuary that separates Tamarindo from Playa Grande. The Ministry of Environment and Energy (MINAE) said it viewed the deaths with concern and that the National System of Conservation Areas (SINAC), working with other competent institutions, will investigate the causes.

The ministry said the assessment will examine the natural closure of the estuary’s mouth, water quality, and possible effects of changing conditions linked to El Niño, including warmer water and shifts along the coast. The mouth of the estuary closed naturally about a week before the discovery, after sand built up where it meets the ocean.

The Tamarindo Integral Development Association (ADIT), which alerted SINAC and requested attention to the case, said the agency attributed the changes at the beach to strong tides and sand accumulation at the outlet. The association has also filed a complaint over the deaths.

Estuaries depend on a steady exchange of water. Seawater pushes in on high tides while rivers bring fresh water from inland. When river flow is too weak to keep the mouth open, a sand bar can form and cut that connection, trapping water and wildlife inside. One hypothesis is that the animals became trapped behind the sand barrier. Even at high tide, the water may not have been deep enough for them to cross back to the sea.

Another possibility is a sharp drop in dissolved oxygen, which can be fatal to fish and other aquatic species in enclosed water. Bull sharks are among the few shark species that tolerate fresh and brackish water, and they are a familiar presence along Guanacaste’s coast, where the species is celebrated each year at the Bull Shark Festival in Playas del Coco.

MINAE stressed that none of these explanations has been confirmed and said it would be premature to attribute the deaths to any specific cause before a technical assessment is complete. The closure comes during a dry year on the Pacific side, as El Niño drought conditions grip Guanacaste. Authorities are also monitoring the estuaries at Avellanas, Bejuco, Ostional, Junquillal and Bongo-Ario, some of which have closed naturally as well.

MINAE asked the public not to alter the estuary mouth without authorization from environmental authorities while the assessment is underway. ADIT likewise urged residents not to dig or bring in machinery to open it, and asked the community to report any new incidents at 8704-6444.

SINAC said it is continuing to monitor the site and other stretches of the coast as the investigation proceeds.

World.title: French Woman Found Shot Dead Inside Her Guanacaste Home
World.content:
A 64-year-old French woman was found dead with a gunshot wound to the head inside her home in Cabo Velas, Santa Cruz, on Friday morning, according to the Judicial Investigation Agency (OIJ). The OIJ received the report at 8:04 a.m., after a worker employed by the woman discovered her body inside the house in the area known as Lomas de Matapalo. The agency identified the victim by the name Bourgeus.

Agents from the OIJ’s Santa Cruz regional office carried out a preliminary examination at the scene and determined that she had a gunshot wound to the head. Authorities are treating the case as a possible homicide. The body was sent to the Judicial Morgue, where an autopsy will establish the cause and manner of death. As of Sunday morning, the OIJ had not publicly reported any arrests, named a suspect or described a possible motive.

Cabo Velas is a coastal area on Guanacaste’s northern Pacific coast that takes in the beach communities of Flamingo, Potrero, Brasilito and Conchal, along with residential developments and vacation rentals in the hills behind them. The case is the second death of a foreigner under investigation in the district in recent months. In August, the OIJ treated the death of a 75-year-old U.S. citizen found in Cabo Velas as an apparent homicide possibly linked to a robbery at the property. In June, a German resident was found stabbed to death on a farm elsewhere in the canton of Santa Cruz.

Elsewhere in Guanacaste, a 22-year-old woman suspected in the killing of an American businessman in Playas del Coco was ordered held in pretrial detention for one year in October while prosecutors build their case. The OIJ asks anyone with information about the case to contact its confidential line at 800-8000-645. The investigation is ongoing.

World.title: Costa Rica’s First Female Extradition Suspect Faces Legal Battle Over Transfer to United States
World.content:
The first Costa Rican woman ordered extradited to the United States will not be handed over for now. Defense attorneys for Shirley Gómez, known as “La Güera,” and her partner, Frankin Viveros, have appealed a San José Criminal Court ruling that authorized their surrender to U.S. authorities. The appeal suspends the transfer while a higher court reviews the case.

The court approved the extradition of both on September 14. They are wanted by the U.S. District Court for the District of Arizona on charges of international cocaine trafficking and conspiracy to distribute cocaine knowing it would be imported into the United States. The defense filed its challenge within the three-day deadline set for appeals.

Neither has been convicted, and the U.S. allegations have not been tested at trial. Gómez, 39, is the only Costa Rican woman to face an extradition proceeding since the country began allowing the surrender of its own citizens in 2025. Viveros, 50, was born in Colombia and later became a naturalized Costa Rican citizen.

The appeal centers on retroactivity. The defense argued that applying the reform to Article 32 of the Constitution would be a retroactive use of the law, because the conduct attributed to the couple began in July 2024. That was nearly a year before the amendment took effect on May 28, 2025.

The judge rejected that argument. The ruling held that international drug trafficking is a continuing offense. It also found that the U.S. filings describe alleged activity lasting until October 1, 2025, well after the reform came into force, so the new extradition framework applies.

The defense also challenged the role of the U.S. Drug Enforcement Administration (DEA). It argued that DEA agents made undercover drug purchases in Costa Rica without a formal international cooperation agreement approved by the Foreign Ministry. The judge ruled that the validity of that evidence is for the courts in Arizona to decide at trial, not for an extradition proceeding.

The retroactivity question has already produced split outcomes. In February, the Criminal Sentencing Appeals Court in San José upheld the extradition of former security minister and magistrate Celso Gamboa Sánchez and of Edwin López Vega, known as “Pecho de Rata,” because their alleged conduct extended past May 28, 2025.

In the same ruling, the appeals court blocked the extradition of a third suspect, Jonathan Álvarez Alfaro, after finding that all the acts attributed to him took place before the reform. Gamboa and López Vega were flown to Texas on March 20, becoming the first Costa Rican nationals extradited in our history.

So far, cases where the alleged conduct runs past the May 2025 cutoff have held up on review, and cases where it ends before that date have not. The Gómez and Viveros appeal will test how the courts treat an investigation that began in mid-2024 and continued into late 2025.

According to the U.S. indictment cited in the extradition ruling, Gómez and Viveros acted as local leaders of a trafficking network with links to Colombia, Panama and Mexico. U.S. prosecutors allege that the couple received cocaine flights from Colombia about every two weeks and ran safe houses used by the organization.

The indictment links the network to the seizure of 273 kilograms (602 pounds) of cocaine hidden in two vehicles in August 2024. U.S. prosecutors identify Óscar Enrique Virula Arredondo, a Guatemalan national based in Panama, as an alleged organizer of shipments by speedboat and aircraft. Six alleged leaders of the network were indicted on October 1, 2025.

U.S. filings state that DEA informants recorded negotiations on video and made controlled drug purchases in San José and in Cali, Colombia. None of these allegations has been proven in court. Costa Rican authorities arrested Gómez and Viveros on March 13, 2026, in an operation coordinated with the DEA. Viveros is held in the maximum-security unit at La Reforma prison. Gómez is held at the Vilma Curling Rivera women’s prison.

If the appeal fails, the handover would still not be immediate. In the Gamboa case, the appeals court made the transfer conditional on formal U.S. assurances that neither man would face life imprisonment or a sentence longer than 50 years, the maximum allowed under Costa Rican law. No date has been announced for a ruling on the new appeal.

The decision will help define how far Costa Rica’s 2025 extradition reform reaches, especially in long-running trafficking investigations that began before citizens could be surrendered abroad. Other extradition cases involving Costa Rican citizens are still before the courts.

World.title: Costa Rica Prosecutors Investigate Pico Blanco Plane Crash That Killed Five
World.content:
Prosecutors in Costa Rica have opened a negligent homicide investigation into the November 2024 crash of a commercial passenger plane on Cerro Pico Blanco, in the mountains above Escazú, that killed five of the six people on board. The Pavas Prosecutor’s Office is handling the case, which aims to determine who could be named as a suspect. No suspects have been publicly identified.

Negligent homicide applies when a person causes another’s death by failing to meet a required duty of care. The prosecutor’s office opened the case after receiving a direct criminal complaint. By then, the Judicial Investigation Agency (OIJ) had already begun its own inquiry.

The aircraft, a single-engine Cessna U206G with registration TI-GER operated by Aero Caribe, crashed on Pico Blanco on November 25, 2024, while flying from Barra del Tortuguero on the northern Caribbean coast toward Tobías Bolaños International Airport in Pavas. Weather had closed the Pavas airport, and the flight was diverted toward Juan Santamaría International Airport before radar and radio contact were lost.

Those killed were Captain Mario Miranda Ramírez, Ruth Pamela Mora Chavarría, Jean Franco Segura Prendas, Gabriela Calleja Montealegre and Enrique Castillo. The sole survivor, Paola Amador Segura, then 31, was found alive that night after a search and rescue operation that stretched for hours across steep, forested terrain.

A provisional statement issued in December 2025 by the accident investigation unit of the Civil Aviation Technical Council found that Aero Caribe’s operating certificate, issued in 2023 and valid until 2031, did not authorize flights in low-visibility conditions. The document classifies the accident as controlled flight into terrain, in which an aircraft under the pilot’s control is unintentionally flown into the ground.

According to the report, weather stations near the route recorded light rain and mist. Satellite imagery showed dense cloud moving from the Caribbean into the Central Valley, producing fog banks along the second half of the flight, and investigators concluded the crash happened in daylight under adverse weather conditions.

The last radar return showed the plane entering the Pico Blanco area at about 240 kilometers per hour (149 mph). It first struck the treetops roughly 20 meters (66 feet) above the ground, hit the slope at an estimated 15-degree angle and slid about 45 meters (148 feet) before stopping beside a tree trunk.

The wreckage came to rest on a hillside at 2,237 meters (7,339 feet) above sea level. The engine separated from its mount while still producing power and was found about 50 meters (164 feet) from the main wreckage. The report identified no irregularity on the part of the pilot, who held a valid medical certificate and had logged 1,160 flight hours, 830 of them on the aircraft type. Toxicology tests on the pilot and the occupant of the right-hand seat found no alcohol or psychoactive substances.

Investigators stressed that the document is technical and provisional, intended to prevent future accidents rather than assign blame. Its findings remain subject to change, and conclusions and safety recommendations will appear in a final report that has not yet been published.

Aero Caribe has disputed the preliminary findings. The company argues the report is imprecise and leaves out variables that, in its view, shield air traffic controllers at the Civil Aviation Authority (DGAC) from responsibility.

In May 2025, the airline and relatives of Miranda, Mora and Castillo filed a criminal complaint for negligent homicide against DGAC air traffic control officials. The complaint alleges that controllers instructed the pilot to hold 1,981 meters (6,500 feet) on a route toward mountainous terrain, in a sector where official charts set a minimum altitude of 3,048 meters (10,000 feet), even though their radar showed obstacles and minimum heights.

Criminal lawyer Federico Campos Calderón, who represents the airline and several of the families, said at the time that they were seeking criminal accountability for the deaths and compensation for damages. The Union of Air Traffic Control Professionals (Sitecna) has called it hasty, premature and irresponsible to issue opinions or assign responsibility before the final technical report is released. The union has urged all parties, particularly Aero Caribe, to wait for the official results.

The DGAC has previously said it could not comment while the technical investigation remains open. No one has been charged, and the prosecutor’s inquiry remains at a preliminary stage. Small aircraft are a common way to reach remote destinations such as Tortuguero, which has no road access. Earlier this year, three people survived a Cessna crash in La Fortuna after an engine failure on takeoff.

Aviation investigators have not announced a release date for the final report on the Pico Blanco crash, which is expected to set out the causes of the accident and safety recommendations.

World.title: Prison Cases at Costa Rica’s Constitutional Court Jump 124% Amid Crackdown
World.content:
Legal challenges over conditions in Costa Rica’s prisons have more than doubled in five years, as the government’s push for a harder prison regime runs up against its legal duty to feed, house and provide medical care to the people it holds. The Constitutional Chamber of the Supreme Court (Sala IV) received 2,130 prison-related cases in 2020.

By 2025 the figure had reached 4,780, an increase of 124%. The cases include amparo petitions, which seek protection of constitutional rights, and habeas corpus petitions, which challenge the legality or conditions of a person’s detention. The pressure has not eased this year. Between January and September 2026, the court logged 4,139 such cases, an average of about 460 a month compared with roughly 398 a month in 2025. Prison matters were the second most frequent subject of the court’s rulings.

The Ombudsman’s Office has recorded a parallel rise. It received 2,681 prison-related complaints in 2025 and another 1,350 between January and July of this year, most of them concerning failures to provide medical care. The complaints describe spoiled food, portions too small to sustain inmates and missed meals for people with conditions such as diabetes who require specific diets. They also cite long delays in medical treatment and difficulty reaching health services.

Twenty people in custody died of natural causes between January and August 2026. Human rights organizations have pointed to the figure as a sign of possible shortcomings in medical care and nutrition inside the prison system. The rise in cases tracks a deliberate hardening of prison policy. Under the previous administration, the Justice Ministry cut back family and conjugal visits, reduced parcels and removed commissaries and cash from maximum-security units.

Since taking office in May, the current government has gone further, removing microwaves and televisions from cells. The most consequential change came on June 1, when Justice Minister Gabriel Aguilar banned daily food deliveries from families across the prison system. Relatives may now bring only two containers of food on visiting days, down from as many as 15 a day previously.

Aguilar said 158,000 parcels were sent to a prison between January and May and that inspecting them required as many as 200 prison officers a day. He said the deliveries were being used to smuggle drugs and that some inmates ran an illegal trade in food and clothing. He has said the government will not reverse the measure and that the prison system can feed its roughly 20,000 inmates.

President Laura Fernández backed the restrictions and urged the minister to tighten them further. She rejected the official description of prisons as institutional care centers, saying they are simply prisons for people convicted of serious crimes. Maureen Esquivel, spokesperson for Familias Penitenciarias Unidas, a group of inmates’ relatives founded in 2019, said families began noticing deficiencies more sharply in 2025, after the new prison rules took effect.

With outside food barred, she said, inmates now depend entirely on prison meals, which she described as never having been sufficient, and many suffer stomach problems including gastritis and ulcers. Esquivel attributed much of the increase in court filings to the restrictions. She said her group has prepared template amparo petitions so families can file cases themselves, and that some relatives turn to the court because inmates are sleeping on floors or in bathrooms.

Overcrowding compounds the problem. The National Mechanism for the Prevention of Torture, the oversight body attached to the Ombudsman’s Office, reported that the number of inmates held above official capacity rose from 2,772 in 2020 to 6,164 in February 2026. The Justice Ministry put the adult prison population at a record 21,173 on Oct. 7, up from 14,907 at the end of 2022. Ministry officials have put overcrowding at 59% and said the new high-containment prison will bring it down to about 15% once it is full.

That facility, the Center for High Containment of Organized Crime, or CACCO, opened on Oct. 14 at the La Reforma complex in Alajuela with space for 5,100 inmates across five modules. It received its first 123 inmates on Oct. 26 and is expected to reach full capacity in December. At its inauguration, Fernández pledged that the human rights of those held there would be respected.

The conditions under which inmates are held are not a matter of discretion. Costa Rica’s Constitution prohibits cruel or degrading treatment, and the country is bound by the American Convention on Human Rights. The United Nations Standard Minimum Rules for the Treatment of Prisoners, known as the Nelson Mandela Rules, call on states to provide food of adequate nutritional value and health care equivalent to that available in the wider community.

The government’s approach has already drawn institutional criticism. In late September, the Ombudsman’s Office condemned a video in which Aguilar confronted inmates, describing their treatment as humiliating. The Justice Ministry has not publicly addressed the court figures. Its stated position has been that the restrictions are necessary to restore order and security inside the prisons.

The growth in prison cases is also adding to the workload of the Constitutional Chamber itself, which had resolved 37,706 matters of all kinds by the end of September and projects more than 45,000 rulings for the year. Whether the CACCO eases conditions in the rest of the system, or simply shifts the pressure, may show up first in the number of cases reaching the court in the months ahead.

World.title: Fire Chief Says Fernández Gave No Order on Ambulance Deal, but a Memo Cites Her
World.content:
The director of Costa Rica’s Fire Department, Héctor Chaves León, said last night that President Laura Fernández gave no instruction on how to buy 40 ambulances now under review by anticorruption prosecutors. Internal procurement documents, however, cite a presidential instruction as the basis for the emergency purchase.

The Fire Department, known here as the Cuerpo de Bomberos, awarded the contract on Sept. 28 to the SGSV-Bem Estar consortium for $13.88 million, about $347,000 per vehicle. It invited only that consortium to submit an offer, using Article 66 of the General Public Procurement Law, which allows exceptional contracting in emergencies.

The consortium joins SGSV Soluciones Tecnológicas Integradas with the Brazilian ambulance maker Bem Estar. Two people linked to SGSV, its legal representative and regional sales director and a company officer who has held that post since 2015, bought political debt bonds from Fernández’s Pueblo Soberano party during the presidential campaign. According to the Supreme Elections Tribunal (TSE), the purchases totaled 43 million colones and 9 million colones, or roughly $95,600 and $20,000.

The TSE has opened a preliminary administrative inquiry into the economic solvency of the two campaign financiers. The inquiry began on Sept. 17 and was expanded on Nov. 4. Separately, the Deputy Prosecutor’s Office for Probity, Transparency and Anticorruption (FAPTA) opened a case on its own initiative on Nov. 2 into alleged influence peddling against the public treasury. No one has been charged, and the investigation is at a preliminary stage.

At a press conference yesterday, Chaves said Fernández had not told the Fire Department which contracting method to use, how many ambulances to buy or which suppliers to consider. He said those were the institution’s own decisions and asked anyone claiming otherwise to produce written evidence such as emails or messages, adding that none exists.

Chaves acknowledged that the president asked in July for prehospital emergency care to be strengthened. He said it was the government’s Health Sector Council that later instructed the Fire Department to speed up the process.

A recommendation report addressed to Chaves and dated Sept. 25, three days before the award, states that the urgent purchase was carried out under the instruction of President Fernández and a July 31 agreement of the Health Sector Council. The report traces that reasoning to a Sept. 4 memo from the department’s Operations Directorate, and a Sept. 10 compliance report from its procurement office treats the presidential instruction as the trigger for the urgency.

Asked about the document, Chaves said it refers to the president’s general instruction to promote prehospital care in the country, not to the purchase method or the choice of suppliers. Two local suppliers that had submitted quotes during the department’s market study were not invited to bid. Comercializadora Técnica Industrial del Oeste (Cotisa) offered all 40 units for $11.57 million, or $2.31 million less than the winning price, while AutoStar Vehículos offered $13.74 million. The Fire Department rejected both, citing delivery times of 240 days as excessive.

Chaves said the speed of delivery was vital. He said the competing offers ranged from 240 to 280 days, while the Brazilian manufacturer proposed 100 days, and that he expects the units next March, whereas other purchasing routes could have pushed delivery into 2027 or 2028.

Under the contract, the supplier is to deliver one prototype first and the remaining 39 ambulances within 100 days of the department’s approval of that prototype. An inspection of the prototype at the factory in Brazil is scheduled for Nov. 19 and 20. The Fire Department has acknowledged that its own failure to specify the exact color code for its red fleet altered the contract schedule, and it approved an extension.

The tender required proof that the bidder had built at least 200 ambulances for five clients over the previous two years. Bem Estar submitted certificates for 210 units for two Brazilian clients. AutoStar asked for the procedure to be annulled over what it called serious defects, and the Fire Department rejected the request as untimely.

Chaves said the ambulances would be advanced life support units equipped with ultrasound, defibrillators and ventilators, assigned to the Southern Zone, Limón, Guanacaste, the Northern Zone and the Central Valley. He said the country handles about 50,000 accidents a year. He also said the Fire Department dealt only with the Brazilian manufacturer, which then sought out a Costa Rican partner to form the consortium.

Chaves said he had sent the full procurement file to the Prosecutor’s Office and to FAPTA, and that he is willing to cooperate with the Comptroller General’s Office. The file is public and can be consulted on the government’s SICOP procurement platform.

Gabriela Chacón, executive president of both the National Insurance Institute (INS) and the Fire Department, announced at Casa Presidencial on Oct. 7 that the 40 ambulances had been awarded and were expected to enter service in February 2027. On Nov. 2, she said she did not know the details of the procedure and attributed its approval to the department’s director or to its administration.

SGSV has won at least five public contracts since 2022, four of them through special procedures, and it was part of a consortium that bid in 2024 for the contract behind the digital marchamo vehicle sticker, a tender the INS later declared void. Opposition lawmaker Claudia Dobles of the Coalición Agenda Ciudadana described the links between the president’s campaign financiers and the winning consortium as vulgar and sharply questioned the process.

The contract remains in force while prosecutors and electoral authorities carry out their reviews and none of the people or companies involved has been accused of a crime.

World.title: Lemonal stevedore slapped with additional charge of damage to property, allowed to remain on previous bail
World.content:
Lemonal stevedore slapped with additional charge of damage to property, allowed to remain on previous bail

By Breaking Belize News Staff: Twenty-seven-year-old Jerry Malique August, a stevedore of Lemonal Village, appeared in the Belize City Magistrate’s Court on Friday, November 6, 2026, where he was charged with damage to property in connection with an incident for which he had previously been charged with aggravated assault.

August appeared before a magistrate in Court #5, represented by attorney Oscar Selgado, and pleaded not guilty to the new charge.

Prosecutors allege that on August 24, 2026, in Bermudian Landing Village, August damaged a four-door Chevrolet Cruze valued at $3,000.

During the arraignment, the magistrate raised the issue of bail, prompting Selgado to explain that his client had already secured High Court bail in connection with an aggravated assault charge arising from the same incident.

Selgado argued that requiring August to obtain bail again would be unfair, particularly since both charges originated from the same circumstances.

The prosecutor agreed with the submission, and August was allowed to remain on his existing bail without having to secure a new bail arrangement.

August had previously been remanded to the Belize Central Prison following his arraignment on the aggravated assault charge before successfully obtaining bail through the High Court.

His next court appearance is scheduled for November 13, 2026, when he is expected to receive disclosure in relation to both charges.

World.title: ‘Our lives were shattered’: Family of slain police officer Arsenio Cus delivers emotional statement as Khris Rosado awaits sentencing
World.content:
‘Our lives were shattered’: Family of slain police officer Arsenio Cus delivers emotional statement as Khris Rosado awaits sentencing

By Breaking Belize News Staff: An emotional victim impact statement from the sister of Police Constable Arsenio Cus brought the devastating consequences of his death into focus in the High Court on Friday, November 6, 2026, as businessman Khris Rosado continued to await sentencing for the fatal traffic accident that claimed the officer’s life.

Rosado, the owner of Thirsty Thursday nightclub, previously pleaded guilty to causing death by careless conduct in connection with the July 28, 2025 collision on the Philip Goldson Highway.

During Friday’s proceedings before Justice Derick Sylvester, Cus’s sister, Paulina Cus, described the profound grief and emotional trauma her family has endured since losing her brother more than a year ago.

“Our lives were shattered. His death left a void that altered our future,” she told the court, describing how the tragedy had changed their family forever.

She recalled how her brother was always willing to help his family, including providing financial assistance during the COVID-19 lockdowns.

Paulina also spoke about the trauma of seeing her brother’s lifeless body in his police uniform and the painful experience of identifying him for a post-mortem examination.

“Do you know what it was to identify your own brother for a post-mortem?” she asked.

She described suffering flashbacks and lasting emotional distress, while reflecting on the birthdays, holidays and family gatherings that her brother would never again share with his loved ones, including his daughters.

The emotional testimony also appeared to affect Rosado, who was visibly moved as he listened to the family’s account of their loss.

Justice Sylvester subsequently adjourned sentencing until Monday, November 9, 2026.

As previously reported by Breaking Belize News, Rosado pleaded guilty on June 16, 2026, to causing death by careless conduct following the fatal collision between Miles 6 and 7 on the Philip Goldson Highway.

Cus, 38, of Silver Creek Village, was riding his motorcycle from Ladyville toward Belize City when a vehicle entered his lane and struck him, causing severe injuries. He subsequently died from multiple blunt force traumatic injuries.

Police later located Rosado at his Ladyville residence, where investigators found a damaged 2009 Honda Ridgeline pickup truck believed to have been involved in the collision.

Forensic testing subsequently linked blood recovered from the vehicle to the deceased officer.

Rosado’s sentencing has been postponed several times since his guilty plea, including an October 1 adjournment.

The family now awaits Monday’s proceedings, when Justice Sylvester is expected to deliver his sentence.

World.title: Garrick Hemmans remains behind bars as firearm assault trial set for March 2027
World.content:
Garrick Hemmans remains behind bars as firearm assault trial set for March 2027

By Breaking Belize News Staff: Thirty-five-year-old Garrick Hemmans, also known as “Tamalito,” remains on remand at the Belize Central Prison after appearing in the Belize City Magistrate’s Court on Friday, November 6, 2026, in connection with allegations that he fired several shots at a man in August.

Hemmans, who remains unrepresented, appeared before a Senior Magistrate in Court #2, where he was provided with 19 pages of disclosure and 12 photographs as evidence in the case.

The magistrate advised Hemmans to familiarize himself with the disclosed material and prepare for his trial, which has been scheduled for March 10 and 11, 2027.

As previously reported by Breaking Belize News, Hemmans was arraigned on August 28, 2026, on a charge of aggravated assault with a firearm upon 32-year-old technician Emory Williams. He pleaded not guilty and was denied bail due to the firearm-related nature of the offence.

The charge stems from a shooting incident on Rio Bravo Crescent in Belize City on August 25, 2026.

According to police, Williams was standing outside a residence around 7:28 p.m. when a maroon Nissan Murano approached from the direction of Tapir Street.

Williams alleged that Hemmans, who was seated in the front passenger seat, pulled out a firearm and fired several shots in his direction.

Fearing for his life, Williams reportedly ran behind a concrete fence and escaped without injury. The vehicle then sped away toward Fabers Road Extension.

Police processed the scene and recovered two expended 9mm Aguila shells and a bullet fragment.

Investigators subsequently located the Nissan Murano parked outside a residence on Jimmy Dyer Street, where another expended 9mm shell was reportedly discovered on the front passenger seat.

The vehicle was impounded, and Hemmans was detained later that night before being formally charged.

Hemmans remains on remand pending trial.

World.title: Devaun Garcia, previously freed of murder charge, granted $6,000 High Court bail in ammunition case
World.content:
Devaun Garcia, previously freed of murder charge, granted $6,000 High Court bail in ammunition case

By Breaking Belize News Staff: Twenty-one-year-old Devaun Garcia, who previously walked free from a murder charge after the prosecution discontinued its case, has been granted $6,000 bail by the High Court in connection with the alleged possession of three live rounds of ammunition.

Garcia appeared before Justice Candace Nanton on Friday, November 6, 2026, represented by attorney David McKoy, who argued that his client deserved bail, particularly since his two co-accused had already been released.

The prosecution raised no objection to bail, and Justice Nanton granted Garcia bail of $6,000, with two sureties of $3,000 each, subject to several conditions.

Garcia must report to the Raccoon Street Police Station every Monday and Friday, observe a curfew between 11:00 p.m. and 5:00 a.m., surrender his travel documents and refrain from contacting prosecution witnesses. He is also prohibited from leaving Belize without permission from the High Court.

The charges stem from an August 2 incident on Caesar Ridge Road in Belize City, where Garcia, along with 19-year-old Esmond Austin and 19-year-old Isani Conorquie, allegedly possessed three live 9mm Aguila rounds without a firearm licence.

According to police, officers responding to reports of an abandoned vehicle near the Yabra Bridge discovered a damaged black Ford Escape. During a search of the vehicle and surrounding area, officers reportedly recovered three live rounds of ammunition.

Police further allege that Garcia attempted to interfere with the investigation by grabbing ammunition from the vehicle and throwing it toward a nearby canal. The ammunition was subsequently recovered, and Garcia was additionally charged with obstruction.

All three men appeared in the Belize City Magistrate’s Court on August 3 and were initially remanded to the Belize Central Prison.

Garcia has previously faced several serious criminal allegations. In April 2025, he and George Hyde were freed from a murder charge involving the 2021 killing of 18-year-old Eaton Thompson of Mahogany Heights after the prosecution entered a nolle prosequi when its main witness could not be located.

In February 2026, Breaking Belize News reported that Garcia was remanded on firearm and ammunition charges following an incident in which police allegedly used drone surveillance to track a suspect who discarded a loaded 9mm pistol. Garcia had also previously secured bail in connection with an armed robbery allegation involving the BelChina Bridge.

Garcia maintains his innocence in the latest ammunition case, claiming that the bullets were planted by police.

His next scheduled appearance in the Magistrate’s Court is December 9, 2026.

World.title: Ector Soler to stand trial for manslaughter in fatal Ladyville motorcycle collision
World.content:
Ector Soler to stand trial for manslaughter in fatal Ladyville motorcycle collision

By Breaking Belize News Staff: Twenty-nine-year-old Ector Danielo Soler has been committed to stand trial in the High Court for manslaughter by negligence in connection with a fatal motorcycle collision that claimed the life of 40-year-old Celia Josefina Carballo Pleitez De Lazaro in May 2025.

Soler, a maintenance worker of Airport Plaza and resident of Ladyville, appeared unrepresented before the Chief Magistrate in the Belize City Magistrate’s Court on Friday, November 6, 2026, where his preliminary inquiry concluded through a paper committal.

He was informed that his case would proceed to the January 2027 session of the High Court, expected to commence in mid-January.

As previously reported by Breaking Belize News, Soler was arraigned on September 26, 2025, on three indictable traffic offences: manslaughter by negligence, causing death by careless conduct, and driving without due care and attention.

The charges stem from a collision on May 25, 2025, between Miles 9 and 10 on the Philip Goldson Highway in Ladyville.

According to police investigations, 24-year-old Francisco Cortez was travelling southbound on a green Lifan motorcycle with his common-law wife, Celia, riding as a passenger.

The couple had reportedly stopped to purchase food near the Lord’s Bank junction and were returning to their home on Baltimore Road.

As Cortez approached the intersection with Marage Road around 8:00 p.m., he reportedly activated his left indicator and slowed down to make a turn.

Police allege that a red Ducati Monster motorcycle driven by Soler collided with the rear of Cortez’s motorcycle, throwing all three individuals onto the pavement.

Cortez and Soler sustained injuries, while Celia, a Guatemalan national, was transported to the Karl Heusner Memorial Hospital, where she was pronounced dead on arrival.

Following an investigation, the case file was submitted to the Office of the Director of Public Prosecutions, which directed police to charge Soler.

Soler was initially granted bail of $7,000 following his September 2025 arraignment.

He will now face trial in the High Court, where the prosecution will be required to prove its case.

World.title: 19-year-old charged in $89,900 Burrell Boom home invasion granted $8,000 High Court bail
World.content:
19-year-old charged in $89,900 Burrell Boom home invasion granted $8,000 High Court bail

By Breaking Belize News Staff: Nineteen-year-old Adam Abraham Reynolds, accused of participating in a violent home invasion in Burrell Boom Village in which a businessman was tied up at gunpoint and robbed of nearly $90,000 in cash and valuables, has been granted bail by the High Court.

Reynolds, a labourer of Vista Del Mar, Ladyville, appeared before Justice Candace Nanton on Friday, November 6, 2026, after spending 16 days on remand at the Belize Central Prison.

His attorney, Norman Rodriguez, successfully applied for bail after the prosecution, representing the Office of the Director of Public Prosecutions, raised no objection.

Justice Nanton granted Reynolds bail in the sum of $8,000, with two sureties of $4,000 each, subject to several conditions.

Reynolds must report to the Burrell Boom Police Station every Friday, surrender his travel documents, refrain from contacting the complainant directly or indirectly, and remain at least 100 yards away from him. He must also attend all scheduled court appearances and avoid being arrested and charged with any new offences while on bail.

As previously reported by Breaking Belize News, Reynolds was charged with aggravated burglary following an October 14 home invasion at El Chiclero Resort in Burrell Boom Village.

Police allege that four men entered the residence of a 53-year-old businessman around 4:50 a.m., assaulted him, restrained him with duct tape and ransacked his home.

The intruders reportedly escaped with $30,000 in cash, gold chains valued at $12,000, electronic equipment and a 2017 Toyota Rush SUV valued at $45,000. The total value of the stolen property was estimated at $89,900.

Police subsequently located the stolen SUV in Santa Familia Village, Cayo District, on October 15. Investigators allege that Reynolds was inside the vehicle when officers approached, but he sped away before crashing and abandoning it.

Reynolds later surrendered to police in the presence of an attorney on October 19 and was arraigned the following day.

His next court appearance is scheduled for December 9, 2026.

Reynolds remains accused of aggravated burglary and has not been convicted.

World.title: Belize Zoo becomes a classroom for young conservationists
World.content:
Belize Zoo becomes a classroom for young conservationists

By Breaking Belize News Staff (HP): Students from St Martin de Porres School traded their classroom for the Belize Zoo last week, spending a morning learning about conservation through games, interactive booths and hands on activities.

The event took place ahead of the evening celebration of Voices of the Corridor, which marked the completion of a key link in the Maya Forest Corridor.

Students explored aquatic ecosystems with the Savanna Field Station and the Wildlife Conservation Society (WCS). They learned about the work of conservation rangers and field enforcement with WCS and Monkey Bay Wildlife Sanctuary, and got a closer look at biodiversity monitoring through camera trapping and bird observation.

Other booths focused on the dangers of fire and how teams protect the Maya Forest Corridor, as well as the role of sustainable agriculture in keeping landscapes healthy. Those activities were led by WCS, the Belize Maya Forest Trust, the Foundation for Wildlife Conservation, the Savanna Field Station and the Ministry of Natural Resources, Petroleum and Mining.

Organizers said the day gave students an introduction to the people, knowledge and daily work behind conservation in Belize.

World.title: Happy birthday, Shyne: Belize’s comeback king turns 48
World.content:
Happy birthday, Shyne: Belize’s comeback king turns 48

By Breaking Belize News Staff (HP): Today, Belizean rapper and former politician Moses “Shyne” Barrow turns 48.

Like him or hate him, few Belizeans have lived a story quite like his.

Born in Belize City on November 8, 1978, Shyne grew up in Brooklyn, New York, and burst onto the hip hop scene in the late 1990s with Bad Boy Records. His debut album went platinum and made him one of the most talked about young voices in the music industry.

Then it all came crashing down. Shyne was convicted in connection with a 1999 New York nightclub shooting and spent close to a decade in prison. After his release, he was deported to Belize in 2009.

Many would have given up. Shyne didn’t.

He rebuilt his life at home, entered politics and in 2020 won the Mesopotamia seat in Belize City. He went on to become Leader of the UDP and Leader of the Opposition. Even after losing his seat in the 2025 general election, he has kept pushing forward.

This year, Brooklyn Borough President Antonio Reynoso declared April 25, 2026 as “Shyne Day” in Brooklyn and presented him with the Key to Brooklyn. He has also told his story in the Hulu documentary The Honorable Shyne, carrying Belize’s name to audiences around the world.

Happy birthday, Shyne.

World.title: Armed gangs backing squatters
World.content:
An aerial view of Flamingo Beach, Trelawny, where some of the land has been overrun by squatters, stalling a proposed development that includes resort and entertainment facilities in addition to a residential component.

Well-known attorney Gordon Brown says armed gang members from outside the community are thwarting his six-year-long effort to curb squatting on sections of 167 acres of land he owns in Flamingo Beach, Trelawny. Even a private security firm, he said, has refused the job of protecting the property from being further overrun.

Brown has submitted plans to the National Environment and Planning Agency (NEPA) and the Trelawny Municipal Corporation (TMC) for an integrated development that includes resort and entertainment facilities in addition to a residential component, but he is unable to proceed as the land is littered with structures at various stages of construction.

In his view, apart from the TMC, which has publicly expressed concern about the stalled development, little has been done by State agencies to help him with his battle.

“Whilst I cannot say exactly how many acres have been squatted upon, what is unequivocal is that, since 2020, both personally and through the several attorneys who have assisted, I have made assiduous efforts to contain the festering squatting problem,” Brown said in a written response to the Jamaica Observer’s Real Estate on the Rock.

“In the supervening five years since filing suit I have respected the rule of law and complied with all orders of the court. Regrettably, my experience has proven yet again that, in our nation, those who abide by the law and show restraint are met with contempt or indifference. Those who flout it are given safe harbour by the authorities, especially if muscular action is visited upon them,” he added.

He listed a litany of failed attempts to arrest squatting taking place on the land, starting with his lawyers’ appeal to NEPA in early May 2020 to use its powers to “require the demolition of all illegal structures on the property”. He said NEPA posted warnings on all the structures on the site, but they were ignored and the squatting continued unabated.

According to Brown, in mid-January 2021, his attorneys served all the squatters with notices to quit, referencing NEPA’s May 2020 warning. In February, he said, his lawyers wrote to the superintendent of police for Trelawny, alerting him that his team may be needed if the squatters got rowdy after being served with notices to leave the property. Then in March 2021 he tried to hire private security to patrol and protect the land in an effort to move the process along.

“They carried out investigations and declined to accept the assignment, as their checks revealed the credible presence of armed gang members from other communities who were in place to resist any efforts to impede the illegal construction,” said Brown.

He said his lawyers then appealed to the commissioner of police, in late March 2021, alerting him to “rampant suspected criminality” in the area and the impact it was having on his property.

“This was copied to several parties, including the chief of defence staff, member of parliament and others, but we received no response, save from the TMC,” said Brown.

“Early April 2021 I met with the TMC to present the estate’s case and its need for coordinated action by the municipality and the police to curtail and demolish the structures. Subsequent to a meeting with the deputy superintendent of works of the TMC on-site, the property caretaker was ambushed by armed thugs who warned him not to erect the signage that we had agreed with the TMC should be put in place to advise the squatters of imminent action,” he added.

Brown then sought help from the courts, filing a suit in May 2021 in which he named all the then-known squatters

— about 10 of them

— and provided a “generic description” of a handful of others who were not known. In the suit, he sought an order for possession of the property. According to Brown, he was “granted an injunction restraining the squatters from damaging the site’s ecology, carrying out further construction activity upon the premises, and other relief”.

However, that did nothing to rein in the squatters, some of whom claim to own the land they occupy.

“Since that time there has been an explosion in the number of occupants. The injunction has been renewed pending final determination of the matter by the court. The occupants have falsely claimed that they have been in occupation of the premises for a period that would give them a possessory title to the parts of the premises occupied by them, but produced no evidence to support their claim. I have tendered video, aerial and geospatial evidence of the state of the premises as of the date of the court action [and before] which prove their claims untenable,” said Brown.

In explaining his claim to the land, he said he was the administrator of the estate of the late Carl Fei, an American who owned several parcels of land in Jamaica, including “approximately 167.25 acres at Flamingo Beach, Trelawny, near to the border of St James”.

“I was registered as the proprietor on November 11, 2005, but have been engaged with the affairs for the estate for many years prior to that date,” Brown told the Sunday Observer.

The Flamingo Beach land issue came to public attention in September when Falmouth Mayor C Junior Gager raised an alarm during the TMC’s regular monthly meeting. He cited Flamingo Beach as one example of the growing problem of squatting in Trelawny which has resulted in the municipal authority being inundated with complaints from frustrated landowners.

“There is a submitted plan here for that property that will help to build Trelawny, but we cannot proceed because there is this problem of squatting,” Gager said of Flamingo Beach, naming Brown as the owner of the land.

During the meeting the mayor also referenced significant squatting on sections of 344.5 acres of land in an area called Tilston, Hague, where one acre has been informally settled; and Hague Cave Island, where four acres of the property have similarly been occupied. He also pointed to Cooper’s Pen in Trelawny

— where approximately 12 acres of the property had been informally occupied

— which had made news headlines following an August 11 early-morning demolition of about 20 structures by the private owner.

There is also a major development planned for Cooper’s Pen and the landowner has been fighting a legal battle for years to get squatters off the land. Brown pointed to similarities between that case and his struggles at Flamingo Beach.

“This débâcle bears all the portents of another Cooper’s Pen, only with more visible, painful results,” he said.

He outlined the ways in which State agencies have failed to act effectively.

“The police have been given statements by parties duped into ‘purchasing’ lots at Flamingo Beach by unscrupulous persons and received necessary information to investigate and prosecute same. No one has been charged,” Brown said.

“I have made several overtures to the police in Trelawny and at the level of the high command for their assistance to address the burgeoning criminality, but with only token support, limited to police escorts whenever court orders are posted on-site. Even equipment bearing insignia and markings of the Jamaica Defence Force has been observed on the site, engaged in illegal activity,” he alleged.

Insisting there can be no excuse for squatting, Brown lay the blame at the feet of successive administrations who have skirted around the issue. He said there has been a “collective refusal” to craft plans to install basic infrastructure on the 550,000 acres of land believed to be in the Government’s possession; pursue transparent divestment methodology and pricing; and put in place the technical staff and enforcement personnel needed in municipal corporations across the country to review and inspect building sites.

Pointing out that the bulk of the country’s housing stock is informal but it is “futile” to demolish them because of non-compliance, Brown argued that many squatters genuinely want to be legitimate owners of property, but the State has failed to put the necessary channels in place.

“Many squatters pay for lands which they occupy

— just not the legitimate owner. Squatters spend large sums for palatial homes on lands they do not own. There is clearly no issue of their ability to afford land, which represents 10 per cent or marginally more of the cost of overall development,” he argued.

“Given an opportunity to acquire lands owned by Government legitimately, those in search of lands [who become squatters] would do so. However, the State must make lands affordable, while ensuring that both the subdivisions and intended development of them are orderly and comply with structural integrity for the safety and health of the intended inhabitants. Formal infrastructure in the form of paved roads and electricity are never a feature of communities that have been squatted,” Brown said.

“These services typically follow after an informal settlement has been established and there is pressure on a member of parliament to support it. These become far more costly to implement because there is no planning of these communities; service roads are twice as long, etc. It is therefore only logical for the State to lead with low-cost, basic infrastructure

— serviced lots in locations with sufficient proximity to main/arterial roads, etc,” Brown added.

He made it clear, however, that he was not excusing the behaviour of those who have stalled his plans at Flamingo Beach.

“These [plans] cannot exist nor be pursued in the context of lawlessness and criminality,” Brown told the Sunday Observer.

World.title: Nurse offers land for proposed Portland hospital
World.content:
Public health Nurse Elaine Linzi making the offer to give up five acres of her land as a site for a new hospital in Portland, last Thursday at the opening of Katus Blakey Dental Clinic in Manchioneal. (Photos: Everard Owen)

MANCHIONEAL, Portland — Hearing Health and Wellness Minister Dr Christopher Tufton saying Government was scouting land on which to house a hospital planned for Portland, United Kingdom citizen and public health Nurse Elaine Linzi last Thursday offered up unused property she owns in the parish. She now works at Manchioneal Health Centre in Portland.

“There seems to be a challenge re identifying a suitable area for the hospital and I’m offering you my land. I have five acres,“ she told Tufton as guests, gathered for the opening of Katus Blakey Dental Clinic in Manchioneal, listened keenly.

”Think out of the box and not always think [about only] Port Antonio. We have wonderful places right here in the east — flat, accessible, cool. All you need is electricity, water, and staff. It is between Kensington and Rural Hill,” Linzi added.

The health minister welcomed the offer, and asked for a round of applause for Linzi.

“It’s a good offer. Send us a note and… all of the team will look at it. The truth is, there’s a lot that goes into building a facility, recognising the needs of the parish in its totality. It’s not necessarily the capital; it could be anywhere on the outskirts… I’m just thinking of a convenient location” said the minister.

“Government is committed and have started a process with land identification. Over the next year we’ll give an update as to where we are to give you a hospital commensurate with the development of the parish,” he promised.

As Tufton noted, the existing hospital in Port Antonio is no longer able to meet the needs of the parish. He pointed out that earlier in the week, Member of Parliament for Portland Eastern Isat Buchanan had raised the issue in the House.

“The truth is, the demand on the facility is higher than the facility’s capacity to deliver. The location of the facility is a problem, because it has no space for expansion. The access to the facility is a challenge, especially when you have an emergency,” he said.

Tufton also pointed to the challenge being faced by many expectant mothers who now have to seek medical care at Annotto Bay Hospital in St Mary.
