“We have to find a way to ensure that we develop our health services in keeping with what is required and the growth and the future prospects of the parish,” said Tufton.

Ahead of Linzi’s offer he indicated that talks are under way with Port Authority of Jamaica, which has plans for a development that is being worked on. He said there have also been discussions with the North East Regional Health Authority, National Land Agency, and “the Urban Development Corporation because they are the largest repository of land”, and there has been a suggestion that he should have a discussion with the College of Agriculture, Science, and Education “because they have a lot of land”.

“We’re going to do some sort of comparison to see what is available and what is the most suitable,” said Tufton.

He added that the Government would draw on lessons learned from projects such as Cornwall Regional and the Children’s Hospital in Montego Bay, as well as work done at Black River, Spanish Town, Falmouth, and Kingston Public hospitals.

“I’m here to announce to you that we appreciate and understand what is coming for Portland. We know that health services have to be improved, and we’re making provisions; we will keep you and your representatives abreast as to the progress. I’m hoping that during the course up to the end of this financial year, maybe sometime in the new year… we should at least have some idea as to where that is,” Tufton shared.

World.title: Romain Virgo bares his soul on My Woman & I
World.content:
Virgo’s latest single, My Woman & I was released on Friday, October 30, 2026Contributed

For Romain Virgo, vulnerability has never been something to shy away from. Whether through his music or in his personal life, the reggae singer believes there is value in allowing people to see the person behind the performer, even when the emotions being shared are difficult.

That openness is at the heart of his new single, My Woman & I, a deeply personal offering inspired by a period of uncertainty in his own relationship and a reminder that committed love is not necessarily love without struggle.

Written about a year ago, the song emerged at a time when Virgo and his wife, Elizabeth, were navigating some of the challenges that can arise in any relationship.

Rather than suppressing those feelings, the singer turned to music to process them, recording what was on his heart.

“Relationships and everything that comes with it, those moments when it feels like things aren’t going to work, that’s how I was feeling about my personal relationship in the moment,” he told the Jamaica Observer. “Relationships are like a roller-coaster ride and sometimes, as musicians, the best way to handle these things is to put it in the music. I put pen to paper and I just wrote how I was feeling and recorded it.”

For Virgo, the decision to draw on such a personal experience speaks to his commitment to authenticity. He wants listeners to recognise themselves in his music, particularly those who have experienced the uncertainty that can accompany a relationship while still believing in the possibility of working through it.

“The world, by now, knows me and knows that I am not afraid to show the real side of me. Whether through music or in real life, I am authentic always,” he said.

That willingness to be candid extends to the conversations surrounding the song at home.

When Virgo first played My Woman & I for his wife, her response was not quite the enthusiastic reception he might have hoped for.

“If I’m going to be as vulnerable as possible, the first time she heard this song, she hissed her teeth while laughing at the same time,” he recalled. “I would trouble her and tell her this is the song that she will probably hate the most.”

The reaction, however, appears to have softened. Virgo recently caught her singing the song, prompting a laugh when she remembered that she had supposedly disliked it.

For him, the moment reflects a growing understanding of how music allows him to work through his experiences, including those that are deeply personal.

His creative process, he explained, means drawing on what he is feeling in the moment rather than shying away from difficult emotions. More importantly, the song is not about presenting a relationship as perfect. Instead, Virgo hopes it will resonate with people who understand that commitment is sometimes tested by circumstances that cannot be resolved overnight.

“I hope this single will give people who look to music for their peace and to express themselves. I hope it gives them a sense of belonging,” he said. “I hope they hear someone who has been through some tough times when it comes to relationships and now that it just something that comes with the territory.”

His message to listeners is simple: Difficulty does not have to mean defeat.

“When you’re committed to something, you have to find ways to work through issues and keep showing up, don’t give up on love,” he said.

Though written a year ago, My Woman & I is only now making its way to listeners. Virgo explained that the timing was not right for its release earlier, particularly in the aftermath of Hurricane Melissa, when he delayed the release and promotion of several songs already in the pipeline.

With the time now right, the single will also serve as a precursor to a larger project currently in development. Sources suggest a 2027 release on Ineffable Records.

“This track will lead into something bigger. We working on a project that we can’t give too much details on just yet. Just know this single is a part of a bigger picture,” he said of the track produced by Mr G and revives the classic Dub Fire rhythm made famous on Dennis Brown’s Promised Land.

For now, My Woman & I offers listeners an intimate look at an artiste willing to turn his own experiences into music, with a message that extends beyond romance. Love, as Virgo presents it, is not simply about the moments when everything falls into place, but also the willingness to keep showing up when it does not.

My Woman & I was released on Friday, October 30, and is available on all digital platforms.

World.title: The 15-year challenge
World.content:
Inter Miami’s Lionel Messi (second left) deftly scores past Cavalier’s goalkeeper Vino Barclett (#1) as Jeovanni Laing (left) looks on during the Concacaf Champions Cup second-leg round-of-16 match at the National Stadium on Thursday, March 13, 2025. (Photo: Garfield Robinson)

When Mount Pleasant FA and Cavalier FC represented Jamaica in the Concacaf Champions Cup it was a proud moment for local football. However, their participation also highlighted the gap between Jamaican clubs and the region’s top teams.

Clubs in Major League Soccer (MLS) and Mexico’s Liga MX have far greater financial resources, with budgets exceeding US$10 million (over $1.5 billion). This puts them well ahead of teams in the Legend Jamaica Premier League (JPL).

The difference is not just about players’ salaries. It also comes down to facilities, technical support, sports science, preparation, and the cost of competing internationally.

Mount Pleasant have done more than most Jamaican clubs to improve their operations. Under owner Peter Gould, the St Ann club has built its own training academy, hired experienced technical staff, and established itself as one of the leading teams in the Caribbean.

However, even with that investment, Mount Pleasant still have work to do to compete with the best in Concacaf.

Mount Pleasant Sporting Director Paul Christie says the club has made significant progress since 2022, but is still some way from achieving its continental ambitions.

“In 2022, when we were given the privilege of carrying out the mandate by owner Peter Gould, Mount Pleasant was 172nd in Concacaf’s club rating and 35th in the Caribbean,” Christie told the Sunday Observer. “Since then, we’re on the cusp of breaking into the top 50 in Concacaf, and we’re the #1 team in the Caribbean. Until we are able to satisfactorily compete at the Concacaf level, there’s still a lot of work to be done.”

The challenge extends beyond individual clubs. Professional Football Jamaica Limited (PFJL) Chief Executive Officer Owen Hill says the league must address several problems if Jamaican teams are to compete more regularly at the regional level.

One of the biggest challenges is the lack of stadiums that meet Concacaf’s requirements. This often forces clubs to play home matches overseas, increasing their expenses and taking away the advantage of playing in front of their supporters.

Hill pointed to Portmore United’s Caribbean Cup campaign as an example of the problem. He explained that the reigning JPL champions had to play a home match in Trinidad because suitable venues were unavailable in Jamaica.

“That was a home game – in Trinidad, why?! Trinidad is not even close to Jamaica, but the reason they played in Trinidad is primarily because of the economics of it. It’s cheaper to play in Trinidad than Jamaica,” Hill told the Observer.

Hill explained that the National Stadium was booked for the Independence Gala period, while Sabina Park was being used for the Caribbean Premier League. He said Portmore had no other suitable venue available and had to travel to Trinidad to fulfil the fixture.

Playing home matches overseas means clubs miss out on ticket sales and other income that could be used to improve their operations. It also limits the support they receive from local fans.

Hill wants clubs to eventually have their own stadiums that meet minimum Concacaf standards. This would not only give them a suitable home venue for international matches but also allow them to build stronger connections with their communities and generate income.

The PFJL is also working with Concacaf and the Jamaica Football Federation to adjust the domestic calendar around international competitions. However, Hill says clubs must also plan their training programmes and squad depth because fixture clashes cannot always be avoided.

The financial demands of international football are another concern. Hill says the PFJL supports clubs that qualify for regional competitions, while Concacaf subsidies have increased. However, the cost of travel, maintaining squads, and preparing for matches remain major challenges.

“Our clubs and, by extension, our economy, are not about to sustain that consistently, so what we try to do is incentivise the opportunities but also ensure that education happens very early,” Hill says.

The PFJL also wants Jamaican clubs to become stronger brands that can attract investment from the Diaspora and international sponsors. Hill admits that the response from overseas Jamaicans has so far been limited, but believes clubs can become more attractive to investors as the professional product improves.

The league has already reached some important milestones, including an expanded sponsorship agreement with Legend Beer, 360-degree broadcast coverage, and venue partnerships with Independence Park Limited.

Hill also sees the proposed redevelopment of Montego Bay Sports Complex as a model for future projects. He believes Jamaica needs at least 10 stadiums of a similar standard over the next decade to improve the facilities available to clubs and other sporting events.

However, better stadiums alone will not close the gap. Hill says clubs also need proper gyms, recovery facilities, and technical analysts who can study opponents and help coaches prepare their teams.

He believes the lack of those resources also affects how Jamaican football is viewed internationally. While the country’s players are recognised for their speed and athleticism, tactical preparation remains an area that needs improvement.

The long-term plan is to build clubs that can generate enough income through sponsorship, commercial activities, and player transfers to reinvest in their operations.

“When I talk about the vision, I’m saying no less than 10 to 15 years of building and toiling before we see some actual results, such as players being sold for solid amounts of money; transfer fees are now back into the club’s ecosystem to develop the club’s infrastructure at a minimum standard,” Hill says.

World.title: Growing appetite for the snip
World.content:
Medical diagram illustrates the human male reproductive system displaying the anatomical structures involved in a vasectomy procedure including the vas deferens ligation and cauterisation process alongside detailed notes on post-vasectomy physiology and the resulting blockage of the normal sperm pathway.

SOME are fathers who say their families are complete. Others are young men in their 20s and 30s who have decided that they never want children. They are among men seeking vasectomies in the Corporate Area, where some urologists say interest and requests are rising in their private practices.

The slight but notable increase suggests that more men are embracing an active role in contraception, say urologists, who point to varied motivations behind their patients’ decisions.

Consultant Urologist Dr Belinda Morrison-Blidgen, co-owner of the newly opened Urology and Cardiothoracic Centre in St Andrew, told the Jamaica Observer that while she has not observed a similar trend in the public health system, requests for the procedure have increased at her private practice.

Known colloquially as the snip, the procedure involves the cutting and then clamping or sealing of the vas deferens, a tube on each testicle that carries sperm to the urethra.

Morrison-Blidgen estimates that she now performs 10 vasectomies annually, a figure she acknowledged may appear modest, but represents a significant shift from a time when she performed none.

“For the men who already have children, they tend to say that they’ve had enough and they don’t want any more. And that’s usually after they’ve had like two or three children,” she said, adding that those patients also cite the expense of child-rearing as motivation for electing the procedure.

For some, the decision is also about sharing a responsibility traditionally left to women. Morrison-Blidgen said some men are choosing vasectomies to ease the burden on their wives, who have experienced side effects from other contraceptive methods.

“The men may have to put on a condom, but the women really are the ones who use permanent methods like implants or tubal ligation. Some of these women have side effects from those options. Women who take the pill, implants or hormonal options, they may have side effects,” she said.

According to the American College of Obstetricians and Gynaecologists (ACOG), hormonal birth control like pills, patches, and vaginal rings often cause mild, temporary side effects, including spotting between periods, mild nausea, headaches, sore breasts, and weight gain.

Conversely, hormone-free options do not alter the body’s chemistry but can cause some discomfort where they are placed. According to the Mayo Clinic, a non-hormonal copper intrauterine device (IUD) avoids side effects like mood swings or nausea, but it can result in heavier menstruation and worse cramps.

“A lot of my patients are married men, and they are sympathetic to their wives and the side effects that they have from these pills or injectables, and they say, okay, they’re going to take that stress away from them,” Morrison-Blidgen said.

“The joy of it for the men is that with the vasectomy, it’s a local outpatient procedure done under local anaesthetic. So they don’t have to be put to sleep and it’s very quick, quick recovery time, minimal side effects, and it’s effective. So, they’ve opted to do that,” explained Morrison-Blidgen.

But perhaps the more intriguing aspect of the growing interest, she noted, is that young, childless men are also seeking vasectomies, having decided they do not want children at all.

“I’ve had a few of them who are in relationships, they’re not married, but they’ve just decided they do not want to have children at all. A lot of times they do not come with their partners, it’s just that they’ve never seen themselves having children and they don’t want it to ever happen.

These are men in their 20s and 30s who have made this decision, and I have to respect that,” she said. Morrison-Blidgen further noted that men who come seeking the operation are usually well informed about the process and are just hoping to move on with their sexual life without having to worry about pregnancies or their partners experiencing side effects.

“Most of the patients who come, they have already done their reading, and their background information is there. So, they know it is permanent. They know it’s simple and easy. They know that nobody can even tell that they’ve done it easily because it doesn’t change your rectal function.

“It doesn’t change your semen volume. You will still ejaculate; you still have a normal semen volume.

It’s just that there will be no sperm in that semen,” she said, adding that while a reversal is possible, the men who visit her practice want a permanent solution.

Dr Elon Thompson, owner of Westminster Medical Centre in St Andrew, told the Sunday Observer that relative to his private practice, those going through with the procedures are middle-aged men, who have children.

“Mostly they would be referrals or people who have developed a need, having thought about it and consulted with their partner, that this is the direction in which they would want to go.

But in terms of referrals for vasectomy, I would say, maybe three in a sixmonth period. But most times it is patients that I am already managing that are interested in doing it,” he noted.

The consultant urologist, who is also a Government senator, shared that he has seen growing interest among younger men, though many may decide against the procedure after learning more about it.

“Interest is one thing and actually doing the procedure is another. So, persons will want to find out what the process is, cost, and things like that and get an idea of what will happen after the procedure: ‘Will I have any pain? Will I have any side effects?’ — those things before they make their final decision.

I will say interest is definitely more than, let’s say five, six years ago, but in terms of the actual procedure, some persons are not necessarily sold for whatever reason,” he explained.

Reasons for electing the operation varied among his patients, he noted. But the most central motive, Thompson said, was to prevent pregnancies. “The main benefit clearly is if someone has satisfied themselves along with their partner, of course, that they want no children or no more children.

This is probably one of the most elective of procedures because persons really have to come forward to have it done after having a discussion with their partner.

And it has to be an informed discussion and decision on the part of the patient,” Thompson said, adding that some patients chose vasectomies because they considered the procedure less risky than the female alternative, tubal ligation.

One father of two teenagers told the Sunday Observer that the idea of getting a vasectomy gained traction over dinner as friends who had already had the procedure shared their experiences.

The man, who is between 40 and 50 years old, said that the prospect of going home the same day appealed to him. He also wanted to enjoy his sex life with his wife without worrying about another pregnancy.

He said condoms and the pill had not worked well for them, and a vasectomy would cost less than having his wife’s tubes tied. “A handful of people recommended that this was one of the best ways they found work best in their marriage.

And it was easy to do. It was a one-day procedure versus being in the hospital for three, four, five days,” he explained.

What he had not counted on was the pain. He recalled feeling a tugging sensation in his lower abdomen during the procedure, which he said took nearly two hours.

“It’s local anaesthesia so you might have a little bit of pain. None of that was explained by my friends.

So, what was supposed to be like a 45-minute to an hour session, it ended up being like an hour and a half, almost two hours for me, which was a little rough,” he recalled.

The recovery, however, was a matter of days and much simpler than what his wife would have to endure with a tubal ligation, he reasoned.

“I don’t think I even needed the medication for more than two days. I normally run and I was able to run a 3K in maybe a week after the whole thing,” he told the Sunday Observer.

He encouraged other men who feel their families are complete to consider a vasectomy, weigh the costs, and check what their insurance covers. “I think if you look at that option and the weigh the pros and the cons as the man, it’s beneficial, because the woman has to go through so much more,” he said.

“I know Jamaicans are still of the mindset that ‘man fi breed woman’ and all sorts of things. But to be honest, as much as Minister [of Health and Wellness] Tufton says we need to have more children, children are expensive.

“So, for those of us who are in committed relationships and planned for kids, if you want to… also have sex without the fear of pregnancy, condoms that you’re allergic to, or pills that cause people to put on weight or have side effects, this is one of the best approaches to take because you don’t have to worry about any of that,” he said, while urging men and their partners to be aware of their status, stressing that a vasectomy does not prevent sexually transmitted diseases.

In August this year a BBC story on why more men in their 20s in England are having vascetomies, reported National Health Service data showing that 26,385 vasectomies were performed at hospitals and clinics during 2024-25.

“This was 16 per cent more than in 2023-24,” the BBC report said.

“Men aged 35-39 had more procedures than any other age group, about 8,400 in 2024-25,” the report added.

Additionally, the BBC reported that “there had also been a slight rise on the previous year in younger men choosing to have the snip — about 950 vasectomies were performed on men aged under 30 in England during 2024-25”.

World.title: Loyalty At Heart
World.content:
In Citizen Magazine Issue 005, award-winning actress Sheryl Lee Ralph shares the spotlight with her daughter, stylist Ivy “Coco” Maurice, for “Loyalty at Heart”. (Photo: Rasaan Wyzard)

Plus…

For Sheryl Lee Ralph, style is a family affair. The Emmy, Critics Choice and Independent Spirit Award-winning actress joined her daughter, stylist Ivy “Coco” Maurice, for a striking fashion moment in Citizen Magazine Issue 005. Photographed in Kingston, Jamaica, in March, the mother-daughter duo wore designs by Bianca Saunders and Diotima, respectively, for ”Loyalty at Heart”, an editorial styled by Mecca James-Williams. Curated in the wake of Hurricane Melissa, the visual tribute turns its lens on Jamaican families, celebrating the bonds that endure and a shared allegiance to one another and home. A sentiment captured in its central message: “Loyal to one another, home in Jamaica”.

World.title: Man suspected of drowning in Alligator Pond
World.content:
People enjoying the river and sea at a beach in Alligator Pond. A no swimming sign is seen in the background. (Photo: Kasey Williams)

MANCHESTER, Jamaica — A man is suspected to have drowned in Alligator Pond, south Manchester on Saturday.

Police identified him as Simon Newman, a resident of Downs near the Manchester/ St Elizabeth border.

Preliminary reports are that about 4:00 pm Newman was swimming in a river when he got into difficulty and went underwater. His body was later removed from the river. Police were called and he was pronounced dead at hospital.

The area, known as River, has been the scene of numerous drowning incidents over the years, especially on holidays.

In August 2023, two people drowned at the location. A local community hero, who saved people from drowning at the same location, also drowned upstream in the river in Alligator Pond, a week after rescuing several people.

READ: Alligator Pond hero found dead in river

A police source said in January 2025 Newman’s twin brother was one of two people who died in a crash on the Buttup main road in south Manchester.

— Kasey Williams

World.title: Manning Cup quarterfinalists decided
World.content:
In this file photo, Kingston College’s Deshawn Byfield (left) and Mona High’s Jermaine Morgan vie for the ball during the ISSA Walker Cup final at Stadium East. (Photo: Naphtali Junior)

Former champions Jamaica College (JC), Mona High and Wolmer’s Boys were the last three qualifiers to the ISSA Manning Cup quarterfinal following the final set of games in the round of 16 on Saturday.

JC drew 1-1 with Eltham and finished second on five points in Zone 4. Eltham won the group with seven points. Norman Manley defeated Tivoli Gardens 4-2 and grabbed third place with three points. Tivoli Gardens ended with a point.

In Zone 1, defending champions Excelsior came from behind to beat St George’s College 2-1 and consolidated their position at the top with nine points. The Light Blues finished at the bottom with a point.

Mona High booked their spot with a comprehensive 4-0 win over St Catherine High and finished with six points and second spot in Zone 1 as St Catherine were eliminated with a point in third spot.

Wolmer’s Boys blanked Hillel Academy 2-0 and finished second in Zone 3 with six points and into the last eight. St Andrew Technical High School (STATHS) topped the group with maximum nine points after whipping St Jago High 5-0.

Kingston College defeated Calabar 1-0 to top Zone 2 with maximum nine points. Calabar, who had already qualified for the quarterfinal, were second with six points.

The quarter final pairings have been decided with Group A consisting of Excelsior high, Eltham High, Wolmer’s Boys and Calabar High while Group B will have KC, STATHS, Mona and JC.

–Howard Walker

World.title: Wirecard fugitive claimed he toppled Sebastian Kurz in messages to Russian spy
World.content:
If substantiated, Marsalek’s claims would be a clear indicator of the Russian state interfering directly in the political leadership of an EU country. The Kremlin has long sought to sow division and destabilize governments across Europe, according to assessments by multiple security agencies.

Marsalek is one of the world’s most wanted men and has been on the run since June 2020 when his company, German tech giant Wirecard, collapsed with a €1.9 billion hole in its books.

Since his escape, he has been accused of working for the Kremlin for more than a decade while British police say he is involved in espionage on an “industrial” scale. He is wanted for fraud and is being investigated for spying in several European countries, including his native Austria.

Kurz was the world’s youngest leader when he first became chancellor of Austria in 2017 at the age of 31. But his stratospheric rise, which saw him hold the post twice, was marred by corruption allegations, including that public money was used for political advertising on his behalf.

When members of Marsalek’s spy ring, led by Roussev, were arrested in the U.K., police seized hundreds of thousands of messages detailing operations plotted from British soil.

Some of these messages were shared with authorities, including Austrian officials, who are currently investigating whether their spies provided information to Marsalek and, in turn, to Russia.

World.title: Europe will be represented in Abu Dhabi talks on Ukraine, French foreign minister says
World.content:
“In recent weeks, Europeans have made their voices heard, expressing to the American mediator that no discussion concerning the future of the continent can disregard our expectations and demands,” Barrot told RTL.

European Commission spokesperson Paula Pinho said Friday the EU executive didn’t yet have details to share, but added that “it’s obviously up to the European Union to decide on matters which affect its security and on matters which are of its competence.”

The EU has scrambled to agree on who should represent it at the peace talks and who, if anyone, should be in contact with Russian President Vladimir Putin.

Italian Prime Minister Giorgia Meloni urged European Council President António Costa to settle the issue in a letter this week, prompting Costa to put it on the agenda of the Nov. 13 leaders’ summit. Meloni’s letter was partly prompted by a phone call Finland’s Alexander Stubb and Norway’s Jonas Gahr Støre made to Putin on Oct. 27, which took some European leaders by surprise.

Meanwhile, the European Commission hosted talks on Ukraine’s reconstruction on Wednesday, bringing together representatives from Ukraine, the U.S., U.K., Germany, France, NATO and the World Bank.

U.S. President Donald Trump spoke late Thursday of a “big, beautiful agreement,” after meeting with Putin’s envoy Kirill Dmitriev, adding: “It’s going to involve more than Ukraine, and I could even say it might involve all of Europe.” The plan has brought anxiety among EU officials, who fear it risks sidelining the continent and emboldening Putin.

“We already have a European security architecture in place — NATO and European Union both have their respective roles,” EU foreign policy chief Kaja Kallas said Friday in response to the U.S. plan. “We must make sure Ukraine is integrated into this architecture. The problem remains that Russia keeps breaking the treaties that underpin it … Putin does not have a veto over European security.”

World.title: Russian strikes leave 600,000 in the dark in eastern Ukraine
World.content:
“Power company workers are already working to restore electricity. Their efforts are being hampered by constant Russian shelling,” said the region’s governor Oleksandr Hanzha, adding that hospitals and critical infrastructure are now relying on generators for power.

The blackout follows shelling in the region on Nov. 3 that damaged infrastructure in a key industrial region bordering active combat areas, and a wider attack the same day across Ukraine targeting energy facilities.

The Zaporizhzhia nuclear power plant also lost power overnight, with the International Atomic Energy Agency saying on Sunday morning it is now relying “on emergency diesel generators for reactor cooling and other essential nuclear safety and security functions.”

The attack comes as Kyiv and Moscow gear up for another round of US-brokered peace talks in Abu Dhabi next week. Following the new wave of attacks on Saturday night Zelenskyy called on international partners to ramp up sanctions on Russia to hamper its capability to acquire or build more missiles.

“It is very important that they be synchronized across Europe and G7 jurisdictions. If the world does not have enough anti-ballistic capabilities to protect Ukrainian skies, then the missiles must be stopped on the production lines,” he said.

World.title: Security Sunday: Die neue Front der Bundeswehr in Litauen – mit Robertas Kaunas
World.content:
Eingeklemmt zwischen Kaliningrad und Belarus liegt die verwundbarste Stelle der NATO. Genau hier entsteht mit der Panzerbrigade 45 das wohl wichtigste Projekt der deutschen Zeitenwende. Bis 2027 sollen fast 5.000 deutsche Soldaten dauerhaft in Litauen stationiert werden.

Doch die Bedrohung durch Russland ist längst nicht mehr nur theoretisch: Drohnen, Desinformation und brennende Infrastruktur zeigen, dass der hybride Krieg Litauen bereits erreicht hat. Im Gespräch erklärt der litauische Verteidigungsminister Robertas Kaunas, wie real die Gefahr einer Invasion ist.

Die Folge beleuchtet, wie sich die baltischen Staaten wappnen und was Europa tun muss, falls die USA als Schutzmacht ausfallen. Eine präzise Einordnung, warum die Abschreckung an der Ostflanke über das Schicksal des Kontinents entscheidet und die Sicherheit in Vilnius letztlich die Sicherheit in Berlin bedeutet.

World.content:
Share on LinkedIn

Die Welt spielt verrückt, doch im Präsidium des Bundestages herrscht überraschende Einigkeit. Bundestagsvizepräsident Bodo Ramelow (Die Linke) gibt im Gespräch mit Gordon Repinski einen seltenen Einblick in die überparteiliche Zusammenarbeit, auch bei Nachtschichten. Dabei wird deutlich, mit welcher Strategie das Gremium den Provokationen der AfD begegnet.

In seiner eigenen Partei brodelt es derweil gewaltig. Ramelow findet deutliche Worte zur Antisemitismus-Debatte innerhalb der Linken und kritisiert das taktische Lavieren einzelner Abgeordneter. Warum er trotzdem eine Gesinnungsprüfung ablehnt, aber klare rote Linien beim Existenzrecht Israels zieht, offenbart die tiefe Zerrissenheit seiner Partei.

Zudem verrät er, warum die Wahrnehmung der Linken im Bundestag derzeit auch von der Gruppe der „Silberlocken“ abhängt, wie sich die Silberlocken regelmäßig absprechen und warum er sich trotz aller Krisen nicht verrückt machen lässt.

Mit den Linken, aber auch der SPD und den Grünen beschäftigt sich auch der neue Podcast von POLITICO und WELT. In „Inside Links“ geht es jede Woche darum, wie in Deutschland womöglich eine neue linke Mehrheit entsteht, zu welchem Preis und wer künftig dabei möglicherweise am Regierungstisch sitzen könnte. „Inside Links“ gibt es auf den Podcast-Plattformen zu hören und zu sehen, unter anderem auch hier.

World.title: Merz’s conservatives poised to nominate Germany’s first woman president
World.content:
BERLIN — Bavarian politician Ilse Aigner is set to become Germany’s next president, making her the country’s first woman to hold the office, according to two senior conservatives with knowledge of the matter.

German Chancellor Friedrich Merz’s conservative bloc and the center-left Social Democratic Party (SPD) will nominate Aigner to succeed outgoing German President Frank-Walter Steinmeier, the officials told BILD, which, like POLITICO, is part of the Axel Springer Global Reporters Network. Both officials were granted anonymity to discuss internal party matters freely. Aigner’s nomination will officially be announced Monday, according to the officials.

Aigner, who previously served as agriculture minister under former German Chancellor Angela Merkel from 2008 to 2013, is currently president of the Bavarian State Parliament. She is also a member of the Christian Social Union (CSU), the Bavarian sister party to Chancellor Friedrich Merz’s Christian Democratic Union (CDU).

World.title: Trump’s ‘big, beautiful’ European security plan isn’t convincing Europe
World.content:
The latest U.S. proposal underscores growing anxiety around Trump’s fresh rapprochement with Russia as he ramps up pressure on Ukraine and his administration attempts to revive long-stalled talks to end Moscow’s full-scale war against Kyiv.

POLITICO spoke to 12 NATO diplomats, EU envoys and European government officials, all of whom were granted anonymity to speak freely on the sensitive issue. NATO allies were not briefed about the American plans in advance, according to three alliance diplomats, and many remain skeptical of the idea.

U.S. President Donald Trump late Thursday talked of a “big, beautiful agreement,” after meeting with Putin’s envoy Kirill Dmitriev, adding: “It’s going to involve more than Ukraine, and I could even say it might involve all of Europe.”

“Our objective is to develop practical arrangements that address the security concerns of all sides, reduce the risk of future conflict, and create a more stable and predictable security environment,” Trump’s son-in-law and envoy Jared Kushner added soon after.

Kushner said the arrangement would have five goals: “Permanent security consultations, reliable crisis communications, greater military transparency, reciprocal measures to reduce escalation risks, and an enduring framework for long-term European security and stability.”

“It is a bit obscure what Kushner meant,” said one NATO diplomat. “The general sentiment in Europe is that any discussion with Russia on the future architecture at the moment will just be used by Moscow to legitimize their arguments ... it will not fly with the European allies.”

World.title: NATO faces €7B shortfall on military aid pledge to Ukraine
World.content:
The shortfall comes ahead of an alliance meeting on Nov. 17 where European capitals are expected to examine ways to boost funding and increase the transfer of critical weapons to Ukraine. While new NATO funding pledges are still expected, it’s possible that allies may fail to meet this year’s target, the diplomats said.

A NATO official speaking on behalf of the organization said that “allies continue to provide essential military support to Ukraine” to fulfill the pledge and “are working to ensure that Ukraine has the support it needs now and into the future.”

The target combines bilateral contributions throughout the year and €30 billion drawn from the EU’s €90 billion loan to Ukraine.

Kyiv has repeatedly urged allies to step up their funding as Russia continues its devastating air assaults; more than 40 people were reportedly killed after a school bombing this week.

During a closed-door meeting with allies Thursday, Ukraine’s ambassador to NATO Alyona Getmanchuk “emphasised the importance for Ukraine of NATO Allies fulfilling the commitment made at the Ankara Summit to provide €70 billion in military support this year,” according to a statement by the Ukrainian mission.

“It is essential to mobilise all partners to the fullest extent, accelerate new decisions, and translate previously announced commitments into concrete deliveries of equipment or transfers of funds,” it added.

World.title: Netherlands: Sea of red fills Amsterdam streets in Gaza protest
World.content:
The demonstration, part of the country's ongoing "Red Line" protest movement, brought large crowds onto streets closed to traffic, including the area around the Van Gogh Museum. Protesters waved Palestinian flags and carried placards reading "Not in my name", "Gaza is being starved" and "Stop the Genocide". Chants of "Free Palestine" and "Shame on you" echoed through the crowds, while marchers demanded action from The Hague. Organisers called for tougher trade sanctions against Israel, a halt to arms sales and official recognition of Israel's actions in Gaza as genocide.

 

The protest comes amid continuing tensions between the Netherlands and Israel over the humanitarian situation in Gaza. Israel strongly rejects accusations of genocide, maintaining that its military campaign followed the Hamas-led attacks of 7 October 2023, which killed around 1,200 people and saw 251 taken hostage.

Israel's subsequent offensive has killed tens of thousands of Palestinians and devastated much of the territory. According to Gaza's health ministry, more than 1,550 Palestinians have been killed by Israeli forces since a ceasefire began in October 2025.

Dutch Prime Minister Rob Jetten, who joined an earlier Red Line demonstration but did not attend Sunday's march, defended his government's approach, saying it was increasing diplomatic pressure on Israel while also pressing Hamas to respect security commitments.

World.title: Poland: Kraków mourns six victims as shooting site reopens
World.content:
Residents and visitors returned to the scene of the attack, where bullet marks were still visible on café windows and candles were being lit in memory of those killed.

 

Footage shows people stopping to examine the damaged glass, while others quietly pay their respects at a makeshift memorial on the edge of the square. One visibly emotional woman is comforted by a man as mourners gather around the candles.

Police officers continued to patrol the area as pedestrians and café customers gradually returned to the normally bustling square.

The attack took place on Saturday 7 November, when a 24-year-old gunman opened fire in the historic centre of Poland's second-largest city. The shooting triggered scenes of panic, with witnesses filming people running for cover as emergency services rushed to the area.

World.title: Pope Leo XIV ends his visit to Uruguay with a tribute to women before departing to Argentina
World.content:
Leo XIV wrapped up his visit to Uruguay on Sunday by praising the women who have passed the Catholic faith on to younger generations, as he highlighted the role the church has played since the founding of Latin America’s most secular country.

 

“You taught your children to pray, and today they no longer do so. You used to attend Mass together, and it has been years since they entered a church,” he said. But he urged them to not despair.

“Mothers and grandmothers: never tire of passing on the faith!"

He travelled to the city of Florida, north of Montevideo, to mark an important local Catholic feast day, of the Virgin of the Thirty-three, for his final event in the country.

Paying homage to the women who passed on the Catholic faith, he also raised awareness about gender-based violence, calling on men to treat their wives with respect.

His homily addressed a prominent issue in Latin America: over the last five years, the region recorded nearly 20,000 femicides, most of them committed by the victim's current or former partner.

Live 'faith with courage'

Pope Leo became the first pope in nearly four decades to visit Uruguay, in hopes of reminding the increasingly secular nation of its Catholic identity.

We must "live our faith with courage, not be afraid to say: I am a Christian, I am a Catholic, I believe in Jesus Christ", the Pope said in front of at least 50,000 worshippers gathered outside the Cathedral of Florida.

"The people of Uruguay are capable of great things", he added, "what we have received and offer freely through the grace of God multiplies, opens up horizons and enriches our lives, giving them new meaning".

In his homily the Holy Father also spoke about the attack in Krakow, saying he was "deeply saddened".

After Uruguay, Argentina

On Sunday evening the pope landed in Buenos Aires, where he received a welcome at the Casa Rosada from the Argentine president, Javier Milei.

The visit is not without political controversy. The Catholic Church has criticized Milei’s austerity measures that have slashed social spending, and his embrace of artificial intelligence.

Milei has staked his presidency on cutting social spending to overhaul Argentina’s troubled economy and deliver a long-elusive budget surplus.

He has called social justice “an aberration” that amounts to stealing, and mocked as “huge stupidity” the increasingly common complaint in Argentina that families squeezed by his austerity program can’t make it to the end of the month.

For Argentine Catholics, though, the visit is hugely important in a spiritual sense, since it sees Leo reconnecting with the path of his predecessor Francis, born Jorge Mario Bergoglio and Argentine by birth, who died on Easter Monday 2025.

World.title: Overcrowded car plunges into lake in Brazil, killing ten, including five children
World.content:
Ten people died after a car plunged into a lake in a rural area of the Brazilian municipality of Barra Mansa, in the state of Rio de Janeiro.

 

The accident happened in the early hours of Sunday, after a passer-by raised the alarm when they noticed the submerged vehicle.

"The victims were already dead when they were removed from the vehicle," said the government of the state of Rio de Janeiro in a statement, quoted by AFP.

On social media, the Rio authorities expressed their condolences over the accident, confirming that the victims included five adults and five children.

Some Brazilian media reported that a baby girl was among the victims. The victims' identities have not been confirmed.

Emergency teams were sent to the scene. Firefighters managed to recover the submerged victims with the help of two divers.

Local authorities have classified the incident as an accident, and the police are investigating the circumstances.

According to media outlet G1, which cites a relative, all the victims belonged to the same family.

The Rio de Janeiro region was hit by heavy rain on Saturday, which caused flooding in several streets, including some in tourist areas such as Copacabana.

World.title: Erdoğan joins Aliyev for Azerbaijan’s Victory Day in Karabakh
World.content:
Azerbaijan marked Victory Day on Sunday with nationwide commemorations celebrating the sixth anniversary of the end of the Karabakh war.

 

Azerbaijan's President Ilham Aliyev led the Victory Day commemorations by laying a wreath at the Victory Monument in Khankendi, where he paid tribute to Azerbaijani soldiers and officers who died during the 2020 war.

Aliyev called the liberation of Shusha on 8 November 2020 the decisive moment of the conflict and congratulated both the nation and the Armed Forces for their victory six years ago.

“The liberation of Shusha effectively decided the outcome of the Second Garabagh War,” Aliyev said.

In a powerful message about the strength of the ties between Turkey and Azerbaijan despite recent differences, Turkish President Recep Tayyip Erdoğan travelled to Azerbaijan to participate in the commemorations at Aliyev's invitation.

Erdoğan and his wife, Emine Erdoğan, were greeted by Aliyev and First Lady Mehriban Aliyeva in Karabakh.

President Recep Tayyip Erdoğan and wife Emine Erdoğan and President Ilham Aliyev and First Lady Mehriban Aliyeva president.az

The visit comes after weeks of diplomatic disagreements between Ankara and Baku, along with criticism of Azerbaijan from within Turkish society.

Yet on a day of considerable historical significance for both countries, the two leaders spoke of their intent to demonstrate the resilience of their long-standing partnership.

Welcoming Erdoğan, Aliyev described the Turkish president's presence at the commemorations in Karabakh as a demonstration of their alliance's strength during a joint press conference.

"This unity will last forever," Aliyev declared. "Your presence with us on Victory Day brings joy to the entire Azerbaijani people."

He added that the two countries were stronger together and that Erdoğan’s visit to Karabakh demonstrated their unity to the world.

In a post on X, Erdoğan said that "six years ago, under the resolute leadership of my brother Ilham, the Azerbaijani people stood united and, with great heroism, restored Karabakh’s freedom."

"This glorious victory remains the finest expression of Azerbaijan’s just cause and a source of pride for the entire Turkic world."

Erdoğan joined Aliyev in reaffirming their special relationship by saying that “those seeking to weaken the Azerbaijan-Turkey brotherhood will never achieve their goals.”

Erdoğan's visit also highlighted the alliance's importance as both countries navigate shifting regional relationships and international priorities, with shared strategic interests even when differences emerge over individual policies.

Erdoğan sought to reinforce the alliance's importance ahead of his visit, countering criticisms of Baku within Turkish society by saying relations with Azerbaijan extended “far beyond conventional diplomatic engagement.”

He also said that the “unbreakable bond” between the countries was a product of “our joint history, culture, destiny, and, God willing, our future.”

“Ties between Turkey and Azerbaijan could overcome all obstacles”, Erdoğan said, and his presence at the Victory Day commemorations appeared to have reinforced that message.

President Ilham Aliyev, Victory Day commemoration on 8 November 2026, Azerbaijan president.az

Aliyev echoed Erdoğan, describing the two countries' relationship as exceptionally close.

“I have said many times that there are no countries in the world as attached to each other as Azerbaijan and Turkey,” Azerbaijan's president said.

'Brotherly Turkish people were by our side'

The relationship was reinforced during the last 44-day war between Azerbaijan and Armenia in 2020, when Turkey provided political and military support to Baku.

Azerbaijan's retaking of the strategically important city of Shusha on 8 November marked a turning point in the conflict, with a Russian-brokered ceasefire agreement signed two days later on 10 November.

The anniversary of Shusha’s capture is now commemorated annually as Azerbaijan’s Victory Day.

Azerbaijan's President Aliyev laying down flowers for Victory Day commemoration president.az

Aliyev acknowledged Turkey's support during the 2020 conflict, whilst directly addressing Erdoğan, stating that “during 44 days, my dear brother, and the brotherly Turkish people were by our side."

The Azerbaijani-Turkish alliance was formalised on 15 June 2021, when the Shusha Declaration on Allied Relations was signed, which strengthened defence and security cooperation.

A shared vision for the future

As the two leaders made this year's Victory Day a powerful symbol of the historical and political relationship between Turkey and Azerbaijan, six years after the war, the South Caucasus is entering a new phase with economic cooperation, reconstruction and regional diplomacy shaping its future.

Turkey and Azerbaijan have had a strong relationship over the last decades, and their cooperation in defence, trade, energy and transport has strengthened connections between the South Caucasus, Central Asia and European markets.

The Southern Gas Corridor, which transports Azerbaijani natural gas through Turkey towards Europe, has become increasingly important as European countries seek to diversify their gas supplies and switch away from Russian gas.

The proposed Trump Route for International Peace and Prosperity (TRIPP) has also become a wider part of discussions about regional connectivity and economic integration.

Speaking alongside Erdoğan on Victory Day, Aliyev said the partnership had implications beyond their national borders.

“Turkey-Azerbaijan unity is an important factor across a vast geographical area, contributing to stability, cooperation, and security,” he said.

President Recep Tayyip Erdoğan and President Ilham Aliyev shaking hands during a joint press conference on Victory Day, 8 November 2026 president.az

Reconstruction and restoration in Karabakh

Earlier in the day in Khankendi, Aliyev highlighted Azerbaijan's post-war reconstruction efforts and the return of displaced communities.

“Today we are building and creating a free Karabakh,” Aliyev said during Sunday's commemorations.

Erdoğan said, “We highly appreciate Azerbaijan’s reconstruction efforts in Karabakh,” adding that Turkey would continue contributing its experience to rebuilding the region.

According to Aliyev, 97,000 people now live, study and work in the territories Azerbaijan regained control of as the government's so-called "Great Return Programme" continues.

Official figures show that more than 40,000 residents have resettled in newly constructed communities, including Fuzuli, Zangilan, Lachin and Shusha.

State infrastructure expenditure across these areas has surpassed €10 billion since 2020.

Engineering projects have completed international airports in Fuzuli, Zangilan, and Lachin, alongside 3,000 kilometres of high-capacity highways. At the same time, green energy initiatives target 2,000 megawatts of renewable power generation capacity by 2030.

Parallel to civil engineering, Azerbaijani state programmes led by the Heydar Aliyev Foundation have focused on heritage rehabilitation across recovered territories.

In Shusha, specialists have restored 27 historical and architectural monuments, including seven mosques, six historical water springs, and seven cultural sites.

Environmental agencies have simultaneously launched nationwide greening drives, planting thousands of Eldar pine and olive trees, alongside forest regeneration in Topkhana.

Civic observances have also expanded across national institutions.

On 3 November, Azerbaijan's national assembly Milli Majlis adopted an official parliamentary statement framing post-war reconstruction as the cornerstone of future economic growth.

Direct bilateral talks and peace treaty framework

After the war, Azerbaijan's national focus shifted towards building a historic peace process with Armenia after decades of tragedies for both sides.

Diplomatic relations between Baku and Yerevan have since shifted from multi-party international mediation formats to direct bilateral negotiations between government commissions as the peace process is built.

Earlier this year, joint border teams completed the formal physical demarcation of a 12.7-kilometre northern border section, erecting the first mutually agreed boundary posts along the frontier.

Bilateral negotiating teams have finalised most articles of a draft comprehensive peace treaty. Core provisions focus on mutual recognition of state sovereignty, territorial integrity, and opening regional transport connections.

Beyond bilateral legal agreements, economic integration forms the primary foundation for post-conflict governance.

Regional transit projects aim to connect landlocked commercial routes across the South Caucasus directly to wider Eurasian transport arteries, including the Middle Corridor.

World.title: Rosstat hack: data obtained suggests over 390,000 Russian deaths in Ukraine war
World.content:
The hacker groups Kiberpartizany BY and Silent Crow claim to have carried out a large-scale breach of Russia's Federal State Statistics Service (Rosstat).

 

According to the hackers, they managed to steal about 23 terabytes of data, including internal documents, demographic and economic statistics, as well as information on Russian losses in the war against Ukraine.

The data obtained enabled the groups to make their own calculations of the number of people killed since the start of Russia's full-scale invasion of Ukraine in February 2022.

According to Kiberpartizany BY, as of 27 August 2026 at least 393,881 Russian citizens have been killed in the war. Silent Crow gives an even higher figure of 450,100 dead.

This significant difference in estimates is due to the use of different methods of counting losses.

Kiberpartizany BY counted deaths in which military action or its consequences were listed as the cause.

Silent Crow, by contrast, not only included those killed in combat, but also added several other categories of deaths: non-combat losses among military personnel, deaths marked as terrorist acts, and deaths of people registered in Russia but who died in occupied territories or in Ukraine where the exact cause of death was not established.

Why these figures are particularly important

Russia has not released official statistics on combat losses since September 2022.

In addition, from 2024 Rosstat stopped publishing annual data on causes of death, which has made an independent assessment of the demographic impact of the war much more difficult.

Against this backdrop, access to the agency's internal statistical materials may make it possible to assess the scale of human losses more accurately.

For comparison, as of 8 November the joint database of BBC News Russian Service and Mediazona, which collects a list of dead Russian servicemen identified by name, contained around 286,000 names. However, this list is known to be incomplete, especially for the most recent months of the war.

In a joint study by Meduza and Mediazona, based on analysis of inheritance registry data, the number of fallen Russian servicemen by the end of 2025 was estimated at roughly 350,000.

In this way, the hackers' estimates are in line with figures from previously published independent studies, although this does not yet prove the accuracy of each individual number.

Verifying the authenticity of the data

Meduza and Mediazona have said they obtained access to the data published by the hackers and have begun checking it.

The journalists aim to establish not only whether the materials are authentic, but also how complete the information is they contain. In particular, they need to rule out the possibility of deliberate data falsification.

Moreover, causes of death given in medical documents do not always reflect the actual circumstances of a person's death.

It should also be noted that Rosstat's internal databases do not contain up-to-date information on people listed as missing. Such individuals may be declared dead only after a long period of time.

Therefore even data from the state statistics agency cannot automatically provide a definitive figure for Russian military losses.

If the authenticity and completeness of the leak are confirmed, the materials obtained could become one of the largest sources of information on the demographic consequences of the war for Russia.

World.title: Watch: Spectacular double waterspout forms off Italy's Capri island
World.content:
A rare double waterspout formed over the Italian island of Capri on Saturday, stretching across its iconic Faraglioni rock formations.

 

The two swirling columns emerged from heavy clouds hovering over the island, creating a striking natural spectacle.

Waterspouts are relatively common over the Mediterranean in late summer and autumn, when cooler air moves over warmer waters.

Capri is one of Italy's most popular tourist destinations, attracting an estimated three million visitors each year. The Faraglioni rock formations are among the island's best-known attractions, although many tourism businesses close during the winter months, leaving the island largely to its residents.

World.title: Nvidia CEO Huang admits affair amid rumors of China spy ties
World.content:
Following reports of Nvidia's chief Jensen Huang becoming involved with a Chinese spy, Huang offered an apology for cheating on his wife. Meanwhile, the US tech company pledged to investigate the alleged espionage.

US tech giant Nvidia said on Sunday it would investigate claims that its CEO Jensen Huang was targeted by "foreign intelligence efforts."

Multiple media outlets, including The Financial Times, recently reported on American intelligence sharing information on Huang's extramarital affair with a Chinese woman. The woman, according to US intelligence sources, had been recruited by China's Ministry of State Security.

Chipmaker NVIDIA profits up, despite trade war challenges To view this video please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser that supports HTML5 video

The reports identified her as Alice Huang, an executive for Singapore-based company Megaspeed. The US is investigating the company over suspicions that it was helping Beijing bypass export restrictions and obtain cutting-edge AI chips. According to The New York Times, the company has bought Nvidia chips worth billions of dollars in the last two years.

US lawmakers have invited the Nvidia chief to brief them on the reports.

Nvidia's Huang as rich as Warren Buffet

On Sunday, Nvidia's top executive admitted to being "unfaithful" to his wife of 40 years.

"My actions hurt her and our children," Jensen Huang wrote in an email sent to Nvidia staff. "There is no excuse for what I did. I am deeply sorry."

Nvidia's AI PC explained: AI agents, speed and data privacy To view this video please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser that supports HTML5 video

He also said he was he committed to protecting the company and "supporting America's national security."

Huang was born in Taipei and spent part of his childhood in Taiwan before moving to the US. In 1993, he and two other people launched Nvidia, a company that grew to become a leading manufacturer of computer graphic cards and then an essential supplier of computer chips in the AI boom.

Nvidia’s Cage for AI: can it prevent disaster? To view this video please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser that supports HTML5 video

The 63-year-old Nvidia CEO is one of the richest people in the world, according to the Forbes magazine, with his $162.2 billion (€145.5 billion) net worth as of Sunday putting him roughly on par with globally renowned investor Warren Buffet.

Huang stays on as Nvidia CEO

In their statement, Nvidia's board of directors said Huang will remain the head of the US-based company while the probe is taking place.

Huang "fully supports the review and has committed to cooperating with it," according to their statement.

The board said a group of "independent directors, assisted by outside independent counsel, will oversee the investigation."

At the same time, the heads of the $4.5 trillion company said they had "no reason to believe that either national security or Nvidia secrets were compromised."

World.title: Iran: Trump says strikes unlikely if peace talks keep moving
World.content:
After weeks of rumors that the US and Israel were preparing new strikes on Iran, President Donald Trump said it was "highly unlikely" that he would order a new escalation as the Iranians "want to make a deal so badly."

In an interview with US broadcaster CNN, President Donald Trump sought to downplay fears that the US is about to relaunch its military campaign against Iran.

"It depends on whether or not they sign a very strong agreement," he told CNN on Sunday. "The answer is highly unlikely it's going to be necessary."

At the same time, Trump restated that the US military was "ready" to launch a new round of strikes and could "finish [Iran] off."

"I've got three aircraft carriers here," he said. "They're fully locked and loaded."

He added that the US military had 38 bridges in their sights "that we can knock down in literally one hour."

US strikes Iran hours before midterm election To view this video please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser that supports HTML5 video

However, Trump also repeated several times that the new escalation is "highly unlikely," saying that Iran was a "failing nation" and "withering away financially" after eight months of hostilities.

"I hit them so hard. You don't know how hard I hit them," he said. "They want to make a deal so badly."

Iran and the US stuck between war and peace

Trump ordered an attack on Iran in late February, after US ally Israel launched what it called a "preemptive strike" on its biggest regional rival. The US president has since repeatedly declared victory, insinuated that Iran was begging the US for a deal, and told the media that a peace deal was done or nearly done.

Iran has repeatedly rejected Trump's account. Despite Trump's claims that Iran was collapsing both economically and militarily, Tehran has been able to repeatedly stage attacks on US allies in the region and maintains at least a partial blockade of the Strait of Hormuz. The Houthi rebels in Yemen, allied with Tehran, are currently targeting high-profile targets in the Saudi capital of Riyadh and elsewhere across Saudi Arabia.

The most tangible diplomatic achievement since the start of the war was reported in June, when Iran and the US signed a memorandum of understanding in Islamabad. But the talks broke down and the memorandum expired in August​​​​​​​, with the two sides still engaged in a military and diplomatic stalemate.

Iranian top diplomat says US still digesting midterms

The conflict has proven to be unpopular with the US public, featuring heavily in the campaign for US midterm election that eventually saw Trump's Republicans lose their majorities in Congress.

Republicans rebuke Trump on Iran war, economy after midterm wipeout To view this video please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser that supports HTML5 video

On Sunday, Iranian Foreign Minister Abbas Araghchi said that that peace mediators did not "travel" since the Tuesday election in the US. Araghchi described the outcome as a "shock."

"We now have to see how long it will take for them to digest these results, in order to determine how we are going to move forward," he said.

Qatar says talks moving behind the scenes

Qatar, which acts as one of the mediators in the conflict, denied rumors that the US and Iran are failing to reach a peace deal. On Saturday, the Qatari prime minister said both sides were still working toward an agreement.

Separately, the Reuters news agency cited a senior Iranian official as saying that Tehran has submitted a proposal on its nuclear program to Washington through Qatar.

The official also noted that further talks would depend on the US meeting Tehran's demands, including the lifting of sanctions, unfreezing Iranian funds and war reparations.

World.title: Germany news: Merz to nominate Aigner for president
World.content:
Skip next section Merz to nominate Aigner as Germany's next federal president

German Chancellor Friedrich Merz announced to the Christian Democrat Union (CDU) party heads his intention to nominate Ilse Aigner as the country's next federal president, according to the dpa, AFP and Reuters news agencies.

She will replace Frank-Walter Steinmeier when he steps down at the end of his term early next year.

Aigner, who hails from Bavaria's conservative Christian Social Union (CSU) and is the president of the Bavarian state parliament, would be the first woman to hold the German president's position should she be elected on January 30.

Steinmeier is a member of the junior coalition partner SPD.

Merz will officially pitch Aigner's name for the job on Monday, when party leaders will gather to choose a joint candidate.

SPD and Green Party representatives have already voiced support for her candidacy.

World.title: Many killed after migrant boat sinks off Senegal
World.content:
The incident occurred near Kebemer off the coast of northwestern Senegal. Authorities on El Hierro in the Canary Islands have declared an emergency after a marked increase in migrant boat arrivals.

At least 34 people were killed after a small boat carrying migrants sank off the coast of northwestern Senegal, according to the Senegalese Press Agency.

Thousands have died in recent years after embarking on boats from the Senegalese coast in order to reach Spain's Canary Islands through the perilous Atlantic route.

Initially, the Senegalese Ministry of the Interior stated that only one person had been rescued from the capsizing and that 21 bodies had been recovered.

The ministry added that the toll was "provisional" and that search operations were still ongoing.

The incident occurred near Kebemer, some 180 kilometers (around 112 miles) north of the capital, Dakar.

On Saturday, the ministry stressed the government's "determination to combat people smuggling networks, notably through strengthened cooperation with neighboring countries."

Senegalese authorities said they intercepted 142 migrants on a similar boat aimed at reaching Spanish territory on Friday. The boat included nationals of multiple West African countries.

Authorities on the island of El Hierro have declared an emergency due to increased migrant arrivals Image: Jesus Cabrera/REUTERS

El Hierro island declares emergency over migrant arrivals

Authorities on El Hierro Island in the Canary Islands declared an emergency on Saturday after a marked increase in migrant boat arrivals.

El Hierro officials say that over 3,300 people have arrived on around 30 boats since the start of the month.

"We are very concerned... by this sharp increase in arrivals," Alpidio Armas, head of the El Hierro regional council, told Spanish television.

"This is precisely what has led us to declare an emergency in order to ensure a framework of cooperation with higher-level institutions," he added.

Armas said that conditions at the island's hospital have become "undesirable."

El Hierro is home to about 11,400 residents.

Migrant arrivals reached a record high of 46,000 in 2024. Afterwards, arrivals have fallen sharply due to increased surveillance and cooperation with African countries.

World.title: South Africa elections: ANC marks its worst-ever performance
World.content:
The African National Congress, the party of late Nobel Prize winner Nelson Mandela, slumped to its worst-ever result in South Africa's municipal election. The voters blame the ANC for water and electricity shortages.

South Africa's African National Congress (ANC) turned in a historically poor election performance, with the the final tally published on Sunday giving them less than 31% of the vote in Wednesday's municipal polls.

Their closes rival, the Democratic Alliance (DA), won just under 25% of the vote.

The ANC also lost its majority in six of the eight metropolitan regions, South Africa's Electoral Commission said on Saturday. With no outright winner declared in several major cities, politicians are expected enter tough coalition talks to form municipal governments.

ANC secretary general says outcome 'catastrophic'

While the ANC remains the most popular party in the country, they have been struggling with growing backlash from voters. In 2026, many South Africans are frustrated by water and electricity shortages, with the ANC taking the blame for the poor state of municipalities. High unemployment, crime, and widespread corruption are high on the public agenda.

ANC leader, and South African president, Cyril Ramaphosa, has not yet addressed his party's poor performance. In his weekly presidential letter, however, he admitted that "municipal failures have contributed to declining public trust and confidence in democratic governance."

On Saturday, ANC Secretary-General Fikile Mbalula told reporters that the ANC needs to work on winning back public confidence.

"We cannot ask the people to trust us merely because of our history," Mbalula said.

"This has been a very catastrophic outcome for the ANC ... as much as we are the largest party, it has been catastrophic for the movement," he added.

The ANC's steady decline with voters

The ANC had governed with an absolute majority for most of its history up until the general election in 2024 saw it lose an outright parliamentary majority for the first time in South Africa's democratic era.

"This is the most severe result that the ANC would have feared," political analyst Daniel Silke told the AFP news agency.

"It's the ANC's worst result in history," Silke said, adding that the result will undermine the ANC's ability to exert authority on the local and national level. The results could also provide a bellwether of voter sentiment ahead of the 2029 general elections.

Once led by Nelson Mandela, the ANC was instrumental in ending apartheid, and took and power in 1994 after South Africa became a democracy.

But over the past decade, it has steadily performed worse in one election after another. In 2024, the ANC secured just over 40% in the 2024 national polls and 46% at the previous municipal elections in 2021.

After losing the absolute majority in 2024, the ANC formed a cross-party national unity government with all the parties represented in parliament, which is still in power.

The ANC's decline comes amid disillusionment over corruption, mismanagement and high unemployment. Smaller parties have also emerged across South Africa's political landscape, cutting into the ANC's voter base.

DA opposition holds large cities

The pro-business, center-right DA is set to keep control of Cape Town after winning an absolute majority. It also performed well in the capital, Pretoria, and economic hub of Johannesburg, and is expected to form coalitions that exclude the ANC.

"All of the cut and thrust that comes with the election is now over, and it is time now... to put together governments that can actually fix these towns and cities," DA leader Geordin Hill-Lewis told reporters.

"We have already reached out to many parties over the last 24 hours and will continue to do so today," he said.

World.title: Egypt train crash leaves several dead, over 100 injured
World.content:
A train derailed after colliding with another train south of Cairo, with authorities confirming several deaths and saying more than 100 passengers were injured. Over 50 ambulances were deployed to the scene.

At least seven people were killed in the train collision in Egypt on Sunday, with authorities also confirming over 100 people were injured.

The collision involved one train hitting the rear end of another while traveling through the Giza province on the line between Cairo and the southern Nile city of Aswan. One of the trains then derailed and several cars flipped, according to the Egyptian authorities.

Authorities said rescue teams and cleanup crews were deployed to the site Image: AP Photo/picture alliance

Officials said 52 ambulances were deployed to the scene some 52 kilometers (32 miles) south of Cairo. Emergency crews and cranes were also working to clear the line and restore railway traffic through Giza's al-Ayyat district.

The cause of the accident was not immediately clear.

El-Sissi says incident being investigated

In a social media post, Egyptian President Abdel-Fattah el-Sissi said he ordered an investigation. He also urged the state agencies to "hold accountable anyone found to have been negligent."

State media reports indicated a large number of injuries Image: AP Photo/picture alliance

The crash tool place in the same area as the worst train disaster in Egypt's history, which saw over 370 people were killed in a train fire in 2002. Several crashes also claimed dozens of lives in the same region in 2009.

In recent years, Egypt has invested billions of dollars into new highways and high-speed rail lines, but is still facing safety issues and repeated crashes while attempting to revamp its aging rail network.

World.title: Israel: Eisenkot officially tasked with forming a government
World.content:
Israeli President Isaac Herzog tasked Gadi Eisenkot with the right of trying to form a government. The opposition leader's way to replacing Benjamin Netanyahu as prime minister is full of political challenges.

Israel President Isaac Herzog has officially tasked Gadi Eisenkot with forming a government.

Eisenkot, the head of the centrist Yashar party, will have 28 days to secure a coalition to replace current Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu's religious-nationalist government, with Herzog having the authority to prolong Eisenkot's mandate by 14 days.

"The conversations with the different parties were open and transparent, while also resurfacing the many voices in Israeli society. They reminded us the fact that all Israeli citizens have an equal voice, from all parts of society," Herzog said.

He stressed that Eisenkot received the clearest support from the majority of Knesset members when it comes to the question of forming the next government.

"The challenges we face are giant. Iran is not waiting a second in its threats. We have to start building a future in the region and proceed with Trump's 20-point plan in Gaza, as well as negotiating the future with Lebanon and other neighbors," the Israeli president said, adding that "Israel needs a stable government that faces these challenges."

Herzog said that he expected Eisenkot to do his best to form a government that would serve all parts of the Israeli people.

Herzog stressed that Eisenkot received the clearest support from the majority of Knesset members Image: Ronen Zvulun/REUTERS

In turn, Eisenkot stressed that he is committed to establishing a national emergency government.

"We do not have the privilege of endless rounds of elections. I will send an official approach to all of the Knesset's members, as parties and individuals, for talks," he added.

Eisenkot also addressed Knesset members. "The public looks up to us... We are in the most complicated political situation since Israel's establishment," he said.

What do we know about forming a coalition

Yashar was Israel's second biggest party in Israel's October elections with 21 parliament seats, behind Netanyahu's Likud with 27. However, more members of the Knesset, the Israeli parliament, recommended Eisenkot as the man who should be given the first right to try and secure a government.

In comparison to Eisenkot's 67 recommendations, Netanyahu received the backing of 46 members, with the ultraorthodox Ashkenazi party United Torah Judaism (UTJ) deciding not to make any recommendations despite having joined Netanyahu's governments of the past 17 years.

Should Eisenkot fail to form a coalition, President Isaac Herzog will have the authority to pass the task on to a different Knesset member, with the second person in line expected to be Netanyahu.

If the Likud leader, too, will not manage to form a government, and if no other parliament member will claim to have enough support to head a government, Israel will likely head to another round of elections.

Eisenkot faces a difficult task

Dividing Israel's Zionist parties into blocs results in Netanyahu's religious-nationalist allies receiving 53 seats, with the Eisenkot-led anti-Netanyahu bloc having 48 seats.

Israel's two Arab parties, which with 19 seats received historic support due to the high turnout in Arab and Palestinian communities, already voiced their willingness to support the Zionist opposition in ousting Netanyahu and his government. Mostly the religious Muslim party Ra'am, led by Mansour Abbas, said it is willing to join a coalition once again in a bid to improve Israel's Arab and Palestinian communities' lives.

In 2021, Ra'am made history in becoming the first-ever Arab party to join an Israeli coalition, signing an agreement with right-wing candidate Naftali Bennet and liberal politician Yair Lapid.

The other Arab party, the Joint List, is a union of several smaller parties. While its members have never joined an Israeli coalition, its politicians did provide political support for an Israeli government from the opposition during Yitzhak Rabin's second term as prime minister as his government pushed through the Oslo Accords with the Palestinians, a term which was cut short by Rabin's murder in November 1995.

Israeli President asks Eisenkot to form government To view this video please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser that supports HTML5 video

Campaign promises at risk

Both sides of Israel's Zionist political divide promised not to rely on votes by Arab parties to form a coalition, meaning Eisenkot's bloc will have to track back on one of its election promises to form a government with them.

However, a poll by the Accord Center of the Hebrew University in Jerusalem carried out two days after the elections found that 59 percent of Israel's Zionist opposition voters would rather have a government with Ra'am, and with the Joint List's abstention, than any other alternative.

Another option touted by Israeli media in the past week was the country's two ultraorthodox parties potentially joining an Eisenkot-led coalition. UTJ and Sepharadi party Shas have seven seats each, but a coalition with any of them would require Eisenkot to backtrack on another campaign promise: to pass through a legislation to secure the army conscription of young ultraorthodox men, which the two parties strictly object, citing fears over the future of religious studies in Israel.

Moreover, Shas supporters are known to hold right-wing views favorable to Netanyahu, with party head Arye Deri being considered as one of the politicians closest to Israel's longest-serving prime minister.

Effects on Palestinians

The government formed is bound to have wide-ranging implications on the lives of Palestinians in the Occupied West Bank and the Gaza Strip.

The Netanyahu-led current coalition also includes far-right parties Otzma Yehudit and Religious Zionism, which received 13 seats in the October election. The two parties support annexing the West Bank — a territory illegally occupied by Israel — as well as re-establishing Israeli settlements in the Gaza Strip and carrying out the so-called "wilful migration," the plan to move Gaza's 2.1 million Palestinians to other countries.
