World.title: Prague Ice Rinks Guide This Winter: Opening Dates, Prices and Locations
World.content:
As temperatures fall, public ice rinks are beginning to reopen across Prague for the 2026–27 winter season.

Several districts have already confirmed opening dates, while others are still finalising their winter programmes. From free skating in Smíchov to rinks beneath the Žižkov Television Tower and on the Letná Plain, residents and visitors will have plenty of options in the coming months.

Here is what has been announced so far.



Prague 1

The Na Františku ice rink is scheduled to open on November 13. Public skating will begin at 8 a.m., with closing times varying between 6:30 p.m. and 8:30 p.m., depending on the day. Skate rentals, refreshments and a heated tent will be available.

A second rink is expected to open on Wenceslas Square on November 28. It will operate daily in four sessions between 9 a.m. and 10 p.m.

A two-hour ticket will cost 200 CZK for adults and 100 CZK for children under 15. Visitors will be able to rent skates and helmets, while skating aids for children, skate sharpening and storage facilities will also be available.

It remains unclear whether the rinks at Ovocný trh and Čapadlo will return this winter.

Prague 2

Three outdoor ice rinks are planned in Prague 2.

The rinks at Havlíčkovy sady, also known as Grébovka, and Svatopluk Čech Park are scheduled to open on November 20. A third rink, located in Folimanka Park beneath the Nusle Bridge, is expected to follow on December 1.

All three venues are expected to operate daily from 9 a.m. to 8 p.m. On weekdays between 9 a.m. and 2 p.m., the ice will be reserved for kindergartens and primary schools in Prague 2. Public skating will take place in the afternoons and throughout weekends.

On December 24 and December 31, the rinks will close at 3 p.m.

Prague 3

Prague 3 will again operate two public ice rinks.

Both are scheduled to open on November 14. One will be located in Mahlerovy sady, beneath the Žižkov Television Tower. A two-hour ticket will cost 150 CZK for adults and 50 CZK for children.

The second rink will return to the Pražačka sports complex. It will be open from 1 p.m. to 8 p.m. on weekdays and from 8 a.m. to 9 p.m. on weekends. All-day admission will cost 120 CZK for adults and 80 CZK for children.

Skate rentals and refreshments will be available at both locations.

Prague 4

So far, one public ice rink has been confirmed in Prague 4.

The rink near the Prague Congress Centre, close to Vyšehrad metro station, is scheduled to open on November 13. It will operate from 1 p.m. to 9 p.m. on weekdays and from 9 a.m. to 9 p.m. during weekends.

Admission will cost 120 CZK per hour for adults and 80 CZK for children. Skate rentals and refreshments will also be available.

The opening date for the public rink in Podolí has not yet been announced.

Prague 5

Residents will once again be able to skate for free at the Aréna sportu on Hořejší nábřeží in Smíchov.

The rink is scheduled to open on November 13, with the official launch of the winter programme planned for the afternoon of November 20.

The venue will also host several themed events during the season, including St. Nicholas on Ice, a superhero-themed skating event and a Valentine’s Day programme.

Prague 6

Two Prague 6 locations are expected to offer outdoor skating this winter.

The rink in Ořechovka is provisionally scheduled to open around November 20, although the final date has yet to be confirmed.

At Vypich, a trial operation is expected to begin on November 27. The official opening is planned two days later and will coincide with the lighting of the local Christmas tree.

Prague 7

The ice rink on the Letná Plain is scheduled to open on November 14 and remain in operation until March 7, 2027.

It will be open daily from 9 a.m. to 9 p.m. A two-hour ticket will cost 150 CZK for adults and 120 CZK for children under 15.

Children under 15 who live in Prague 7 or attend school in the district will be able to skate free of charge.

Prague 8

Three outdoor ice rinks are planned in Prague 8.

On November 17, rinks are scheduled to open in Libeňské podzámčí and near the Krakov Cultural Centre in Bohnice. A third location near the Ládví swimming pool is expected to open on November 20.

Further information on admission and operating hours is expected to be announced by the district.

Prague 9

The rink in Park Přátelství in Střížkov has already opened for the season.

It has been operating since November 5 and is open daily from 9 a.m. to 9 p.m. Morning hours are reserved for schools, while skate rentals are available to visitors.

Another rink will open in Zahrádky Park on December 5. It will also operate daily from 9 a.m. to 9 p.m.

On weekdays between 9 a.m. and 2 p.m., schools will be able to reserve the ice. Visitors will have access to skate rentals and refreshments from Café Park Zahrádky.

Prague 10

Prague 10 will again open a public ice rink in Heroldovy sady in Vršovice.

The rink is scheduled to open on November 29, 2026, and is expected to remain in operation until February. The final closing date will depend on weather conditions.

With opening dates spread throughout November and early December, Prague’s winter skating season is now gradually getting underway. Several districts are still expected to release further details, and visitors should check local announcements before heading to the rink.

World.title: St. Martin’s Day 2026 in Prague: Where to Enjoy Traditional Goose
World.content:
St. Martin’s Day, which Czechs celebrate on November 11, is a holiday of good food and drink. Autumn slowly alternates with winter, and it begins to snow.

In the past, the economic year was ending at this time, and the landowners were preparing a feast for their people as a form of thanks, when they were also paid out their wages.

St. Martin’s Day in restaurants

You can be sure that almost every restaurant around mid-November will be offering its visitors a special St. Martin’s Day menu. What does it feature?

According to a tradition that has lasted for several centuries, geese were always roasted in the autumn, fresh cabbage was processed, and wine or beer was drunk. And today’s restaurants and pubs remain faithful to these basic ingredients.

Typically, you will be served liver pâté as an appetizer, followed by a strong broth with liver dumplings and noodles, which the chefs usually leave to simmer overnight, with the main course being roast goose with red or white cabbage and dumplings.

Where to taste St. Martin’s menu?

Restaurant Salabka (November 6 – 14): Choose from 3 to 5 courses featuring seasonal autumn ingredients and contemporary gastronomy. Available from November 6, alongside the regular autumn tasting menu.

More info here.

Restaurant Obecní dům: (November 7–11): Enjoy a festive menu combining traditional roast goose with creative starters, including smoked duck and goose prosciutto carpaccio. A special St. Martin’s brunch takes place on November 8, while the restaurant’s beer hall joins the celebrations from November 9 to 15.

More info here.

Restaurant Masaryčka: Here the highlight is a tender goose leg confit with caraway, served with braised red cabbage, plums and assorted dumplings (499 CZK). Alternatively, guests can enjoy homemade potato lokše filled with pulled goose meat, onion cabbage and apples (359 CZK). To finish on a sweet note, the menu offers apple strudel with vanilla sauce, walnuts, honey and cinnamon crumble (149 CZK).

More info here

Restaurant Deer: a special four-course menu by chef Lubomír Dolejš, available until November 11. The menu features goose breast, traditional goose soup (kaldoun), confit goose leg with cabbage and bread dumplings, followed by miniature St. Martin’s pastries. The full menu costs 1,295 CZK per person, with individual dishes also available.

More info here

Le Petit Beefbar at the W Hotel: the “Made the List – Holiday 2026 Edition” program features everything from St. Martin’s goose and Advent brunches with oysters and champagne to Christmas dinners at Le Petit Beefbar au Grand Café, culminating in a New Year’s Eve celebration. Starting November 11, the restaurant will host “St. Martin’s Week,” serving slow-roasted goose with all the traditional sides during dinner service.

More info here

World.title: Prague Welcomes Tea Experts and Producers from Around the World
World.content:
Prague will welcome tea producers, experts and enthusiasts from around the world next weekend as Euro Tea Expo returns to the Czech capital for its second edition.

The two-day event, taking place on November 14 and 15, will bring together 37 exhibitors and focus on tea traditions from different parts of the world.



This year’s theme is “Chinese White Tea – The Heritage of Fuding.”

One of the main guests will be Master Lin Zhenchuan, a recognised inheritor of the traditional Fuding white tea-making techniques and founder of PINPINTEA.

Fuding white tea production is listed as part of China’s National Intangible Cultural Heritage.

With more than 30 years of experience, Master Lin will introduce visitors to the craftsmanship and history behind Fuding white tea through presentations and guided tastings. Guests will also be able to compare fresh and aged white teas and learn more about the ageing process.

The programme will feature demonstrations and presentations covering several tea traditions, including a traditional Shē ethnic group white tea performance, Sichuan gaiwan tea culture and long-spout teapot demonstrations.

Visitors can also learn about Kenyan tea, Japanese hojicha, ancient tea trees in Guangxi and the connection between tea and wellbeing. Beyond tea, the programme includes Taiji sessions, a tea and Taiji performance, and a Japanese Nerikiri confectionery workshop.

Organisers say this year’s edition will also expand beyond tea. Five European vegan brands will present plant-based products and sustainable lifestyle concepts as part of the event.

The first Euro Tea Expo was held in Prague in 2025 and brought together 33 exhibitors from 15 countries, attracting around 960 visitors. The organisers say the event aims to further strengthen connections between tea producers, professionals and consumers across Europe.

Event information

Dates: November 14–15, 2026

Opening hours: 10:00–18:00

Venue: U Slavie 1540/2a, Prague 10 – Vršovice

Theme: Chinese White Tea – The Heritage of Fuding

Exhibitors: 37

World.title: Canva Closes Prague Office as More Than 1,200 Jobs Are Cut Worldwide
World.content:
Canva is shutting down its Prague office, leaving only six employees from a workforce of around 50 as part of a company-wide restructuring affecting more than 1,200 people.

According to a former employee familiar with the situation, staff first received a company-wide email from Canva CEO Melanie Perkins outlining major changes.

Around 20 minutes later, employees whose positions were being eliminated received individual notifications.



Those affected were reportedly given about a week to collect their belongings. Access to most internal work systems was cut immediately, with employees retaining access only to services such as Slack and email.

The Prague closure comes during what has been described as the largest restructuring in Canva’s history and the company’s first major round of mass layoffs.

The changes are expected to affect 1,271 employees, equivalent to roughly 22 percent of the company’s workforce.

Prague Staff Point to Structure and AI Costs

A former member of the Prague office said two factors appear to have contributed to the decision.

The first is the company’s organizational structure. Responsibilities were divided across several layers, making communication and decision-making more difficult. The problem was further complicated by the ten- to eleven-hour time difference between Central Europe and Sydney.

The second issue, according to the former employee, involves the cost of artificial intelligence.

Canva has invested heavily in AI tools and technology, initially facing significant costs associated with computing power. Over the past month, the company has begun introducing its own models, although it remains unclear how much this could reduce the cost of processing graphics and other AI-related tasks.

The company has integrated tools and services linked to platforms such as ChatGPT and Claude. At the same time, users are increasingly able to generate images, designs and other visual content directly through competing AI systems without relying on Canva’s traditional platform.

World.title: No Price Cap, No Limits: Tourist Charged CZK 8,000 for a 3 km Taxi Ride
World.content:
Prague received 70 complaints from taxi passengers during a three-week period when the city’s maximum taxi fares were temporarily not in force, according to information published by the Chamber of Taxi Service Operators.

The complaints included several cases involving foreign visitors who were charged thousands of crowns for relatively short journeys. In one of the most extreme cases, a passenger paid CZK 8,096 for a 3.2-kilometre trip from Duplex Club to Na Františku Hospital.

Another passenger was charged CZK 9,955 for a journey through Prague but was reportedly unable to provide the exact route when filing a complaint. The published list of cases shows that, with one exception, the complaints involved foreign tourists.



Among the other reported fares were more than CZK 7,500 for journeys of around 15 kilometres between central Prague and Václav Havel Airport.

According to the list, a passenger travelling from the city centre to the airport paid CZK 7,560 for a 15-kilometre journey. A similar trip from Smetana Embankment cost CZK 7,554.

The issue was highlighted by the Chamber of Taxi Service Operators, which asked Prague City Hall how many complaints had been submitted during the period when fare limits were not being applied.

“There were 70 in total. Some of them really did not hold back,” Štěpán Hradečný, speaking on behalf of the chamber, wrote on Facebook.

Prague City Hall confirmed that the complaints related to the period when taxi price regulation was temporarily absent.

“These complaints relate to a period when taxi price regulations were not in effect. When prices are not regulated by the city, the only regulator is the market itself,” City Hall spokesperson Vít Hofman told *Blesk*.

The situation followed the removal of Prague’s maximum taxi fare limits on September 30. According to Prague Deputy Mayor for Transport Jaromír Beránek of the Pirate Party, the move was not intended as a political decision by the city’s leadership.

Beránek said he had asked the relevant department to prepare materials for a discussion on taxi fare regulation. Instead, the preparatory process resulted in the limits being removed altogether.

The price caps remained absent until October 20, leaving a 21-day period during which taxi fares were not subject to the city’s maximum limits.

World.title: Two-Michelin-Starred Austrian Chef Comes to Prague for Exclusive Dinner
World.content:
Prague’s Zlatá Praha restaurant will host an exclusive four-hands dinner bringing together two-Michelin-starred Austrian chef Andreas Döllerer and Maroš Jambor for one evening of contemporary fine dining.

The special collaboration will see the two chefs create on November 22 a bespoke menu combining their individual culinary styles, seasonal ingredients and modern interpretations of gastronomy.



Based in Golling, Austria, Andreas Döllerer is one of the country’s most acclaimed chefs.

His restaurant, awarded two Michelin stars, is known for its distinctive approach to Alpine cuisine, which reinterprets traditional regional ingredients and culinary influences through contemporary techniques.

For the occasion in Prague, Döllerer will join forces with Maroš Jambor, creating a menu that brings together their respective approaches to fine dining.

The four-hands concept offers guests the opportunity to discover the work of both chefs through a single, specially designed dining experience.

The exclusive menu is priced at CZK 6,000 per person and includes a welcome drink and water. Guests can also opt for a wine pairing at an additional CZK 2,500 per person.

The event requires full prepayment. Reservations are available online.

World.title: American Man Suspected of Racist Assault at Prague’s Želivského Stop
World.content:
Police are investigating an alleged racist assault at the Želivského tram and metro stop in Prague’s Vinohrady district after an English-speaking man reportedly attacked a passerby and damaged his phone.

The suspect has since been identified, although police have not confirmed reports linking him to an American previously detained in Russia.

The incident took place on the morning of November 4 on Vinohradská Street, close to the Želivského stop.



According to the victim, an Arab man who has lived in the Czech Republic for several years, the confrontation began when a stranger started shouting racist remarks in public.

The man allegedly called for the deaths of Black people, Jews and Arabs.

The victim challenged the statements, telling the stranger that racist abuse and threats against people because of their background were unacceptable.

He then began recording the encounter on his mobile phone, fearing that the situation could turn violent.

“I started recording in case I was attacked—and, unfortunately, that is exactly what happened,” he later wrote in the Facebook group Vinohradská parta.

Footage of the confrontation shows the alleged attacker directing insults at the victim. At one point, he raises his phone and says, “Hello, Trump?” He also appears to threaten the other man with death before the confrontation turns physical.

The suspect then allegedly grabbed the victim’s mobile phone and threw it into the road. According to the victim, the device was struck by a passing truck. Although he managed to recover it, the phone was damaged.

The victim said he had reported the incident to the police and called on local residents to help identify the alleged attacker.

“I am dealing with this through the police, but the perpetrator has vanished. Let’s find him and show that violence and racism have no place in Vinohrady,” he wrote.

The original Facebook post containing the video was subsequently removed. The victim suggested that its disappearance might have been connected to the ongoing police investigation.

Police later confirmed that they were dealing with the case as a suspected criminal offence.

“We are handling the matter as a suspected criminal offense, and we have identified the suspect,” police spokesperson Eva Kropáčová told Czech tabloid Blesk.

Suspect reportedly linked to Russia

The investigation has also raised questions about the man’s identity.

The suspect could be an American citizen who previously faced criminal proceedings in Russia and was ordered by a Russian court to undergo compulsory psychiatric treatment.

The man was reportedly accused of assaulting a female police officer in Russia. Media reports have also suggested that he holds Czech citizenship and travelled from Russia to Prague, where he is currently staying.

However, Czech police have not confirmed whether the individual identified in connection with the Želivského incident is the same American mentioned in the Russian case.

World.title: Fake Apartments and Rental Scams Target Students in Prague, Police Warns
World.content:
Prague Police are warning about a growing number of rental fraud cases, with international students among the groups most vulnerable to fake apartment listings.

Leaving everything you know behind is the beginning of a new chapter. A new city. A new home. A new life.

After weeks of searching, you finally have the keys to your apartment in Prague. You climb the stairs of an old building, find the right door and put the key in the lock.

But it will not turn.

You try again. You check the address, look at the contract and reread your messages with the supposed landlord. Everything appears to be in order, except for one crucial detail: the apartment was never yours.

The address exists. The building is real. But the home you thought you had rented does not belong to you.



A Key That Opens No Doors

Rental scams are an increasingly common problem in Prague’s housing market, with international students among the most vulnerable targets.

Many arrive in the Czech capital without knowing the local rental system or having the opportunity to view an apartment in person. The pressure to secure accommodation before the start of the academic year can also make students more vulnerable to convincing-looking fraudulent listings.

In 2024, Czechia ranked ninth among Erasmus+ programme countries for incoming higher education mobility, with approximately 17,000 arrivals, according to Dům zahraniční spolupráce.

The growing number of international students in Prague has also increased the demand for accommodation.

Charles University, one of the city’s largest universities, has repeatedly warned prospective international students about rental fraud. According to its 2024 annual report, the university had 11,455 international students from 139 countries, out of a total student population of more than 54,000.

The university advises students to watch out for several warning signs, including requests for deposits or other payments before a contract has been signed, pressure to finalise an agreement unusually quickly, and landlords who claim to be living abroad.

Offers that appear too good to be true should also raise suspicion.

Three Cases, Nearly CZK 150,000 in Losses

Prague Police have also warned about an increasing number of rental fraud cases involving apartments.

In mid-January, three cases were reported within a single week, resulting in combined losses of nearly CZK 150,000, or approximately €6,000.

One increasingly common method involves collecting deposits from prospective tenants for apartments that are never actually rented out. In some cases, fraudsters advertise properties they do not own or have no right to rent.

Police have not ruled out the possibility that the suspect involved in the January cases may be connected to other similar incidents, meaning the number of victims could be higher.

For international students, the consequences can be particularly severe.

Police and universities therefore advise prospective tenants to verify listings carefully, avoid sending money before signing a contract and viewing the property, and remain cautious of unusually cheap offers or landlords who create pressure to pay quickly.

World.title: Budapest apartment gutted by fire, 15 residents evacuated from smoke-filled building
World.content:
A flat was gutted by fire in a four-storey residential building in Budapest’s District III on Sunday, filling the entire building with smoke. Firefighters evacuated 15 residents, including some who had to be brought outside using rescue masks.

According to the National Directorate General for Disaster Management, the fire broke out in a flat on Pozsonyi Street. Budapest’s professional firefighters arrived at the scene in large numbers and extinguished the flames using water jets.

Under the direction of the disaster management operations service, firefighters also dealt with remaining hot spots and inspected and cooled the building’s external façade and roof.

Residents evacuated, gas supply suspended in five flats

Fifteen people were evacuated from the building. Some residents were taken outside wearing rescue masks, while an ambulance was also dispatched to the scene.

A heated emergency bus was provided for residents while the situation was being dealt with. Gas utility specialists inspected the building, but the gas supply was not restored to five flats.

The local municipality is arranging temporary accommodation for the owner of the flat affected by the fire, while eight other residents are making their own arrangements for temporary housing.

The disaster management authority shared footage of the incident on its social media page, showing the emergency response in the residential area.

Fatal fire in Budapest in October

World.title: Hungarian defence minister’s warning: European plane bomb threats could be coordinated
World.content:
Hungary’s Defence Minister Romulusz Ruszin-Szendi has warned that the recent wave of bomb threats targeting passenger aircraft across Europe could be part of a coordinated campaign aimed at disrupting air travel and testing security systems. He also explained why Hungarian Gripen fighter jets are scrambled during such incidents and under what circumstances they could use weapons.

In a Facebook post on Sunday, the minister pointed to the unusual frequency, geographical spread and timing of the threats. On one recent day, Hungarian authorities ordered three separate alerts within a few hours, while similar incidents were reported in other European countries.

According to Ruszin-Szendi, the pattern raises the possibility of coordinated action. If that is the case, the objective may not necessarily be to cause direct physical damage, but rather to disrupt European aviation, create uncertainty and undermine public confidence, while testing how quickly national and allied security systems respond.

Make things easier with professional support in English. Explore Daily News Hungary’s Services in English and find the help you need.

Why are Hungarian Gripens scrambled?

The minister stressed that the role of the Hungarian Air Force’s JAS-39 Gripen fighter jets goes beyond simply escorting threatened passenger aircraft.

Their tasks include identifying the aircraft, checking its position and monitoring its movements. This can be particularly important if a plane unexpectedly deviates from its declared route, fails to follow air traffic control instructions or behaves in a way that could pose a threat to the population or critical infrastructure.

Ruszin-Szendi also highlighted that the Gripens are armed combat aircraft. Under the appropriate legal and military conditions, and with the necessary authorisation, they can use force against an immediate threat from the air.

However, he emphasised that a bomb threat or an unexpected change of flight path alone does not justify the use of weapons. Any such decision is subject to strict legal, operational and command requirements.

More details: Hungarian Gripen jets scrambled 3 times over bomb threats to passenger planes

The security lessons of 11 September

To explain why such capabilities are necessary, the minister referred to the 11 September 2001 terrorist attacks in the United States, when hijacked passenger aircraft were used as weapons. The attacks demonstrated how a civilian plane could become a serious threat to human lives and national security.

Ruszin-Szendi said Hungary maintains continuous air defence readiness as part of NATO’s Integrated Air and Missile Defence System. Hungarian Gripen pilots and the military personnel supporting them remain on standby around the clock to protect the country’s airspace.

He described the fighter jets’ take-offs not as a show of force, but as evidence of a defence capability that operates continuously and can respond when an aircraft presents a potential threat.

The minister also stressed the importance of rapid decision-making, preparedness and cooperation with NATO allies in responding to both conventional military threats and more difficult-to-identify hybrid challenges.

World.title: Hungary expands energy cooperation with Poland and Czechia in new regional agreement
World.content:
Hungary has expanded its regional energy cooperation with Poland and Czechia, which have joined a broader coalition involving Italy and several Central and Southern European countries. The agreement was signed in Zagreb, where energy ministers also discussed access to Black Sea natural gas, supply diversification and Hungary’s planned green energy investments.

Hungary’s Minister of Economy and Energy, István Kapitány, announced the development in a Facebook video on Sunday. According to his statement, the discussions focused on strengthening energy security by giving participating countries access to more supply sources and transport routes.

The expanded cooperation brings two more members of the Visegrád Group (V4) into the initiative. Poland and Czechia join Hungary, Croatia, Romania and Italy in a regional framework intended to improve energy market integration.

One of the key topics was diversifying gas procurement routes. Hungary aims to work more closely with Croatia and Romania to secure access to alternative energy sources, including natural gas extracted in the Black Sea region.

“Our goal is for Hungary to obtain energy from an increasing number of sources, safely and at affordable prices,” Kapitány said.

Make things easier with professional support in English. Explore Daily News Hungary’s Services in English and find the help you need.

Hungary eyes Black Sea gas supplies

During the meeting in Zagreb, Kapitány also held separate talks with Romania’s new energy minister. The two sides reviewed how Hungary could play a more active role in purchasing natural gas produced in the Black Sea and facilitating its transport to the region.

The Black Sea is expected to become an increasingly important source of natural gas for Central and South-Eastern Europe as new production projects are developed. However, access to these supplies also depends on available infrastructure, transport capacity and agreements between the countries involved.

Kapitány described his discussion with his Romanian counterpart as constructive and said the two ministers would continue their talks in Bucharest in two weeks.

The Zagreb meeting also covered Hungary’s major energy development projects, particularly its efforts to expand green energy capacity.

For Hungary, closer cooperation with neighbouring countries could help diversify its energy imports and reduce reliance on individual supply routes. This agreement shows a stronger regional approach, although its practical impact will depend on the projects and supply arrangements that follow.

World.title: Budapest’s iconic City Park Ice Rink opening date announced – How much could a family visit cost?
World.content:
Budapest’s historic City Park Ice Rink is set to welcome skaters back on 20 November, with an opening event celebrating the 100th anniversary of its mechanisation. However, a family outing could prove costly: although this season’s ticket prices have not yet been announced, last winter’s rates offer an indication of how much visitors may need to budget.

The rink announced on its social media channels that the 2026/27 skating season is scheduled to begin on Friday, 20 November, at 5 pm. The date is still subject to weather conditions, and any changes will be communicated through the venue’s official channels.

The opening celebration will run from 5 pm to 9 pm, with organisers promising ice sports demonstrations, music and activities for all age groups. More details about the programme are expected later.

The occasion also marks 100 years since the rink’s mechanisation. The venue itself is much older: it first opened on 29 January 1870, making it one of Europe’s oldest outdoor ice rinks. Euronews has also included the Budapest attraction in its selection of outdoor ice rinks worth visiting across Europe this winter.

How much did skating cost last season?

The rink has not published its 2026/27 ticket prices yet. The official website still lists the rates from the previous season, so these should be treated as a guide rather than confirmed prices.

(1 euro = 363 forints)

According to Pénzcentrum, last winter, an adult ticket cost HUF 3,500 during normal periods and HUF 4,500 during peak periods, which included Friday evenings and weekends. Student and pensioner tickets were HUF 2,500 and HUF 3,500, respectively.

Discounted family tickets were also available for groups with children under 14. A four-person family ticket, requiring at least two children, cost HUF 9,500 during normal periods and HUF 12,500 at peak times. The three-person and five-person options were also available at different rates.

For a family of four consisting of two adults and two children, the previous season’s weekend admission would therefore have cost HUF 12,500.

Skate rental could push the bill above HUF 25,000

Visitors without their own equipment also need to budget for rentals. Last season, hiring a pair of skates cost HUF 3,500, with a refundable HUF 2,000 deposit per pair. Helmet rental was HUF 1,500, while younger children could hire a skating aid for HUF 1,000 per half-hour.

If all four family members rented skates, that would add HUF 14,000 to their admission bill. At last season’s rates, the total for a weekend visit would therefore have reached HUF 26,500, excluding deposits and any additional services.

Regular visitors could save money with multi-entry passes. A 10-entry adult pass cost HUF 31,500 last season, bringing the price per visit down to HUF 3,150.

What parents should know

Children under six can enter free of charge. Those under 12 must skate with a parent or another adult, while children aged 12 to 14 need written parental permission. The rink does not offer a separate spectator ticket, so accompanying adults must also buy admission.

Tickets for the new season are expected to become available online closer to the opening date. The length of the season will depend on the weather.

World.title: New Hungarian-language book explores why Indian students are learning the language
World.content:
A new Hungarian-language book featuring interviews with 26 Indian university students has been launched at the University of Delhi, offering insight into their experiences of learning Hungarian and what inspired them to take up the language.

Story by: Gopalan Rajamani

Titled Beszélgetőkönyv: Egy delhi magyar lektor interjúi indiai egyetemistákkal (roughly translated as A Conversation Book: Interviews with Indian University Students by a Hungarian Lecturer in Delhi), the 204-page publication was written by Dr Margit Köves, Assistant Lecturer of Hungarian Language and Culture.

The book brings together conversations with 26 students, conducted on different dates. Through their accounts, readers can discover what first attracted them to Hungarian and how they have experienced learning the language in India.

Dr Margit Köves: Beszélgetőkönyv: Egy delhi magyar lektor interjúi indiai egyetemistákkal

A closer look at Hungarian language learning in Delhi

Dr Margit Köves has a postgraduate degree in Philology from ELTE University in Budapest and a doctorate in Buddhist Studies from the University of Delhi. She teaches Hungarian at the University of Delhi and the Liszt Institute – Hungarian Cultural Centre in Delhi, where she is a popular educator.

Published by Tiszatáj Könyvek, based in Szeged, the book also features an introduction by Hungarian author and guitarist Gábor Lanczkor, a member of the band Médeia Fiai.

Students share their experiences at book launch

The launch event was organised by the Department of Slavonic and Finno-Ugrian Studies at the University of Delhi. Several students whose interviews appear in the publication spoke at the event about their personal journeys of learning Hungarian.

The gathering was attended by university professors, students and other guests, bringing together members of the academic community interested in Hungarian language and culture.

The publication offers a glimpse into the growing academic and cultural connections between Hungary and India, told through the experiences of the students themselves.

World.title: Budapest property price gap exceeds EUR 275,000 between its most and least expensive districts
World.content:
The average value of residential property transactions in Budapest’s most expensive district was more than HUF 100 million (approximately EUR 275,000) higher than in one of the capital’s cheapest areas in the third quarter of 2026, according to data from OTP Ingatlanpont. The figures also point to cooling demand in the capital, while family houses continue to dominate property sales in several parts of rural Hungary.

In Budapest, the average transaction value across the districts stood at HUF 73.7 million. District V, which covers the historic city centre, recorded the highest figure at HUF 150.2 million. It was followed by District XXII at HUF 119 million, District II at HUF 88 million and District XII at HUF 87 million.

At the other end of the scale, the average transaction value in District XIX was just HUF 42.8 million. Districts XVII, XXI and VII also recorded relatively low averages, at around HUF 50–51 million.

Budapest property market shows signs of cooling

The high prices appear to be increasingly testing buyers’ budgets. The number of property sales in Budapest fell by nearly 17% in the third quarter compared with the previous quarter, according to OTP Ingatlanpont.

Dezső Varga, the company’s Budapest regional director, said buyers were becoming more selective and paying closer attention to the relationship between price, location and the condition of a property.

Smaller, well-maintained flats priced between HUF 40 million and HUF 70 million remain attractive to many buyers. In Buda, larger properties suitable for families continue to find customers, provided they offer a good layout and are appropriately priced.

Illustration. Photo: depositphotos.com

Family houses dominate rural property sales

The picture is different outside the capital, where family houses account for a substantial share of transactions.

In Southern Transdanubia, nearly 90% of property sales involved family houses. Buyers in the region are particularly interested in more affordable homes, including properties priced below HUF 10 million, although well-maintained houses in higher price categories also attract demand.

In North-Eastern Hungary and the Southern Great Plain, family houses accounted for 74% of transactions in both regions. The average floor area of the family houses sold was 95 square metres.

Meanwhile, the Balaton region continues to attract buyers in the premium segment, with developments around Balatonfüred and Veszprém catering to demand for higher-quality properties in sought-after locations.

Affordability increasingly shapes buying decisions

According to OTP Ingatlanpont’s regional experts, affordability, technical condition and realistic pricing have become increasingly important across Hungary.

Buyers are also paying closer attention to renovation and maintenance costs, as well as whether they can secure suitable financing. The figures suggest that the Hungarian property market is far from uniform, with substantial differences between Budapest districts, rural areas and popular tourist destinations.

World.title: Freezing rain and frost to bring a taste of winter to Hungary next week
World.content:
Hungary is in for a changeable start to the week, with cloudier skies, rain and overnight frosts following a mostly sunny Sunday. Temperatures will generally reach 5–13°C during the afternoons, but freezing conditions are expected in some areas overnight, while light freezing rain cannot be ruled out locally in the Northern Hungarian Mountains.

According to the latest forecast from HungaroMet, Sunday will remain mostly sunny and dry across much of the country, although cloudier areas may develop in western Hungary. Afternoon temperatures will reach 8–13°C, while the mercury could drop below freezing in some northern and north-eastern areas overnight.

Freezing rain possible in the Northern Hungarian Mountains

Clouds will increase from the south-west during Sunday evening, bringing isolated light rain or showers to parts of southern and central Hungary overnight. HungaroMet also says that light freezing rain is possible in the northern foothills of the Mátra and Bükk mountains during the early hours of Monday.

Fog may form in places, particularly in western Transdanubia, and could make driving more difficult. However, the meteorological service says the overall likelihood of weather events reaching its hazardous-weather warning criteria remains low.

What to expect on Monday and Tuesday

On Monday, western Hungary will mostly enjoy sunny weather. East of the Danube, clouds will gradually break up, although some areas may remain overcast, with a little precipitation possible in the morning.

Afternoon highs will generally range between 7 and 12°C, while temperatures in persistently cloudy areas may remain as low as 5–7°C.

Tuesday will bring another change, as clouds move in from the west. Rain and showers are expected in several parts of the country, mainly from the afternoon onwards, although western Transdanubia may stay mostly dry.

Morning temperatures will range from around -4°C to +4°C, rising to 5–13°C by early afternoon. The mildest weather is expected in the south-west.

Cloudy weather to continue on Wednesday

Wednesday is expected to be mostly cloudy or overcast across much of Hungary, with more sunshine likely only in the north-east and south-west. There may be fewer showers during the day, but isolated showers could develop again later in the evening.

Afternoon temperatures are forecast to reach 5–15°C, with cooler conditions in the north and slightly milder weather in the south and south-west.

With overnight frost, local fog and a chance of freezing rain in some areas, drivers should pay particular attention to changing road conditions early in the week.

World.title: New road planned to ease summer traffic to Lake Balaton’s popular city – Unfinished M76 section to get new connection
World.content:
A new seven-kilometre road is being planned to improve access to Keszthely, one of the most important tourist destinations on Hungary’s Lake Balaton. The government is also preparing three cycling infrastructure projects in the region, while dropping plans to extend the M76 expressway towards Sármellék over environmental concerns.

Transport and Investment Minister Dávid Vitézy announced the developments in a Facebook post, explaining that the aim is to make travelling around the western part of Lake Balaton easier and safer for residents and visitors alike.

New road could ease summer congestion

Although Keszthely is the largest town in the region and a major tourism centre, its road connections are currently inadequate, according to the minister.

Traffic arriving from the M76 expressway is diverted onto main road 71 at Fenékpuszta. This creates regular congestion, particularly during the busy summer tourist season.

To address the problem, the government will begin planning a roughly seven-kilometre, single-carriageway road with one lane in each direction. The new route would connect the current terminus of the M76 with main road 75, partly following a new alignment. It would also be designed so that it could be expanded later if traffic demands require it.

The development is intended to provide faster and safer access to Keszthely while reducing traffic on the Fenékpuszta section of main road 71, which is also due for renovation. Plans are also being prepared to upgrade main road 76 between Fenékpuszta and the Sármellék junction.

The new connection could also improve journeys towards Zalaegerszeg.

What will happen to the unfinished M76?

The announcement also clarified the future of the unfinished M76 expressway, originally intended to improve the road connection between Zalaegerszeg and the M7 motorway.

However, the project was halted in 2022, when the government withdrew the procurement procedure for the section between Fenékpuszta and Zalaegerszeg amid a wider investment freeze. Vitézy said in a comment under his Facebook post that the decision to stop the M76 project towards Zalaegerszeg had been made by János Lázár in 2022.

He also stressed that extending the expressway through the Kis-Balaton area towards Sármellék had been off the agenda for years, including under the previous government. According to the minister, the route would cause unacceptable environmental damage to the protected natural area.

Instead, the current government has decided to connect the existing, unfinished section of the M76 to main road 760 via a new bypass road. This would give the already-built section a practical connection to the surrounding road network and, according to Vitézy, improve access towards Zalaegerszeg as well.

Three cycling projects also planned

Alongside the road developments, preparations will begin for three cycling infrastructure projects in the western Balaton region:

A cycling connection between Fenékpuszta and Sármellék;

Cycling route improvements around the Festetics-major estate;

Modernisation of the Balaton Bike Circuit between Keszthely and Vonyarcvashegy.

The minister stressed that transport development around Lake Balaton should take all forms of mobility into account. The planned projects are intended to support everyday travel for local residents, improve access to the region and benefit tourism.

For visitors heading to Keszthely and the western shore of Lake Balaton, the proposed road could eventually offer an alternative to one of the area’s current traffic bottlenecks. However, the projects are at the planning stage, and no construction timetable has been announced.

World.title: Week in Review: Between Hope and Apathy
World.content:
Bulgaria has a newly elected president – government-backed candidate Iliana Iotova. In the November 1 run-off for the presidency, she won 57.6 per cent of the votes cast to her challenger Andrey Gyurov’s 39.5 per cent.

Yet unlike their neighbours in Serbia, who voted in record numbers in recent elections, Bulgarians voted in record low numbers. Only 29.1 per cent of eligible voters cast ballots in the run-off, slightly more than in the first round. Our analysis looks at why many Bulgarians are tuning out of politics altogether.

World.title: With Change of Power, Serbia Can Reinvigorate EU Accession Bid
World.content:
“Catastrophic” - that’s how Dragana Djurica describes the current state of Serbia’s European Union accession process.

On Wednesday, the bloc’s executive arm, the European Commission, delivered its annual assessment of the progress made - or not - by countries bidding for membership. One of the main takeaways was the substantial progress made by Montenegro; another was the dramatic backsliding by Serbia.

“This is not a progress report, as it is officially called, but a report on backsliding,” said Djurica, head of the European Movement in Serbia, an NGO that advocates for Serbia’s EU integration.

“It is one of the most critical, and I would even say the worst, reports Serbia has received from the European Commission since the start of accession negotiations.”

World.title: Turkey Arrests Former Minister Over Stock Market Fraud Scandal
World.content:
A court in Istanbul on Friday ordered the arrest of Fatma Betul Sayan Kaya, a former minister and deputy chair of Turkey’s ruling Justice and Development Party, AKP, over her alleged role in a major stock market financial fraud.

The Istanbul Prosecutor’s Office accused Kaya of “being a member of an organised crime group and violating stock market law”.

Her husband, Ilyas Kaya, and a former chair of the Capital Markets Board, Ibrahim Omer Gonul, were given a travel ban but not arrested.

Fatma Betul Sayan Kaya, who was family and social policies minister from 2016 to 2018, resigned in September as a deputy chair of President Recep Tayyip Erdogan’s ruling AKP after allegations emerged about share transactions by her and her husband.

She is accused of illegally profiting through share-price manipulation after she received 2.17 billion Turkish lira (about 38.4 million euros) after reportedly investing 163 million lira (about 2.7 million euros) in an investment fund.

The couple deny wrongdoing. They have transferred some of the profits to an account designated by the banking regulators.

The AKP and the government welcomed the arrest order as proof of their good governance.

“We move forward by renewing ourselves! We are constantly reborn. We part ways with those who do wrong and those who succumb to their own desires, and we continue on our path stronger than before,” Turkish Justice Minister Akin Gurlek wrote on X after Sayan Kaya’s arrest on Friday.

The investigation has already resulted in more than 100 detentions while Turkey’s Capital Markets Board has ordered the liquidation of 131 investment funds managed by seven portfolio management companies.

According to Reuters, the funds’ assets are worth around 18.8 billion euros, involving about 353,000 investors. A Turkish television channel put the total number of investors at more than 514,000.

Kaya comes from a family with experience of public office. Her brother, Omer Fatih Sayan, a former telecommunications regulator chief and deputy transport minister, was appointed to the Energy Market Regulatory Board in July.

Her sister, Ayse Hilal Sayan Koytak, previously ambassador to Kuwait and Bahrain, was appointed ambassador to Finland in September. Another sister, Nazmiye Sumeyye Sayan, previously served on Istanbul’s municipal council.

World.title: Serbia’s Anti-Terrorism Unit Chief Detained Over Alleged Abuse of Protesters
World.content:
A court in Belgrade on Friday ordered up to 30 days of detention for nine current and former employees of Serbia’s Interior Ministry, including the commander of the Special Anti-Terrorist Unit, Igor Zmiric, over allegations of abusing and torturing students and others inside the government building following protests in August 2025.

According to the court, the nine suspects were remanded in custody over concerns that they could influence witnesses and obstruct criminal proceedings. The court also cited the seriousness of the alleged offence and the public concern it had caused, which could jeopardise the fair conduct of the proceedings.

The suspects are accused of jointly committing the criminal offence of abuse and torture.

According to the prosecution, the suspects used force and threats to inflict pain and suffering on students and other people in the government building’s garage between 10.30 p.m. on August 14 and 1 a.m. the following morning, with the aim of obtaining information, intimidating and unlawfully punishing them.

At the time of the offence, they were working as officers of the JZO, a police unit used to protect high-ranking state officials and major government buildings.

The suspects were arrested earlier this week. Among them is Milan Vukovic, a retired JZO officer who is now acting director of the detention facility where former JZO chief Marko Kricak is being held.

Kricak, who headed the unit at the time of the alleged abuse, has also been arrested, but in connection with a separate investigation into a murder in Belgrade.

During the mass anti-government protests of the past two years, some protesters have accused Kricak of using excessive force. Student Nikolina Sindjelic alleged that Kricak had threatened her with rape while she was detained in the garage beneath the government building in August 2025.

At least 15 people were detained in the garage beneath the government building on the night of August 14, 2025, amid anti-government protests, BIRN reported.

BIRN obtained testimonies given to prosecutors by four detainees and interviewed five others, who described being beaten, threatened with sexual violence and death, and having their personal belongings destroyed. Rights groups Amnesty International and Civil Rights Defenders warned that the alleged treatment could amount to torture and violate international law.

At the time, the Interior Ministry rejected the allegations, insisting that the officers had acted in accordance with the law. Then President Aleksandar Vucic later announced that the ministry’s internal affairs unit would investigate the allegations made by Sindjelic.

At the time of BIRN’s investigation, it was not clear whether the promised internal probe had been carried out.

World.title: Albania’s ‘Coordinator’? The Rapid Rise and Sudden Fall of Ergys Agasi
World.content:
On the afternoon of August 26, as the sun was setting over Durres beach, police in several unmarked vehicles pulled over a black Audi on the southern outskirts of the Albanian port city. Inside the car was Ergys Agasi, a businessman and former official at the environment ministry who had been on the run for the past eight months.

In video released by the police, 39-year-old Agasi is seen in a white T-shirt and shorts, hands cuffed behind his back, head bowed.

Albania’s Special Prosecution Against Corruption and Organised Crime, SPAK, accuses Agasi of leading an organised criminal group that manipulated public tenders linked to the National Agency for Information Society, AKSHI, sometimes through violence.

Less than a month after his arrest, investigators moved against the head of the State Intelligence Service, SHISH, Vlora Hyseni, accusing her of aiding Agasi to evade arrest and providing him with classified information. Hyseni was placed under house arrest and dismissed from SHISH.

World.title: Serbian President’s Controversial Last-Minute Pardons Face Legal Challenges
World.content:
This Friday, a court in Belgrade was supposed to hear the verdict in the case against a man who rammed a car into a 20-year-old female student, Sonja Ponjavic, who was blocking a traffic intersection during an anti-government protest in the Serbian capital in January 2025.

The blockade was one of many rallies organised by students in memory of victims of the November 2024 Novi Sad railway station disaster – an incident that transformed Serbian politics and ultimately led to the ousting of the government led by Aleksandar Vucic’s Serbian Progressive Party at last month’s elections.

However, now the driver might not be punished for hitting the student because Vucic pardoned him in one of his last actions as President before stepping down to run for the premiership in the elections.

World.title: Transnistria’s Separatist Leader Decorated by Moscow, Denounced by Moldova
World.content:
In a ceremony at the Kremlin on Wednesday, Russian President Vladmir Putin formally pinned the Order of Honour award on the lapel of Vadim Krasnoselsky, the leader of Transnistria - a separatist region of Moldova where Moscow has maintained a military presence since the Soviet bloc disintegrated.

Putin said the decoration was awarded to recognise Krasnoselsky’s efforts to "strengthen ties" with Russia and amidst "pressure" from the West. Moldova is seeking to join the EU, but separatist Transnistria remains a potentially disruptive Russian lever of influence that Moscow wants to preserve.

“Despite difficult conditions and attempts at external pressure, the republic [Transnistria], under his leadership, is developing consistently. Its inhabitants, who are of various nationalities, defend their rights and interests together, uphold the historical truth and preserve the Russian language,” Putin explained.

Located on Moldova’s border with Ukraine, and home to 1,600 Russian troops, Transnistria is strategically important for the Russian leader. Speaking in Moscow, Krasnoselsky seemed happy to fall into line.

World.title: Hundreds of bags of red pepper wash up on beach near Bulgaria’s Plovdiv
World.content:
As is traditional, a Remembrance Sunday service was held at the Commonwealth War Graves cemetery in Bulgaria’s city of Plovdiv on November 8.

Remembrance Sunday, held annually on the Sunday closest to Remembrance Day on November 11, commemorates and honours the dead in the wars of the 20th century. The November 11 date arises from the anniversary of the Armistice at the close of the First World War.

In Plovdiv, the service was led by British ambassador Nathaniel Copsey and Father Patrick Irwin, and attended by military veterans from Britain and the Commonwealth, as well as members of the public.

The Lesson was read by Lieutenant Colonel Matthew Walker, and 10-year-old Charles Copsey delivered the Exhortation:

“They shall grow not old, as we that are left grow old,

Age shall not weary them, nor the years condemn.

At the going down of the sun, and in the morning,

We will remember them.”

(Photos: Clive Leviev-Sawyer)

World.title: Hundreds of bags of red pepper wash up on beach near Bulgaria’s Plovdiv
World.content:
Hundreds of bags of red pepper have washed up on the beach near the village of Sinemorets on Bulgaria’s Black Sea coast, Tsarevo municipality’s mayor Marin Kirov said on November 8.

Officials from the Regional Inspectorate for Environment Protection and Water in Bourgas and the Basin Directorate are taking samples of the sea water near Sinemorets to determine if there is any pollution.

According to the Bourgas district administration, the cargo was likely transported in a shipping container that opened at sea and currents carried the sacks to shore.

The incident also follows recent incidents of drones sinking or severely damaging merchant ships off Bulgaria’s coast, in attacks widely blamed on Russia.

The results of the checks on the sea water are expected next week. However, reaching the beach is a serious challenge for the inspectors themselves, as they have to walk nearly two kilometres through difficult terrain.

Kirov, in a post on Facebook, said that although though the beaches are exclusive state property, “we fully recognise the gravity of the situation regarding the hundreds of sacks of red pepper found on an undeveloped beach in Sinemorets”.

He said that the municipality was in constant contact with the district governor, and would assist in the cleanup of the beach.

“Naturally, I would like to make a point: such incidents are likely to become more frequent, and a formal mechanism for cleaning the coastline needs to be established,” Kirov said.

“Should this recur—given that the sea frequently washes various types of cargo onto our beaches and rocky shores—the state must allocate funds to the Bourgas district administration to cover these cleanup operations,” he said.

(Photo via Kirov’s Facebook page)

World.title: Bulgarian Navy team destroys Russian drone found near Shabla
World.content:
A Bulgarian Navy team destroyed on November 6 a drone – identified as a Russian Gerber-2 – that had been found near Shabla on Bulgaria’s northern Black Sea coast, according to a statement by the Defence Ministry.

At 10am, a signal was sent by the operational duty officer of the Ministry of Interior about the presence of a drone in the area of the beach north of the lighthouse on Cape Shabla, the ministry said.

A specialist team from Varna Naval Base established that the aerial drone probably fell into the sea and was subsequently thrown ashore.

According to the Defence Ministry, there were no inscriptions on its hull and it was classified as a Russian Gerber – 2. This contradicts earlier media reports that the drone was marked as a Shahel, a type that is of Iranian manufacture and which is used by Russia.

The drone was destroyed on site, with strict observance of all safety measures. It was established that it did not carry an explosive, the Defence Ministry said.

The incident is the latest of more than 100 in which drones or parts of drones have been found in Bulgarian waters or on beaches since the beginning of 2026, against the backdrop of Russia’s war on Ukraine.

(Photo: Ministry of Defence)

World.title: Two aircraft land at Sofia Airport following latest bomb threats – report
World.content:
Two civilian aircraft that were travelling from London and Brussels landed at Vassil Levski Sofia Airport on November 6 following e-mailed bomb threats, Bulgarian National Television (BNT) said, citing the Transport Ministry.

The aircraft were checked by Border Police teams and no explosive devices were found, BNT said.

The planes landed without any problems.

This is the latest of a succession of disruptions of flights in Europe because of e-mailed bomb threats. On November 5, three aircraft that were the subject of bomb threats landed at Bulgarian airports – two in Sofia and one in Plovdiv.

Director of Air Traffic Management Ivan Dyaksov told Nova Televizia on November 6 that the e-mails were sent by “unknown organisations” whose goal is to sow discord.

There have been at least 24 such cases across Europe in the past week,” Dyaksov said.

National security expert Colonel Assen Peychev told Nova TV: “There are two countries in the world that have an interest in destabilising Europe – Russia and Iran”.

“They aim to both drain resources and test how Nato countries react,” cybersecurity expert Lyubomir Tulev said.

(Photo: Sofia Airport)

World.title: Eurostat: Bulgaria had EU’s third-highest annual increase in retail trade volume in September 2026
World.content:
Dr. Konstantin Trenchev, founder and honorary president of the Podkrepa labour confederation, has died at the age of 71 after a short illness, Podkrepa said on November 6.

“There are individuals whose names remain inextricably linked to a certain historical era,” Podkrepa said.

“For the Bulgarian independent trade union movement and the democratic changes after 1989, this name is Dr. Konstantin Trenchev.”

A doctor by profession, a public figure, a dissident by conviction and a leader by vocation, Trenchev was the man who, in 1989, laid the foundation for the first independent trade union in Bulgaria – Podkrepa, the statement said.

At a time when free association was impossible and the protection of human and labour rights was subordinated to state power, he chose the most difficult path – to oppose the system and give hope that free trade unionism was possible, it said.

The creation of Podkrepa was not simply the establishment of a new organisation, the labour confederation said. “It is an act of civic courage and protection of the dignity of Bulgarian workers”.

Because of this activity, Dr. Trenchev was subjected to repression, was arrested and spent several months as a political prisoner.

“Instead of being crushed, he became one of the symbols of the struggle for democracy, freedom of speech and the right to independent trade union association.”

After the fall of the communist regime, he became one of the founders of the Union of Democratic Forces and participated in the processes of democratic transition in the country, including in the National Round Table between the ruling party and the opposition.

After the democratic changes, Trenchev devoted more than a quarter of a century to building Podkrepa.

Thanks to his efforts, Podkrepa became the first Bulgarian trade union organisation accepted into the international and European trade union family.

He was the first Bulgarian elected as Vice-President of the European Trade Union Confederation, as well as as Vice-President of the International Confederation of Free Trade Unions – “a recognition not only of his personal authority, but also of Bulgaria’s place in the European social dialogue”.

In 2015, after 26 years at the helm of Podkrepa, he handed over the leadership to the next generation of trade union leaders and was elected honorary president of the confederation – recognition for his exceptional contribution to the development of the organization and the Bulgarian trade union movement, Podkrepa said.

(Photos via the Podkrepa website)

World.title: Eurostat: Bulgaria had EU’s third-highest annual increase in retail trade volume in September 2026
World.content:
Bulgaria had the third-highest annual increase in retail trade volume in the European Union in September 2026, according to figures released on November 6 by EU statistics agency Eurostat.

Among EU member states for which data are available, the highest annual increases in the total retail trade volume were recorded in Cyprus (7.6 per cent), Sweden (6.9 per cent) and Bulgaria (5.7 per cent).

The largest decreases were observed in Germany (-2.4 per cent), Romania (-2.3 per cent) and Spain (-1.5 per cent).

In September 2026, compared with September 2025, the calendar adjusted retail sales index increased by 0.4 per cent in the euro area and by 0.9 per cent in the EU, Eurostat said.

(Photo: Ngaulin)

World.title: NSI poll: Consumer confidence in Bulgaria plummets
World.content:
A regular three-monthly poll by the National Statistical Institute (NSI), the results of which were released on November 6, shows that consumer confidence in Bulgaria has dropped by 6.9 percentage points.

The NSI found it to be slightly down in February. This was followed by a downturn in May, then an improvement in the poll reported in August.

In October 2026, there was decreased confidence among both urban and rural dwellers, by 5.3 and 11 percentage points, respectively, the NSI said.

Those polled were more pessimistic in their views of the economic situation in Bulgaria over the past 12 months and the coming 12 months.

Compared to July, their assessments and expectations about the changes in the financial situation of their households were also more negative.

In October, consumers’ assessments about the change of consumer prices over the past 12 months were more unfavourable. However, inflation expectations over the next 12 months were less intense, the NSI said.

While overall expectations were that unemployment in Bulgaria would slightly decrease over the coming 12 months, those living in cities expected that it would increase.

Most consumers saw the current economic situation in Bulgaria as unfavourable for savings.

Their attitude regarding intensions of spending on major purchases of durable goods and home improvements over the next 12 months was also negative, the NSI said.

World.title: Bulgarian sculptor and former Speaker of Parliament Vezhdi Rashidov dies
World.content:
Renowned sculptor and former Speaker of Bulgaria’s National Assembly Vezhdi Rashidov has died at the age of 74, it was confirmed on November 6.

Rashidov was born on December 14 1951 in Dimitrovgrad.

In 1970, he graduated from the Iliya Petrov Art School of Fine Arts in Sofia, and in 1978, he graduated from the Sculpture Department at the National Academy of Arts in Sofia.

From 1978, Rashidov participated in national and international exhibitions, biennials and symposiums.

He presented his works at the International Sculpture Biennale in Ravenna and the World Art Fair in Basel.

Among his solo exhibitions are those at Unesco in Paris in 1989, in Tokyo in 1992 and at the Oscar Wilde Museum in Dublin in 2006. In addition to sculptures, he exhibited drawings and watercolours.

Among his awards are the Vatican’s Dante Alighieri Gold Medal in 1981, the first prize at the International Biennial of Humor and Satire in Gabrovo in 1983, and the Vera grand prize for sculpture at the “Traditions and Modernity” International Festival in Moscow in 2009.

Rashidov was awarded the Order of the Stara Planina with Ribbon and is a Corresponding Member of the Bulgarian Academy of Sciences. He was an honorary citizen of Sofia, Dimitrovgrad, and Kurdzhali, among other cities. His works are held in Bulgarian galleries and in collections abroad, including the Uffizi Gallery in Florence, the Pushkin Museum in Moscow, and the Israel Museum in Jerusalem.

Rashidov was Minister of Culture in the first and second Boiko Borissov governments. He held the post from July 27 2009 to March 13 2013 and from November 7 2014 to January 27 2017.

Rashidov was a member of parliament in seven parliaments. On October 21 2022, he was elected Speaker of the 48th National Assembly and held the position until the end of his term in February 2023.

In the 49th National Assembly, he was an MP from Borissov’s GERB-UDF. On September 1 2023, his resignation was approved by Parliament.

World.title: Zagreb Engineers Turn a Garage Hobby into a Global Tech Business
World.content:
November the 8th, 2026 – Zagreb engineers managed to turn a garage hobby into a truly global tech business, and it all started with hiding cigarettes from inspectors…

In a smaller industrial zone in Rudeš, a Croatian technology company has been working on innovative solutions that are used in the products of large global companies, from Europe to the USA. Paula Hadjur reports for Index that Matija Puškar, one of the founders of Byte Lab, revealed more about exactly what their team is engaged in. Their job is not to create finished products, but to develop technological solutions that make them smarter, simpler and more accessible to customers. For example, after receiving a specific request, their team designed a device that measures performances in motocross, which is then placed on the drivers’ helmets.

“we’re currently working on an electronic nose…”

“The most successful path to a good product is to talk to people who are deep in that niche. We’re exclusively an engineering company that carries out their own ideas. Someone has a problem and from that, a technical solution arises,” he explained.

They are currently busy working on a so-called electronic nose, an idea that arose in their innovations department in which an entire team works on all projects that seem interesting and useful to them for companies that have not yet developed those ideas themselves. “The idea evolved to the level that we went to our standard clients and showed them the technology. Some clients said it wasn’t particularly interesting to them, but there were those to whom it was very interesting. For example, that the nose, just from the smell of the coffee, understands which brand it is and how much it is roasted and on the basis of that automatically adjusts the coffee preparation process,” he says.

cooperation with the rest of europe and even the usa

They cooperate the most with the USA, Puškar explained, but also with European countries such as Switzerland, Germany, the Benelux countries and the United Kingdom. They also work with Middle Eastern countries. “That distribution is quite natural. We are part of the EU so we give the greatest value to clients in Europe. Prototypes that are produced today in our ground floor can already tomorrow at 9 o’clock be delivered to them,” he says. However interesting and abstract the innovations are, perhaps the most valuable thing in this story is the way it arose. In a garage in Špansko two friends, still as kids, started learning about electronics over the summer.

“The whole story started 10 years before the company was founded. Danijel Babić and I were kids from Špansko who were playing around with electronics,” he says. The first more concrete projects Danijel and he carried out still during their studies at the Faculty of Electrical Engineering and Computing (FER), when they developed a system intended for medical diagnostics, such as gait analysis in persons with amputation, because of which they also received the Tesla’s Egg recognition of the VIDI e-novation competition back in 2007. As their desire for innovations did not diminish even with the years, and the projects became larger and larger, both decided to finally open their company, which somewhat later was also joined by their friend and colleague from FER Ivan Dodig.

“In 2011, we came to the situation that the colleague was finishing faculty, I was in the final year. We saw that we already had some revenues and came to the conclusion that we need to formalise so that the whole story would have its head and tail,” he says.

from smart bikes to electric gas meters…

We also went down into Byte Lab’s production plant. Everything starts from an empty board, Puškar explained to us while he was leading us, on which electronic components are placed that are then soldered in ovens, after which additional controls and correctness tests follow, with the help of human hands. That is how some of their most recognisable solutions arose – electric gas meters, smart bicycles and even devices that track performances of motocross races. “If you do motocross, you don’t know how you’re managing to ride, unless you have a friend who times you while you’re passing. We made a device that tracks the complete analytics of entering corners, jump heights, speed tracking,” Puškar says, and subsequently it was interesting for him to hear from clients that that product was later also used among skiers.

“From the standpoint of data, what’s the difference?” Puškar asks himself.

their first product was a cigarette controller

Today, the Byte Lab team, which achieved around 4.5 million in revenue last year alone, still keeps the first product they ever sold as part of the company, in the drawers of the office in which today they close most of their deals with world-famous brands. “We were making cigarette controllers,” Matija laughs. “Advertising of cigarettes was already banned then, and we got the task to make a controller that by pressing a button opens and automatically closes the shutters under which the cigarettes stand, so that traders would reduce the risk of fines.”

Today, they’re a company with around 90 employees, with their own plant, production and a whole series of long-term partners. But, Puškar says, they never thought that the whole story could reach such proportions. “We like to joke that for us the development of new products is like running is for Forrest Gump: you ask yourself where you’re running, you don’t know, but it doesn’t matter. We love creating something new, we strongly nurture that curiosity and it motivates us. The nicest thing is that we work really broadly, from appliances to medical devices. It’s nice to see your products on shelves in shops, in concert halls and at airports,” he concluded.
