World.title: Alex Eala suffers season-ending stunner as Liu dominates Hong Kong final
World.content:
MANILA, Philippines – Filipina tennis superstar Alex Eala met a disappointing end to what was otherwise a prolific Hong Kong Open run, and a historic 2026 season overall, as American foe Claire Liu cruised to a dominant 6-3, 6-0 title-winning finale on Sunday, November 8.

With the stunning win over the world No. 17 Eala, world No. 102 Liu finally earned a breakthrough career singles title at the WTA 250 level after earning two WTA 125 championships.

Liu’s title win marked a second consecutive upset at the Filipina icon’s expense, as the 26-year-old, then world No. 305, booted the top-50 Eala at the 2025 Guangzhou Open first round in their only other head-to-head meeting.

With that footnote likely in the back of their minds, Liu kept her aggression up from the get-go, seizing the opening frame with a 3-0 finish from a competitive 3-3 deadlock to set the tone, 6-3.

Desperate to turn the tide, Eala poured everything she had into the first game of the second set, denying four break points in a prolonged back-and-forth point trade before finally losing her serve and the first point to Liu.

Likely out of gas and definitely out of momentum, Eala faded quicker as the points piled on, losing her serve in the third and fifth games before Liu finally put the Filipina out of her misery with a stunning bagel finish, 6-0, and nine straight won games for the title.

The 6-0 burial marked a dim end to a monumental 2026 season for Eala, who proved worthy of her lofty world ranking with a sensational rise to the Hong Kong Open final and a career milestone WTA 500 Washington DC Open championship last August.

“First and foremost, I want to congratulate Claire on an amazing tournament, a great week and a great match. Very, very well deserved congratulations. I’d like to thank the tournament staff and the organizers for the amazing hospitality, the physios for keeping me together,” Eala said.

“And of course, the fans, thank you, thank you, thank you. I mean, wrapping up this year, you guys do not know how much meaning you add on top of what I do, and how much of a pleasure it is to go about my life sharing these moments with you all. So I’m forever grateful.”

Eala soon heads home to bask in her career highs and 2026 season overall with a big homecoming event, “Alex Eala Live: Game. Set. Celebrate,” at the massive Philippine Arena on December 8. – Rappler.com

World.title: Tesla to pull the plug on Cybertruck after years of poor sales
World.content:
CYBERTRUCK. A Tesla Cybertruck sits in the parking lot of a Tesla facility in the Queens borough of New York City, U.S., September 16, 2026.

Tesla will add an extra production shift to try to complete outstanding Cybertruck orders before dismantling the line next year for a planned expansion of Cybercab production

Tesla will wind down Cybertruck production at its Texas gigafactory around mid-2027, CEO Elon Musk said on Friday, November 6, after years of persistently weak sales for a futuristic model once touted as a rival to legacy pickup trucks.

The move is a major retreat from what has been one of Musk’s pet projects. In an X post, Musk said the wind-down would let Tesla make more of the Cybercab, a robotaxi he has made central to the automaker’s autonomous-vehicle ambitions, but one that has yet to prove itself commercially.

The announcement comes at the end of a bruising week for Musk, as his record political spending of nearly half a billion dollars yielded little in Tuesday’s US midterm elections, with the vast majority of the Republican candidates he backed losing their races.

Combined, his companies were on track to lose more than $180 billion in market capitalization for the week.

Tesla will add an extra production shift to try to complete outstanding Cybertruck orders before dismantling the line next year for a planned expansion of Cybercab production, CEO Elon Musk said Saturday.

“The Cybertruck order backlog is currently far more than Tesla can make before dismantling the line for Cybercab expansion around June/July next year,” Musk said in a post on X.

In response to a user on X, Musk called the Cybertruck the “best vehicle Tesla has ever made” and the wind-down the “end of an era.”

Tesla has been shifting its focus to robotics and autonomy, a transition analysts say comes at the expense of the electric-vehicle business it helped pioneer as Chinese rivals gain ground.

The US EV maker began delivering the Cybertruck to customers in late 2023. According to automotive data platform Kelley Blue Book, the company only sold 20,237 Cybertrucks in the US last year, down 48% from 38,965 in 2024. Around the start of production in 2023, Musk had predicted annual sales of 250,000 units.

“It doesn’t make sense to keep it going when it’s not meeting its targets,” said former Aston Martin CEO Andy Palmer. “Every rational auto guy would say the same.”

“It will no doubt only be a rounding error on Tesla’s balance sheet, but the statistics speak for themselves.”

Musk’s SpaceX was one of the model’s biggest customers last year and bought Cybertrucks worth $131 million from Tesla in 2025 at list price, according to its IPO filing.

‘Cybertruck won’t go, can’t go’

Right from its unveiling in 2019, the Cybertruck was a controversial choice for Musk. Pickup truck purists mocked its angular design, and safety experts predicted it would be hard to gain approval for sale in key markets like Europe.

The unveiling event itself was marred when Musk tried to prove that its windows were shatterproof by having metal balls thrown at them — only to leave massive cracks in two of them.

During Cybertruck’s official launch in 2023, Musk touted it as a futuristic competitor to pickup trucks from General Motors and Ford, saying “finally, the future will look like the future.”

But the model has struggled to meet those expectations. Tesla has issued 11 recalls for the Cybertruck since it went on sale in late 2023, according to the National Highway Traffic Safety Administration. Some vehicles required physical repairs, while others were fixed with over-the-air software updates.

Automotive analyst Felipe Munoz said that although the Cybertruck has been called a failure because of its poor sales, electric pickups from Ford and others have also flopped in the US market.

“All of them lost the competition because electric pick ups aren’t popular in the US,” Munoz said.

But Cybertruck’s sharp-edged stainless-steel design limited its prospects in markets like Europe where EVs are more popular. Regulatory approval was impossible for Europe because of rules there concerning pedestrian impact.

“Anywhere where you have crash regulation that takes into account pedestrian impact, that Cybertruck won’t go, can’t go,” former Aston Martin CEO Palmer said.

Musk’s new bet

The Cybercab, which has butterfly doors and no steering wheel, pedals or mirrors, is one of Musk’s key bets in his push to turn Tesla into an AI and robotics company rather than just an automaker.

Musk has said he sees it as Tesla’s main autonomous model supplying a global network of robotaxis.

After years of delays to Musk’s self-driving targets, Tesla began offering paid rides in a small fleet of Cybercabs in Austin in September. However, the automaker still has to answer the US auto safety agency’s questions on whether it has properly self-certified Cybercab to demonstrate compliance with federal motor vehicle safety standards.

The National Highway Traffic Safety Administration opened an audit in September to review the basis for that certification.

“Cybertruck was an incredible technology development platform and lives on through Cybercab,” Cybertruck lead engineer Wes Morrill said on X.

However, the Cybercab is unlikely to make up for lost Cybertruck volumes soon. The two-seater robotaxi is still a small program, with production beginning only earlier this year. Tesla has listed an installed capacity of more than 125,000 units.

About 570 of the more than 1,200 Tesla robotaxis operating in Texas are Cybercabs, with the rest mainly Model Y vehicles, according to the state’s Department of Motor Vehicles. – Rappler.com

World.title: [Inside the Newsroom] The struggle with declaring #WalangPasok
World.content:
President Ferdinand Marcos Jr.’s new executive order seems to be an EO that Malacañang itself badly needs, after a string of blanket class suspensions

“Talaga lang ha?” was my initial, no-filter reaction when Malacañang announced that President Ferdinand Marcos Jr. had signed an executive order (EO) establishing a framework for class suspensions and resumptions.

EO No. 130 explicitly allows for area- and school-level decisions to be made on when to suspend or resume classes — a targeted approach as opposed to blanket orders covering entire provinces or even regions.

Hello, I’m Acor Arceo, head of news operations at Rappler. I also oversee our coverage of the education sector and disasters, among others, which explains why I was probably the most skeptical in our newsroom when Marcos’ new EO was publicly released on Tuesday, November 3.

When I instructed our education reporter Jelo Ritzhie Mantaring to write an article on the EO, I also pointed out that Malacañang had often been the one to step in and declare blanket class suspensions — in trigger-happy fashion, really.

It was like the Palace gave itself the order it badly needed.

Let’s backtrack a bit to 2025. Remember when Interior Secretary Jonvic Remulla drew flak for his flippant way of announcing class suspensions? The approach that made him a social media star as Cavite governor had the opposite effect when he took it to the national stage. At the time, the focus was on Remulla’s choice of words and overall tone, which lacked the formality befitting his position and the gravity of the situation.

There were also instances when Remulla’s announcements somehow excluded one or more affected provinces, raising even more questions about whether or not he was making well-informed decisions.

Thankfully, the poorly worded social media announcements from the Department of the Interior and Local Government eventually stopped. What didn’t stop back then, however, was Malacañang’s blanket class suspension policy.

Up until last September, the Palace was still suspending face-to-face classes for entire areas, seemingly disregarding the fact that these areas were facing different weather conditions and varying risk levels. Sure, there was a line in each Malacañang memorandum acknowledging the authority of local chief executives to decide for their respective cities, municipalities, or provinces, but who would deviate from an order that already came from the top?

In one instance, the Palace suspension order came late afternoon, when school and work hours were almost over. People could only shake their heads and wonder: a) Is this supposed to be for tomorrow? b) Is Malacañang in a different timezone? c) Is this even for real?

The executive branch also seemed to have forgotten that every school day counts in a country facing a severe learning crisis. This is not to say that we should make students go to class at all costs, without care for their safety. It’s about ensuring that those who can safely attend classes are actually able to do so, instead of them automatically being lumped together with students in areas facing harsh conditions.

Implementing guidelines for Marcos’ new EO are expected to be released within 30 days. Join us in scrutinizing the guidelines once they’re out. – Rappler.com

World.title: VP’s defense begins amid calls for her to testify
World.content:
Inquirer photo/Niño Jesus Orbeta

MANILA, Philippines — Vice President Sara Duterte’s lawyers face the task of disproving allegations that she amassed unexplained wealth while in office as her Senate impeachment trial resumes today, after a nearly monthlong recess and amid growing pressure for her to take the witness stand.

Senate impeachment court spokesperson Reginald Tongol said the court has already served 22 of the 24 subpoenas requested by the defense panel ahead of the presentation of their evidence.

Tongol said Suzette Balucanag-Punay, the corporate counsel of GenCorp Industries Inc. and Metro City Chow Foods Corp., would be the first defense witness to take the stand when the proceedings resume.

Article continues after this 

However, Batangas Rep. Gerville Luistro said the prosecution team received a notice that Balucanag-Punay would be unable to attend the hearing due to a scheduled magnetic resonance imaging (MRI) scan.

READ: VP’s lawyers didn’t dispute authenticity of financial records – prosecution

“That is correct, and the anticipated date for her presentation will be on Wednesday because the subpoena issued to [Balucanag-Punay] I believe is from Monday to Wednesday. But with the excuse of having this scheduled MRI, definitely, she will not be there tomorrow,” Luistro told dzBB on Sunday.

Tongol on Saturday said in an interview with dwIZ, “She will testify on the general information sheets and audited financial statements submitted by those corporations from 2022 to 2025 according to the purpose stated by the respondent in their manifestation.”

READ: Hontiveros: Too early to say there’s already a number for VP conviction

Article continues after this 

The defense panel had initially sought subpoenas for 25 individuals, including former law school dean Ralph Sarmiento, who declined to testify.

The recess in the trial was marked by exchanges between prosecutors and the Vice President’s camp over whether evidence established her undisclosed fortunes by failing to truthfully disclose her assets since taking office in 2022.

Article continues after this 

Luistro said “it will be difficult” for Duterte’s lawyers to refute the records filed by the prosecutorial team and admitted by the impeachment court as evidence.

“It is difficult to dispute evidence anchored in a document submitted by none other than the respondent,” she told dzBB in Filipino on Sunday. “How do you disown your own documents? How do you contradict a document that you personally filed?”

Luistro, chief prosecutor, challenged Duterte to take the witness stand so she could personally shed light on the accusations fueling the ouster drive against her.

“The lone person who can truly explain what happened is none other than the Vice President herself,” she said.

Duterte has not attended her trial since proceedings began in July. She has repeatedly denied any wrongdoing, dismissing the effort to remove her from office as politically motivated.

“As we’ve said, if the defense is truly claiming that she committed no wrongdoing and no violation, why not come out into the open?” Luistro asked. “Take the witness stand, defend yourself.”

Asked what it would mean if the Vice President refuses to take the stand to testify, Luistro said it would show that “she is not interested in defending herself,” leaving the prosecution’s allegations unrefuted.

Public sentiment also heavily favors Duterte personally addressing the unexplained wealth charge against her, lawyer Benjamin Tolosa Jr., a private prosecutor and the team’s legal spokesperson, said.

“The recent stats show that if people want to hear the Vice President’s explanation, it means they see the merit and weight of the evidence we presented,” he told the Saturday News Forum in Filipino, based on a Sunday statement. “That’s precisely why they want her to address it.”

A Social Weather Stations Survey last month showed that 78 percent of Filipinos believe Duterte should testify in her trial.

Mansions, properties

Drawing on testimony from forensic financial analyst Alexander Cabrera, prosecutors claimed Duterte may have concealed at least P817.87 million in assets, though broader projections from his assessment suggest her total undisclosed wealth could top P1.5 billion.

“What is the explanation regarding the allegation of over P800 million in unexplained wealth as computed and calculated by our financial analyst?” Bicol Saro Rep. Terry Ridon asked at the Saturday News Forum, according to a statement on Sunday.

Ridon, an impeachment prosecutor, said that as defense witnesses take the stand, they must address the claims of Duterte’s wealth and properties tied to her.

“During the presentation of witnesses, particularly these local officials from Davao City and the Island Garden City of Samal, it is crucial for these individuals, who are their own witnesses, to explain the mansions and properties that the NBI claims are owned by the Duterte family, specifically by our Vice President,” he said.

Among the prosecution’s evidence are land titles for two properties registered to Duterte’s husband, lawyer Manases Carpio, which were not listed in her statements of assets, liabilities and net worth (SALNs).

The questioned properties include a 379-square-meter parcel of land in Huna Subdivision, Davao City, purchased for P6 million in 2024, as well as a Kembali Coast property valued at about P3.45 million.

Trial schedule

Beyond properties, prosecutors also introduced bank, tax and corporate records linking Duterte to commercial ventures that they say were prohibited for officials, while zeroing in on discrepancies in her SALNs.

Tongol said after Punay, city assessors from Davao City and the Island Garden City of Samal, an accountant from Davao and the barangay captain of Matina Crossing would next take the witness stand.

Bank representatives are also scheduled to testify after the other defense witnesses.

Impeachment court presiding officer Sen. Francis “Chiz” Escudero earlier outlined the schedule for Duterte’s trial.

The impeachment court will hold proceedings throughout November, with full-day hearings scheduled from 10 a.m. to 6:30 p.m. on Nov. 10, 12, 13, 19 and 20.

The Nov. 9 proceedings will be suspended at 3 p.m. to give way to the Senate plenary session before resuming trial afterward.

The same arrangement may be applied on Nov. 11, if necessary. On the other hand, a shorter hearing is scheduled on Nov. 23, from 10 a.m. to 2 p.m.

The trial calendar covers Nov. 9 to 13 and Nov. 19, 20, and 23. The trial will be suspended on Nov. 30, a nonworking holiday in observance of Bonifacio Day.

World.title: Gov’t workers to get bonus, cash gift
World.content:
Inquirer file photo

MANILA, Philippines — Government employees will receive their year-end bonus equivalent to one month’s salary and a P5,000 cash gift with their November pay, with the Department of Budget and Management (DBM) directing agencies to ensure the benefits are released on schedule.

The DBM said it had released P82.998 billion to cover the benefits of qualified civilian employees and military and uniformed personnel, reminding agencies to include the payments in their first November payroll instead of releasing them separately at a later date.

Under DBM Budget Circular No. 2024-3, qualified personnel are entitled to a year-end bonus equivalent to their basic monthly salary as of Oct. 31, plus a P5,000 cash gift.

Article continues after this 

Budget Secretary Kim Robert de Leon said on Saturday the funds had already been released to concerned agencies. “We know that this will be a big help to our employees and their families, especially with Christmas approaching,” he said.

READ: DBM streamlines release of pay, benefits for gov’t workers

“More importantly, this is our way of recognizing and thanking our government workers for their hard work, dedication, and continued service to the Filipino people,” he added.

More incentives

Of the total allocation, P73.449 billion is earmarked for year-end bonuses and P9.549 billion for the cash gifts.

To qualify, employees must have rendered at least four months or 120 days of aggregate service from Jan. 1 to Oct. 31 and must still be in government service as of Oct. 31.

Article continues after this 

READ: Public school teachers, personnel may get 2024 bonus before December

The benefits cover personnel holding regular, contractual or casual positions in the national and local governments, including those who took authorized leave with pay.

Article continues after this 

The November benefits are separate from other incentives that government workers may receive in December.

These include the P5,000 Productivity Enhancement Incentive, traditionally paid starting mid-December; the Service Recognition Incentive of up to P20,000, which requires presidential authorization and cannot be paid earlier than Dec. 15; and the Collective Negotiation Agreement incentive of up to P30,000, subject to agency savings and existing agreements.

PBB still pending

Meanwhile, the release of the 2024 Performance-Based Bonus (PBB) remains pending for most eligible government agencies, despite President Marcos’ directive to prioritize teachers and personnel in public schools.

The PBB, equivalent to 45.5 to 65 percent of an employee’s monthly basic salary, is a separate incentive based on individual performance and agency accomplishments.

As of Oct. 30, only two of 315 eligible agencies had secured funding, according to the DBM’s online tracker.

The DBM issued special allotment release orders on Oct. 29 for Central Luzon State University, amounting to P24.39 million, and Nueva Ecija University of Science and Technology, worth P1.146 million.

Another 258 agencies, or 82 percent, remained under validation, while 51 had submitted Form 1.0, listing employees qualified to receive the bonus.

The Department of Education submitted its form on Oct. 7, but the DBM returned it on Oct. 28 for revisions.

The DBM was also reviewing submissions from the Department of Labor and Employment, Palawan State University, and the University of the Philippines System. Their funding will be released once the submitted employee lists are verified.

World.title: P7.2-T budget, tax relief among legislative agenda
World.content:
Inquirer file

MANILA, Philippines — The Senate will put the P7.2-trillion 2027 budget on top of its agenda when it resumes session on Monday after its month-long break, with senators vowing tighter scrutiny and greater budget transparency.

The House of Representatives, meanwhile, is seeking to fast-track President Marcos’ priority measures, including tax relief for workers, the removal of system loss charges from electricity bills and reforms to the partylist system.

Under the Senate calendar, interpellations on the budget’s general principles will run from Nov. 23 to Dec. 1. The chamber is scheduled to approve the measure on second reading on Dec. 3 and third reading on Dec. 7. Bicameral conference committee deliberations are set for Dec. 10 to 12, with the report to be signed on Dec. 21 and ratified on Dec. 22.

Article continues after this 

Bicam transparency

Sen. Panfilo “Ping” Lacson said the Senate would push for livestreaming of bicameral proceedings and transcripts to establish who proposed amendments and who pushed for realignments in the final budget.

READ: Senate to release transcripts of 2027 budget bicam proceedings – Lacson

“In the bicam, the minutes of the proceedings should be recorded through a transcript. The budget bill is the only measure whose bicameral proceedings do not have a transcript, so we cannot trace who made what amendment,” Lacson said in a radio interview on Sunday.

“There should be a transcript containing the minutes so it will be clear who initiated amendments and who pushed for realignments,” he added.

READ: JV, Lacson: Budget ‘bicam’ open to all, sparing none

Article continues after this 

He warned that some lawmakers made insertions twice—first in the National Expenditure Program submitted by the executive, and again after it was transmitted to Congress.

“It’s double kill,” he said.

Article continues after this 

He urged budget advocacy groups not only to be vigilant but also to “resort to shaming lawmakers who sneak in questionable realignments.”

Questionable projects

Earlier, Senate President Sherwin Gatchalian vowed to remove P8.836 billion worth of infrastructure projects from the proposed budget because the Department of Public Works and Highways (DPWH) failed to provide essential technical documents.

“The Senate is committed unequivocally in weeding out unsubstantiated line items, including those lacking concrete and verifiable technical support, to ensure that every item in the final version is shovel-ready,” Gatchalian said last Tuesday.“Unverifiable line items will not receive a single peso of public funding,” he added.

Gatchalian’s office found that 7,107, or more than 62 percent, of 11,395 infrastructure projects examined had at least one major budgetary irregularity, including missing station numbers or geographic coordinates, lump-sum allocations, overlapping projects and conflicting work descriptions.

Civil society watchdogs have separately flagged more than P1 trillion in allocations in the House-approved budget that they consider questionable or vulnerable to political patronage.

The People’s Budget Coalition and other groups classified the items into P695 billion in “hard pork,” P210 billion in “soft pork” and P112 billion in “shadow pork.”

Malacañang has warned that Marcos will veto amendments lacking proper documentation, clear project descriptions and legitimate purposes.

“The President’s directive is clear: public funds must not be abused. Public funds should be used for the people, not go into anyone’s pockets,” Palace Press Officer Claire Castro said.

House priorities

In the House, Speaker Faustino “Bojie” Dy III has cited tax relief and lower electricity costs among the administration’s priorities

The proposed tax measure would raise the annual personal income tax threshold to P350,000 from P250,000, increasing take-home pay for lower- and middle-income workers.

“That is why we are pushing for tax relief for workers,” Dy said in October. “This also includes proposals aimed at improving the supply and lowering the price of electricity.”

Lawmakers are also pushing to remove system loss charges from power bills, which critics say add to the burden on households facing high electricity costs.

The House is likewise pursuing reforms to the partylist system, designed to give marginalized sectors representation but criticized over claims that wealthy interests and political dynasties have captured the mechanism.

Tingog Rep. Jude Acidre, a member of the House committee on suffrage and electoral reforms, said the proposed bill seeks to ensure partylist groups genuinely represent the constituencies they claim to serve.

World.title: 13 years after Yolanda, Tacloban carries lessons into every typhoon
World.content:
Inquirer file photo

TACLOBAN CITY, LEYTE, Philippines — For 38-year-old Marian Edano, moving forward 13 years after Super Typhoon Yolanda (international name: Haiyan) devastated this city does not mean forgetting the husband and relatives she lost to the disaster.

Edano lost her husband, Jesus, and several relatives when their house in Sitio Alimasag, Barangay 88, San Jose district, was swept away by Yolanda’s massive storm surge on Nov. 8, 2013.

On Sunday, she visited her husband’s grave at the Holy Cross Memorial Garden with their 13-year-old daughter and 15-year-old son, joining other families in commemorating the typhoon’s 13th anniversary.

Article continues after this 

“Although it is very difficult to move on without remembering the loss, we have continued with our lives and are looking forward to a better future,” she said.

Edano said her family has since learned to take no chances whenever a typhoon threatens Tacloban, preparing to evacuate even before authorities issue official advisories.

READ: Act on environmental woes, learn from Yolanda catastrophe, says church

Her experience reflects the lessons that Mayor Alfred Romualdez urged residents to carry forward as the city marked the anniversary, emphasizing the importance of disaster preparedness and early evacuation.

Mass grave

Romualdez made the call during the commemoration at Holy Cross Memorial Garden, where about 2,200 victims were hastily buried in a mass grave.

Article continues after this 

He said the annual gathering was not only an occasion to remember those who perished but also an opportunity to thank the international community and the national government for the assistance extended to Tacloban after the disaster.

READ: This Taclobanon lived to tell the story of Yolanda

Article continues after this 

More importantly, the commemoration should prompt residents to assess how far the city has come and whether they have learned from the tragedy, Romualdez said.

For one, he noted that residents have become more conscious of disaster risks, particularly the need to evacuate ahead of an approaching storm.

Before Yolanda, the city government often struggled to convince residents, especially those in high-risk communities, to leave their homes and move to safer grounds, he recalled.

“Since then, we have registered zero casualties due to typhoons,” Romualdez said.

20 evacuation facilities

The city government has identified more than 20 evacuation facilities, including public schools and the Tacloban City Astrodome, to accommodate residents threatened by severe weather.

Yolanda, one of the most powerful storms worldwide, struck the Philippines on Nov. 8, 2013, devastating coastal communities across Eastern Visayas, with Tacloban among the hardest-hit areas. It left 6,300 dead and 1,061 missing.

The commemoration culminated in the evening with the tolling of church bells and the lighting of candles along streets across the city.

Other communities in Eastern Visayas devastated by Yolanda, including Palo and Tanauan in Leyte and Guiuan in Eastern Samar, also held activities to honor the victims and remember the destruction.

Environmental crisis

Meanwhile, the Diocese of Borongan also urged communities to turn the lessons of Yolanda into action against environmental destruction and to protect vulnerable populations.

In a pastoral message on Sunday, the diocese called on the faithful to “see, judge, and act” in addressing the worsening environmental crisis, urging them to oppose destructive mining, protect forests and mangroves, reduce waste and prepare for disasters.

“Remembering is not enough. Yolanda asks something of us today, in the midst of an environmental emergency that grows more urgent each year,” it said. —With a report from Dianne Sampang

World.title: LTO summons bus driver, operator in Quezon road accident
World.content:
Inquirer file photo

MANILA, Philippines — The Land Transportation Office (LTO) has issued a show-cause order against the driver of a passenger bus and its operator after a loose engine cover flew off and struck a bystander on the side of the road in Atimonan, Quezon, killing the victim.

In a statement on Saturday, the LTO directed the bus driver and operator to appear before the Intelligence and Investigation Division (IID) at its central office in Quezon City on Nov. 13.

The passenger bus was traveling on the northbound lane of Maharlika Highway in Barangay Tagbakin when its engine cover detached and hit the victim who was standing by the roadside while waiting for a ride to Manila.

Article continues after this 

The victim suffered serious injuries and was brought to Doña Maria Hospital but was declared dead on arrival. The accident happened around 5 a.m. on Nov. 5.

READ: Bus engine cover turns deadly for Quezon traveler

The LTO said the driver and operator must submit statements explaining their side of the incident, along with supporting documents, in connection with the alleged violations.

The driver faces a reckless driving charge, while the bus operator is being investigated for employing a reckless driver and breach of franchise conditions.

READ: College student dies in motorcycle-bus collision in Quezon

Article continues after this 

As part of its immediate action, the LTO suspended for 90 days the driver’s license which must be surrendered to the IID while the bus involved in the accident was flagged.

“Negligence in ensuring that a passenger bus is properly maintained should never result in loss of life,” LTO chief Assistant Secretary Markus Lacanilao said.

Article continues after this 

“Every part and component of the vehicle must be checked to ensure it is safe and in good condition before it is allowed to travel, as even a single oversight can lead to a road tragedy,” Lacanilao added.

The LTO warned that it would hold accountable those found violating transportation laws and regulations. /cb

World.title: Bishops in Visayas, Romblon renew opposition to Boracay casino
World.content:
GAMBLING DEBATE Tourists enjoy the white beach on Boracay Island in this photo, taken in May. Catholic bishops in the Western Visayas and Romblon renewed their opposition to casino operations on the island, citing its potential harm. —Photo courtesy of Enjoy Life Boracay

ILOILO CITY, Philippines — Catholic Church leaders in Western Visayas and Romblon province have renewed their opposition to casino operations in Boracay, warning that gambling could undermine family welfare and expose vulnerable communities to social and economic risks.

In a joint statement made public on Sunday, the Church leaders expressed support for Kalibo Bishop Cyril Villareal’s opposition to gambling and the operation of a casino in Boracay, Malay, Aklan.

“We recognize the importance of tourism, investment, and employment in Boracay. However, development must serve the human person, not sacrifice human dignity and family welfare for profit,” the bishops said.

Article continues after this 

READ: Capiz bishops urge leaders to address concerns over Boracay casino

The statement was signed by Jaro Archbishop Midyphil Billones, who is also apostolic administrator of the Diocese of Kabankalan in Negros Occidental; Archbishop Emeritus Jose Romeo Lazo of Jaro; San Carlos Bishop Gerardo Alminaza; Bacolod Bishop Louie Galbines; San Jose de Antique Bishop Marvyn Maceda; and Bacolod Bishop Emeritus Patricio Buzon.

The other signatories were Capiz Archbishop Victor Bendico, Romblon Bishop Narciso Abellana, Kalibo Bishop Emeritus Jose Corazon Tala-oc and Villareal.

READ: AGI building $300-M Boracay casino resort

The prelates warned that gambling addiction could lead to mounting debts, depleted savings, marital conflict, broken trust and neglect of children. Money intended for food, education and healthcare, they said, could instead be lost in the pursuit of quick winnings.

Article continues after this 

Citing the Catechism of the Catholic Church, they said that “the passion for gambling risks becoming an enslavement.”

Potential harm

They also raised concerns about possible social risks associated with expanded casino operations, including human exploitation, prostitution, human trafficking, substance abuse, gambling-related fraud and other crimes.

Article continues after this 

The bishops clarified that these consequences should not automatically be attributed to every casino, but said the potential harm to individuals and communities should be weighed against the profits such businesses could generate.

They appealed to the national government, the Aklan provincial and Malay municipal governments, national agencies and business leaders to consider the long-term social costs of casino operations, listen to affected communities, and prioritize families and vulnerable people.

The statement also called on Catholic communities and people of goodwill to promote honest work, responsible use of resources and compassion for those struggling with gambling addiction, who need understanding, support and appropriate assistance.

“No to gambling casinos in Boracay. Yes to development that protects families, dignifies work, and serves the common good,” the statement said.

The bishops said Boracay’s economic future should instead be built on responsible tourism, environmental stewardship, dignified employment and opportunities that strengthen families and communities. They maintained that economic progress need not depend on gambling casinos.

The joint appeal followed Villareal’s Oct. 5 pastoral statement opposing the opening and operation of a casino on the island.

Bendico and Abellana had also issued a separate statement of solidarity with Villareal and the Diocese of Kalibo on Oct. 7.

The statements came after the opening of Kaban Hotel and Casino Boracay, the island’s first hotel casino.

The property, part of a 23-hectare development by Golden TW Realty and Development Corp., began operations on Sept. 16 and held its grand opening on Oct. 11 at Station 0 in Barangay Yapak.

World.title: Myanmar Regime Plans April Vote in 55 Constituencies Despite Continued Clashes
World.content:
Myanmar’s regime plans to hold elections in 55 constituencies across 37 townships on April 4, 2027, including 12 townships where it has regained at least partial control from resistance forces in recent years. Voting was not held in those 12 townships during the regime’s general election in December 2025 and January 2026, which was widely dismissed as a sham.

In an announcement Thursday, the regime said it would hold voting in 34 Lower House constituencies, using the first-past-the-post (FPTP) system; five Upper House constituencies; and 16 regional/state parliament constituencies across the country.

The townships include Tonzang and Falam in northern Chin State and Tigyaing, Banmauk and Indaw in Sagaing Region, all recaptured by the regime this year, as well as Singu and Mogoke in Mandalay Region, which it recaptured in 2025.

Also included on the regime’s list of townships scheduled to vote in April are Sagaing’s Kawlin, which the Myanmar military recaptured in 2024, and the Sagaing resistance strongholds of Pale, Yinmarbin, Shwebo and Taze.

A military analyst pointed out that the regime only controls the towns in Pale, Yinmarbin, Shwebo, Taze, Tigyaing, Banmauk and especially Indaw.

“The regime wants to show it is able to control the whole country, and that its administration is operating,” said Zin Yaw, a military defector who has monitored Myanmar’s conflicts since defecting after the coup.

The absence from the list of southern Chin State towns that the regime has been trying to retake since May 2026, as well as Arakan Army-controlled towns in Rakhine State, amounts to an admission by the regime that it hasn’t been able to restore its authority in these areas, he said.

The regime announced Lower House elections in Myeik, Tanintharyi Region; Nyaunglebin, Pauk Khaung and Padaung in Bago Region; Chauk and Minbu in Magwe Region; Pyin Oo Lwin, Meiktila, Natogyi, Singu and Mogoke in Mandalay Region; Kyaikmayaw in Mon State; Mayangone, Shwepyithar, Hlegu, Tamwe, Cocokyun and Hlaing Tharyar in Yangon Region; Kyaukme, Monghpyak, and Mong Pan in Shan State; Maubin in Ayeyarwady Region; and Zabuthiri, Dekkhinathiri and Ottarathiri in Naypyitaw.

The Upper House constituencies on the list are in Kachin State, Chin State, Magwe Region, Bago Region and Mandalay Region.

The list also includes state/regional parliament constituencies in Tonzang and Falam in Chin State; Tigyaing, Banmauk, Indaw, Kawlin, Pale, Yinmarbin, Taze and Shwebo in Sagaing Region; Zigon and Thegon in Bago Region; Natogyi, Singu and Mogoke in Mandalay Region; and Yegyi in Ayeyarwady Region.

The Myanmar military recently suffered heavy losses to resistance ambushes in Indaw Township. Clashes continue there and in upper Sagaing.

Despite the ongoing armed conflicts in many areas, political parties cooperating with the regime’s electoral process said they are making preparations for the vote.

Saw Than Myint, joint secretary of the Shan and Ethnic Democratic Party (SNDP), which secured 37 seats in the regime-backed general election, said the party plans to compete in the upcoming by-election but is still discussing details.

People’s Pioneer Party (PPP) chair Saw Han Aye said the party hopes to field candidates in at least one-third of the 55 constituencies, as required under the Political Parties Registration Law for parties competing at the national level.

He acknowledged that security concerns remain in some areas, adding that participation would ultimately depend on individual candidates’ willingness.

The PPP was founded by Thet Thet Khine, a former regime minister who was barred in October 2025 from running in the general election on grounds of violating rules on personal debts.

The Irrawaddy contacted People’s Party chair Ko Ko Gyi, a former 88 Generation student protest leader, about the party’s plans but received no response.

Coup leader Min Aung Hlaing’s regime organized the nationwide election in three phases in December 2025 and January 2026, with voting in 263 out of 330 townships. Civilian leaders, including Aung San Suu Kyi, remained imprisoned, while major opposition parties had been dissolved.

With only nine parties participating at the national level, the election was dominated by the military-backed Union Solidarity and Development Party (USDP) and allied parties, allowing the USDP to secure a majority of the seats.

Since installing himself as president in April, Min Aung Hlaing has launched a diplomatic campaign in an effort to gain legitimacy for his regime, visiting China, Russia, Belarus, Thailand, Vietnam, Laos, Cambodia, Malaysia and India, while his military forces continue targeting civilians in attacks and atrocities. The absence of elections in the 55 constituencies has underlined his regime’s lack of legitimacy, observers say.

World.title: Over 2m Myanmar Migrants in Thailand Reject Regime’s Identity Document
World.content:
Over 2 million Myanmar migrant workers in Thailand have participated in a poll calling on the parallel National Unity Government (NUG) to issue identity documents amid a mass boycott of the regime’s new Certificate of Identity (CI) process.

The poll also aims to demonstrate to the Thai government that they recognize the NUG as their legitimate government, not the military regime.

Thailand hosts an estimated 4 million Myanmar workers, both documented and undocumented. Migrant worker groups estimate that at least 600,000 are required to apply for CIs in this round. However, most are staying away from the regime’s newly opened Thai CI centers in protest against new tax and remittance rules that critics condemn as extortion. To apply, workers must prove they have remitted 25 percent of their wages through official regime channels and paid 2 percent annual income tax. The vast majority are refusing, fearing payment would help fund the regime’s war on civilians while lending it political legitimacy.

Meanwhile, Thai opposition lawmakers and labor rights groups have urged the government to review or scrap the centers, branding them a threat to national security and sovereignty.

The workers themselves made their overwhelming opposition clear in a weeklong online poll launched Sunday by the Myanmar Migrant Workers’ Representative Coordinating Committee in Thailand (MMWRCCT). Many appealed to Thai authorities to grant them work and residency permits without the CI document.

The poll result reflected resounding support among migrant workers for an alternative identification process managed by the NUG, Khin Soe of the MMWRCCT told The Irrawaddy.

“The regime CI process is a trap to extract foreign currency and information for military conscription,” he said. “The workers know this, so they don’t want to apply.”

He said the poll result would be sent to the NUG’s Labour Department to push for worker ID issuance, while a separate workers’ online petition would be delivered to the Thai government.

“The Thai government may argue it has to cooperate with the regime on the CI process to ensure national security, but we are appealing to them on humanitarian grounds. If they need an alternative authority to issue identity documents, this poll shows that millions of workers want the NUG to do it. As guests living under Thai law, we are not making demands, we are simply presenting these results as a respectful request,” Khine Soe said.

Launched on October 18, the campaign and petition contain four requests, including the right to stay and work legally without a CI, and has drawn support from Thai labour rights groups and politicians.

Among them is MP Anuson Tamajai, a prominent economist who urged the government to review or cancel the CI centers, arguing their unchecked operations compromise national security and sovereignty.

Highlighting migrant workers’ indispensable role in Thailand’s economy, he also called for an investigation into whether demanding remittance and tax payments in exchange for ID certificates violates Thai law.

The Thailand Migration Reform group recently warned that allowing Naypyitaw to control migrant registration “undermines Thai sovereignty and fuels corruption.” It urged Thai authorities to revert to the Pink Card system for migrant workers.

On Friday, Thai Labor Minister Julapun Amornvivat told media after a meeting of the Foreign Workers Management Policy Committee that CIs are required by migrants’ countries of origin for identity verification, but the process operates entirely within Thai territory.

He said his ministry will send a formal letter to its regime counterpart expressing opposition to the mandatory remittance policy, arguing it undermines migrant worker rights and fails to align with international standards.

Dismissing the backlash, the cash-strapped regime has doubled down on its push to skim foreign currency from low-paid overseas workers. Newly appointed Labor Minister Maung Myint has threatened workers with legal action and a ban on returning home if they don’t make tax and remittance payments.

However, the boycott shows no sign of weakening, with only a trickle of applicants reported at the five CI centres across Thailand since they opened on October 14.

World.title: China Wields Carrot and Stick at Beijing Meet, Regime Seeks Elections in Shan, and More
World.content:
We’ll always hold your hand, Beijing promises Myanmar regime

“China will always be a strategic partner that Myanmar can rely on,” Chinese Foreign Minister Wang Yi told Myanmar investment minister Aung Kyaw Hoe on the sidelines of the 11th Lancang–Mekong Cooperation Foreign Ministers’ Meeting on Tuesday.

The reassurance came as part of a carrot-and-stick package amid alarm in Beijing over recent meetings between U.S. and Myanmar officials that seemed to augur the start of re-engagement.

The U.S. has released an Integrated Country Strategy for its mission in Myanmar, which identifies goals for expanding Washington’s diplomatic, economic and humanitarian influence in the country. Besides singling out scam networks, it also sets goals for boosting American exports to the impoverished war-torn country and gain access to Myanmar’s “bountiful” rare earth resources—besides aiming to “counter China’s influence.”

Myanmar is China’s most important external source of rare earth minerals and a major global source of heavy rare earth elements, particularly dysprosium and terbium, which are essential for electric cars, wind turbines, advanced electronics and military technologies. But mines are concentrated in areas beyond the reach of the regime in Kachin and Shan states.

Online scam operations have become a major point of convergence and competition in the two superpowers’ approach toward Myanmar. During the meeting with Aung Kyaw Hoe, Wang urged his regime to prevent the “resurgence of chaos” in Myawaddy, referring to the vast scam compounds that flourished there.

China grows impatient over stalled investment projects

But in the same meeting Wang applied plenty of stick, urging Myanmar’s regime to get a move on in realizing long-stalled projects that form part of the planned China–Myanmar Economic Corridor (CMEC) that would provide Beijing with overland access to the Indian Ocean. Wang told Aung Kyaw Hoe the two sides must “coordinate development and security” so they can “steadily advance” key CMEC projects.

Wang’s message echoed remarks made by his President Xi Jinping during regime leader Min Aung Hlaing’s visit to Beijing in June, when Xi also called for swift implementation of CMEC projects.

The corridor’s flagship schemes include the Kyaukphyu deep-sea port and special economic zone in Rakhine State and a planned railway linking Kyaukphyu with Yunnan via Mandalay and Muse. On China side, the railroad is already entering its final phase but on the Myanmar side fighting continues across many parts of the route.

Aung Kyaw Hoe promised the regime is doing all it can but, true to form, also used the occasion to beg for even more Chinese investment.

Border trade gates reopen as armed groups consolidate control

China has significantly eased restrictions on trade through several Myanmar border crossings controlled by Beijing-linked ethnic armed organizations, allowing fuel, medicines, construction materials and other previously banned goods to enter northern Shan and Kachin.

The move suggests China is adjusting its border policy to accommodate new realities on the ground, where it appears the military regime in Naypyitaw has permanently lost control. With Operation 1027, key border trade gates and routes in northern Shan fell into the hands of the ethnic Chinese Myanmar National Democratic Alliance Army (MNDAA), and its erstwhile partner in the Brotherhood Alliance, the Ta’ang National Liberation Army (TNLA).

Beijing initially closed the crossings to pressure them into making peace with the generals, but trade has long resumed and is now growing exponentially.

According to Chinese Customs at the Mengding crossing with MNDAA-controlled Chinshwehaw, the total value of trade there and at nearby Mangka eached 4.92 billion yuan in the first eight months of this year, up 49.3 percent on-year.

Customs figures also show increased trade through Namhkam crossing controlled by the Ta’ang National Liberation Army, as well as through the Kyin San Kyawt gate controlled jointly by the Brotherhood Alliance in Muse Township, which once accounted for some 70 percent of cross-border trade. The regime still controls a couple of crossings in Muse, where it bans the import of fuel from China.

In a move to prevent those groups from financing their armies through cargo taxation, the cash-strapped regime is now reduced to blocking routes south of Lashio, imposing a crackdown on what it calls “smuggled” goods—which in reality means roadside extortion.

Late last month, Min Aung Hlaing urged his ministers to intensify their crackdown on illegal trade and make sure that cross‑border commerce is conducted only through “legal” channels, i.e. those his regime controls. Myanmar’s consul general in Kunming met with the customs department director this week to discuss facilitating flows of “officially traded goods” between the neighbors and improving cooperation on customs procedures.

Naypyitaw seeks to roll out elections into Shan borderlands

Defence Minister Yar Pyae who also chairs the junta’s peace negotiation committee, this week visited areas held by China-linked ethnic armed groups with a view to rolling out the regime’s sham elections across their part of the country as well.

Yar Pyae went to Panghsang, the headquarters of United Wa State Army (UWSA), and Mongla, the fiefdom of the National Democratic Alliance Army (NDAA) near the Chinese border. The visit comes after Chinese Special Envoy to Myanmar Deng Xijun urged granting “high-level” autonomy to ethnic minorities.

Together with the MNDAA, they are widely regarded as being under heavy Chinese influence, with Chinese widely spoken and the yuan used as the major currency in their territories.

All three trace their origins to the 1989 mutiny that fractured the Communist Party of Burma. Most people in NDAA territory are ethnic Chinese with roots in Yunnan, but the Wa are a Mon‑Khmer-speaking people more closely related to the Palaung.

Both the UWSA and NDAA have long upheld ceasefires they signed with the military in 1989 in return for de-factor autonomy in their areas, sustained by cross‑border trade and Chinese investment.

In Mongla, Yar Pyae discussed holding the vote, which was omitted there when the regime orchestrated polls in the parts of Myanmar it controls in the winter of 2025-26 that led to military dictator Min Aung Hlaing declaring himself president. Naypyitaw is aiming for next April, regime media said. But none of the townships under the control of the UWSA or NDAA were included on the junta’s recently announced list of constituencies slated for catch-up and by-elections.

Historically, no national elections have been conducted either in Mongla or Panghsang, although voting has taken place in some townships of the constitutionally defined Wa Self-Administered Division where government administration was present. Formally, the UWSA is stuck at a stage of demanding official statehood, and the NDAA is demanding official autonomous status.

World.title: Arakan Army Faces Second Front at Bangladesh Border
World.content:
Amid intensified fighting as the Arakan Army (AA) closes in on the Arakan (Rakhine State) capital of Sittwe, a second front is heating up along the border with Bangladesh, where regime-aligned Rohingya armed groups are escalating conflict.

These attacks are not isolated border incidents. They reflect a history of cooperation between Myanmar’s military and Muslim armed organizations during the 2024 battles for Buthidaung and Maungdaw. For Bangladesh, they raise difficult questions about its security interests and the prospects of repatriating the hundreds of thousands of Rohingya refugees now within its borders. For the AA, they raise the question whether it can maintain stability across its home state.

A major concern is that armed networks established during the military regime’s territorial retreat are continuing to exert pressure on the AA while the main body of its forces confronts the regime elsewhere.

From cooperation to proxy warfare

During the 2024 Arakan offensive, the military suffered major territorial losses. Facing the AA’s advance, it cast around for additional manpower and local allies, and alighted on armed organizations that, ironically, were associated with a population it had systematically persecuted. One of them was the Arakan Rohingya Salvation Army (ARSA).

The International Crisis Group has documented the regime’s ammunition supplies to ARSA, along with recruitment arrangements that transferred Rohingya refugees to military facilities for training.

ARSA and another armed group, the Rohingya Solidarity Organization (RSO), received training, weapons and tactical support during the fighting while maintaining contacts with regime personnel after the AA captured Maungdaw in December 2024, according to the Transnational Institute.

Here was the military that was responsible for the 2017 atrocities that drove hundreds of thousands of Rohingya into Bangladesh, brazenly cooperating with Rohingya armed organizations against the AA.

For the junta, however, the strategic advantages outweighed any qualms it might have had. Armed groups operating along the state’s northern frontier could challenge AA positions even after its own conventional military bases had fallen, and thereby divert precious resources from the AA’s other battlefronts.

As a bonus for a regime that has long sustained itself by divide-and-rule tactics, it risked deepening mistrust between the state’s Arakanese and Muslim communities.

Maungdaw remains a strategic front

Thus when the AA eventually captured Maungdaw, it transformed the military balance along the Bangladesh border but could not fully eliminate the armed groups operating through remote terrain and cross-border networks.

In September last year, ARSA fighters attacked an AA border security position near Inn Chaung village in northern Maungdaw. AA forces subsequently retook the position, while the attackers reportedly fled to Bangladesh.

Further clashes followed, and by late October this year, residents reported that ARSA was renewing recruitment, armed movements and attacks against AA outposts in northern and southern Maungdaw.

“ARSA activities have resurged in both northern and southern Maungdaw Township,” one resident told my news organization, Development Media Group.

With the AA confronting regime forces around Sittwe, repeated ARSA attacks could now force it to divert much-needed troops, intelligence resources and supplies to the border.

This would benefit Myanmar’s military even without direct command of these operations.

There is an important caveat. ARSA, RSO and a third militia active at the border, the Arakan Rohingya Army (ARA) have distinct leadership structures and interests. Their historical cooperation with the military regime does not mean that every recent attack was centrally coordinated.

Bangladesh’s border dilemma

A further complication lies in Bangladeshi involvement in these skirmishes. The AA accuses certain officers of the Border Guard Bangladesh (BGB) of providing the Rohingya armed groups with logistical assistance, ammunition and intelligence, and allowing them to operate near border security positions.

The International Crisis Group, too, has documented the complicated relationships between these groups and elements of Bangladesh’s security establishment.

The allegations require credible investigation, but any such shenanigans must also be distinguished from official Bangladeshi government policy. Publicly, the BGB has denied supporting ARSA or the RSO.

Bangladesh faces legitimate challenges involving border security, with more than 1 million Rohingya refugees and the prospect of their eventual repatriation creating a massive headache for Dhaka.

But it will eventually have to confront the reality that the territory from which the refugees fled is now controlled by the AA, and that fundamentally changes the political realities.

Some Bangladeshi security personnel may still regard these avowedly Muslim armed organizations as potential leverage over the AA. But helping them with their cross-border attacks would now in fact undermine border stability and make peaceful repatriation more difficult.

In other words, Bangladesh’s security interests would be better served by stopping ARSA and co. from exploiting refugee communities, and instead maintaining effective communication with the AA authorities controlling the opposite side of the border.

Beyond armed groups and military control

The motivations behind Rohingya armed mobilization long predate any cooperation with Myanmar’s military.

Decades of discrimination, statelessness, displacement and uncertainty have created grievances that armed organizations can exploit. Refugees facing declining humanitarian assistance and limited opportunities are particularly vulnerable to recruitment and intimidation. But that cannot justify attacks on civilians, abductions or forced recruitment.

Nor should ARSA, RSO and ARA be treated as representative of Muslim communities as a whole. The Arakanese, Muslim and other communities in Maungdaw face threats from armed violence, disrupted livelihoods and insecurity. Abuses by all armed participants, including the AA, require impartial investigation and accountability.

The AA’s territorial gains have brought responsibilities extending beyond military security. Effective governance means it must protect civilians regardless of ethnicity or religion, address grievances and prevent communal tensions from escalating.

The Maungdaw conflict demonstrates that territorial control does not necessarily end a war.

Myanmar’s military has lost most of its positions in Arakan, yet its airpower, remaining military strongholds and historical relationships with armed groups continue to complicate the AA’s security calculations.

Preventing further escalation requires credible investigation of alleged weapons supplies and cross-border assistance, effective border management, protection of refugees from coercive recruitment, and sustained engagement between Bangladesh and the AA.

It also requires meaningful dialogue with Muslim civilian representatives and equal protection for all communities.

Unless the networks and grievances sustaining violence are addressed, no lasting peace can come to Arakan.

Aung Marm Oo is the editor-in-chief and executive director of Development Media Group, a news agency based in Arakan. He faces charges under Myanmar’s Unlawful Associations Act and has been in hiding since May 2019.

World.title: Hurry Up With Our Investment Projects, China tells Myanmar Regime
World.content:
Chinese Foreign Minister Wang Yi has renewed Beijing’s call for the Myanmar regime to “steadily advance” key projects under the China-Myanmar Economic Corridor (CMEC), which is designed to give Beijing direct access to Indian Ocean.

Wang made the remarks during a meeting on Tuesday with Myanmar Investment and Foreign Economic Relations Minister Aung Kyaw Hoe, who is in Beijing for the 11th Lancang–Mekong Cooperation Foreign Ministers’ Meeting.

A clearly exasperated Wang stressed the need for the two sides to “coordinate” development and security, as many parts of Myanmar are plagued by civil war, making it hard for the China-backed projects to proceed.

In turn, Wang promised Chinese support for the rebranded regime’s efforts to achieve international recognition. “China will always be a strategic partner that Myanmar can rely on,” he said.

The remarks come as the U.S. shows signs of re-engaging with Naypyitaw in search of business.

Wang also called for stronger efforts to combat scams and online gambling. He urged Myanmar to prevent the “resurgence of chaos” in Myawaddy, referring to online scam operations that flourished along the Thai-Myanmar border.

He urged Naypyitaw to do more to ensure the safety of Chinese nationals, organizations and projects operating in the country.

Aung Kyaw Hoe, for his part, promised that his regime does want to accelerate the CMEC projects and step up cooperation with China and regional countries in combating online scam operations. He duly thanked his hosts for supporting Myanmar in international forums, according to a statement from the Chinese Embassy.

When Myanmar’s putschist leader Min Aung Hlaing last visited Beijing in June after declaring himself president, Chinese President Xi Jinping also urged him to speed up the CMEC projects, a key component of Beijing’s Belt and Road Initiative (BRI).

He too urged the regime to provide stronger security guarantees for Chinese personnel and investments in Myanmar, many of which are in areas now controlled by the resistance or ethnic armed organizations over which Beijing holds no sway.

The planned corridor includes several flagship projects, notably the Kyaukphyu deep-sea port in Rakhine State and a railway linking Kyaukphyu through Mandalay and Muse with China’s Yunnan Province.

The Kyaukphyu Special Economic Zone and deep-sea port project is particularly important for Beijing because it would provide China with direct access to the Indian Ocean while supporting economic development in Yunnan and other southwestern Chinese provinces.

But other than pay lip-service to the plans and hold out its hand for more investment, the Myanmar regime has done little to advance these projects, instead losing itself in dreams of reviving the long-mothballed Myitsone Dam Project in quite a different part of the country.

In its frustration, China has now reopened border crossings with areas controlled by ethnic armed organizations in northern Shan State to allow lucrative trade to resume, whether the regime likes it or not.

A China analyst told The Irrawaddy that Beijing “knows very well that Min Aung Hlaing’s stubbornness is holding everything up. The fighting is still going on, the peace talks haven’t delivered any results, there’s been no progress in northern Shan State, and the border crossings are still not operating normally.”

For the CMEC projects to move forward, Min Aung Hlaing “has to engage in talks with the ethnic armed groups first,” she added. “In that sense, I think China was quite deliberately sending that message.”

World.title: Kyat Slump Disrupts Thai Border Trade as Import Costs Rise
World.content:
The rapid depreciation of Myanmar’s currency has disrupted border trade with Thailand, prompting some traders and money changers along the border to suspend transactions as they struggle to cope with volatile exchange rates and mounting import costs.

The currency weakened to around 680 baht per 100,000 kyats this week, down from more than 700 baht in recent weeks. The currency also fell against the U.S. dollar, with the market exchange rate rising from just above 4,700 kyats per dollar at the end of October to more than 4,900 on Wednesday. The rate was just around 4,400 kyats in early October.

The latest slump is fueling concerns over another wave of inflation in a country heavily reliant on imports from Thailand. Myanmar imports a wide range of goods from its neighbor, including electrical appliances, household products, cosmetics, construction materials and foodstuffs, making fluctuations in the baht exchange rate significant for consumers.

Market insiders attributed the kyat’s latest decline to the regime’s plan to borrow 2.1 trillion kyats from the Central Bank of Myanmar to finance a budget shortfall for fiscal year 2026-27, which ends on March 31. The regime has already sold treasury bonds worth trillions of kyats, leading to speculation that it will simply print banknotes to cover the deficit.

They also pointed to Myanmar’s continued inclusion on the Financial Action Task Force (FATF) blacklist, delays in export licensing and policy inconsistencies between ministries as factors undermining confidence in the market.

The swift depreciation of the kyat has left traders struggling to price goods and manage working capital.

“A gradual rise doesn’t create much difficulty. The problem is when rates surge rapidly,” a trader in Myawaddy told The Irrawaddy.

“If exchange rates rise further, we will need more capital to restock. Some traders have temporarily stopped trading and making payments, and are waiting to see where the market moves.”

The uncertainty has spread beyond traders. Some major money changers in Myawaddy and across the border in Thailand suspended transactions on Wednesday, opting to wait for the next day’s opening rates before resuming business, according to border exchange operators.

The volatility is not confined to the Thai border. Traders in Muse, on Shan State’s border with China, are facing similar difficulties as the kyat continues to weaken against the yuan, market sources said.

Traders warn that prolonged instability in foreign exchange markets could further squeeze trade. Importers say their profits are shrinking, but are reluctant to increase prices for fear that demand may decline further.

A trader in Myawaddy said transport costs remain a major contributor to rising prices, with expenses along trade routes increasing because of checkpoints and demands for unofficial payments.

“Price increases are caused more by transport costs than exchange rates,” he said. “Costs at checkpoints rise sharply whenever authorities announce crackdowns or tighter controls.”

Exporters also say the weaker kyat is raising shipping costs because freight charges, container fees and port services are paid in U.S. dollars. At the same time, they complain that mandatory foreign-exchange conversion rules prevent them from fully benefiting from higher market exchange rates.

Under existing regulations, exporters must convert 35 percent of their export earnings at the Central Bank’s official rate, creating a significant gap between official and market rates. The Central Bank’s official reference rate remains 2,100 kyats per dollar, while its market trading rate is about 3,660 kyats per dollar. The market rate was around 4,900 kyats on Thursday. Before the coup, the kyat traded at roughly 1,300-1,400 per U.S. dollar.

An exporter from Mon State explained that the depreciation of the kyat has sharply increased the capital required to buy export commodities such as corn and onions.

“Previously, we could buy a container of goods for 10 million kyats from local producers. Now it can require more than 15 million kyats,” he said.

Traders say prices of Thai imports, particularly electrical goods, household products, cosmetics, construction materials and food items, are already climbing as a result of the stronger baht and rising transportation costs.

World.title: Thai Foreign Minister to Visit Myanmar Ahead of ASEAN Summit
World.content:
BANGKOK—Thailand’s foreign minister said he will visit Myanmar on November 12, days before a regional summit where Bangkok will be pressing to normalize ties with the war-torn country.

Sihasak Phuangketkeow’s trip also comes during raised tensions along the countries’ shared border, where Bangkok said clashes between Myanmar’s military and ethnic rebels caused property damage and injured a Thai civilian in Thailand on Thursday.

His visit, announced late Tuesday, is scheduled shortly before a November 16-18 summit of leaders of the Association of Southeast Asian Nations (ASEAN) in Manila.

Myanmar’s leaders have not been invited to high-level ASEAN meetings since former general Min Aung Hlaing led a 2021 military coup that ousted democratic leader Aung San Suu Kyi, triggering a civil war.

Sihasak told reporters in Beijing his government wants to “hear Myanmar’s latest position” ahead of the summit.

“De-escalation by all parties will help create a conducive atmosphere for essential dialogue and the peace process,” he said.

“If there is progress on these fronts, it will be a positive factor for ASEAN to consider at the leaders summit, as we decide how to move forward on the situation in Myanmar, including Myanmar’s participation in ASEAN meetings,” he added.

Sihasak, who last visited Myanmar in April, said he would meet his counterpart, Tin Maung Swe, on November 12, and a meeting with Min Aung Hlaing was “in the works”.

In July, Bangkok hosted a meeting between Tin Maung Swe and foreign ministers of several ASEAN member states, the first such gathering since the 2021 coup.

The following month Min Aung Hlaing met with Thai Prime Minister Anutin Charnvirakul in Bangkok, with the two nations’ military chiefs holding talks two weeks after.

Min Aung Hlaing took over as civilian president in April following elections widely dismissed by monitors as a charade.

Since then he has been given a red-carpet welcome across the region, in India, China and several ASEAN nations.

Myanmar is expected to send a senior civil servant to the Manila summit.

Thailand has stepped up security on its western frontier following last week’s cross-border fire.

On Wednesday, Myanmar’s military blamed “terrorist insurgents”—the term it commonly uses to refer to ethnic-minority armed groups and pro-democracy forces—for wounding a Thai national, according to a statement in state media.

World.title: Myanmar’s NUG Warns US Against Prioritizing Its Interests Over Peace
World.content:
In response to the new U.S. Mission Strategy for war-torn Myanmar, the parallel civilian National Unity Government (NUG) and observers urged Washington to help solve the country’s political crisis first instead of prioritizing its own security and economic interests.

Speaking with The Irrawaddy, NUG Deputy Foreign Affairs Minister David Gum Awng said that if the U.S. had a genuine desire to see sustainable peace and economic development in the country, the root cause of the political crisis must be solved first.

“An approach that sidelines the core principles such as democracy, human rights and establishment of a federal union in favor of prioritizing its [own] security and economic interests is not sufficient and lacks the comprehensive scope needed to solve the Myanmar crisis,” he added.

The U.S. State Department recently published its latest strategy for Myanmar, prioritizing the fight against online scam networks that target Americans, increasing U.S. investment, and access to rare earth minerals. Additional objectives include expanding U.S. regional influence and brokering a peace agreement by 2030.

Recently, U.S. officials held talks with junta leaders in Naypyitaw and Tokyo, increasing Washington’s engagement with the internationally isolated coup regime that ousted the democratically elected civilian government led by pro-democracy leader Aung San Suu Kyi in 2021.

Washington said in its latest statement that facilitating dialogue and supporting multi-stakeholder engagement would help lay the groundwork for lasting peace and national reconciliation.

However, Gum Awng argued that peace cannot be achieved simply by forcing stakeholders to sit together at a negotiating table, noting that the primary challenge is whether the regime is genuinely willing to give up its dictatorship and accept real change.

“Without the definitive end of the military dictatorship, the emergence of an inclusive political process involving all stakeholders (including ethnic groups), and the establishment of robust monitoring mechanisms to guarantee agreements, any hastily brokered peace driven by a specific timeline will only temporarily de-escalate the conflict without solving the underlying root problem.”

Regarding the U.S. goal of building regional influence, the NUG minister said Myanmar cannot be viewed solely as a proxy battleground for U.S.-China influence, adding that the sovereignty and the right to self-determination of the nation’s people remain paramount.

“If the U.S. wishes to build long-term, sustainable influence, engaging with the military council alone is insufficient. The U.S. must respect the democratic will of the Myanmar people, increase its engagement with federal democratic forces, and prove through practical actions that it is a reliable partner,” Gum Awng said.

“U.S. influence cannot be measured solely by its ability to counter China. It depends entirely on earning the trust of the Myanmar people and participating constructively in the building of a future federal democratic nation.”

Regarding U.S. efforts to gain access to rare earth minerals through its peace efforts, the NUG’s deputy foreign minister warned that the country’s resources cannot be treated merely as a component of a peace process or a political compromise, since they are directly tied to the long-term interests of the people, the rights of ethnic groups, and the resource management rights of the future federal union.

Regarding Washington’s move to boost engagement with the regime, Debbie Stothard, founder and coordinator of the Alternative ASEAN Network on Burma, said a strategy based on appeasing the root cause of Myanmar’s notorious transnational crime hubs is doomed to fail. U.S. citizens, along with the people of Myanmar and the region, continue to suffer due to this irresponsible approach, she said.

“It is like engaging serial killers in order to persuade them to kill fewer people instead of acting to stop their crimes,” she said.

“It is both illogical and immoral to bribe [coup president] Min Aung Hlaing’s junta with trade and aid to secure rare earths while looking away from the security, economic and humanitarian crises he is intensifying every day.”

She also warned that the U.S. was in danger of falling into Min Aung Hlaing’s trap, in which he is able to pit Moscow, Beijing and Washington against each other to secure more weapons, more cash and more legitimacy without concrete solutions.

Regarding U.S. peace efforts, Myanmar political analyst Htin Kyaw Aye said, “I don’t think it [a U.S.-brokered peace plan] will work. Myanmar’s political situation and its underlying problem cannot be resolved easily or quickly. Its peace plan is likely either a strategic miscalculation or merely a gesture to show the U.S. is interested in it.”

World.title: Three Kazakh Traditions Move Closer to UNESCO Recognition
World.content:
ASTANA – UNESCO’s Evaluation Body has recommended adding Kazakhstan’s Salburyny hunting festival, traditional embroidery and feltmaking to the Representative List of the Intangible Cultural Heritage of Humanity, according to a document published by the organization.

Salburyn

Rooted in nomadic traditions, Salburyny is an annual equestrian festival featuring Tazy hunting dogs and golden eagle falconry. Usually held between late autumn and early winter, the weeklong celebration brings together falconers, musicians, storytellers and young people.

Participants learn horseback riding, falconry, dog care and hunting, while the tradition promotes respect for animals, environmental awareness and cooperation across generations.

The UNESCO document said the inscription would raise awareness of an ancient tradition that combines falconry, dog breeding, horsemanship, oral traditions, music and close interaction with nature. It would also promote wildlife conservation, sustainable tourism and traditional crafts while strengthening cultural identity and intergenerational knowledge-sharing.

Salburyny was added to Kazakhstan’s National List of Intangible Cultural Heritage in 2013. The Kiran Federation, Zhalayr Shora and the Kansonar Association took part in preparing the nomination.

Art of embroidery

Kazakhstan submitted the nomination for the art of embroidery jointly with Tajikistan and Uzbekistan.

Embroidery is a traditional craft involving decorative and symbolic patterns sewn with colorful threads onto cotton, wool, silk and, in some cases, leather. It is used to decorate wall hangings, pillows, clothing, accessories, headdresses and household textiles.

Techniques vary across regions, while patterns often draw on nature and mythology, featuring flowers, animals and celestial symbols with meanings specific to local communities. The craft is practiced mainly by women, who work individually or in groups. Beyond decorating clothing and household items, embroidery provides a source of income.

Traditional feltmaking

Kazakhstan joined Azerbaijan, Iran, the Kyrgyz Republic, Mongolia, Tajikistan, Türkiye and Uzbekistan in submitting a joint nomination for traditional feltmaking. The UNESCO document praised the countries’ “exemplary cooperation” in promoting a shared cultural tradition that transcends geographical boundaries.

Felt, traditionally made from wool, is used for carpets, prayer mats, yurt coverings, clothing and accessories. The labor-intensive process involves cleaning and dyeing wool, laying it on a mat, rolling and tightening it, and then stretching and drying the material.

Feltmaking is closely linked to the cultural identity of the communities that practice it. The collective process strengthens social ties and connects generations.

A total of 59 nominations were submitted for inclusion on the Representative List this year. The Evaluation Body recommended 56 for inscription, while returning three others to the submitting countries for revisions.

The final decision is expected to be made at the session of UNESCO’s Intergovernmental Committee for the Safeguarding of the Intangible Cultural Heritage, scheduled for Nov. 30-Dec. 5 in Xiamen, China.

World.title: Kazakhstan’s Snow Leopard Population Doubles as Scientists Begin Tracking Altai
World.content:
