World.title: Azerbaijan celebrates November 9 - National Flag Day
World.content:
BAKU, Azerbaijan, November 9. National Flag Day in Azerbaijan is celebrated on November 9, following a decree signed by President Ilham Aliyev on November 17, 2009.

The Azerbaijani tricolor was first adopted as the national flag on November 9, 1918, during a meeting of the government of the Azerbaijan Democratic Republic (ADR), which lasted until May 1920.

After Azerbaijan regained its independence in 1991, the Supreme Soviet of Azerbaijan declared the tricolor, featuring an eight-pointed star and crescent, as the State Flag of the Republic of Azerbaijan on February 5.

In November 2009, an amendment was made to Article 105 of the Labor Code, designating November 9 as National Flag Day and a non-working holiday.

The "State Flag of the Republic of Azerbaijan" law provides a detailed description of the flag.

The flag symbolizes the sovereignty of Azerbaijan and consists of three horizontal stripes of equal width: a blue stripe on top, followed by a red one, and a green stripe at the bottom. In the middle of the red stripe, on both sides of the flag, there is a white crescent and an eight-pointed star.

On September 1, 2010, President Ilham Aliyev inaugurated the National Flag Square in Baku. The decree to create the square was signed on November 17, 2007.

To note, the flag weighs over 500 kilograms, with a width of 36 meters and a length of 72 meters, making it one of the largest flags in the world.

At the initiative of President Ilham Aliyev, a Museum of the State Flag was established at the square to further honor the flag's significance.

World.title: Azerbaijani gymnasts win three medals at World Championships (PHOTO)
World.content:
BAKU, Azerbaijan, November 8. The Azerbaijani national team performed successfully at the World Trampoline and Tumbling Championships, held from November 4–8 in the Chinese city of Nanjing, the Azerbaijan Gymnastics Federation reports.

According to the report, a total of 367 gymnasts from six continents took part in the prestigious competition, where 16 world championship titles were contested across various disciplines. Azerbaijani gymnasts delivered strong performances, winning one gold and two silver medals.

The national team's greatest success came in the tumbling team event. The Azerbaijani team, comprising Mikhail Malkin, Tofiq Aliyev, Adil Hajizada, and Alexey Karatashov, finished the qualification round in first place and advanced to the final as leaders.

Maintaining their strong performance in the decisive round, the gymnasts scored 25 points to become world champions. In the final, the Azerbaijani team finished one point ahead of Denmark and five points ahead of the United States, claiming the top spot on the podium.

This victory continued the national team's successful run in international tumbling competitions. Following their triumphs in 2023 and 2025, the Azerbaijani team claimed the world championship title in the team event for the third time, becoming three-time world champions.

The national team also celebrated a medal in the individual tumbling event. Tofiq Aliyev scored 29.700 points in the final to claim the silver medal at the World Championships. This marked the gymnast's first individual silver medal at a world championship.

Portugal's Vasco Peso won gold in the final, while American gymnast Kaden Brown took bronze.

Another Azerbaijani representative, Mikhail Malkin, concluded his individual campaign in the round of 16.

In the individual tumbling event, Alexey Karatashov scored 54.400 points in the first qualification round, finishing 11th and advancing to the second qualification round. He then scored 26.800 points to finish 13th.

Adil Hajizada scored 52.900 points in the first qualification round, placing 19th and ending his individual competition.

It should be noted that Alexey Karatashov made his debut at the World Championships in the senior category. He was also among the members of the national team that won gold in the team event.

Azerbaijani representatives also achieved a historic result in trampoline gymnastics. Competing in the mixed synchronized event, Seljan Mahsudova and Maqsud Mahsudov successfully advanced through the qualification and semifinal rounds to reach the final.

In the decisive round, the brother-and-sister duo scored 52.010 points to win the silver medal at the World Championships. Thus, Seljan Mahsudova and Maqsud Mahsudov made history as the first Azerbaijani gymnasts to win a world championship silver medal in the mixed synchronized event.

In the final, representatives of Belarus took first place, while gymnasts from Japan finished third.

Seljan Mahsudova also delivered a strong performance in the individual event. She scored 56.140 points in the semifinal, finishing sixth and qualifying for the final. At this stage, the Azerbaijani gymnast finished six places ahead of Paris 2024 Olympic champion Bryony Page, securing her place in the final among the world's top trampoline gymnasts.

In the final held on November 8, Seljan Mahsudova scored 56.580 points to finish sixth at the World Championships.

In the men's individual event, Maqsud Mahsudov scored 37.850 points in the semifinal and finished 20th.

In the men's synchronized event, Maqsud Mahsudov and Huseyn Abbasov scored 50.900 points in the first qualification round, advancing to the second round. The Azerbaijani pair finished 15th in the next stage. It should be noted that Huseyn Abbasov also made his debut at the World Championships in the senior category.

Thus, the Azerbaijani national team concluded the World Championships in Nanjing with one gold and two silver medals.

World.title: Search resumes for man missing in Gold Coast Broadwater
World.content:
A major air and sea search is underway for a boatie missing on the Gold Coast.

Emergency services were called to the Boykambil Esplanade Boat Ramp at Hope Island about 5pm yesterday after reports the man was heard yelling for help.

Gold Coast water police are searching for the missing man. (ABC Gold Coast: Heloise Vyas)

Police say the 55-year-old man, who lives on a sailboat in the Broadwater, went missing when he tried to paddle his broken-down tinnie he had been working on onshore back to his sailing boat.

"Somehow he became separated from his boat and he's obviously ended up in the water," Acting Inspector Peter Venz said.

"The circumstances around that we don't know."

The tinnie was found at nearby Coombabah Creek last night.

Acting Inspector Peter Venz spoke to media earlier today. (ABC Gold Coast: Mark Rigby)

Acting Inspector Venz said the man was reported to be a strong swimmer with no known medical conditions, but he had badly cut his foot on barnacles earlier in the day.

"We've got our fingers crossed he's safely been able to swim to shore," he said.

Police scoured the area into the early hours of this morning and resumed their search at first light today.

Marine Rescue Queensland crews, water police, the Polair aircraft and a rescue helicopter have joined the search, as well as the police dive team.

World.title: Young retail workers allegedly strangle accused shoplifter in Katherine
World.content:
A 33-year-old man was allegedly punched, stomped and strangled by two young shop employees in Katherine before "losing consciousness", after allegedly stealing items from the store.

In a statement, NT Police said the incident happened at 10:35am on Saturday at a store at a Katherine shopping centre.

Police said the 33-year-old allegedly stole items from the counter area inside the shop before fleeing, with the two retail workers chasing after him.

When the 18- and 20-year-old workers caught up with the man a short distance away, police allege they began a "prolonged physical assault", including "punching, kicking and stomping on him".

"It is alleged he was also strangled," NT Police said.

"He lost consciousness as a result of the assault, with nearby bystanders intervening to prevent further from occurring."

The 33-year-old man was taken to hospital and was subsequently discharged.

Police said the two store workers were also taken to hospital, having "injured their hands" in the alleged assault.

All three men were remanded in custody and will face Katherine Local Court today.

The 33-year-old is facing robbery charges, while the two young men will face charges related to the alleged assault, including an acts intended to cause serious harm offence and strangulation.

Police are urging any witnesses to the incident to contact them.

World.title: Police appeal for couple who helped friend of missing teenager
World.content:
A 17-year-old boy missing in Victoria's alpine region has likely spent the weekend in just shorts and boots as snow fell on nearby mountains overnight.

William, whose surname has not been released by authorities, was camping with another teenager in Walhalla East, near Cowwarr, when he walked a short distance to another part of their camp near Stoney Creek Road and T2 Track, but failed to return.

Victoria Police Superintendent Melanie Hamshere said the teenager had taken his shirt off in warm weather on Friday afternoon because he expected a 20-minute walk.

"They'd gotten quite warm so he took his T-shirt off, as boys do, and he walked back up towards the location where he'd been dropped off to pick up some more stuff to bring down," she said.

" So at the time he went missing he was only wearing shorts and boots. "

William went missing near Walhalla on Friday, November 6. (Supplied: Victoria Police)

William had gone back to collect an esky, two pillows, a fishing tackle box and a brown tabletop and did not take his phone with him.

The esky was found a short way up the track.

Weekend snow

A cold snap brought a late dusting of snow to some of Victoria's mountain ranges over the weekend.

At Mount Baw Baw, about 45 minutes' drive north-east of Walhalla, overnight temperatures dropped to below zero degrees Celsius on Saturday and Sunday.

On Sunday, William's mother Elizabeth Barclay told the ABC he was an inexperienced camper with a poor sense of direction in an unfamiliar area.

Police have resumed the search for the teen today and have set up a staging area at Cowwarr Recreational Reserve.

Authorities are hoping to speak with a bearded man and a woman who helped William's friend on Friday night. They were in an older white ute with a black canopy.

The teenager flagged the car down when he began looking for William.

"We're appealing to the public to try and identify that couple," Superintendent Hamshere said.

About 70 people searched for William on Sunday, supported by a police helicopter, water police and the dog squad.

World.title: Families face 150km daily drive as more regional childcare centres close
World.content:
After working as a police officer across Western Australia for more than a decade, Julienne Slade made the switch to teaching to spend more time with her family.

The veteran officer worked in rural towns in the state's Great Southern and Pilbara regions before moving back to her hometown of Mount Barker, 370 kilometres south of Perth, to settle down with her husband and begin a teaching career.

However, news that one of the town's two childcare centre will close in December has cast a cloud over her plans.

"I couldn't believe it because that's the daycare centre I went to when I was a child. It's been operating for at least that long, if not longer," she said.

Julienne Slade says families have received little notice of the centre's closure. (ABC News: Andrew Chounding)

Three centres closing

The family is not alone, with childcare provider Uplyft announcing it will close centres in the neighbouring towns of Mt Barker, Kojonup and Katanning in the next six months.

Affected parents say they will have to drive hundreds of kilometres each day to access alternative services, or join waitlists for closer centres.

Ms Slade's husband works in agriculture and they both said the closure would impact their careers.

"We'll have to adapt work. I'll either need to take leave or my husband will have to not work," Ms Slade said.

"If he's home looking after the kids, that's lost income, sometimes up to $5,000 or $6,000 a day because of how sporadic his work is."

Uplyft will close two centres next month and a third in June. (ABC News: Andrew Chounding)

Uplyft announced closures to some of its centres across WA in October.

The company's chief executive, Jo Sadler, said Mount Barker and Katanning's closure were due to lease conditions and also resulted in the Kojonup branch being unviable.

"As a result of these two events, it will be unfeasible to continue with an isolated service operating out of Kojonup," she said.

"At this stage, the Mt Barker and Katanning centres will close by the end of December 2026, while Kojonup will close in the first half of 2027."

The ABC spoke to several impacted families who said they were scrambling to secure places at alternative centres, but faced waitlists and limited availability.

Ryan Colman says he will have to drive more than 150km a day to access another childcare service. (ABC News: Andrew Chounding )

No other options

Kojonup mechanic Ryan Colman sends his two-year-old child to Uplyft five days a week, and said he does not know what he will do when the town's only centre closes.

"We don't have another option, unless we're driving 80 kilometres return twice a day … That's the only real option, but that throws another financial burden into the mix because it's more fuel," he said.

"We've got mortgages and bills and that's not helping with interest rates always going up."

Data from the Early Learning and Care Council of Australia shows 152 services permanently closed between 2024 and mid-2026, with a further 276 services at risk of closure by July 2027.

Nesha Hutchinson says hundreds of centres across Australia are under financial strain. (Supplied: Nesha Hutchinson)

Australian Childcare Alliance vice-president Nesha Hutchinson said rising inflation and high running costs were driving the closures.

"It's absolutely a problem — not just in Western Australia but across the country — that regional, rural, remote services are being pushed to the brink of financial viability," she said.

"Month by month … we're hearing of hundreds of services closing across the country … It's not going to get any better in the short term."

World.title: Khawaja says one state was best at ball tampering in Sheffield Shield
World.content:
Usman Khawaja says ball tampering was common at Sheffield Shield level and the Victorians were the best at it.

Following his explosive claims that all Australian players and staff knew about the ball tampering during the South Africa tour of 2018, Khawaja has made a further claim that tampering was common at Sheffield Shield level.

"The Victorians were probably the best at it. The MCG used to be dead and flat. Reverse swing and a bit of spin was the only way you could win a game there," Khawaja wrote in his new book Sabr, which is set to be released to the public on Tuesday.

"I personally never tampered with a ball — in terms of scratching it or anything — but I knew everything that was going on and I wasn't against it which made me complicit.

"The Victorians of that 2000s and 2010s era were genius at it. Throwing it into the wicket and doing other dark arts to rough it up and make the shiny side relatively shinier. It was all fair game."

Khawaja named former Australian ODI fast bowler Mick Lewis as someone who was caught out changing the state of the ball.

Mick Lewis was caught raking the ball across concrete in 2016. (Supplied)

"It was no surprise when, years later, Victoria's bowling coach, Micky Lewis, was caught on cameras scraping the ball in the gutter when it got hit for a boundary. This kind of stuff was very normal," Khawaja wrote.

"There were plenty of times we hoped a spinner got hit for a six so someone could fetch the ball and scrub it while no one was watching and we could reverse swing it.

"To be honest, everyone knew what was going on in those teams I played in growing up. So whether you did it personally or not we were all complicit. The world game was the same. Reverse swing on those older, flatter Test wickets was how you won the matches, come day four and five.''

The former Australian Test batter also claimed an unnamed player had used super glue to tamper with the ball.

Loading...

"One of the players had super glue on his towel,'' Khawaja wrote about his first year in Sheffield Shield.

"He'd get the ball on the rough side and scrub it against the dried-up super glue. It worked a treat and the ball would always reverse."

Khawaja's claim about the prevalence of ball tampering matches comments made by former Australian coach Darren Lehmann on ABC Sport's Summer Grandstand on Saturday.

Lehmann, who has joined the ABC's Cricket Podcast as co-host this season, said ball tampering had been a "big part of the game" until the Australians were caught in South Africa.

"You do know ball tampering is going on because it's been happening for 150 years," Lehmann said.

"I can only speak to what I know, and I know ball tampering was a big part of the game of cricket. Now it is obsolete.

Darren Lehmann stood down as Australian coach after Cape Town. (AP: Halden Krog)

"That doesn't make it right either, but that's the case, and we paid a heavy price for that."

Khawaja has been on the media trail promoting his book for the past two weeks, but the chapter about ball tampering had been redacted until Saturday morning.

The batter has been criticised for sitting on the information for eight years, however Khawaja defended the timing in a social media post while saying he felt he had not thrown anyone "under the bus" with his revelations.

Cricket Australia has continuously denied all players and staff knew about the South African ball tampering.

World.title: Shooter's medical care focus of inquest into Floreat double murder
World.content:
A coronial inquest into the double murder of Perth mother Jennifer Petelczyc and her daughter Gretl is expected to begin today, focusing on the medical care provided to their killer in the lead-up to the fatal shooting.

WARNING: This story contains details that may distress some readers

Mark Bombara, 63, shot and killed his estranged wife's best friend, Jennifer Petelczyc, 59, and her daughter, Gretl, 18, in their Floreat home, before turning the gun on himself.

He had gone to their house in May 2024 looking for his estranged wife and his daughter.

Bombara made menacing phone calls, triggering a massive police response, but when officers arrived at the Berkeley Crescent home Bombara and Jennifer Petelczyc were dead.

Gretl was rushed to Royal Perth Hospital but died a short time later.

It was a tragedy that shocked the state, exposed police failings and forever changed the state's gun laws.

What will the inquest examine?

A pre-inquest hearing in June heard the coroner's primary focus would be investigating the medical care Bombara received in the lead-up to the shooting.

An expert neurological report on Bombara was requested, but no detail has been provided on Bombara's medical history or why the report was ordered.

The actions of police officers, the state's gun laws and how family and domestic violence played a role are also expected to be examined over five days.

The internal police investigation

Bombara's daughter, Ariel, had been trying to warn police for weeks that her father had a history of family and domestic violence and was a real and imminent threat.

Ariel Bombara says she repeatedly warned police about her father. (ABC News: Phil Hemingway)

She and her mother had fled the family home weeks earlier, fearing for their lives, and had told officers that one of Bombara's 13 guns was missing, but no action was taken.

A WA Police investigation found eight officers did not perform their duty and internal disciplinary action was taken.

No officer was sacked.

Probe finds eight police officers at fault before Floreat murders An internal investigation into the actions of WA Police officers in the weeks before Mark Bombara killed two women in the Perth suburb of Floreat finds eight officers did not perform their duty.

"The finding is that officers did not correctly assess the risk, therefore the available powers under the Restraining Orders Act and Firearms Act were not exercised appropriately," WA Police Commissioner Col Blanch said in January 2025.

Ariel Bombara's response to the police report was scathing.

"We told you he was going to murder us. So did you not believe us? Or did you just not give a sh*t?" she said at the time.

"This was the perfect storm of apathy and compassion fatigue from officers combined with shoddy systems, outdated policies and insufficient training and support that resulted in a lethal outcome."

The two women were slain in May 2024 at their home. (ABC News: Julian Robins)

One of the recommendations from the police report was for a family violence coordinator to always be present at the state Operations Command centre to allow officers to seek expert advice.

Australian Bureau of Statistics data shows WA Police are responding to one family and domestic violence incident every 20 minutes.

Changes to WA gun laws

Mark Bombara legally owned 13 guns, including 11 firearms on a recreational licence and two handguns on a collector's licence.

That is no longer possible.

WA's gun laws are now among the toughest in the nation. (ABC News: Sam Clark)

Less than a week after the double-murder suicide, the WA Parliament vowed to change the state's gun laws.

The reforms came into effect in March 2025 and are now the toughest in the nation. They have reduced the number of licensed guns in the state by a quarter.

Recreational licences no longer exist, and collectors' licences are much stricter.

There are limits of 10 guns and a requirement for a mental health check every five years.

But what are likely to make the biggest difference are the disqualification orders, which allow for the immediate removal of a person's firearms when a report of domestic or family violence has been made.

Warnings 'broken system' led to Floreat murders The WA Labor government has put tackling family and domestic violence at the top of its agenda. In spite of this, eight police officers did not perform their duties in lead-up to the Floreat murders, according to an internal report.

It removes the ability for police officers to use discretion to assess whether the risk threshold has been met.

The changes were met with backlash from The Nationals and the WA Firearms Community Alliance who suggested they were an overreach affecting law-abiding gun owners, while not targeting illegal guns in the community.

A 2024 record-breaking ePetition in Parliament was signed by more than 31,000 people who also were against the changes.

Family violence failings

The deaths of Jennifer and Gretl Petelczyc were a turning point for the state's response to domestic and family violence, but in the two years since, the number of women and children killed by violence has continued to climb.

According to Australian Femicide Watch, 60 women and 28 children across Australia have been killed by violence so far this year.

What more needs to be done to protect Australian families will be heard in the inquest, which is expected to sit for five days.

World.title: Nvidia investigates reports CEO had affair with Chinese spy
World.content:
Technology giant and artificial chip manufacturer Nvidia says it is launching an independent investigation after a media report that its founder and CEO Jensen Huang had been the target of a foreign intelligence effort.

Top Republican members of Congress in the US House of Representatives have called on Mr Huang to brief Congress this month about a New York Times report in October alleging he had a close relationship with a Chinese businesswoman who passed information to Beijing.

The media outlet reported last month that US authorities were investigating Alice Huang, a former executive of Singapore-based company Megaspeed, which buys AI chips from Nvidia.

Jensen Huang and Netspeed's Alice Huang in Taipei in 2024, in an image shared to LinkedIn at the time by software company Net Thunder. (Supplied: NetThunder/LinkedIn)

US authorities have scrutinised Megaspeed over suspicions it helped Beijing gain access to advanced AI chips barred from shipment to China.

Nvidia said on Sunday, local time, that while its board had no reason to believe that either US national security or Nvidia secrets were compromised, its inquiry would examine all available information.

"The NVIDIA Board is initiating an independent investigation in light of recent reporting that founder and CEO Jensen Huang has been the target of a foreign intelligence effort," a statement said.

"A committee of independent directors, assisted by outside independent counsel, will oversee the investigation."

Jensen Huang has forged a close working relationship with US President Donald Trump amid the country's race to develop AI faster than China. (Reuters: Evan Vucci)

Mr Huang fully supports the review and has committed to cooperating with it, the company said.

Axios reported on Sunday, citing a draft email by Mr Huang to employees, that he admitted to having a romantic relationship with a suspected Chinese spy and took full responsibility for his actions.

"I was unfaithful to my wife. My actions hurt her and our children. There is no excuse for what I did," Mr Huang said in the draft email seen by Reuters.

Addressing his colleagues, board, partners and shareholders, Mr Huang said: "My responsibility is to serve you and be worthy of your trust. I have fallen short of that responsibility. I am fully committed to NVIDIA and will work to earn back your confidence."

An Nvidia spokesperson said Mr Huang was "committed to continuing to lead NVIDIA as CEO without interruption."

Jensen Huang has previously pushed for a relaxation of US restrictions against Nvidia in the interest of accelerating the global adoption of its technology.

Jensen Huang's memo to staff I owe my family and all of you an apology. I was unfaithful to my wife. My actions hurt her and our children. There is no excuse for what I did. I am deeply sorry. Throughout my life, my family has given me love and support. They deserve my honesty and loyalty. Instead, I let them down and damaged the life we built together. I take full responsibility for what I did and the hurt I caused, and I accept the criticism that comes with it. To my wife and family: I love you. I know an apology cannot undo what I have done. I hope our family will heal and that, over time, I can earn back your trust. To my colleagues at NVIDIA, including those I have worked alongside for decades, and to our board, partners, and shareholders around the world: you deserve better from me. Leading NVIDIA is the privilege of my life. My responsibility is to serve you and be worthy of your trust. I have fallen short of that responsibility. I am fully committed to NVIDIA and will work to earn back your confidence. Regarding the national security concerns raised in news reports, NVIDIA's Board of Directors has initiated an independent investigation. I support the investigation and will cooperate fully. I love our country and our company, and I am committed to protecting NVIDIA and supporting America's national security. I am proud and grateful to be an American. My family bears no responsibility for my choices. I do. Please give them privacy. Jensen Huang Source: Bloomberg

Who is Jensen Huang?

Mr Huang is a central figure in the global push toward AI development, and has forced a close working relationship with United States President Donald Trump.

He has previously encouraged the White House to lift restrictions on the sale of advanced AI chips to China, arguing the measures accelerate Beijing's own development of the technology.

Who is Jensen Huang? The founder of the world's most valuable AI company has the ear of Donald Trump when it comes to the risks and potential of the cutting-edge technology.

Nvidia is valued at about $US5.4 trillion ($7.7 trillion), making it the world's most valuable company as demand for AI hardware and data centres has skyrocketed.

Mr Huang was born in Taiwan and raised in Thailand before he emigrated alone to the US to attend a boarding school at the age of 10.

He has previously described AI as the world's next industrial revolution and argues that whichever country has its technology adopted the most worldwide will win the AI race.

ABC/Reuters

World.title: Beau Lamarre-Condon trial live updates: Former NSW Police officer’s cross-examination continues over alleged murders of Jesse Baird, Luke Davies
World.content:
Hello and welcome to our live coverage of Beau Lamarre-Condon’s criminal trial in the NSW Supreme Court in Sydney.

Lamarre-Condon, 31, has pleaded not guilty to two counts of murder over the deaths of Jesse Baird, 26, a former TV presenter, and Luke Davies, 29, a Qantas flight attendant, in Paddington on February 19, 2024. His case is that he acted in self-defence, the 15-person jury has been told.

The former NSW police officer started giving evidence on Thursday and returns to the witness box at 10am today for cross-examination by Crown prosecutor Brett Hatfield, SC.

Here are the key parts of his evidence on Friday:

Lamarre-Condon said he entered Baird’s Paddington share house through an open door on February 19, 2024, to collect some of his belongings – including a $25,000 Cartier ring and Casablanca shirts worth thousands – after their relationship ended in November 2023. He said he also had a key with him that Baird had cut for him in November.

He said his relationship with Baird was romantic but was not exclusive. He believed nobody was home despite the door being ajar when he entered the home, he said.

The accused had his police weapon with him because he had contemplated taking his own life on February 18 over work-related trauma and had intended to return it to Miranda police station later that day, he said.

He said he struck upon an idea that morning to dress as an Uber Eats delivery rider and used a motorcycle helmet, high-visibility clothing and bags he saw on a bike in Paddington. “I was worried if I knocked on the door it may be perceived as harassment ... because Jesse told me, ‘please refrain from contacting me’,” Lamarre-Condon said.

He entered the home after knocking three times and saying hello loudly and receiving no reply.

He ran upstairs and hid when he heard noises in the home and came back downstairs later, encountering Baird in the kitchen. He said he took off the high-visibility jacket upstairs and his firearm was “secreted under my shirt. You could not see it. It was actually to the rear of me on a plain-clothes holster so no one could be under the impression that I had a firearm on me”.

Baird did not recognise Lamarre-Condon with the helmet on and lunged at him with a knife, he said. He said at one stage the knife “tore my whole blue shirt open” and he was pinned to a wall in the kitchen.

He shot Baird once in the shoulder to disarm him and accidentally in the head when they fell to the floor.

“I 110 per cent stand by that first shot because if I didn’t do it Jesse Baird would be sitting here in the box today, and he would have to explain why he drove a knife into my throat,” he said.

“Jesse did not have his finger on the trigger,” he said. “It was my fault. I’ve said from the start I am guilty of manslaughter and I’m responsible for his death, but it wasn’t intentional.”

Lamarre-Condon said he found a phone and called Triple Zero and went into “police mode” to try to “save” Baird.

The accused said Davies grabbed the gun and pointed it at him, and later pulled the trigger and shot himself in front of Baird’s bedroom door. The Crown case is that Lamarre-Condon shot Davies through the door.

He admitted to cleaning Baird’s house and disposing of the men’s bodies before turning himself in to police on February 23, 2024.

Support is available from the National Sexual Assault, Domestic Family Violence Counselling Service at 1800RESPECT (1800 737 732), the Men’s Referral Service on 1300 766 491, and Lifeline on 13 11 14.

David Jones is restocking shelves for a busy Black Friday period after shoppers swarmed to visit the collapsed department store for what they thought could be the last time over the weekend.

World.title: Shoot for the MICHELIN stars, land close to home
World.content:
When the first MICHELIN Guide to Australia was launched in mid-October, with 12 coveted stars awarded, alongside 16 Bib Gourmand awards and 50 MICHELIN-selected establishments, it reiterated what so many of us already understood: South Australia is a serious player on the global food and wine scene.

This is a state that produces about 50 per cent of Australia’s wine, 80 per cent of Australia’s premium wine, across some of the country’s best-known regions, the places we associate with legendary names such as Penfolds and Wynns.

It’s also a gastronomic hotspot, the home of Adelaide Central Market, Barossa shiraz, Maggie Beer, Coffin Bay oysters and genuine star chefs such as Jake Kellie, Fabian Lehmann and Scott Huggins.

This is, in short, the natural home for the MICHELIN Guide, and an incredibly exciting destination for those who like to wine and dine.

These are South Australia’s best regions for gastronomes, and what to look out for while you’re there.

Magill Estate Restaurant has made history as the first venue in Australia to be awarded two MICHELIN stars.



Adelaide

The South Australian capital now boasts six MICHELIN stars, not to mention 12 Bib Gourmand awards, and plenty of standard inclusions in the French restaurant guide’s first foray into Australia.

To understand Adelaide, you should begin at the Adelaide Central Market. Wander at your own pace or take a tour – the sprawling facility has been around since 1869 and remains the heart and soul of the city’s food scene, with some of the finest produce around.

Then, experience the city’s high-end dining at MICHELIN-starred arkhe, Aurora, Esmay, Restaurant Botanic and, of course, the now two-starred Magill Estate Restaurant.

And sample the cuisines of the world at the likes of Parwana (Afghan), Osteria Oggi (Italian), Ong (Vietnamese), and many more.

1 / 3 Adelaide Central Market is the heart and soul of the city’s food scene. Supplied 2 / 3 Two-starred fine diner Magill Estate Restaurant. Supplied 3 / 3 arkhe in Norwood, South Australia, has been awarded one MICHELIN star. Supplied Previous Slide Next Slide

Barossa

Few wine regions and varietals in Australia can make a genuine claim to global fame, but Barossa shiraz is one of them. Penfolds Grange is iconic; Peter Lehmann Wines, Yalumba and Henschke are legends. This region is home to some of the oldest vines not just in Australia but in the world – that’s some serious history.

In the Barossa you will also discover an exciting new wave of winemakers and cellar doors that includes Spinifex, Rieslingfreak and Artisans of Barossa. You could tour the Barossa just sampling drops and you would be happy – Small Batch is a wonderful wine tour operator with which to do so.

There’s more to this region, however, than one grape varietal. The Barossa is a hotbed of gastronomic talent. Check out fermentAsian for seriously good Vietnamese-influenced cuisine, Bib Gourmand-awarded Fino at Seppeltsfield for a long lunch in the sun, Vino Lokal for wine-bar-style dining, Vintners for a regional classic, and Appellation at The Louise for fine-dining. And don’t miss Hentley Farm, recently awarded one MICHELIN star for its modern Australian cuisine.

1 / 3 Hentley Farm in the Barossa Valley, South Australia, has been awarded one MICHELIN star. Supplied 2 / 3 Hentley Farm executive chef Kyle Johns. Supplied 3 / 3 Johns’ menus celebrate seasonal ingredients and a true sense of place. Supplied Previous Slide Next Slide

McLaren Vale

It seems almost unfair when you consider the riches on Adelaide’s doorstep compared with other capital cities. The Barossa is only an hour’s drive away, and it’s not even the closest wine region to the state capital – nor is Adelaide Hills. Because, in the city’s southern outskirts, so begins McLaren Vale, a world-class producer of wine and food right there for the visiting.

Let’s begin with the cellar doors that should be on everyone’s list: d’Arenberg is instantly recognisable thanks to The Cube, its unique, five-storey headquarters that looks like a slightly twisted Rubik’s Cube. New-wave labels such as Bondar, SC Pannell, Ministry of Clouds and Alpha Box and Dice are also well worth trying. Stay in Adelaide CBD, and a tour with the likes of Taste the McLaren or Groovy Grapes will deliver you from cellar door to door in with ease.

And as with any good wine region, there’s also great food. Start with one MICHELIN star: Maxwell Restaurant is a must-visit where the food feels like an extension of the winery itself, and every dish is designed with the winery’s own wines and ginger-spiked meads in mind. Or head to The Salopian Inn, newly awarded a Bib Gourmand, for a farm-to-table feast which draws from the organic bounty of its surrounding garden.

Maxwell Restaurant in McLaren Vale, South Australia, has one MICHELIN star.

Adelaide Hills

Adelaide Hills also has its share of gems, including some of the most exciting new winemakers in Australia. Its band of young, forward-thinking vignerons is pushing the Australian scene forward. Check out Ngeringa, Vinteloper, Hesketh, Murdoch Hill, Koerner, Bottle Shock and CRFT, to name a few.

And of course, you want to dine in the Hills. Hardy’s Verandah is epic fine dining with a view – and a beautifully curated wine program which has earned head sommelier Maxime Martin a prestigious MICHELIN sommelier award. CRFT does grazing plates to pair with wine tastings. And those one-MICHELIN-starred restaurants: LVN Restaurant at Bird in Hand, Aptos and Anvers now all have that famous red badge at their front door.

1 / 3 LVN Restaurant at Bird in Hand has been awarded one MICHELIN star. Supplied 2 / 3 LVN Restaurant at Bird in Hand. Supplied 3 / 3 Anvers in Kangarilla, South Australia, now has one MICHELIN star. Supplied Previous Slide Next Slide

Clare Valley

Around 90 minutes from Adelaide, the Clare Valley is boutique area where creativity runs deep and rich rewards and ripe for the taking – and tasting.

Clare wineries are best known for their world-class riesling, made by the likes of Grosset and Jim Barry, though cellar doors such as Knappstein, Shut the Gate and Kilikanoon provide ample reason to hang around in the Clare and sample as much as possible.

This is also the home of a MICHELIN star. Skillogalee Barrel House is run by chef Dan Moss, who serves set menus of modern Australian cuisine, pairing French techniques with the finest local ingredients. Antidote Kitchen, another Clare Valley favourite, received a Bib Gourmand award for its approachable, Indian-influenced cuisine. This, clearly, is a place to wine and dine, and it’s just 90 minutes from Adelaide.

Skillogalee Barrel House in Sevenhill, South Australia, has been awarded one Michelin star.

Further afield

The chance to sample great food and wine in South Australia doesn’t begin and end at Adelaide and its surrounding wine regions. Look a little further and you will still discover plenty of high-quality culinary experiences.

Take Kangaroo Island, for example, where the likes of the Islander Estate, Dudley Wines and Kangaroo Island Spirits offer approachable, delicious food to pair with their more famous liquid products.

This is also the home of Southern Ocean Lodge, the winner of three MICHELIN keys – the organisation’s rating for hotels – and itself home to an excellent on-site restaurant. And don’t forget Tirage, recently awarded a Bib Gourmand award by MICHELIN for its easy-going wine bar fare.

Win the ultimate South Australian foodie escape with a former MICHELIN Guide Inspector.

The Ultimate Reservation is a money-can’t-buy journey into South Australia’s food culture, taking you beyond the table to discover its restaurants, regions, producers and people, with a former MICHELIN Guide inspector joining you along the way.

Think it should be you? Take a video of up to 60 seconds about why you’d love to experience The Ultimate Reservation for your chance to win for you and a companion. Visit southaustralia.com/ultimatereservation to enter.

World.title: ASX edges up, Wall Street steadies as AI stocks rebound
World.content:
Updated BusinessMarketsWorld markets ASX edges up, Wall Street steadies as AI stocks rebound Stan Choe Updated November 9, 2026 — 10:05am ,first published 5:20am Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Gift icon Gift Gift icon 0 / 3 No gift articles left You've used all of your gift articles. 3 more will become available on the 1st of every month. Close Share A A A

The Australian sharemarket has made a steady start to the week after Wall Street closed last week with gains after AI stocks clawed back some of their heavy losses suffered following the midterms. The S&P/ASX 200 was up 2 points in early trade to 9022.9. The Australian dollar was trading lower at US68.60¢ at 10.05am AEDT. On Friday on Wall Street, AI stocks bounced back and recovered some of their selloff following a whirlwind few days of Wall Street trying to sort out what this week’s sweeping victories by Democrats in the US midterm elections will mean for the economy. Wall Street steadied after a volatile week. AP The S&P 500 rose 0.3 per cent and trimmed its loss for the week to 2.7 per cent, which was its worst since President Donald Trump shook markets in April 2025 with his “Liberation Day” tariffs. The Dow Jones Industrial Average dropped 237 points, or 0.5 per cent, and the Nasdaq composite climbed 1.1 per cent.



The relative steadiness for Wall Street halted what had been a worldwide tumble for stocks. Indexes dropped 6 per cent in Tokyo and in Seoul following the US market’s plunge on Thursday. European indexes have fewer stocks tied to the artificial-intelligence industry, but Germany’s DAX nevertheless lost 1.9 per cent. Friday’s biggest lift for the S&P 500 came from Nvidia, the chip company that’s become the face of the boom and possible bust of the AI frenzy. Its stock climbed 2.8 per cent, coming off drops of 9.3 per cent and 3.2 per cent. Related Article Analysis

Cryptocurrencies Crypto’s Trump-fuelled Washington boom comes to an abrupt halt It and other companies tied to the build-out of AI data centres tumbled this week on worries that Democratic victories in statehouses across the country could mean a slowdown in further construction, particularly in Texas. Voters across political parties say they’re wary about AI and don’t like increases to power bills caused by data centres. That built on top of worries already rattling the industry that further construction of AI data centres may slow because of how expensive it’s become to borrow money. Before that, even, critics were saying AI stock prices had shot too high and were in a bubble.



But political power in Washington will still be split between a Democratic Congress and a White House run by the Republican Trump, who retains the power to veto. That could limit federal efforts to rein in the AI industry. In the meantime, companies in the industry still see strong growth. IREN, a company that delivers data centres, compute and software for AI training, reported stronger results for the latest quarter than analysts expected. Its stock jumped 20 per cent, and it also announced two new contracts signed since the end of the quarter. World.content:
The English view SportAustralian cricket Pat Cummins has to front up and explain all on ball-tampering scandal Nick Hoult November 9, 2026 — 10:03am Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Gift icon Gift Gift icon 0 / 3 No gift articles left You've used all of your gift articles. 3 more will become available on the 1st of every month. Pat Cummins is no stranger to wading into public debates. He has been the most vocal current cricketer to join public appeals for humanitarian treatment of Imran Khan. He has spoken about climate change, co-founding the Cricket for Climate action group and did not take part in sponsorship appearances for Cricket Australia backer Alinta Energy. He has supported changing the date of Australia Day in support of Aboriginal and Torres Strait Islanders; political opinions and interventions that have copped him a lot of criticism in a country where its athletes are expected to stay in their lanes. Usman Khawaja (right) in his playing days with Australian fast bowlers Mitchell Starc, Pat Cummins and Josh Hazlewood, who all played in the infamous Cape Town Test of 2018. Getty Images On the field, he has been a magnificent leader for Australia. Truly one of the great fast bowlers and competitors who has led Australia to home Ashes series wins, and beat India in the 2023 World Cup final, silencing 100,000 supporters in Ahmedabad. He was exactly the clean-cut family man Australian cricket needed when searching for a captain after scandals brought down Steve Smith and Tim Paine – one for cheating on the field, the other for cheating on his marriage.



But for someone who likes to share opinions publicly, the one debate he strives to steer clear of is what happened in Cape Town in February 2018. That will be much harder now. What did he know? Was he aware of the sandpaper plot that Usman Khawaja says was widely discussed in the dressing room? Did he know it happened in Port Elizabeth, before it was publicly exposed in the next Test? Was he one of the two players that Khawaja says refused the plan to take collective blame? Is this upstanding cricketing poster boy really telling us he knew nothing was going on? Loading Fast bowler Chadd Sayers played in the final Test in Johannesburg and claimed: “Everything Usman says in his article is accurate”. What does Cummins think of that?



We will probably have to wait for some time to find out. Khawaja is at the centre of most criticism in Australia for ratting on his mates. That is the way it works. He is accused of profiteering on a book he wrote himself without the aid of a ghost. Well, that is kind of the point of writing a book, although considering other topics include his opinions on Palestine, race and the immigrant’s experience in Australia, his motivation is clearly more than making a few dollars. As current captain of the national team, Pat Cummins won’t be able to avoid questions about the sandpaper saga. Getty Images Cummins was a co-signatory to a letter in 2021 along with Mitchell Starc, Nathan Lyon and Josh Hazlewood that stated the bowlers in the Cape Town Test were unaware of what was going on. It was this that tipped Khawaja over the edge because it reinforced that David Warner, Smith and Cameron Bancroft were accused as the only plotters. It never made sense and was laughed at by figures in the game.



“If you are playing sport at the highest level you know your tools that good it’s not funny. Can you imagine that ball being thrown back to the bowler and the bowler not knowing about it? Please.” That was Michael Clarke, the former Australia captain. Cummins and the other bowlers are standing by their 2021 statement and will add nothing to it, but silence cannot hold for ever. Cummins will speak before the Test series against New Zealand starts on December 8. Will he add to what he said last month as Australia prepared for their first series in South Africa since the sandpaper saga? Mitchell Marsh, the white-ball captain, was on that tour and played in the Cape Town Test. He will speak this week before the white-ball series against England. Warner is on commentary and Smith is rarely away from a press conference microphone.



Related Article Analysis

Australian cricket ‘A nightmare for Pat Cummins’: Why Khawaja claims are set to dog Australia captain “It’s going to be obviously a nightmare for Pat Cummins and the team leading into the summer of cricket,” former Test captain and CA board member Mark Taylor said. Cricket Australia is likely to resist re-opening the case despite the emergence of new evidence: Khawaja saying it went on in Port Elizabeth, which contradicts the official findings, and that everyone knew. Testimony is evidence. Ignoring it without testing it is dereliction and undermines future investigations. Nobody has come out of this well. Smith was a captain who let this fester and take hold. Where were the leaders in the dressing room? Where was the moral compass at the time, during the investigation and the years of silence? Khawaja at least had the guts to say they should all share the blame.



Cummins is a brave, tough cricketer. Will those broad shoulders now share some of the weight of scandal? The Telegraph, London News, results and expert analysis from the weekend of sport sent every Monday.

World.title: Beau Lamarre-Condon trial live updates: Former NSW Police officer’s cross-examination continues over alleged murders of Jesse Baird, Luke Davies
World.content:
Hello and welcome to our live coverage of Beau Lamarre-Condon’s criminal trial in the NSW Supreme Court in Sydney.

Lamarre-Condon, 31, has pleaded not guilty to two counts of murder over the deaths of Jesse Baird, 26, a former TV presenter, and Luke Davies, 29, a Qantas flight attendant, in Paddington on February 19, 2024. His case is that he acted in self-defence, the 15-person jury has been told.

The former NSW police officer started giving evidence on Thursday and returns to the witness box at 10am today for cross-examination by Crown prosecutor Brett Hatfield, SC.

Here are the key parts of his evidence on Friday:

Lamarre-Condon said he entered Baird’s Paddington share house through an open door on February 19, 2024, to collect some of his belongings – including a $25,000 Cartier ring and Casablanca shirts worth thousands – after their relationship ended in November 2023. He said he also had a key with him that Baird had cut for him in November.

He said his relationship with Baird was romantic but was not exclusive. He believed nobody was home despite the door being ajar when he entered the home, he said.

The accused had his police weapon with him because he had contemplated taking his own life on February 18 over work-related trauma and had intended to return it to Miranda police station later that day, he said.

He said he struck upon an idea that morning to dress as an Uber Eats delivery rider and used a motorcycle helmet, high-visibility clothing and bags he saw on a bike in Paddington. “I was worried if I knocked on the door it may be perceived as harassment ... because Jesse told me, ‘please refrain from contacting me’,” Lamarre-Condon said.

He entered the home after knocking three times and saying hello loudly and receiving no reply.

He ran upstairs and hid when he heard noises in the home and came back downstairs later, encountering Baird in the kitchen. He said he took off the high-visibility jacket upstairs and his firearm was “secreted under my shirt. You could not see it. It was actually to the rear of me on a plain-clothes holster so no one could be under the impression that I had a firearm on me”.

Baird did not recognise Lamarre-Condon with the helmet on and lunged at him with a knife, he said. He said at one stage the knife “tore my whole blue shirt open” and he was pinned to a wall in the kitchen.

He shot Baird once in the shoulder to disarm him and accidentally in the head when they fell to the floor.

“I 110 per cent stand by that first shot because if I didn’t do it Jesse Baird would be sitting here in the box today, and he would have to explain why he drove a knife into my throat,” he said.

“Jesse did not have his finger on the trigger,” he said. “It was my fault. I’ve said from the start I am guilty of manslaughter and I’m responsible for his death, but it wasn’t intentional.”

Lamarre-Condon said he found a phone and called Triple Zero and went into “police mode” to try to “save” Baird.

The accused said Davies grabbed the gun and pointed it at him, and later pulled the trigger and shot himself in front of Baird’s bedroom door. The Crown case is that Lamarre-Condon shot Davies through the door.

He admitted to cleaning Baird’s house and disposing of the men’s bodies before turning himself in to police on February 23, 2024.

Support is available from the National Sexual Assault, Domestic Family Violence Counselling Service at 1800RESPECT (1800 737 732), the Men’s Referral Service on 1300 766 491, and Lifeline on 13 11 14.

World.title: Why additional MPs may cost millions
World.content:
Audio player for " What will cost me more, cooling my house down or heating it up? " removed for printing Visit page to play audio: https://www.rnz.co.nz/news/eyJhbGciOiJIUzI1NiJ9._v0.KrRTFtoPsaA8nSDloPZ4KejQJr59ANQpD9ULgGwzaM0/politics_election-2026/2459965%2Fwhy-additional-mps-may-cost-millions

What will cost me more, cooling my house down or heating it up? No Stupid Questions with Susan Edmunds Download MP3 11m

An overhang resulting in additional MPs could end up costing about $5 million more in the first year.

On the preliminary results, the typical 120-seat Parliament is expected to increase by 11 MPs, with both National and Te Pāti Māori winning more electorate seats than their party vote entitles them to.

National has an extra seven "overhang" MPs, while Te Pāti Māori has an extra four.

Victoria University associate professor in public management and policy Barbara Allen pointed to the new Speaker's Determination for 2026 which gives members of parliament who are not ministers a staff allocation of $25,818 in their first year in parliament, and a non-staff allocation of $62,145.

They also receive a salary of about $180,000 a year, a basic expense allowance of $19,300, IT hardware funding of $10,400 and $13,682 once per term in staff IT costs.

That adds up to a total of about $500,000 per member of parliament in the first year.

With 11 extra MPs, that adds at least another $5.5 million.

"That's based on an additional non-ministerial list MP. That doesn't include other allowances they might get," Allen said.

In addition, parties receive funding according to the number of members in their caucus.

"There's $26,500 per caucus member. That seems to be an extra amount that's not directly related to the MP themselves."

Offices would need to be found for the additional MPs.

She said overall the cost of the additional members of parliament would still be small in the scheme of the overall cost of government.

Simplicity chief economist Shamubeel Eaqub said data showed the average cost per member of parliament had dropped a little from more almost $750,000 in 2012, in 2025 dollars, to less than $700,000.

He said the bulk of that cost related to the wider business of running parliament rather than directly to the MPs themselves.

"The bigger issue is the erosion of trust, we have record low trust in government, in politics. This kind of stuff makes it worse."

Geoff Plimmer, associate dean of research in the school of business and government at Victoria University agreed the additional cost was a drop in the bucket.

"It's trivial when the government spends billions and billions every year. We need to pay our MPs reasonably well to get quality people. This is the democratic process at work. There are other discussions to be had about whether we need to look at the design of MMP but those are for down the line."

He said it could be moot whether another 10 seats could be added to Parliament's relatively small debating chamber.

"They're often not all always there. Maybe they can hot desk in parliament and experience what life is like for many public servants and others."

World.title: Election reminder: These are Opportunity's five non-negotiables for a coalition
World.content:
The Opportunity Party could be kingmaker after the final vote count, and its leader Qiulae Wong says both National and Labour should be able to get on board with the party's five bottom lines.

The party's new MPs arrived at Parliament for the first time on Monday.

Speaking outside it, Wong said she would like to meet with all party leaders over the next few weeks - but would leave any negotiations to after the final vote count.

Video player removed for printing https://players.brightcove.net/6093072280001/default_default/index.html?videoId=6408112099112

Wong said the party's five bottom lines remained and were "very reasonable" and if party leaders could not meet it they would have to explain to the New Zealand public why they could not.

"Being in coalition means we would really need to be comfortable with the overall direction the government is going in, that's going to be how we determine what role we play," she said.

She declined to say which ministerial portfolios she'd want Opportunity MPs to hold, but indicated climate change, environment, commerce and consumer affairs were areas where it had strong policy.

Opportunity Party leader Qiulae Wong arriving outside Parliament for the first time. RNZ / Mark Papalii

The Opportunity Party's five bottom lines:

Giving the Commerce Commission more teeth and greater independence to tackle excessive market power in supermarkets and other uncompetitive sectors, bringing down prices. Wong had said the problem was broadly agreed, and it was time to do something about it.

Regulating lobbying and capping political donations to "clean up politics". "New Zealanders deserve to know who is trying to influence their government, and no one should be able to buy disproportionate political influence," she previously said.

Developing a 10-year plan to "fix the health system" alongside health professionals, with clear commitments on funding, workforce and infrastructure. "A 10-year plan would give the health system a stable direction for its workforce, infrastructure and funding."

Phasing out bottom trawling, working with industry, iwi and coastal communities to fairly manage the transition.

Recommitting to Paris Agreement emissions reduction obligations and protecting the Climate Change Commission's independence. "We will not support a government that walks away from our international obligations or undermines the independent Climate Change Commission," Wong had said.

On talks with the National Party, Wong said she knew they would eventually call.

National Party Leader Christopher Luxon said he intends to speak with Wong shortly.

However prior to Saturday, the National Party leader had repeatedly ruled out working with the party.

Luxon told Morning Report on Monday one of the big lessons from the campaign was the need for more cross-party collaboration.

Wong said she would call Luxon in the next few days if she had not heard anything.

She was not surprised to hear Luxon mention Opportunity and cross-party collaboration in his election night speech.

Wong earlier told Morning Report she had received congratulatory phone calls from Labour's Chris Hipkins and the Greens' Chlöe Swarbrick.

She said there were no discussions about potential governing arrangements.

On election day, Wong's party made history as the first to enter Parliament from the outside under the MMP electoral system - securing six percent of the vote, provisionally winning seven seats.

World.title: 'Coalition united': No-confidence motion against Vanuatu PM Napat withdrawn before vote
World.content:
A motion of no confidence in Prime Minister Jotham Napat has been withdrawn before it could go to a vote in Vanuatu's parliament.

On Sunday, Napat, who leads a coalition government of five parties, said that he felt confident he would see the motion off after it was lodged at the beginning of last week by opposition MPs.

The reasons listed in the motion included the unfair allocation of ministerial portfolios and alleged misuse of government investment funds.

"Despite the many confusing reports circulating ahead of [Monday's] vote, the Government wishes to reassure the people of Vanuatu that the five coalition partners in Government are united and ready to defeat the motion," the Vanuatu Prime Minister's Office said in a statement.

"We have assessed the motion. The Opposition has no valid grounds."

In mid-October, Napat shut down claims that he could be facing a leadership challenge when parliament resumed this week.

Napat said the government acknowledged that there were areas of governance that needed strengthening and that it had been saddled with issues left unattended for many years.

But he said that the no-confidence motion, in large part, had "no substance."

Napat was elected as Vanuatu's prime minister in February 2025 - the country's fifth in as many years.

World.title: Rotorua primary school ransacked by group of teenagers
World.content:
A Rotorua primary school is facing at least $80,000 in damage after a group of teenagers ransacked classrooms, its principal says.

Five teenagers aged 13 to 15 broke into Western Heights Primary school in Rotorua on Sunday and threw acrylic classroom paint over ceilings, walls, furniture and carpets.

Principal Brent Griffin said seeing the damage was devastating.

"Heart-wrenching to see everything we've worked for in these classrooms just destroyed in such a short period of time, and aimless disregard for anyone else."

Facebook / Western Heights Primary Rotorua

Griffin said it was difficult to comprehend how much damage the group had caused.

"It was rough, I can't really describe it, it was just when you walked in the door you couldn't really believe what you were seeing."

Griffin said there was CCTV footage of the offenders, who were not connected to, or known by the school.

He expected the damage to cost $80,000 to $120,000 to clean up.

Facebook / Western Heights Primary Rotorua

Griffin said despite how devastating the vandalism was, it had shown what a great community the school had.

"Their kindness, their willingness to support, start up Givealittle pages... as negative as this whole thing is, the positives that have come from this just shows what a brilliant place Rotorua really is."

He said teachers had come in on their day off, hundreds of people had called to wish them well and Cafe Dynasti in Ngongotahā had brought in morning tea for the staff.

Griffin said the school was completely closed until 12pm on Monday, when some students would be allowed back, and commercial cleaners were aiming to have things ready for all students to return on Tuesday morning.

Facebook / Western Heights Primary Rotorua

Police inspector Ewan Dunsmuir said they were making enquires after a report of a burglary at a school in Rotorua at 4:50pm on Sunday.

She said she would reach out directly to Luxon "in the next few days or the next week or so" if he did not call first.

Speaking to Morning Report, Luxon took responsibility for a big loss of talent in National's caucus.

National won the most seats in Parliament despite its party support plummeting to 29 percent. Its electorate success means they'll have no list MPs, leaving heavy hitters Nicola Willis, Paul Goldsmith, Gerry Brownlee, and probably Chris Bishop out of a job.

Luxon said that was a bittersweet result and as leader, that lies with him.
